Add a squirt of dish soap and a few drops of orange food coloring.
Pour in half a cup of vinegar and step back, the volcano erupts out of the grin.
Ask the science question: what made it foam? (The acid and the base react and release gas.) Repeat with more vinegar.
activities.tagline: A jack-o'-lantern that erupts: baking soda, vinegar, and dish soap, straight out of the grin.

variations.easier: Skip the carving. Draw the face with marker and use an uncut pumpkin with the top off.
variations.harder: Test variables: does warm vinegar erupt more than cold? Does more soap make taller foam? Run it like an experiment.

activities.name: Candy Chromatography

photo.alt: Paper chromatography strips separating ink colors in a glass of water
photo.caption: Paper chromatography strips separating ink colors in a glass of water.
photo.credit: Photo: Unicorno rosa 9, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Check the candy against the class allergy list. This is a look-don't-lick experiment, no tasting during the science.
activities.setup: Sort candies by color, one color per filter. Cut coffee filters into strips and draw a pencil dot (not pen!) near the bottom of each.
steps: Place one candy on the pencil dot and add a single drop of water on top of it.
Watch: the color bleeds out and creeps up the filter in a ring.
Wait two minutes, then lift the candy off. Look at the rings left behind.
Compare colors: which candy's dye split into two colors? Which stayed one?
The reveal: one 'single' color is often a mix of dyes, the filter pulled them apart.
activities.tagline: Candy dyes split into rainbow rings on a coffee filter, real separation science, Halloween edition.

variations.easier: Use brown and green candies only. They show the clearest splits.
variations.harder: Predict first, then test: write down which candies you think hide two dyes, and check your predictions.

activities.name: Monster Slime Lab

photo.alt: Purple slime: a photograph for Monster Slime Lab
photo.caption: Purple slime.
photo.credit: Photo: TarnishedPath, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Slime is for hands, not mouths, no tasting, and wash hands when you're done. Skip this one for kids who still mouth everything, and check for skin sensitivities to glue or saline.
activities.setup: Cover tables, slime finds everything. Pre-measure: half a cup of glue and half a cup of water per batch, mixed in each bowl.
steps: Stir half a teaspoon of baking soda into the glue-water mix.
Add food coloring and glitter. This is the monster's skin and fur.
Add one tablespoon of saline solution and stir; add a second if it's still sticky.
Knead it with your hands for two minutes. The stickiness works itself out.
Press in the googly eyes: your monster is alive. Stretch-test: how far before it snaps?
activities.tagline: Classic slime, monster-fied: googly eyes, glitter 'fur,' and stretch tests.

variations.easier: The teacher mixes the base; kids only do the coloring, glitter, and eyes.
variations.harder: Run the stretch test like an experiment: does more saline make it stretchier or snappier? Chart three batches.

activities.name: Haunted House Blueprints

photo.alt: Granby Manor Blueprints 1
photo.caption: Granby Manor Blueprints 1.
photo.credit: Photo: Michaeelaln, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.setup: Hand out graph paper and rulers. One set per designer or pair. Set the design rule up front: silly-spooky only, nothing that would scare a kindergartner.
steps: Draw the floor plan: entrance, three scare rooms, and a clearly marked EXIT.
Design one silly scare per room, a tickle tunnel, a room where the 'ghosts' compliment you, a floor that squeaks on purpose.
Add one secret passage and label how it works.
Trade blueprints with a neighbor: can they find the exit? Would a little kid laugh or cry at your scares?
Revise once based on the feedback, then post the blueprints as the Haunted Hallway gallery.
activities.tagline: Design a not-scary haunted house on paper: silly scares, secret passages, and a marked exit.

variations.easier: Design just one room instead of three, with a big EXIT arrow.
variations.harder: Add a materials list and a budget: what would your haunted house actually cost to build?

materials.item: a knife and cutting board (adult only)

activities.name: Apple Tasting Party

photo.alt: People tasting apples at a long table covered with baskets of different apple varieties
photo.caption: An apple tasting in a barn: baskets of varieties down the table and tasters working through them.
photo.credit: Photo: Bob Embleton, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Adults do all the cutting. Check for apple and fruit allergies before tasting day, and keep the slices separate from other snacks.
activities.setup: An adult slices the apples into tasting wedges. Kids don't do the cutting. Label the varieties A, B, C so the tasting is blind.
steps: Taste variety A: crunchy or soft? Sweet or tart? Everyone gives a thumbs up, sideways, or down.
Repeat for B, C, and D, cleanse the palate with a sip of water between.
Vote: one sticker per kid on the chart for your favorite.
Reveal the names. Did the class favorite surprise anyone?
Graph it: bar chart of the votes, and one sentence about what the winning apple tasted like.
activities.tagline: Taste-test apple varieties blind, vote for the class favorite, and graph the results.

variations.easier: Two varieties only, and vote with a show of hands.
variations.harder: Add descriptive words to the chart. Have tasters invent the vocabulary (snappy, honeyed, zippy).

materials.item: a large paper wreath cutout or paper-plate ring

activities.name: Harvest Gratitude Circle
activities.setup: Cut a big wreath ring from butcher paper, or tape paper-plate rings together. Cut paper leaves, one per kid plus extras.
steps: Sit in a circle. Each person names one thing from this season they're thankful for, a person, a food, a moment.
Write it on a paper leaf (or dictate it for young writers).
One by one, tape your leaf to the wreath and say the word out loud.
When the wreath is full, hang it where the whole program can see it.
Closing: one thing you're looking forward to before winter.
activities.tagline: One thankful thought each, added to a paper harvest wreath. The season's quiet anchor.

variations.easier: Draw the thankful thing instead of writing it.
variations.harder: Write the why, not just the what, one sentence about why it matters.

materials.item: a scooped pumpkin's pulp and seeds

activities.name: Pumpkin Guts Sensory Bin

photo.alt: Pumpkin Guts (Unsplash)
photo.caption: Pumpkin Guts (Unsplash).
photo.credit: Photo: Shaun Holloway shaunholloway, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Pumpkin seeds are a choking hazard for the littlest kids. Close supervision, and seeds stay in the bin, not in mouths. Wash hands before and after.
activities.setup: An adult scoops the pumpkin ahead of time. Kids get the pulp, not the knife. Spread a sheet under the bin; this is gloriously messy.
steps: Tip the whole pumpkin's insides into the bin, pulp, seeds, strings, all of it.
Free explore: squish it, smell it, describe it. Slimy? Stringy? Cold?
The sort challenge: tweezers only, seeds in one cup, pulp in another.
Count the seeds in teams of ten. Which team harvested the most?
Save the seeds for roasting or planting; compost the pulp.
activities.tagline: Scoop, squish, and sort: pumpkin pulp and seeds in the bin, tweezers for the scientists.

variations.easier: Hands only, no tweezers, just explore and describe.
variations.harder: Weigh the seed cups: does the biggest pile always weigh the most?

materials.item: big paper for the parking-lot map

activities.name: Trunk-or-Treat Planning

photo.alt: Fort Bliss Trunk or Treat 141017 A ZZ999 003
photo.caption: Fort Bliss Trunk or Treat 141017 A ZZ999 003.
photo.credit: Photo: Photo by Capt. Olivia Cobiskey, 402nd Field Artillery Brigade, First Army Divisi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Cars stay parked with engines off for the whole event, and adults monitor the lot entrance. Plan the route so kids never walk behind reversing cars.
activities.setup: Sketch the real parking lot outline on the big paper, or walk it first and pace it off. Make the volunteer sign-up sheet.
steps: Map it: draw every parking space on the lot map and number the trunks.
Theme brainstorm: each team pitches a trunk theme, under-the-sea, mad scientist, book characters, and claims a space.
Plan the traffic flow: one-way walking lanes, an entrance and an exit, so nobody bottlenecks.
Assign jobs: greeters, the allergy-safe treat table crew, the cleanup crew.
Send the sign-up sheet home: which family brings which trunk, and who staffs the allergy-safe table.
activities.tagline: Kids design the parking-lot Halloween: trunk themes, a traffic map, and the allergy-safe table.

variations.easier: The teacher maps the lot; kids only pitch themes and vote.
variations.harder: Kids write the family letter themselves. Date, time, what to bring, where to park.

activities.name: Reverse Trick-or-Treat

photo.alt: A man in a Spider-Man costume carries a costumed child holding a pumpkin treat bucket toward a waiting car, waving, during Naval Station Rota's reverse trick-or-treat
photo.caption: We go to them: at Naval Station Rota's reverse trick-or-treat the treats travel, and a costumed child with a pumpkin bucket meets the parade at the kerb.
photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Navy photo by Lt. Lyndsi Gutierrez, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Small groups, an adult with every group, daylight or well-lit routes only. Sealed, store-bought treats only, nothing homemade for giving away. Check the allergy-safe options before packing.
activities.setup: Line up the delivery route ahead, a nearby senior center, or neighbors who've said yes. Buy sealed treats; check the allergy-safe options.
steps: Decorate the bags, Halloween on the outside, kindness on the inside.
Pack each bag: two or three sealed treats and one handmade thank-you card.
Walk the route in small groups, each with an adult.
Knock, smile, hand over the bag: 'Happy Halloween. This one's for you!'
Back at home base: share one reaction each. Who lit up the most?
activities.tagline: Flip the script: kids pack treat bags and deliver them to seniors and neighbors.

variations.easier: Deliver within the building, the front office, the custodians, the younger classrooms.
variations.harder: Kids plan the route and write the ask-note to the senior center themselves.

materials.item: teal paint or a teal pumpkin sign

activities.name: Teal Pumpkin Project

photo.alt: FARE Teal Pumpkin Flyer
photo.caption: FARE Teal Pumpkin Flyer.
photo.credit: Photo: Alexander Klink, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Keep the non-food treats truly separate from the candy, different box, different scoop, no mix-ups. Check that small non-food items aren't choking hazards for the youngest visitors.
activities.setup: Paint the pumpkin teal ahead of time, or let the kids do it as the craft. Set up TWO treat containers: candy, and the teal non-food box.
steps: The meaning: a teal pumpkin on a porch means 'we have allergy-safe, non-food treats here.'
Paint your teal pumpkin, or make a teal pumpkin sign for the door.
Stock the teal box: stickers, pencils, glow bracelets, bouncy balls, nothing edible.
Practice the line: 'Would you like candy or a teal treat?' Every kid gets asked, every kid gets a choice.
Put the teal pumpkin where trick-or-treaters can see it, with the teal box right beside the candy.
activities.tagline: Paint a pumpkin teal and run the allergy-safe treat table, Halloween for every kid.

variations.easier: Print a teal pumpkin sign instead of painting, same meaning, zero dry time.
variations.harder: Kids survey the neighborhood: how many teal pumpkins can they spot on Halloween night?

materials.item: printed neighborhood maps or big paper

activities.name: Trick-or-Treat Route Map
activities.safety: This is the safety activity: daylight planning for a nighttime event. The standing rules, reflective gear or glow sticks, an adult with every group, no entering homes, get said out loud and written on the map.
activities.setup: Print simple street maps of the neighborhood around the school or program, or draw the main streets on big paper together.
steps: Mark home base on the map. That's where the route starts and ends.
Trace the route: stick to well-lit streets and sidewalks, and mark every street crossing with an X.
Pair up: every kid gets a buddy, and buddies never separate. Draw the pairs on the map's corner.
Mark the safe stops: houses of people you know, the teal pumpkin houses, the well-lit corners.
Walk the rules out loud: stay on sidewalks, cross at corners, one adult per group, home by the agreed time.
activities.tagline: Map the safe route before the big night: lit streets, buddy pairs, and crossing points.

variations.easier: The teacher pre-marks the route; kids add the buddy pairs and safe-stop stickers.
variations.harder: Kids plan a second route for a different start point and compare which is safer.

activities.inclusion: Pre-cut pieces for little hands; dictate thankful thoughts for pre-writers.
activities.name: Thankful Turkey Handprints
activities.safety: Scissors stay at the table; little kids get pre-cut bodies and feathers.
activities.setup: Trace a hand template on brown paper, one body per kid. Cut colored paper into feather strips, about 8 inches long.
steps: Trace your hand on brown paper and cut it out. The fingers are the turkey's tail feathers.
Cut a round body and a smaller head from brown paper; glue the head on top.
Add googly eyes or marker eyes, an orange triangle beak, and a red wattle.
Write one thankful thought on each paper feather, then glue the feathers in a fan behind the body.
Line the turkeys up on the wall, a whole flock of gratitude.
activities.tagline: A handprint turkey with a feather for every thankful thought.

variations.easier: Use a pre-traced hand and write the thankful thoughts for the youngest kids.
variations.harder: Make the feathers 3D, fold each one down the middle, and write a whole paragraph of thanks on the back of the body.

activities.inclusion: Pre-rolled cones available; partner rolling for limited grip strength.

materials.item: large brown paper or grocery bags

activities.name: Paper Cornucopia
activities.safety: Scissors stay at the table. Big cones get a tape ring on the seam so they hold their shape.
activities.setup: Cut brown paper into 18-inch squares. Set out colored paper for the fruit and vegetables.
steps: Roll a paper square into a cone, overlap the edges and tape the seam. This is the horn.
Curl the narrow end slightly to one side, the way a real cornucopia curves.
Draw, color, and cut out paper apples, pumpkins, grapes, and corn, big and bold.
Stuff the harvest into the wide end so it spills over the rim.
Set the cornucopias down the center of the table as the feast centerpiece.
activities.tagline: A rolled-paper horn of plenty, stuffed with a paper harvest.

variations.easier: Make mini horns from half-sheets and fill them with three paper fruits only.
variations.harder: Weave thin paper strips over the cone in a basket pattern before stuffing it.

activities.inclusion: Draw instead of write; name cards can be dictated.
activities.name: Friendsgiving Place Cards
activities.setup: Fold cards in half so they stand like tents. Write every guest's name on a slip of paper for the draw.
steps: Draw a name from the pile. That's the guest you're honoring.
Write their name big on the front of the tent card.
Inside, finish the sentence: 'I'm glad you're at this table because...'
Decorate the card with their favorite things. Ask around if you're not sure.
Set the cards at the friendsgiving table before anyone sits down.
activities.tagline: Hand-drawn place cards with one reason each guest is loved.

variations.easier: Write the name and one word ('funny', 'kind') instead of a sentence.
variations.harder: Add a tiny portrait of your guest on the back of the card.

activities.inclusion: Wide strips for easier weaving; pre-cut strips for the youngest.
activities.name: Harvest Weave Placemats
activities.safety: Scissors stay at the table; pre-cut strips for the youngest weavers.
activities.setup: Cut one sheet per kid into a 9x12 frame (leave the middle open) for the warp, and cut 1-inch strips in harvest colors for the weft.
steps: Lay the frame flat. These are your straight-up-and-down strips.
Weave a colored strip over, under, over, under across the frame.
Push each strip snug against the last and keep going to the bottom.
Glue the strip ends to the frame edges so nothing slides loose.
Optional: cover both sides with clear contact paper so the placemat survives the feast.
activities.tagline: Paper-strip weaving in harvest colors. The table sets itself.

variations.easier: Use wide 2-inch strips. Fewer weaves, same harvest look.
variations.harder: Weave a pattern: two orange, one brown, repeating, or spell initials with strip colors.

activities.inclusion: Walking-only rounds; a seated 'barn guard' role keeps everyone in the game.

materials.item: pool noodles or flag belts (one per farmer)

activities.name: Turkey Tag
activities.safety: Noodle taps stay gentle and below the shoulders. Clear the field of holes and sticks first.
activities.setup: Set boundaries with cones. Pick 2 farmers to start; everyone else is a turkey. Farmers hold pool noodles; turkeys tuck nothing. Just run.
steps: Turkeys scatter inside the boundaries when you shout 'Gobble!'
Farmers chase and tag turkeys with a gentle noodle tap.
Tagged turkeys freeze and flap their wings until a free turkey high-fives them back in.
After three minutes, switch farmers so everyone gets to chase.
Last round: one farmer, and the turkeys who survive get to pick the next game.
activities.tagline: The farmers are coming. Gobble, dodge, and don't get caught.

variations.easier: Play with walking only and shrink the boundaries for little legs.
variations.harder: Add a safe 'barn' zone. Turkeys inside are safe but can only stay five seconds.

activities.why_it_works: Played in short 3-minute rounds, it works as a structured movement break, research finds active breaks under 10 minutes improve on-task behavior (Deakin University, IJRESS Jan 2026).

activities.inclusion: Move the line closer; bigger buckets for easier success.

materials.item: mini pumpkins or orange beanbags (6 per team)
chalk or tape for the throw line

activities.name: Pumpkin Bucket Toss
activities.safety: Real mini pumpkins only, nothing heavy enough to hurt. Toss toward the buckets, never at people.
activities.setup: Set buckets 6 feet from the throw line for little kids, 10 for older ones. Split pumpkins evenly between teams.
steps: Teams line up behind the throw line, pumpkins in hand.
One at a time, toss a pumpkin toward your team's bucket.
Count only the pumpkins that land IN the bucket. Rim bounces don't count.
Move the line back two feet every round the whole team scores.
Winning team picks the harvest song for cleanup.
activities.tagline: Toss mini pumpkins into harvest buckets from the line.

variations.easier: Use big laundry baskets close up, and let little kids step over the line.
variations.harder: Score it: far bucket 3 points, middle 2, near 1, teams aim for the big total.

activities.inclusion: Walk instead of run; carry two crops to shorten the distance.

materials.item: one basket or box per team

activities.name: Harvest Basket Relay
activities.safety: Keep the running lanes separated so nobody collides at the pile.
activities.setup: Pile the 'crops' at the far cone. Give each team a basket at the start line.
steps: First runner sprints to the pile and grabs ONE crop.
Carry it back, no throwing the crop to a teammate.
Drop it in the team basket and tag the next runner.
Keep going until the pile is empty, then count the baskets.
Fullest basket wins. Then everybody helps carry the harvest inside.
activities.tagline: Teams fill their harvest basket one armload at a time.

variations.easier: Walk instead of run, and let kids carry two crops at a time.
variations.harder: Each runner must name something they're thankful for before they can grab a crop.

activities.inclusion: Build flat shapes instead of towers; partner roles for every step.
activities.name: Cranberry Structures

photo.alt: Red berries hanging on a thin branch against a blue sky
photo.caption: Red berries hanging on a thin branch against a blue sky.
photo.credit: Photo: Jongsun Lee, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Toothpicks are pointy. Build on the table, never sword-fight. Check the class allergy list before using real cranberries; pom-poms build exactly the same.
activities.setup: Rinse the cranberries and pat dry, wet ones slide off the toothpicks. Hand out 30 cranberries and a pile of toothpicks per kid.
steps: Sketch your tower first: triangles hold weight, squares wobble.
Push a toothpick into a cranberry. That's your first joint.
Build a triangle base, then stack triangles upward.
Test as you go: does it stand on its own? Wobble means rebuild the base wider.
Measure the finished towers. Tallest freestanding tower wins the harvest crown.
activities.tagline: Toothpicks and cranberries: who builds the tallest harvest tower?

variations.easier: Build flat shapes on the table, stars, snowflakes, letters, instead of towers.
variations.harder: Add a weight test: how many pennies can the top hold before it tips?

activities.inclusion: Big pom-poms, short distance; two hands on the baster.

materials.item: cones for start and finish lines

activities.name: Turkey Baster Relay
activities.safety: Basters point at pom-poms, never at faces. Allergy-safe by design: the 'cranberries' are pom-poms, so there are no food allergies to check. Wash basters before and after if they were ever near real food.
activities.setup: Set a bowl of pom-poms at the start line and an empty bucket at the finish line, about 10 feet apart, per team.
steps: Squeeze the baster bulb, press the tip against a pom-pom, and let go, suction grabs it.
Carry the pom-pom to the finish bucket without touching it with your hands.
Drop it in, run the baster back, and hand it to the next runner.
Dropped it? Pick it up with the baster only. Fingers don't count.
First team to move all their cranberries wins. Then talk: what made the grip work, air pressure pushing back in.
activities.tagline: Move the 'cranberries' with nothing but a turkey baster and air.

variations.easier: Use big pom-poms and a short carry distance; let little kids use two hands on the baster.
variations.harder: Blow-only round: no suction allowed, push the pom-pom across the table with baster air.

activities.inclusion: One big group jar with 30-second shake turns; timer role for dairy-free kids.

materials.item: small jars with tight lids (one per pair)

activities.name: Shake-a-Jar Butter

photo.alt: A person pulling ropes to churn butter in a traditional churn pot
photo.caption: Butter by arm power: churning cream the slow way, like the shake jar speeds up.
photo.credit: Photo: Madan subedi01, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Dairy check first: kids with dairy allergies take the official timer role and observe the science. No tasting without an adult's say-so. Jars stay closed while shaking.
activities.setup: Pour cream into each jar. Fill only halfway. Screw the lids on tight. Check the class allergy list before you start.
steps: Shake the jar hard, the cream sloshes, then thickens into whipped cream. Keep going.
Keep shaking past the whipped stage: suddenly a yellow lump separates from thin liquid. That's butter and buttermilk.
Pour off the liquid, add a pinch of salt, and give it five more shakes.
Spread it on a cracker and taste the science. You made that.
Talk it through: shaking smashed the fat droplets together until they stuck.
activities.tagline: Cream, a jar, and ten minutes of shaking: that's butter.

variations.easier: One big jar for the whole group. Everyone takes a 30-second shake turn.
variations.harder: Run a race: salted jar vs. unsalted. Does one turn to butter first?

activities.why_it_works: Hands-on making beats screen time: the APA's Sept 2026 report finds learning sticks when kids apply knowledge off-screen, and nothing is more off-screen than shaking cream into butter.

activities.inclusion: Fixed 3-dish menu option; jobs assigned by interest, not just volunteers.
activities.name: Friendsgiving Potluck Plan
activities.safety: Check the class allergy list BEFORE the sign-up goes home. Every dish needs its ingredient card, and keep one table nut-free.
activities.setup: Draw the feast table on the big paper: drinks, mains, sides, desserts. Some families say 'harvest feast' instead of 'friendsgiving'. Both names are welcome here.
steps: Brainstorm the menu together. Every kid names one dish they'd love to see.
Sort the dishes into drinks, mains, sides, and desserts on the table map.
Families sign up for ONE dish each, nobody cooks the whole feast.
Every signed-up dish gets an ingredient card: list everything in it.
Assign jobs for the day: greeters, table setters, drink pourers, cleanup crew.
activities.tagline: The class plans its own friendsgiving feast, sign-up sheet and all.

variations.easier: Teacher picks a simple fixed menu (three dishes) and kids only do the sign-up and jobs.
variations.harder: Kids cost out the feast: price each dish and build the shopping list on a budget.

activities.inclusion: Share one thankful word instead of a story; listening counts fully.
activities.name: Friendsgiving Story Circle
activities.setup: No setup, just a circle of chairs and two minutes of quiet to think of a favorite memory with a friend.
steps: Pair up with someone you don't know well.
Each person tells their partner one favorite memory, two minutes each.
Come back to the circle. Now INTRODUCE your partner and retell THEIR story.
The partner gives a thumbs-up if the retelling got it right.
Close: one word each about what makes a good friend.
activities.tagline: Pair up, trade a favorite memory, introduce your partner's story.

variations.easier: Skip the retelling, partners just share one thing they're thankful the other person taught them.
variations.harder: Make it a story chain: each pair's memory has to connect to the last pair's somehow.

activities.inclusion: Team play for shy kids; passing allowed on any letter.
activities.name: Gratitude Alphabet Circle
activities.setup: No setup. Circle up and pick who starts with A.
steps: First kid says something they're thankful for that starts with A. 'Apples', 'Aunt May'.
Next kid takes B, then C, all the way around.
Stuck on a letter? The group gets ten seconds to shout suggestions.
Letters like Q, X, and Z allow 'thankful for' plus any word, no shame in 'xylophones'.
Finish at Z with a group cheer for the alphabet of thanks.
activities.tagline: A to Z around the circle: one thankful word per letter.

variations.easier: Do it in teams. Each team takes every other letter.
variations.harder: Hard mode: no repeats from last week's circle, and X must be a real word.

activities.inclusion: Draw or dictate slips; anonymous by default.
activities.name: Thankful Jar Shares
activities.setup: Set the jar where everyone can reach it all week. It fills up before the share day.
steps: All week, kids drop in slips: 'I'm thankful for...'. Names optional.
On share day, circle up and shake the jar.
Draw slips one at a time and read each aloud.
After each one, the group guesses who wrote it, or the writer claims it.
Save the week's slips in an envelope: the year's gratitude archive.
activities.tagline: Slips of gratitude in a jar, drawn and read aloud.

variations.easier: Do it in one sitting. Five minutes of writing, then read them all.
variations.harder: Sort the slips into categories (people, places, things, moments) and graph which wins.

activities.inclusion: Draw instead of write; sharing always optional.
activities.name: Gratitude All Year
activities.setup: Give every kid a small booklet. This is their all-year gratitude log. Say it plainly: not every family celebrates Thanksgiving, and gratitude doesn't need a holiday.
steps: Decorate the cover: 'My Gratitude Log' and your name.
Write or draw three good things from TODAY. Tiny counts: warm socks, a joke, lunch.
Share one with a partner if you want to. Sharing is optional, always.
Set the rhythm: one page a week, every week, all year.
Check back monthly: flip through and notice how the good things stack up.
activities.tagline: A gratitude practice for everyone, no holiday required.

variations.easier: Draw instead of write, three pictures of good things per page.
variations.harder: Add a monthly 'gratitude letter': write one real thank-you note to someone outside the program.

activities.inclusion: Poster, counter, and greeter roles for every mobility level.
activities.name: Food Drive Planning

photo.alt: Donated canned food packed inside a metal sorting cage at a food bank
photo.caption: Donations sorted and ready: canned food collected for a food bank.
photo.credit: Photo: USDAgov, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Cans only. No open or homemade food in the bins. Heavy boxes get carried by adults.
activities.setup: Call the local food bank or pantry first (teacher job) to confirm what they accept and when to deliver.
steps: Set the goal together: 100 cans? One can per kid per week?
Make posters: what to bring, where the bins are, the deadline.
Build the collection bins from boxes, decorate them loud.
Assign the crew: bin monitors, counters, delivery team.
Count day: tally everything, celebrate the total, deliver together.
activities.tagline: Kids plan the whole canned-food drive: goal, posters, collection crew.

variations.easier: Run a one-day mini drive: goal of one bag per kid, counted the same afternoon.
variations.harder: Kids write the thank-you notes to every family that donated.

activities.inclusion: One giant class card option; dictate the message.
activities.name: Thank-You Cards for School Staff
activities.setup: List the staff the kids actually see: custodians, cafeteria crew, bus drivers, office staff, crossing guards.
steps: Each kid picks one staff member. No doubles until everyone is covered.
Write what that person DOES that helps you: 'You keep our halls clean.'
Add a drawing of them doing that job, capes optional.
Sign every card from the whole class.
Deliver them in person as a group. The delivery is the best part.
activities.tagline: Cards for the custodians, cafeteria crew, and bus drivers, the holiday heroes.

variations.easier: Make one giant class card per staff member instead of individual ones.
variations.harder: Kids interview their staff member first: 'What's the hardest part of your day?'. Then write the card.

activities.inclusion: Seated assembly line; decorating counts as full participation.

materials.item: sealed store-bought snacks (granola bars, fruit cups)
socks, hand warmers, or travel toiletries

activities.name: Blessings Bags

photo.alt: Packing up food DVIDS135748
photo.caption: Packing up food DVIDS135748.
photo.credit: Photo: Seaman Christopher A. Baker, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Sealed store-bought snacks only, nothing homemade or opened. Check snack labels against the class allergy list if any bags stay in the room.
activities.setup: Confirm the drop-off spot first (teacher job): a shelter, pantry, or community fridge. Buy sealed snacks only.
steps: Decorate each bag with markers, bright and kind.
Assembly line: one snack, one drink box, one pair of socks, one toiletry per bag.
Tuck in a handwritten note: 'Someone in your neighborhood packed this for you.'
Count and stack the finished bags.
Deliver together to the drop-off spot the same week.
activities.tagline: Pack snack-and-supply bags for neighbors who need them.

variations.easier: Pack two bags as a whole group. One bag, everybody adds one item.
variations.harder: Kids plan the next round: what would YOU want in a bag on a cold night?

activities.inclusion: Symbol bank for a head start; drawing-only codes welcome; encode in a home language with a translated key.
activities.name: Turkey Code Feathers
activities.safety: Scissors stay at the table; pre-cut bodies and feathers for little kids.
activities.setup: Cut a simple turkey body and 8 feather shapes per kid. Feathers get taped on after the coding is done.
steps: Invent your symbols: draw one symbol for each letter A–Z (younger kids do A–M). This is your code key. Keep it secret.
Pick a true turkey fact and encode it, one letter per feather.
Tape the coded feathers onto your turkey body.
Trade turkeys with a partner and decode theirs using THEIR key.
Share the most surprising fact the group decoded.
activities.tagline: Invent a symbol code, encode a turkey fact on feathers, trade and decode.

variations.easier: Use a ready-made symbol bank and encode just 3 letters.
variations.harder: Encode a whole riddle across two turkeys and let another pair crack it.

activities.inclusion: Pre-rolled cone templates; seated tossing; rules can be dictated and scribed.
activities.name: Cornucopia Catch
activities.safety: Scissors stay at the table. Toss paper produce only, never at faces.
activities.setup: Set out paper and tape per team of 3–4. Cut a pile of paper produce up front so building starts fast.
steps: Build 3 paper cornucopias sturdy enough to hold, catch, and toss.
Test: toss paper produce between teammates and catch it in the horn.
Now invent your own game: teams write the rules, the scoring, and a name.
Rotate: play another team's game exactly by their rules.
Vote: funniest rules, trickiest catch, best team name.
activities.tagline: Build paper cornucopias, then invent your own catch game, rules and all.

variations.easier: Build one big team cornucopia and play catch in a circle.
variations.harder: Add a points zone on the floor, long catches into the horn score double.

activities.why_it_works: Student-designed endings, inventing the game's rules, are the 2026 STEM flourish research flags as most engaging: kids own the challenge instead of just following it.

activities.inclusion: Thicker skewers for easier grip; team roles (planner, builder, tester); test narrated aloud so everyone follows the results.
activities.name: Thanksgiving Table Build
activities.safety: Toothpicks are pointy. Build on the table, never sword-fight. Check glue bottles for clogs before frustrated squeezing starts.
activities.setup: Cover the table with wax paper, glue peels right off. Hand out toothpicks and glue per team.
steps: The constraint: a table with AT MOST 4 legs, standing on its own.
Sketch the leg design first, triangles beat squares for strength.
Build on the wax paper; let the glue set (build one day, test the next if you can).
Load books one at a time onto the tabletop; record the max before it fails.
Compare: which leg designs held the most? What would you change?
activities.tagline: Toothpicks and glue: build a table with at most 4 legs that holds the feast.

variations.easier: Build with thicker skewers and test with paperback books only.
variations.harder: Limit it to 20 toothpicks total, the constraint forces smarter design.

activities.name: Elf Zipline Delivery

photo.alt: A rider hanging from a zip line cable high above a green gorge
photo.caption: Mid-flight on the zip line, the ride the elf delivery run copies in miniature.
photo.credit: Photo: Boholmission, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Keep the line below shoulder height; no loops of string around necks or fingers.
activities.setup: Pre-cut string lengths and poke a hole near the rim of each cup for the paper-clip hook.
steps: Tie the string tight between two points, one end higher than the other.
Hook a paper cup to the line with a paper clip so it slides freely.
Load a pom-pom gift into the cup and release it from the high end.
Time the trip. Try a steeper line and a flatter line. Which delivers faster?
Challenge: deliver two gifts in one trip without losing either.
activities.tagline: String a zipline across the room and race to deliver the gifts fastest.

variations.easier: Use a short line between two chairs and deliver one gift at a time.
variations.harder: Add a marked drop zone and score points for landing the gift inside it.

materials.item: small cardboard trays or box lids
books or a board for the ramp
cotton balls or small blocks (the gifts)

activities.name: Sleigh and Slope Run
activities.safety: Test sleds on the floor, not off tables; clear the landing zone of feet.
activities.setup: Stack books at one end of a table to make a sturdy ramp; tape the top so it can't slide.
steps: Build a sled: tape straws under a cardboard tray as runners.
Load three cotton-ball gifts onto the sled.
Release the sled from the top of the ramp.
If gifts fall off, redesign: add sides, lower the load, or change the runners.
Final run: which team's sled carries all three gifts the farthest?
activities.tagline: Build a mini sled that carries gifts down a ramp without spilling.

variations.easier: Run the sled empty first, then add gifts one at a time.
variations.harder: Steepen the ramp and time the runs; fastest clean run wins.

materials.item: small clear plastic jars with lids
glitter, foam beads, and paper-hole-punch dots (the snow)
a spoonful of clear glue (optional, slows the fall)
small waterproof figurines or bottle-brush trees

activities.name: Snow Globe Slow-Fall Lab

photo.alt: A snow globe with white flakes settled around a tiny tower
photo.caption: A snow globe with white flakes settled around a tiny tower.
photo.credit: Photo: Alzinous, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Plastic jars only for kids; adult tightens and tapes the lid shut.
activities.setup: Set out jars and snow ingredients in separate cups; hot-glue trees to lids ahead of time if kids are under 7.
steps: Glue a tiny tree or figure to the inside of the jar lid and let it set.
Fill the jar nearly full with water and add a spoonful of clear glue.
Try one kind of snow at a time. Shake, then time how long the snow takes to settle.
Record each snow type's fall time on a chart.
Pick the slowest snow for the final globe, then seal the lid with tape.
activities.tagline: Build a real snow globe, then hunt for the slowest-falling snow.

variations.easier: Skip the timing; just build the globe with the snow you like best.
variations.harder: Graph all the fall times and write one sentence about why the slowest one won.

materials.item: a toy animal or pom-pom (the reindeer)

activities.name: Reindeer Shelter Storm Test
activities.safety: Fan stays on low; fingers and loose string stay away from the blades.
activities.setup: Mark a test line on the table two feet from the fan; sort building materials into bins.
steps: Build a shelter big enough to fit your reindeer inside.
Set the shelter on the test line and place the reindeer inside.
Turn the fan on low for ten seconds: the blizzard is here.
Did the roof lift? Did the walls fall? Rebuild the weak spots.
Test again on a higher fan speed for the brave.
activities.tagline: Build a tiny barn that survives a ten-second blizzard from a fan.

variations.easier: Test with a hair dryer on cool from far away instead of a fan.
variations.harder: Add a rule: the shelter must have a door the reindeer can walk through.

materials.item: a small gift bag with blocks inside (the weighted stocking)

activities.name: Stocking Holder Build
activities.safety: Test on sturdy low tables only; stand clear in case the holder tips during testing.
activities.setup: Fill each gift bag with the same number of blocks so every stocking weighs the same.
steps: Design a holder that clamps or hooks onto the table edge.
Hang the weighted stocking from your holder.
Let go slowly. If the table tips or the holder slides, redesign.
Test three times in a row. It counts if it holds all three.
Decorate the winning holders and vote on the cleverest clamp.
activities.tagline: Engineer a hook that hangs a full stocking off a table edge without tipping.

variations.easier: Start with a clothespin clip design; improve it from there.
variations.harder: Add a weight rule: hold two stockings at once.

materials.item: two tables or chairs (workshop and sled stations)

activities.name: Gift Conveyor Design
activities.safety: Keep the conveyor off the floor where feet walk; tape joints so tubes can't roll away.
activities.setup: Set the two stations about six feet apart; sort tubes and rails where teams can reach them.
steps: Plan a path for the presents: rails, tubes, or a string pull-belt.
Build your conveyor between the two stations.
Launch a present from the workshop. No hands after it starts moving.
If a present gets stuck, find the jam and rebuild that section.
Run a full delivery of five presents. Fastest jam-free line wins.
activities.tagline: Move presents from the workshop to the sled with no hands after launch.

variations.easier: Shorten the run to three feet and use one straight tube.
variations.harder: Add a hill: the present must climb before it rolls down.

activities.name: Cookie Dissolve Race

photo.alt: A plate of homemade cookies
photo.caption: Cookies ready for the race: drop one in water and time how long it takes to fall apart.
photo.credit: Photo: Ann from Detroit, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Check for dairy, egg, wheat, and nut allergies first; use dairy-free milk and allergy-safe cookies where needed. Wash hands before tasting.
activities.setup: Pour milk into cups ahead of time; keep cookie packages sealed until the activity starts.
steps: Look at the three cookies. Predict which will dissolve first and write it down.
Drop one cookie into each cup of milk at the same time.
Watch and wait. Note the order the cookies soften and fall apart.
Taste-test a fresh cookie of each kind after the race.
Compare results to predictions. Did the crunchiest cookie win or lose?
activities.tagline: Drop three kinds of cookies in milk and time which one melts first.

variations.easier: Race just two cookie kinds and skip the chart.
variations.harder: Try warm milk vs cold milk and compare the times.

materials.item: instant snow powder (sold as faux snow)

activities.name: Instant Snow Polymers

photo.alt: Fresh snow settled on dry golden grass
photo.caption: Fresh snow settled on dry golden grass.
photo.credit: Photo: Mikhail Elfimov, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Not edible: nobody tastes the powder or the snow. Adult pours the powder for kids under 8.
activities.setup: Pre-measure powder into small cups; set out water pitchers and bowls.
steps: Look at the dry powder with a magnifying glass. Describe it.
Add water one spoonful at a time and stir.
Watch it puff up. Keep adding until it stops growing.
Scoop the snow with your hands. How does it feel compared to real snow?
Write one sentence about what you think the powder did with the water.
activities.tagline: Turn a spoonful of powder into a bowl of fluffy snow and figure out why.

variations.easier: Make one big shared bowl and explore it together.
variations.harder: Test two water amounts and compare which snow is fluffier.

activities.name: Dancing Cranberries

photo.alt: Workers gathering cranberries floating on a flooded cranberry bog
photo.caption: Cranberries afloat by the thousand at harvest, berries riding the water.
photo.credit: Photo: Keith Weller, USDA-ARS, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Vinegar fizz can splash: keep faces back from the cup and wipe spills right away.
activities.setup: Set out cups, a cranberry bowl, and measured spoons of baking soda.
steps: Fill a cup halfway with water and stir in a spoonful of baking soda.
Drop in five dried cranberries. Watch: they sink.
Slowly pour in a splash of vinegar.
Watch the cranberries rise, dance, and sink again as bubbles grab them.
Try more or fewer cranberries. How many can dance at once?
activities.tagline: Make dried cranberries bounce and bob in a fizzy cup.

variations.easier: Do it as a group demo with one big cup everyone can see.
variations.harder: Count how many trips one cranberry makes in a minute.

materials.item: stickers (stars, trees) for the start and finish

activities.name: Paper Maze Swap

photo.alt: People play a game using a maze on a piece of paper while at a table during the day
photo.caption: People play a game using a maze on a piece of paper while at a table during the day.
photo.credit: Photo: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: None beyond the usual pencil rules.
activities.setup: Hand out graph paper; keep extra sheets nearby for maze redesigns.
steps: Draw a maze on graph paper with one clear start and one finish.
Hide a holiday prize inside: a star sticker at the finish.
Test-solve your own maze to prove it can be finished.
Swap mazes with a partner and solve theirs without lifting your pencil.
Rate it: too easy, just right, or impossible? Tell the designer.
activities.tagline: Draw a holiday maze, swap it, and race to solve someone else's.

variations.easier: Draw on plain paper with wide paths and no dead ends.
variations.harder: Add a rule: the solver must collect three hidden stars before the finish.

activities.name: Gift Wrap Measure-Up

photo.alt: Wraps a gift while playing a game (8801847)
photo.caption: Wraps a gift while playing a game (8801847).
photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Matthew Morales, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Scissors safety for younger kids; pre-cut starter pieces if needed.
activities.setup: Wrap nothing in advance; keep boxes and paper at a measuring station.
steps: Pick a box. Guess how many paper squares it would take to cover it.
Wrap the box for real and count the paper you used.
Measure each side of the box with a ruler and write the numbers down.
Try a second box. This time measure first, then predict.
Was your second prediction closer? The measurer's edge is real.
activities.tagline: Estimate the paper a box needs, then measure and see who was closest.

variations.easier: Wrap one box and just compare guess vs result.
variations.harder: Compute the box's surface area from your measurements and compare.

materials.item: reindeer tokens (paper clips or small toys)

activities.name: Reindeer Grid Coding
activities.safety: None beyond the usual paper-and-scissors rules.
activities.setup: Print grids ahead; cut arrow-card sets into envelopes, one set per kid.
steps: Place your reindeer on the start square and a star on the barn square.
Lay out arrow cards to plan the whole route before moving anything.
Run the program: move the reindeer one square per card.
Bug! If you crash into a wall, go back and fix the cards.
Trade grids with a partner and run their route.
activities.tagline: Program a reindeer across a grid with arrow cards: no screens needed.

variations.easier: Use a 3x3 grid with the barn two squares away.
variations.harder: Add blocked squares the route must go around.

materials.item: washable paint, thinned with a little water
big paper sheets or a tray

activities.name: Ornament Pendulum Paint

photo.alt: A large shiny pendulum ball swinging over a round sand pit
photo.caption: A giant pendulum mid-swing, its ball like a huge ornament on the move.
photo.credit: Photo: Chase Bohannon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Wear smocks; cover the table. Paint stays off faces and mouths; wash hands after.
activities.setup: Poke a small hole in the bottom of each cup; tie the bell inside and the string outside. Set up one station at a time to avoid collisions.
steps: Hang the cup from a chair back or a held stick so it swings freely.
Tape big paper under the cup.
Pour a little thinned paint into the cup and pull it to the side.
Let go and watch it drip-paint spirals as it swings.
Change the pull length or add a second color and compare the patterns.
activities.tagline: Swing a jingle-bell pendulum and let it drip-paint a holiday swirl.

variations.easier: Swing one color over a small paper plate.
variations.harder: Time the swings and try to paint matching patterns twice.

materials.item: clear plastic bottles with tight lids

activities.name: Blizzard in a Bottle

photo.alt: The United States Capitol and its grounds covered in snow during a blizzard
photo.caption: A real blizzard's work: deep snow over everything, the storm the bottle copies.
photo.credit: Photo: USCapitol, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Adult tightens the lid, then tapes it shut. Oily bottles stay on the table, not on laps.
activities.setup: Pre-fill bottles two-thirds with water; keep oil and glitter in pourable cups.
steps: Add a splash of oil and a pinch of glitter to your bottle.
Add one drop of white paint for cloudy storm water.
Cap it tight. Adult tapes the lid.
Shake hard: blizzard! Then set it down and watch the snow settle.
Tip it slowly side to side and watch the glitter swirl like wind.
activities.tagline: Shake up a winter storm in a bottle and watch the glitter settle like snow.

variations.easier: Use water and glitter only; skip the oil.
variations.harder: Time how long the storm takes to calm for three different glitter amounts.

activities.name: Dreidel Spin Math

photo.alt: Fair dreidel, biased dreidel and fair die (photomontage) (14302528039)
photo.caption: Fair dreidel, biased dreidel and fair die (photomontage) (14302528039).
photo.credit: Photo: UCL Mathematical & Physical Sciences from London, UK, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Small tokens are a choking hazard for kids under 4; keep them off the floor.
activities.setup: Print the four dreidel letters and their meanings on a chart: nun (nothing), gimel (all), hey (half), shin (put one in).
steps: Learn the four sides: nun takes nothing, gimel takes all, hey takes half, shin puts one in.
Each player spins 10 times and tallies every result.
Add up your tallies. Which letter came up most?
Compare with the table: did everyone get similar results?
Play a real round with tokens in the pot, using the letter rules.
activities.tagline: Spin the dreidel, tally the letters, and find out which side wins.

variations.easier: Just spin and act out the letter: gimel means a big cheer.
variations.harder: Track 50 spins as a group and graph which letter won.

materials.item: a printed list of the seven principles (Nguzo Saba)

activities.name: Kwanzaa Principle Cards
activities.safety: None beyond the usual classroom rules.
activities.setup: Write the seven principles with one-line meanings on the board: Umoja (unity), Kujichagulia (self-determination), Ujima (collective work), Ujamaa (cooperative economics), Nia (purpose), Kuumba (creativity), Imani (faith).
steps: Make two cards for each principle: one with the name, one with a kid action (for Umoja: 'include someone new at lunch').
Shuffle all 14 cards face down.
Flip two at a time. Keep the pair if the name matches its action.
Read each match out loud when you win it.
Finish by naming which principle your family or class already lives.
activities.tagline: Match the seven principles to everyday kid actions in a memory game.

variations.easier: Play with the principle list visible on the board.
variations.harder: Invent your own eighth action card for a principle and defend the match.

materials.item: one wrapped gift (or a wrapped box of treats to share)

activities.name: Story Gift Pass
activities.safety: Pass gently; no grabbing. If treats are inside, check allergies before sharing.
activities.setup: Wrap the gift; print or write a short story packed with the words left and right.
steps: Sit in a circle. One person holds the wrapped gift.
The reader reads the story slowly.
Every time you hear 'left', pass the gift left. 'Right' passes right.
Keep listening; the gift keeps moving.
Whoever holds it when the story ends unwraps it (or shares the treats).
activities.tagline: Pass the gift left and right as the story says, and see who unwraps it.

variations.easier: Use a ball instead of a gift and skip the unwrapping.
variations.harder: Write your own left-right story as a group first.

materials.item: a bird feeder nearby helps a lot

activities.name: Winter Bird Watch Tally

photo.alt: A close shot of children birdwatching
photo.caption: A close shot of children birdwatching.
photo.credit: Photo: Walton LaVonda, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Watch from inside or a safe spot; never approach or touch wild birds.
activities.setup: Set up near a window with a view of a tree or feeder; print simple tally sheets.
steps: Sit quietly for ten minutes and watch.
Make a tally mark every time a bird lands.
Note the color and size of each visitor: big brown, tiny gray, red chest.
Compare sheets: did everyone see the same birds?
Repeat on another day and see if the numbers change.
activities.tagline: Spend ten quiet minutes counting the birds that visit in winter.

variations.easier: Just count total birds; skip colors and sizes.
variations.harder: Graph a week of counts and spot the busiest visiting time.

materials.item: cotton balls or tissue for smudging
white paint pens or chalk for stars

activities.name: Northern Lights Pastels

photo.alt: Farthest north northern lights
photo.caption: Farthest north northern lights.
photo.credit: Photo: Nansen, Fridtjof, 1861-1930, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Oil pastels stain: wear smocks and wash hands after. Keep pastels away from mouths.
activities.setup: Cover tables with paper; set out pastel sets and smudging cotton.
steps: Draw wavy ribbons of green and purple across the black paper.
Smudge the colors upward with a cotton ball to make them glow.
Add a dark mountain silhouette along the bottom.
Dot tiny white stars above the lights.
Hang the finished skies together as a winter gallery.
activities.tagline: Smudge oil pastels into glowing auroras on black paper.

variations.easier: Use one color ribbon plus stars.
variations.harder: Layer three colors and blend them into a smooth gradient.

activities.name: Snow Paint Spray

photo.alt: Fresh snow sparkling in sunlight
photo.caption: A fresh snow surface, the blank canvas for spray bottle painting.
photo.credit: Photo: USFWSAlaska, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Food coloring stains clothes and gloves; dress for mess and cold. Spray at snow, never at faces.
activities.setup: Mix a few drops of food coloring into each spray bottle ahead of time.
steps: Head outside to clean, fresh snow.
Spray big shapes first: circles, zigzags, your initials.
Layer colors to make new ones where they overlap.
Work together on one giant mural across the snowbank.
Step back and admire it before it melts.
activities.tagline: Spray colored water onto fresh snow and paint the whole yard.

variations.easier: Use one color and paint footprints.
variations.harder: Plan the mural on paper first, then spray it to scale.

materials.item: small mason jars or clear cups with lids

activities.name: Snowman Soup Gift Mix

photo.alt: A mug of hot cocoa topped with big marshmallows
photo.caption: A mug of hot cocoa topped with big marshmallows.
photo.credit: Photo: DanielPenfield, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Use only sealed, store-bought ingredients; check dairy and nut allergies. Wash hands before handling food.
activities.setup: Open sealed bags into pouring bowls just before the activity; set out jars and tags.
steps: Spoon cocoa mix into the jar: about half full.
Layer chocolate chips, then mini marshmallows on top.
Seal the jar and tie ribbon around the lid.
Write the recipe tag: mix with hot water or warm milk.
Give it to someone who could use a warm-up.
activities.tagline: Layer cocoa, marshmallows, and chocolate chips into a gift-ready jar.

variations.easier: Use one jar size and a printed tag to copy.
variations.harder: Design your own tag art and write a personal note.

materials.item: paper and pencils for the route plan
lanterns or jar candles (real walk) or drawings (planning only)
a printed map of the block or school grounds

activities.name: Solstice Lantern Stroll

photo.alt: Jersey Tourism Fête dé Noué Jèrri 2008 Lantern Parade 1
photo.caption: Jersey Tourism Fête dé Noué Jèrri 2008 Lantern Parade 1.
photo.credit: Photo: Jersey Tourism, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Real flames stay with adults only; kids carry battery candles. Walk in a group with an adult leader and wear reflective gear.
activities.setup: Print simple maps; confirm the walk route and adult helpers with the program lead first.
steps: Learn what the winter solstice is: the longest night of the year.
Draw a safe walking loop on the map: start, middle stop, finish.
Assign jobs: route leader, lantern carriers, song starter, caboose.
Make or decorate the lanterns.
Walk the loop together as the sky goes dark.
activities.tagline: Plan a lantern walk for the longest night of the year.

variations.easier: Plan the walk and do a daytime practice loop instead.
variations.harder: Write the invitation and lead the whole event yourselves.

materials.item: bins labeled recycle, trash, and keep

activities.name: Holiday Cleanup Crew Game
activities.safety: Adults handle anything sharp or broken; kids sort paper and packaging only.
activities.setup: Label the bins and place them where everyone can reach them.
steps: Split into crews: Wrappers, Recyclers, and Keepers.
Set the timer for ten minutes.
Sort everything into the right bin; one point per correct item.
Pause at five minutes: which crew is winning?
Final count. The winning crew picks the closing song.
activities.tagline: Turn the post-party mess into a timed team mission.

variations.easier: Skip the points; just beat the timer together.
variations.harder: Add a 'mystery item' round: sort tricky items like tape rolls and ribbons.

activities.name: Snowflake Statue Balance
activities.safety: Clear floor space; no balancing on heads while moving.
activities.setup: Cut or fold a stack of paper snowflakes; clear a play area.
steps: Each player gets a paper snowflake.
The caller names a body part: elbow, knee, shoulder.
Balance the snowflake there while the music plays.
When the music stops: freeze like a statue.
Drop your snowflake and you're the next caller.
activities.tagline: Balance a paper snowflake on your elbow, knee, or nose: freeze!

variations.easier: Balance on your palm only.
variations.harder: Two snowflakes at once, on two different body parts.

materials.item: a red and a green paper circle (the reindeer nose signals)
cones or tape for the start and finish lines

activities.name: Red Nose Green Nose
activities.safety: Play on a clear, flat surface; no running into walls or furniture.
activities.setup: Mark a start line and a finish line about 30 feet apart.
steps: One player is the reindeer, holding the red and green circles.
Runners line up at the start.
Green nose means go. Red nose means freeze.
Anyone caught moving goes back to the start.
First runner to tag the reindeer becomes the reindeer.
activities.tagline: A holiday red-light-green-light: freeze when the reindeer nose turns red.

variations.easier: Play walking speed only.
variations.harder: Add a yellow nose: hop on one foot.

materials.item: a jingle-bell hat or headband for the seeker

activities.name: Winter Hide and Seek
activities.safety: Set hiding boundaries before the first round; no hiding in locked rooms, closets that latch, or outside the boundary.
activities.setup: Walk the play area together and agree on the boundary lines and home base.
steps: One seeker puts on the jingle hat and counts to 30 at home base.
Everyone else hides inside the boundary.
The seeker searches. The jingle bell gives them away if they move.
First person found becomes the next seeker.
Play three rounds and crown the best hiding spot.
activities.tagline: Classic hide and seek with a snowy twist: the seeker wears the jingle hat.

variations.easier: The seeker counts to 60 for more hiding time.
variations.harder: Sardines style: everyone squeezes into one hiding spot.

activities.name: Dice Fitness Roll

photo.alt: A blue twenty-sided die resting in a dice tray with other dice around it
photo.caption: The roll decides: a game die at rest after landing its number.
photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Sarah Spadie, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Keep spacing so arms do not hit neighbors; low-impact swaps always allowed.
activities.setup: Clear a little floor space. Assign each number 1-6 a move on the board.
steps: Assign moves: 1 = jumping jacks, 2 = squats, 3 = arm circles, 4 = high knees, 5 = toe touches, 6 = teacher's choice.
A kid rolls the dice and calls the number. Everyone does that many of the matching move.
Keep rolling for five minutes, new roller each throw.
Last round: the roller picks any two numbers and combines the moves.
activities.tagline: Roll the dice, do the moves, a different workout every throw.

variations.easier: Roll once and do the moves seated or marching in place.
variations.harder: Roll twice and add the numbers. That is your rep count.

activities.name: Squat and Spell
activities.safety: Knees track over toes; anyone can do half-squats.
activities.setup: Everyone stands with room to squat.
steps: Teacher demos: say your name out loud, one squat per letter. 'M-A-Y-A' is four squats.
Go around the circle: each kid squats through their own name while the group counts the letters.
Round two: spell a vocabulary word from this week instead of names.
Finish: the longest name in the room leads one final group squat-spell.
activities.tagline: Spell your name with your legs, one squat per letter.

variations.easier: Do it as toe-touches or marching in place instead of squats.
variations.harder: Spell it backwards, one squat per letter, no peeking at the spelling.

activities.name: Mirror March
activities.safety: Keep the arm's-length gap so nobody bumps elbows.
activities.setup: Pair up facing each other with an arm's length between partners.
steps: Partner A marches in place with big arm swings; Partner B mirrors every move exactly.
After one minute, the teacher calls 'switch', B leads, A mirrors.
Round three: leaders add a silly move every ten seconds for the mirror to catch.
End with both partners inventing a three-move mirror routine and showing the room.
activities.tagline: Copy your partner's march exactly, then steal the lead.

variations.easier: Mirror only the arms while marching gently in place.
variations.harder: No talking. The switch happens on a silent hand signal from the teacher.

activities.name: Beat the Bell Burst
activities.safety: Good form beats fast reps; stop if anything hurts.
activities.setup: Pick three moves before you start: one legs, one arms, one full-body.
steps: Set the timer for 60 seconds. Everyone does move one, as many good reps as they can.
Thirty seconds of rest and water. Set the timer again for move two.
Repeat for move three. Each round, try to beat your own count from last time. Nobody else's.
Cool down: walk it out for one minute while the teacher calls the high counts.
activities.tagline: Three 60-second movement bursts against the timer.

variations.easier: Thirty-second rounds instead of sixty; march in place between rounds.
variations.harder: Combine all three moves into one 60-second circuit, no rest between.

activities.name: Clock Lunges
activities.safety: Keep the front knee behind the toes; small steps are fine.
activities.setup: Everyone stands in their own spot with room to step forward.
steps: Imagine a clock face on the floor around you: 12 straight ahead, 6 behind.
Teacher calls numbers: '3!', lunge sideways to 3 o'clock, then back to center.
Call faster: mix 12, 4, 8, 2. Hold each lunge for two breaths.
Final round: kids take turns calling the numbers for the group.
activities.tagline: Lunge around an imaginary clock face, twelve numbers, twelve lunges.

variations.easier: Step-touches to each number instead of full lunges.
variations.harder: Add the time math: 'half past the number' means lunge halfway between two hours.

activities.name: Popcorn Pops

photo.alt: 202108009 FNS UNC
photo.caption: 202108009 FNS UNC.
photo.credit: Photo: USDAgov, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Land soft with bent knees; keep spacing on the pop.
activities.setup: Everyone crouches low with space around them.
steps: Teacher assigns each kid a popcorn word: 'butter,' 'salt,' 'caramel,' 'cheese.'
Teacher calls words in any order. When you hear yours, pop up high with arms up, then crouch again.
Speed up the calls until the whole room is popping like a hot pan.
Last round: kids call the words for each other.
activities.tagline: Crouch low like a kernel. Pop high when your word is called.

variations.easier: Stand and do a big stretch up instead of jumping.
variations.harder: Two words per kid, pop on either one.

activities.name: Traffic Cop
activities.safety: Jog in place means feet stay under you, no traveling across the room.
activities.setup: Everyone spreads out. One volunteer is the traffic cop up front.
steps: Cop's signals: arms up = jog in place, arms out wide = freeze, spin finger = turn around once.
Practice each signal together until the room responds instantly.
Play: the cop mixes signals fast for two minutes. Slow responders do a silly bow.
New cop takes over, the old cop picks them.
activities.tagline: One kid directs the room's traffic. Jog, freeze, or turn.

variations.easier: Walk in place instead of jogging; only two signals.
variations.harder: Add a fourth signal: both hands on head = crouch low.

activities.name: Zip Zap Zop
activities.safety: Point with an open hand, not a jab. Keep it playful.
activities.setup: Stand in a circle. One player starts with hands together, pointed at someone.
steps: The starter points and says 'ZIP!' The pointed-to player points at someone else: 'ZAP!'
Third player points and says 'ZOP!', then the cycle restarts at ZIP.
Anyone who says the wrong word or hesitates too long does a bow and the game restarts.
Speed up each round until the circle is a blur of zips, zaps, and zops.
activities.tagline: Point, pass the energy, and do not break the chain.

variations.easier: Allow a three-second pause; the group chants the next word as a hint.
variations.harder: Add a rule: you cannot point back at the person who just pointed at you.

activities.name: Alphabet Lineup
activities.safety: Walk, do not shove, while sorting. Keep hands to yourself.
activities.setup: Everyone stands in a loose group. No talking from this point on.
steps: Without speaking, arrange yourselves in one line from A to Z by first name.
Use gestures, finger-spelling in the air, or pointing to sort it out.
When the line looks right, everyone says their name down the line to check.
Time it. Then try to beat your time sorting by last name.
activities.tagline: No talking: line up A to Z by first name.

variations.easier: Talking allowed. The challenge is just the sorting.
variations.harder: Sort by middle name, or by birthday within the same first letter.

activities.name: Word Ball Toss
activities.safety: Mime the throw gently, no real throwing, no lunging.
activities.setup: Stand in a circle. Teacher names a category: animals, foods, colors.
steps: The starter mimes throwing a ball to someone while saying a category word: 'Elephant!'
The catcher says a new word and throws to someone else: 'Giraffe!'
No repeats. A repeated word means you do a victory spin and the game continues.
New category each round; let a kid pick the category.
activities.tagline: Toss an invisible ball, catch it with a word from the category.

variations.easier: Repeats allowed for younger kids. The toss is the fun part.
variations.harder: Two invisible balls in play at once.

activities.name: Two-Minute Mingle
activities.safety: Keep voices at conversation level. Mingles get loud.
activities.setup: Pair up. Each pair gets one question from the teacher.
steps: Round one: 60 seconds. 'What is something you are good at?' Take turns, 30 seconds each.
Rotate: find a new partner. Round two: 'What is the best thing you ate this week?'
Come back to the circle. Introduce your round-two partner and share their answer.
The group votes on the most surprising answer, winner picks the next mingle question.
activities.tagline: Sixty-second chats, two rotations, then introduce your partner.

variations.easier: One round only, with the teacher asking the question to the whole circle.
variations.harder: No repeats: your partner's answer cannot match anyone else's introduction.

activities.name: Secret High-Five
activities.safety: Walk, do not run, to your person, watch for crossing paths.
activities.setup: Everyone stands spread out. On the teacher's signal, each kid silently picks one person across the room.
steps: Point at your person in your head only, no pointing fingers, no telling.
Teacher counts down: 3, 2, 1, everyone walks to their person for a high-five.
The room becomes a happy traffic jam of crossing paths and high-fives.
Go again with a new secret person. Try to pick someone you have not high-fived yet.
activities.tagline: Pick someone across the room in secret, then cross and high-five at once.

variations.easier: Pick someone close by instead of across the room.
variations.harder: Add a secret handshake you invent on the spot with your person.

activities.name: Pass the Face
activities.safety: Silly faces only, nothing that mocks anyone.
activities.setup: Sit or stand in a circle where everyone can see each face.
steps: The starter makes a silly face at the person next to them.
That person copies the face exactly, turns to the next person, and changes it into a new silly face.
The face morphs around the circle. Watch it get weirder every pass.
Full circle: the last face comes back to the starter. Everyone votes on the silliest face.
activities.tagline: Copy the silly face, change it, pass it on.

variations.easier: Just copy without changing. The copying is the game.
variations.harder: Add a sound effect to every face.

activities.name: Guess the Leader
activities.safety: Moves stay small and seated-friendly if space is tight.
activities.setup: One volunteer leaves the room or covers their eyes. The group silently picks a leader.
steps: The guesser returns to the middle. The leader starts a simple repeating move, clapping, head nods.
Everyone copies the leader's move. The leader changes moves every few seconds; the room follows.
The guesser gets three guesses to name the leader. The room keeps copying without giving it away.
New guesser, new secret leader. Play again.
activities.tagline: One guesser, one secret leader. The whole room copies the moves.

variations.easier: The leader stays in one spot so the guesser can scan the room.
variations.harder: The leader changes moves only when the guesser blinks or looks away.

activities.name: Rhythm Echo Clap
activities.safety: Clap at medium volume, protect ears in small rooms.
activities.setup: Everyone seated or standing with hands free.
steps: Teacher claps a short pattern: clap-clap, pause, clap. The room echoes it back.
Make patterns longer and trickier each round. Add stomps and snaps.
A volunteer becomes the leader and invents the pattern; the room echoes.
Final round: chain three kids' patterns together into one long echo.
activities.tagline: The teacher claps it, the room claps it back, then a kid leads.

variations.easier: Echo with just two claps at a time.
variations.harder: Echo it backwards.

activities.name: Body Percussion Build-Up
activities.safety: Stomp lightly. Floors and downstairs neighbors count.
activities.setup: Stand in a circle. Teacher keeps a steady count: 1-2-3-4.
steps: Everyone stomps on beat 1 only. Keep it going. That is layer one.
Add claps on beat 2. Then thigh-pats on beat 3. Then finger snaps on beat 4.
Run the full four-layer groove for one minute, listen to the room lock in.
Split the circle: half does beats 1 and 3, half does 2 and 4. Trade parts.
activities.tagline: Layer stomp, clap, snap, and pat into a four-part groove.

variations.easier: Two layers only: stomp and clap.
variations.harder: One kid solos an 8-beat pattern over the group's groove.

activities.name: Volume Dial Chant
activities.safety: Full voice, never screaming. The dial stops before it hurts.
activities.setup: Pick a short chant everyone knows, a class motto, a counting rhyme, a name cheer.
steps: Teacher is the volume dial: hand low = whisper the chant, hand high = full voice.
Run the chant while the teacher slowly raises and lowers the hand.
Freeze the dial halfway. Hold the chant at medium volume for a full round.
A kid becomes the dial. The room follows their hand exactly.
activities.tagline: One chant, whispered to shouted and back. You control the dial.

variations.easier: Just two levels: whisper and normal voice.
variations.harder: The dial moves fast. The room has to track sudden jumps.

activities.name: Hum Line Guess
activities.safety: Keep volume friendly, humming, not belting.
activities.setup: No materials. Agree on fair game: songs everyone in the room would know.
steps: One volunteer hums the melody of a well-known song, no words, no hints.
The room calls out guesses. First right guess becomes the next hummer.
Keep a running list of guessed songs on the board.
Lightning round: 20 seconds per hum, as many songs as you can name.
activities.tagline: Hum the tune, hide the words. The room names that song.

variations.easier: Hum with the group humming along once someone guesses it.
variations.harder: Hum it backwards, melody in reverse.

activities.name: Silent Beat March
activities.safety: March in place. Feet stay under shoulders, no traveling.
activities.setup: Everyone stands with room to march in place.
steps: Teacher raises a hand and starts pulsing it up and down. That is the beat. Everyone marches in place to it.
Teacher speeds up and slows down the hand. The room's feet follow exactly.
Fist in the air = freeze mid-step. Open hand = march again.
A volunteer takes the beat. Try to trick the room with a sudden tempo change.
activities.tagline: No music, no counting. March to the teacher's silent hand beat.

variations.easier: Seated version: tap knees to the silent beat instead of marching.
variations.harder: Half the room marches the beat while the other half claps double-time.

activities.name: Silent Count to Twenty
activities.safety: None needed. This is a still, seated game.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle, eyes closed. No planning who goes when.
steps: The group counts to 20 together, but only one person may say each number.
If two voices overlap, everyone takes a breath and starts back at one.
No signals, no pointing. Listen for the tiny pause that means it is your turn.
When you reach 20, open your eyes. Try it again and beat your restart count.
activities.tagline: Eyes closed, one voice at a time, if two speak, start over.

variations.easier: Count to 10 instead of 20.
variations.harder: Count backwards from 20 to 1.

activities.name: Rose, Thorn, Bud
activities.safety: Sharing is always optional. 'Pass' is a complete answer.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle. Teacher explains: rose = something good, thorn = something hard, bud = something coming.
steps: Everyone gets 30 seconds of silent thinking to pick their three.
Go around the circle: each person shares their rose, thorn, and bud in one breath.
No fixing anyone's thorn, just listen. Nods are enough.
End with the teacher naming one bud for the whole group.
activities.tagline: One good thing, one hard thing, one thing you are looking forward to.

variations.easier: Just rose and bud, skip the thorn.
variations.harder: Write them down first, then share, compare what changed.

activities.name: One-Word Weather Report
activities.safety: All weather is welcome, no fixing, no judging.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle. No wrong answers. Weather is weather.
steps: Teacher starts: 'My energy weather today is partly cloudy with a chance of giggles.'
Go around: each person reports their energy as weather in a few words.
Notice the room's forecast, lots of sunshine? A storm front moving in?
Close: everyone names one thing that could clear their skies today.
activities.tagline: If your energy were weather today, what would it be?

variations.easier: Just the weather word, no explanation needed.
variations.harder: Report the weather you WANT by the end of the day, and one step toward it.

activities.name: Tense and Release
activities.safety: Tight means firm, not painful, ease off if anything aches.
activities.setup: Sit comfortably with feet flat and hands in laps.
steps: Squeeze both fists as tight as you can for five slow counts.
Release. Notice the warm, tingly feeling in your hands.
Shoulders up to your ears, hold five counts, drop them.
Finish: scrunch your whole face tight, then let it melt into a soft smile.
activities.tagline: Squeeze everything tight. Then let it all go.

variations.easier: Just the fists, squeeze and release three times.
variations.harder: Work down the body: fists, shoulders, belly, toes.

activities.name: Crumple and Toss
activities.safety: Nobody reads anyone else's paper. Toss means private.
activities.setup: Everyone gets a scrap of paper and a pencil. Put a bin or box in the middle.
steps: Write or draw one worry or annoyance from today. One or two words is enough.
Crumple the paper into the tightest ball you can.
On the count of three, everyone tosses their worry-ball into the bin.
Sit for 30 quiet seconds. Notice how the room feels lighter.
activities.tagline: Write the worry, crumple the paper, toss it in the bin.

variations.easier: Draw the worry instead of writing it. Scribbles count.
variations.harder: On the back, write one thing you will do about it, toss only the front.

activities.name: Hand Squeeze Pass
activities.safety: Gentle squeezes only. Firm enough to feel, never hard.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle holding hands, eyes closed.
steps: Teacher squeezes the hand of the person to their right. That is the signal.
Each person passes one gentle squeeze to the next hand. No talking, eyes closed.
Time how long the squeeze takes to travel the full circle.
Try to beat your time. Then try it with two squeezes going opposite directions.
activities.tagline: One silent squeeze travels the whole circle, eyes closed.

variations.easier: Eyes open for the first round.
variations.harder: Pass a pattern: squeeze-squeeze-pause, and the next person must copy it.

activities.name: Gratitude Minute
activities.safety: Small gratitudes count double, a warm drink, a good song, dry socks.
activities.setup: Everyone sits comfortably. Teacher sets a timer for 60 seconds.
steps: Timer starts: 60 seconds of silence. Think of three good things from today. Small counts.
When the timer dings, everyone opens their eyes.
Go around fast: each person shares just ONE of their three.
End together: the whole room says 'thank you' to the day, out loud, once.
activities.tagline: Sixty silent seconds, three good things, then share one.

variations.easier: Thirty seconds and one good thing.
variations.harder: The shared one cannot be something anyone else already said.

activities.name: Finger Count Breathing
activities.safety: Slow and easy. Never hold your breath until it feels uncomfortable.
