activities.setup: Hold one hand up, fingers spread. Breathe normally to start.
steps: Touch your thumb to your pointer finger. Breathe in slowly through your nose.
Move to the middle finger, breathe out slowly through your mouth.
Keep going: ring finger in, pinky out. That is one round.
Do three full rounds, slower each time. Notice your shoulders drop.
activities.tagline: Touch thumb to each fingertip, one slow breath per touch.

variations.easier: Just pointer and middle finger, in, out, done.
variations.harder: Close your eyes and count ten full rounds without losing your place.

activities.name: Silent Sketch Minute
activities.safety: This is sketching, not art class. No judging anyone's drawing.
activities.setup: Everyone gets paper and crayons. Teacher sets a timer for three minutes.
steps: Think of your favorite moment from today, the funniest, kindest, or proudest.
Three silent minutes: draw it. Stick figures welcome, masterpieces optional.
When the timer dings, pencils down, even mid-line.
Pair up and show your sketch: 30 seconds each to explain it.
activities.tagline: Three silent minutes: draw today's favorite moment.

variations.easier: Draw with your non-dominant hand. Everyone's art matches.
variations.harder: No lifting the crayon: one continuous line for the whole sketch.

materials.item: a ball of yarn or string

activities.name: Appreciation Web
activities.safety: Toss underhand and gentle, aim for hands, not faces.
activities.setup: Stand in a circle. One person holds the yarn ball.
steps: The holder names something they appreciate about the person across from them, holds the yarn end, and tosses the ball to them.
The catcher holds their bit of yarn, names an appreciation for someone else, and tosses.
Keep going until everyone holds a strand, a web stretches across the circle.
Gently lift the web together, then carefully pass the ball back to wind it up.
activities.tagline: Toss the yarn, name an appreciation. Watch the web grow.

variations.easier: Appreciations can be about the whole group, not one person.
variations.harder: Each appreciation must name something specific the person DID this week.

activities.name: Human Machine
activities.safety: Parts connect with air space between, no climbing on each other.
activities.setup: Stand in a circle with room to move arms.
steps: One volunteer starts: pick a repeating motion and sound, a piston arm going 'pssh.'
The next person connects to them with their own motion and sound, a gear turning, 'click-click.'
Keep adding parts until everyone is connected into one wild machine.
Run the machine for 30 seconds. Then the teacher calls 'slow motion', the machine winds down.
activities.tagline: Every person is one moving part. Together you are a machine.

variations.easier: Just three parts: start a tiny machine with three volunteers.
variations.harder: The machine has to 'make' something, act out what it produces.

activities.name: Helping Hands Pledge
activities.safety: Pledges are promises to the group. Keep them kind and keepable.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle. Teacher starts with their own pledge.
steps: Each person names one specific, doable way they will help the class this week.
Keep it small and real: 'I will stack the chairs,' 'I will help Sam with spelling.'
Go around fast, one sentence each, no discussion.
Teacher writes the pledges on the board. Revisit at week's end: who kept theirs?
activities.tagline: Name one way you will help the class this week. Then do it.

variations.easier: Pledge as table groups instead of individuals.
variations.harder: Pledges must help a specific person, named out loud.

activities.name: Shout-Out Sixty
activities.safety: Shout-outs lift people up, kind words only.
activities.setup: Teacher at the board with a marker. Timer set for 60 seconds.
steps: Timer starts: call out shout-outs as fast as you can, 'Shout-out to Priya for sharing her markers!'
Teacher scribes every one on the board, rapid-fire.
When the timer dings, read the whole list back together.
Leave the list up all day, the wall of shout-outs.
activities.tagline: Sixty seconds of rapid-fire shout-outs, teacher scribes them all.

variations.easier: Shout-outs can be for the whole class, not individuals.
variations.harder: Every shout-out must name something specific from TODAY.

activities.name: Circle of Strength
activities.safety: Echo exactly what they said, no upgrades, no jokes.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle. Teacher frames it: strengths are not bragging. They are inventory.
steps: Each person names one strength they bring to the group: 'I am good at staying calm,' 'I notice details.'
The group echoes it back: 'Maya stays calm!'
Go around the full circle. Everyone gets echoed.
Close: teacher names the team's combined superpower from what they heard.
activities.tagline: Name one strength YOU bring to this team.

variations.easier: Strengths can be simple: 'I am funny,' 'I am on time.'
variations.harder: Name a strength AND one way you will use it this week.

activities.name: Word of the Day Vote
activities.safety: All nominated words must be kind. The teacher can veto.
activities.setup: No materials. Just voices and a show of hands.
steps: Teacher asks: 'What one word should guide us today?' Take three nominations.
Each nominator defends their word in one sentence.
Vote by show of hands. The winner is today's word.
Write it on the board. Catch each other living it. Call it out when you see it.
activities.tagline: Nominate it, vote it, live it, one word for the whole day.

variations.easier: Teacher picks three words; the group just votes.
variations.harder: The word must be one nobody has used before this month.

activities.name: Window Weather Sketch
activities.safety: Stay inside. This is a watch-the-weather activity, not a go-into-it one.
activities.setup: Everyone gets paper and a pencil near a window view of the sky.
steps: Look out for 30 seconds without drawing, really see the sky.
Sketch what you see: clouds, rain lines, light, movement. Fast and loose.
Add three labels: what you see, what you hear, what the air feels like.
Pair up and compare skies, same window, different drawings.
activities.tagline: Five minutes, one window, the whole sky.

variations.easier: Just the drawing, skip the labels.
variations.harder: Sketch the same window again tomorrow and spot three differences.

activities.name: Indoor Picnic Memory
activities.safety: Imaginary food only, no real snacks needed.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle on the floor, picnic style.
steps: First player: 'We are having a picnic and I am bringing apples.'
Next player repeats the list and adds one: '...apples and cheese.'
Keep building the picnic list around the circle.
If you forget an item, the group chants it back to you. Nobody is out, the picnic just grows.
activities.tagline: We are having a picnic, and I am bringing... can you remember it all?

variations.easier: Keep the list short: restart after eight items.
variations.harder: Alphabetical picnic: each item must start with the next letter.

materials.item: a shallow bin or tray of water

activities.name: Paper Boat Race

photo.alt: Barche Paper Rapid Race
photo.caption: Barche Paper Rapid Race.
photo.credit: Photo: Kazelsama, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Water stays in the bin, towels nearby for splashes.
activities.setup: Everyone gets one sheet of paper. The water bin sits in the middle.
steps: Fold a simple paper boat, teacher demos the five folds slowly, once.
Set a 3-minute timer: finish your boat before it dings.
Line the boats up at one end of the bin. On 'go,' blow them across, no touching.
First boat to touch the far side wins. Race again with the losers' bracket.
activities.tagline: Fold it fast, float it fast, whose boat crosses first?

variations.easier: Teacher pre-folds the tricky steps; kids finish the easy folds.
variations.harder: One redesign round: change one fold and race again.

activities.name: Shadow Guess

photo.alt: Chimera hand shadow Flickr muffinn
photo.caption: Chimera hand shadow Flickr muffinn.
photo.credit: Photo: Mike Finn from Worcester, United Kingdom, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Hands only, no whole-body shadows that block the light for everyone.
activities.setup: One lamp or bright light aimed at a blank wall. Lights low.
steps: One volunteer stands between the light and the wall, back to the group.
They shape their hands into an animal or object. The shadow lands big on the wall.
The group calls out guesses. First right guess becomes the next shadow-maker.
Lightning round: 30 seconds per shadow, as many guesses as you can.
activities.tagline: Hands on the wall, shadows on the wall, guess the shape.

variations.easier: The shadow-maker announces the category: animal, food, or thing.
variations.harder: Two-person shadows: build the shape together.

activities.name: Puddle Poetry
activities.safety: Poems are gifts, listen like it matters.
activities.setup: Everyone gets a paper scrap and pencil. Listen to the rain for 30 seconds first.
steps: Listen to the rain, or imagine it, for 30 quiet seconds.
Write two lines about it. They do not have to rhyme.
Volunteers read theirs aloud. Snap instead of clapping.
Collect the poems on the board, the class rain anthology.
activities.tagline: Two lines about the rain. That is a whole poem.

variations.easier: One line is a complete poem.
variations.harder: Both lines must include a sound word: pitter, splash, drum.

activities.name: Chalk Number Dash
activities.safety: Watch for other dashers, slow down near the numbers.
activities.setup: Write big numbers 1-20 scattered on the pavement with chalk.
steps: Teacher calls a math question: 'What is 7 plus 5?'
Kids dash to the chalk number that answers it and stand on it.
Check: everyone on 12 does a victory jump.
New caller each round, a kid picks the next question.
activities.tagline: Teacher calls the math. Dash to the chalk answer.

variations.easier: Teacher points to numbers; kids just dash to the named one.
variations.harder: Two-step problems: '8 plus 4 minus 2.'

activities.name: Bird Call Count

photo.alt: A group of men stand birdwatching
photo.caption: A group of men stand birdwatching.
photo.credit: Photo: Ryan Hagerty, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Stay in the agreed boundaries, listening ears, watching feet.
activities.setup: Find a sitting spot outside. Agree on silence before you start.
steps: Settle in. For three minutes, just listen.
Count every bird call you hear, on your fingers, silently.
When time is up, compare counts. Why are they different?
Try again: this time, notice which direction the calls come from.
activities.tagline: Three silent minutes. How many bird calls can you count?

variations.easier: Just listen for one minute, no counting.
variations.harder: Tally different TYPES of calls separately: chirps, caws, songs.

activities.name: Stick Shape Sprint
activities.safety: Fallen sticks only, and sticks stay low, never waved around.
activities.setup: Set boundaries for stick collecting. No breaking branches, fallen sticks only.
steps: Two minutes: collect fallen sticks, as many as you can carry.
Teacher calls a shape: 'Triangle!' Build it with your sticks on the ground.
New shape every minute: square, star, the first letter of your name.
Gallery walk: tour everyone's shapes before the timer dings.
activities.tagline: Five minutes, found sticks, three shapes. Go.

variations.easier: Build any shape you want. Free build for five minutes.
variations.harder: Shapes must use exactly ten sticks.

activities.name: Cloud Drift Race

photo.alt: A boy lying in the grass with his hands behind his head, watching the clouds
photo.caption: Cloud watching: lie back, pick your cloud, and watch it drift.
photo.credit: Photo: Josephine Bruce, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Sun check: do not stare near the sun, pick clouds away from it.
activities.setup: Lie back or sit where everyone can see the same patch of sky.
steps: Everyone picks one cloud and points at it.
Predict: which way will it drift in three minutes? Point where you think it will go.
Watch in silence for three minutes.
Closest prediction wins, winner picks the next cloud.
activities.tagline: Pick a cloud, predict its drift, three minutes to be right.

variations.easier: Just watch the clouds drift, no predictions.
variations.harder: Predict AND name the cloud's shape at the start and end.

activities.name: Leaf Catch
activities.safety: Stay clear of the trunk and low branches while watching the sky.
activities.setup: Stand under or near a tree on a breezy day. Hands ready.
steps: Watch the tree. When a leaf lets go, catch it before it touches the ground.
One point per caught leaf. Dropped leaves do not count.
Two minutes of catching. Count your points.
Winner demonstrates their catching stance for the group.
activities.tagline: Catch a falling leaf before it lands. Harder than it looks.

variations.easier: Catch leaves a partner tosses gently in the air.
variations.harder: Catch with one hand only, or with your non-dominant hand.

activities.name: Origami Corner Bookmark

photo.alt: White origami figures on a table: a plane, a bird, a frog and a crane
photo.caption: One sheet, many animals: folded origami figures ready to inspire the next fold.
photo.credit: Photo: ManuelJünior7000, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Scissors cut paper only. Carry them closed and pointed down.
activities.setup: Everyone gets a paper square, cut from a sheet if needed.
steps: Fold the square corner-to-corner into a triangle.
Fold the two bottom corners up to the top point, crease hard.
Tuck those flaps into the pocket that formed. That is the bookmark.
Decorate the front with markers. It slides onto any page corner.
activities.tagline: Three folds and your book has a new corner pocket.

variations.easier: Teacher pre-folds step one; kids do the rest.
variations.harder: Fold a second one and decorate it as a gift.

activities.name: Accordion Paper Fan

photo.alt: A painted paper folding fan in a museum case
photo.caption: A painted paper folding fan in a museum case.
photo.credit: Photo: Rept0n1x, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Crease with your nail, not your teeth.
activities.setup: Everyone gets a sheet of paper. Decorate FIRST. It is easier flat.
steps: Decorate your paper however you like, both sides.
Fold it accordion-style: forward, back, forward, back, one-inch folds.
Pinch one end tight and tape it. That is the handle.
Fan the other end open and wave. Test whose fan moves the most air.
activities.tagline: Fold, pinch, wave, a working fan in five minutes.

variations.easier: Wider folds. Fewer folds to make.
variations.harder: Two papers taped together for a giant fan.

activities.name: Paper Cup Telephones

photo.alt: HKMH 香港玩具傳奇 Legend of Hong Kong Toys 香港歷史博物館 HK Museum of History March 2017 IX1 paper cup telephone
photo.caption: HKMH 香港玩具傳奇 Legend of Hong Kong Toys 香港歷史博物館 HK Museum of History March 2017 IX1 paper cup telephone.
photo.credit: Photo: DAIMANdald, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Keep the string taut but gentle, no yanking cups toward faces.
activities.setup: Pair up. Each pair gets two cups and a length of yarn.
steps: Poke a small hole in the bottom of each cup. Teacher helps the poke.
Thread the yarn through both holes and knot each end inside its cup.
Partners walk apart until the string is tight. One talks, one listens.
Whisper a secret message. Did it come through? Trade roles and try again.
activities.tagline: The classic: two cups, one string, real voices.

variations.easier: Teacher pre-pokes all the holes.
variations.harder: Try it with a slack string. What changes? That is the science.

activities.name: Mini-Me Flag
activities.safety: Markers stay on paper, caps back on when you pause.
activities.setup: Everyone gets paper and markers. No wrong flags.
steps: Draw a flag shape, rectangle, triangle, any shape.
Fill it with three things that represent you: a color, a symbol, an animal.
Add one word on your flag. Your motto, your name, your power.
Flag parade: hold them high and march once around the room.
activities.tagline: Design a flag that flies for exactly one person: you.

variations.easier: Just colors and one symbol. Keep it simple.
variations.harder: Design a flag for your whole table group. Everyone must agree.

activities.name: Gratitude Chain
activities.safety: Tape tears, do not bite it, and watch fingers with the dispenser.
activities.setup: Cut paper into strips ahead of time, or have kids tear them.
steps: Write one thank-you on a strip: a person, a thing, a moment.
Loop your strip into a ring and tape it shut.
Link your ring through a classmate's ring. The chain grows.
Hang the finished chain where everyone can see it all week.
activities.tagline: One link per thank-you. Watch the class chain grow.

variations.easier: Draw the thank-you instead of writing it.
variations.harder: Every link must thank a different person. No repeats until everyone is named.

activities.name: Shadow Size Test

photo.alt: Children making shadows2
photo.caption: Children making shadows2.
photo.credit: Photo: Ramjchandran, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Do not stare into the lamp, watch the wall.
activities.setup: One lamp or bright light aimed at a blank wall. Lights low.
steps: Hold your hand close to the wall. Look at the small, sharp shadow.
Slowly move your hand toward the light. Watch the shadow grow and blur.
Move it back. Small and sharp again.
Ask the room: why does closer to the light mean bigger shadow? Take three theories.
activities.tagline: Move your hand closer, watch the shadow grow. Why?

variations.easier: Just play with the sizes, no theories needed.
variations.harder: Predict the size before you move: 'halfway to the light means...?'

activities.name: Gravity Drop Race
activities.safety: Drop from shoulder height, no climbing for extra altitude.
activities.setup: Everyone gets two sheets of paper. Stand on chairs only if the teacher says so. Floor is fine.
steps: Crumple one sheet into a tight ball. Keep the other flat.
Everyone predicts: which hits the floor first?
On 'drop,' release both from the same height at the same time.
The ball wins, but WHY? Take theories, then test: flat versus loosely crumpled.
activities.tagline: Flat sheet versus crumpled ball, place your bets.

variations.easier: Just race them. The surprise is the lesson.
variations.harder: Redesign the flat sheet (fold it?) to fall faster, race again.

activities.name: Balloon Static Pickup

photo.alt: Attractive electric force between hair and balloon
photo.caption: Attractive electric force between hair and balloon.
photo.credit: Photo: MikeRun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Balloons stay away from faces, and pick up every scrap after.
activities.setup: Tear paper into tiny bits on each table. One balloon per group.
steps: Rub the balloon on your hair or sweater, ten fast rubs.
Hold it just above the paper bits. Watch them jump up and stick.
Count how many bits you can lift at once.
Test: does it still work after five minutes? What about on a sleeve versus hair?
activities.tagline: Rub the balloon, lift the paper, invisible force, visible result.

variations.easier: Just the rub-and-lift. The wow is enough.
variations.harder: Race: whose balloon holds its bits the longest?

materials.item: tape (for the start and finish lines)

activities.name: Breath Power Race
activities.safety: Blow, do not spit, and give each other breathing room.
activities.setup: Tape a start line and a finish line on each table. One paper scrap per kid.
steps: Place your scrap on the start line. Hands behind your back.
On 'go,' blow your scrap toward the finish. Steady breaths win.
First scrap across wins the heat. Losers' bracket races next.
Experiment: big fast puffs versus slow steady blowing. Which wins?
activities.tagline: No hands, blow your paper scrap across the finish line.

variations.easier: Shorter track. Move the finish line closer.
variations.harder: Blow around an obstacle: a cup sitting mid-track.

activities.name: Feel the Hum
activities.safety: Gentle humming only, no shouting into your own throat.
activities.setup: Everyone puts two fingers gently on the front of their throat.
steps: Hum a low note. Feel the slow, big buzz under your fingers.
Slide up to a high note. Feel the buzz get fast and small.
Hum your name. Feel the buzz jump with each syllable.
Ask the room: what do you think is buzzing in there? Take three theories.
activities.tagline: Hand on throat, hum high, hum low. Feel the buzz change.

variations.easier: Just hum high and low. Feel the difference.
variations.harder: Hum with your mouth closed versus open. What changes?

activities.name: Season Sort Sprint
activities.safety: Corners need space, no crashing into the walls.
activities.setup: Designate four corners: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter.
steps: Teacher calls an item: 'pumpkin!' 'sunscreen!' 'rain boots!'
Everyone dashes to the season corner it belongs to.
Tricky ones get debated: 'birthday!'. Birthdays are every season!
A kid becomes the caller. Try to stump the room.
activities.tagline: Pinecone? Swimsuit? Snowflake? Sort it into the right season, fast.

variations.easier: Caller gives a hint with each item.
variations.harder: Items must be sorted by season AND explained in one sentence.

activities.name: Weather Compare
activities.safety: Observations only, no weather-chasing.
activities.setup: No materials, just memory and the window.
steps: Look out the window for 30 seconds. Notice everything.
Name three ways today's weather differs from yesterday's.
Vote: is today better, worse, or just different?
One prediction: what will tomorrow's weather do?
activities.tagline: How is today different from yesterday? Three observations.

variations.easier: One difference is enough.
variations.harder: Track it for a week, spot the pattern.

activities.name: Season Stretch
activities.safety: Stretch gently. Growing trees do not force it.
activities.setup: Everyone stands with arm room.
steps: Spring: crouch small, then grow tall with arms reaching up.
Summer: sway side to side like a tree in a warm breeze.
Fall: let your leaves drop, arms flutter down to the ground.
Winter: curl small and still. Hold it. Then spring comes again. Grow!
activities.tagline: Grow like spring, sway like summer, drop like fall, sleep like winter.

variations.easier: Just the four poses. Hold each one.
variations.harder: Add a sound to each season.

activities.name: Celebration Circle
activities.safety: Every tradition is welcome, curiosity only, no comparisons.
activities.setup: Sit in a circle. Every family's celebrations count.
steps: Each person shares one sentence: a celebration or tradition their family enjoys.
One sentence only. The short version is the whole point.
Listen for celebrations you have never heard of.
End with the teacher naming one thing all the celebrations share.
activities.tagline: One sentence: a celebration your family loves.

variations.easier: Just name the celebration, no sentence needed.
variations.harder: Share the food, the sound, or the smell of it, one vivid detail.

activities.name: Gift Wrap Speed Round

photo.alt: Christmas preparations 1960 (JOKAMT2Ku19 2)
photo.caption: Christmas preparations 1960 (JOKAMT2Ku19 2).
photo.credit: Photo: Erkki Voutilainen, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Tape tears, do not bite. Scissors stay with the teacher if used.
activities.setup: Pairs get paper, tape, and a paper plate to wrap as their 'gift.'
steps: Three minutes on the timer: wrap your paper plate however you like.
Creativity counts more than neatness, weird folds welcome.
Parade the gifts. The room votes: neatest, funniest, most surprising.
Unwrap carefully, save the paper for the next round.
activities.tagline: Three minutes, one paper plate, judged on creativity. Go.

variations.easier: Five minutes instead of three.
variations.harder: Wrap it so the plate cannot be seen at all, no gaps.

activities.name: Thank-You Sprint
activities.safety: Kind and true, if you cannot say it kindly, pick someone else.
activities.setup: Everyone gets three paper scraps and a pencil.
steps: Think of three people you are thankful for. School counts.
Five minutes: write one thank-you note to each. Two sentences is plenty.
Fold them and write the name on the outside.
Deliver them today, or save them for the week's end.
activities.tagline: Five minutes, three thank-you notes. Who gets yours?

variations.easier: One note instead of three.
variations.harder: The notes must name something specific the person did.

activities.inclusion: Monsters can be described aloud instead of drawn; the choice-only version skips dice entirely.
activities.name: Roll-a-Monster Dice Draw
activities.safety: Dice are small - keep them on tables, not in mouths.
activities.setup: Draw a 6-column chart on the board: eyes / horns / mouth / arms / pattern / extra. Fill each column with 6 options (1 = one big eye, 6 = six tiny eyes...).
steps: Roll the dice six times - once per column - and write down each result.
Draw your monster exactly as the rolls say. No re-rolls: weird is good.
Give it a name and one silly power (shoots glitter, naps standing up).
Monster meet-and-greet: introduce yours to the table in your monster voice.
activities.tagline: Roll the dice, draw the parts: every monster comes out gloriously different.

variations.easier: Choice-only version: pick parts from the chart instead of rolling.
variations.harder: Two dice per kid - roll for each body part twice and pick the better roll.

activities.why_it_works: Pen-and-paper making beats a screen: a Sept 2026 survey of 2,501 teachers (DonorsChoose/EdWeek) found more hands-on analog work was the most-cited classroom change this year.

activities.inclusion: Respectful learning framing: we study a real holiday of remembrance; nobody dresses it up as a costume or invents new rituals.
activities.name: Marigold Paper Flowers

photo.alt: Families making Day of the Dead crafts. (14066234 f53e 478f b198 0fb8efab3069)
photo.caption: Families making Day of the Dead crafts. (14066234 f53e 478f b198 0fb8efab3069).
photo.credit: Photo: NPS Photo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Scissors stay at the table; younger kids get pre-folded fans.
activities.setup: Cut tissue into 6-inch squares, 8 sheets per flower. One pipe cleaner per flower for the stem.
steps: Stack 8 tissue squares and fold them back and forth like a fan.
Pinch the middle and twist a pipe cleaner tightly around it.
Round the fan ends with scissors - these become the petals.
Gently pull each tissue layer up toward the center, fluffing into a bloom.
While you work: marigolds (cempasuchil) guide loved ones home on Dia de los Muertos, Nov 1-2 - a real Mexican holiday of remembrance.
activities.tagline: Tissue-paper cempasuchil - learning about Dia de los Muertos through making.

variations.easier: Use 4 sheets instead of 8 and skip rounding the ends.
variations.harder: Make a full garland: tape finished flowers to a long string for the room.

materials.item: orange and black paint or markers

activities.name: Pumpkin Seed Mosaics

photo.alt: A close-up of roasted pumpkin seeds piled together
photo.caption: Roasted seeds by the handful: mosaic tiles that start as pumpkin guts.
photo.credit: Photo: Daniel Schwen, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Check the seed supply against the class allergy list - seeds are food. No tasting the craft seeds; painted seeds are not for eating.
activities.setup: Rinse and fully dry pumpkin seeds ahead of time (damp seeds won't glue). Tint half the seeds orange with paint the day before, or leave natural.
steps: Draw a big pumpkin outline on your cardboard square.
Glue seeds inside the outline, overlapping like scales - orange outside.
Fill the stem with green-tinted or natural seeds.
Add a black-seed jack-o'-lantern face: triangles for eyes, zigzag mouth.
Set flat to dry. Sign the back - gallery wall ready.
activities.tagline: Roasted seeds become jack-o'-lantern mosaics - zero-waste art from pumpkin guts.

variations.easier: Skip the face - a plain seed-filled pumpkin still looks great.
variations.harder: Sort seeds by size first and work in shaded rows, like a real mosaic artist.

materials.item: black paper party hats or cones

activities.name: Decorate-a-Witch-Hat
activities.safety: Keep small stickers away from mouths for the youngest kids.
activities.setup: Set out the decorating supplies in trays - one tray per table keeps the line moving.
steps: Claim a hat and try it on - check the fit before you decorate.
Wrap ribbon or paper strips around the base for the hat band.
Add the spooky-cute: paper bats, stars, a buckle cut from foil.
Write your witch name on the inside brim in marker.
Witch hat runway: strut, pose, and introduce your hat's magic power.
activities.tagline: Plain black hats in, runway-ready witch hats out - the costume station classic.

variations.easier: Pre-cut the paper shapes so it's stickers-and-glue only.
variations.harder: Engineer a hat that survives the playground: reinforce the cone seam.

materials.item: film canisters or small snap-lid tubes

activities.name: Ghost Rocket Fizz
activities.safety: Safety glasses on for the launcher. Everyone behind the line before the lid snaps - never point a loaded canister at anyone.
activities.setup: Work outside with a clear launch zone. Draw ghost faces on tissue squares and tape one loosely around each canister - decoration only, nothing blocking the lid.
steps: Put one spoonful of baking soda in the canister.
Pour in vinegar to about one-third full - then snap the lid on FAST.
Set the canister lid-down on the ground and step back 10 feet.
Watch: fizz builds pressure until POP - the ghost launches.
Try it again: more baking soda or more vinegar - which flies higher?
activities.tagline: Film-canister rockets in ghost costumes - chemistry does the launching.

variations.easier: The teacher does the snap-and-set while kids watch from the line.
variations.harder: Time the launches and graph height vs. spoonfuls of baking soda.

activities.name: Glow Stick Temperature Lab
activities.safety: Don't cut glow sticks open; the liquid inside stays inside. Cracked or leaking sticks go straight in the trash - wash hands after handling.
activities.setup: Fill the three cups: ice water, room-temp water, warm tap water. Label them COLD, ROOM, WARM. Crack each glow stick to activate right before the test.
steps: Drop one activated glow stick in each cup at the same time.
Dim the lights and compare: which cup glows brightest right now?
Wait 5 minutes and compare again - did the order change?
Feel the cups: the warm cup's stick fades fastest. Heat speeds the chemical reaction up - and uses it up faster.
Write the rule in your own words: warmer = brighter but shorter.
activities.tagline: Same glow sticks, three cups of water - temperature changes the light.

variations.easier: Teacher runs the demo up front while kids call out observations.
variations.harder: Add a fourth cup - freezer-cold vs. fridge-cold - and time the fade with a stopwatch.

materials.item: paper plates with the centers cut out

activities.name: Spiderweb Weight Bridge
activities.safety: Scissors at the table only. Keep yarn below shoulder height.
activities.setup: Cut the center out of each paper plate, leaving a 2-inch rim - the web frame. Tape one end of yarn to the rim.
steps: Weave yarn across the plate ring: spokes first, then spiral around them. Tie off the end.
Set your web across two books with the middle hanging free.
Add pennies one at a time to the center of the web. Count as you go.
Record the breaking point - the number of pennies your web held.
Rebuild round two: tighter spiral or double yarn - beat your record.
activities.tagline: Weave a yarn web, then load it with pennies - how strong is your silk?

variations.easier: Weave a simple 6-spoke web and test with crayons instead of pennies.
variations.harder: Real spiders vary silk thickness - test thin yarn vs. thick yarn webs.

activities.name: Vampire Teeth Acid Test
activities.safety: Vinegar is food-safe but stings eyes - no splashing, wash hands after. This is a model, not a mouth: eggshells stand in for enamel.
activities.setup: Rinse eggshell halves and label cups: VINEGAR, WATER, (MILK). One shell half per cup. Set up the day before you want results.
steps: Drop one eggshell half in each cup - these are our stand-in 'teeth.'
Predict: which liquid will change its shell the most by tomorrow?
Wait 24 hours. Lift each shell: look, feel, and compare.
The vinegar shell turns soft and bubbly - acid wears the shell down. Water barely changes it.
Connect it: that's why dentists nag about brushing - acid is the enemy.
activities.tagline: Eggshell 'fangs' soak overnight - which liquid is toughest on teeth?

variations.easier: Teacher sets up the cups; kids observe and vote on predictions.
variations.harder: Test more liquids: juice, soda, soapy water - rank them toughest to gentlest.

activities.inclusion: Riders set their own speed; walking the course counts fully.
activities.name: Witch Broomstick Relay
activities.safety: Clear the course of anything trippable. Noodles are for riding, not dueling.
activities.setup: Set two cones 30 feet apart per team. Hand each team a pool noodle 'broomstick.'
steps: First rider straddles the noodle like a broomstick - hands on the front.
Ride to the far cone, circle it, and ride back. Noodle stays between your legs the whole way.
Hand off the broomstick to the next witch in line.
Fallen off? Pick it up, climb back on, keep riding - no penalty.
Winning team takes a victory lap with their best witch cackles.
activities.tagline: Ride a pool-noodle broomstick around the cones - cackling encouraged.

variations.easier: Shorten the course and let kids walk the noodle instead of running.
variations.harder: Add a spell-casting stop: freeze at the far cone and shout your spell before riding back.

activities.why_it_works: Short active bursts reset focus - reviews of classroom brain-break research (IJRESS) find under-10-minute movement breaks counter cognitive fatigue.

activities.inclusion: A seated 'home base' role: frozen players can also be freed by a buddy calling their name from base.
activities.name: Ghost Freeze Tag
activities.safety: Tag is touch-only, never push. Play away from walls and furniture.
activities.setup: Pick 2 ghosts (taggers). Everyone else haunts the play area. No equipment needed.
steps: Ghosts chase; a touch turns you into a frozen statue - arms up, spooky face.
Unfreeze a statue by floating past and whispering 'BOO!' - then both float away.
A frozen player can't be tagged again until they're freed.
Rotate ghosts every 3 minutes so everyone gets to haunt.
Last round: EVERYONE is a ghost and the teacher is the only haunter.
activities.tagline: Tagged? Freeze like a ghost. A teammate's 'BOO!' sets you free.

variations.easier: One ghost only, and a smaller play area.
variations.harder: Frozen ghosts must freeze mid-pose from a category: animals, monsters, dancers.

activities.why_it_works: Freeze-play mixes sprinting with stillness - short movement breaks in this format are what brain-break reviews (IJRESS) link to recharged attention.

activities.name: Monster Movement Dice
activities.safety: Clear a wide circle first - flapping bats need elbow room.
activities.setup: Draw the chart on the board: 1 = zombie shuffle, 2 = bat flap, 3 = ghost glide, 4 = witch swoop, 5 = mummy march, 6 = monster's choice.
steps: Everyone stands in a circle with room to move.
Roll the big dice - the whole group moves like that monster for 30 seconds.
Roll again: new monster, new movement. Keep the energy up.
Monster's choice: the roller picks any move and everyone copies.
Cool-down roll: whatever you roll, do it in slow motion.
activities.tagline: Roll the die, move like the monster: zombie shuffle, bat flap, ghost glide.

variations.easier: Roll once and move like that monster for the whole round.
variations.harder: Kids invent moves 7-12 on a second chart for two-dice chaos.

activities.name: Zombie Walk Relay
activities.safety: Monster walks stay in the lane - no wandering zombies near other teams.
activities.setup: Mark a there-and-back lane with cones. Deal each team four monster-walk cards in order.
steps: Leg 1: the zombie shuffles to the cone and back - arms out, groaning.
Leg 2: the witch swoops - bent over, 'flying' low and fast.
Leg 3: the bat flaps - arms as wings, quick little steps.
Leg 4: the ghost glides - slow, silent, arms floating.
Tag the next monster with a high-five. Best monster walk wins the round - the team votes.
activities.tagline: Each leg is a different monster walk - zombie shuffle to ghost glide.

variations.easier: Two legs instead of four; walking pace for every monster.
variations.harder: Add a fifth mystery leg: the team invents a brand-new monster walk.

activities.inclusion: Answers can be choral; every riddle is read twice; picture clues on the board support multilingual learners.
activities.name: Halloween Inference Riddles
activities.safety: No materials, no hazards - just voices. Keep the volume neighbor-friendly during the lightning round.
activities.setup: None - read from this bank (or make your own): 1) 'I have a face but no eyes, I glow but I'm not a lamp' (jack-o'-lantern) 2) 'I fly at night but I'm not a bird, I sleep upside down' (bat) 3) 'I'm orange, I wear no costume, kids paint my grin' (pumpkin) 4) 'I say boo but I'm not scary, I'm made of an old sheet' (ghost costume).
steps: Read a riddle aloud - slowly, twice.
Hands up when you think you know it - but answers need a clue citation: 'I know because it says...'
The group decides: did the clue really prove it?
Kids take turns being the riddle-reader for the next round.
Lightning round: everyone writes one riddle of their own for tomorrow.
activities.tagline: Read the riddle, cite your clue: inference practice in a witch hat.

variations.easier: Give the answer bank up front - kids match riddles to answers.
variations.harder: No answer bank, and riddles must cite TWO clues instead of one.

activities.why_it_works: Inferring from clues is reading comprehension in disguise - and it's fully unplugged, the direction the Sept 2026 DonorsChoose/EdWeek teacher survey points.

activities.inclusion: Stamped prints need no drawing skill to start - the monster emerges from the print, not from a blank page.
activities.name: Thumbprint Monsters
activities.safety: Washable ink only. Wipe hands before touching anything else.
activities.setup: Set out ink pads and paper. Keep wet wipes in the middle of every table.
steps: Press your thumb on the ink pad, then stamp it on the paper - one print per monster.
Turn the print: which way looks most like a monster body?
Add the features with fine marker: eyes, horns, fangs, arms, spots.
Give it a name and write one sentence about what it does all day.
Gallery walk: line them up and vote - spookiest, silliest, most likely to hug.
activities.tagline: One ink thumbprint becomes a monster: add eyes, horns, and attitude.

variations.easier: Use finger-paint dots instead of ink pads for the youngest kids.
variations.harder: Thumbprint monster comic: three prints, three panels, one tiny story.

activities.why_it_works: Low-stakes making with real materials: a Sept 2026 survey of 2,501 teachers (DonorsChoose/EdWeek) found more hands-on analog work was the most-cited classroom change this year.

activities.name: Halloween Dots & Boxes
activities.safety: Pencils stay on paper - no sword fights.
activities.setup: None - each pair draws their own 5x5 dot grid. No printing needed.
steps: Draw a 5x5 grid of dots on your paper.
Take turns drawing one line between two dots - horizontal or vertical.
Complete a box and it's yours: initial it AND draw a tiny pumpkin face inside.
Most boxes wins. Ties broken by silliest pumpkin face - group vote.
Rematch round: 6x6 grid, and every box needs a different face.
activities.tagline: The pencil-and-paper classic, Halloween edition: claim boxes, draw the face.

variations.easier: 4x4 grid, and the teacher plays alongside the youngest kids.
variations.harder: Mystery grid: play on a 7x7 and track your score as a running total.

activities.inclusion: Photo-based version works for anyone who can't get to the webs; sketching needs no art skill - labels count as success.
activities.name: Spiderweb Sketch Study

photo.alt: An orb-weaver spider at the center of its dew-covered web among grass stems
photo.caption: A real web in morning dew: the spokes and spirals this sketch study slows down for.
photo.credit: Photo: Shenandoah National Park from Virginia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Look with eyes and magnifiers only - never poke a web or its spider.
activities.setup: Scout the area ahead of time for real webs - fence corners, playground equipment, bushes. Morning dew makes them easy to spot.
steps: Find a web and settle in - no touching, just looking.
Sketch what you see: the anchor lines, the spokes, the spiral. Slow is the whole point.
Label the parts: spokes (the straight lines), spiral (the sticky circle), anchor (where it ties off).
Watch for 5 quiet minutes: does the spider move? Does anything land?
Back inside: compare sketches - no two real webs match.
activities.tagline: Find a real web, sketch it slow, label the spokes: quiet science.

variations.easier: Sketch from a printed photo of a web at the table.
variations.harder: Measure your web's diameter and count the spokes - real field data.

activities.why_it_works: Slow looking is attention training: close observation and sketching give selective attention a real workout.

activities.inclusion: Dairy-free chips swap in with no recipe change; kids who can't have banana make ghost cups with the same faces.
activities.name: Ghost Banana Pops
activities.safety: Check the class allergy list first (chocolate contains milk/soy). Adults handle any sharp knives; kids use plastic table knives on the soft banana. Treats are made to take home or eat at the party - not during craft time.
activities.setup: Peel bananas and cut each in half crosswise. Set out chips in small bowls. Freeze the finished ghosts at least 2 hours before serving.
steps: Push a craft stick into the cut end of each banana half.
Press two mini chocolate chips in for eyes - and one for the mouth.
Stand the ghosts upright in a cup and freeze until solid.
Serve straight from the freezer: cold, sweet, and not remotely scary.
activities.tagline: Frozen banana ghosts on sticks - the two-ingredient Halloween treat.

variations.easier: Skip the sticks - banana ghost bites in a cup with a spoon.
variations.harder: Dip in yogurt before freezing, then add the chip faces.

activities.inclusion: Allergy-safe kids get the same job with safe ingredients - nobody sits out the assembly line.
activities.name: Monster Mix Bags
activities.safety: Check the class allergy list BEFORE buying anything - nuts, gluten, and dairy are all common in trail mix. Keep ingredient labels out so kids can read them. No double-dipping scoops.
activities.setup: Pour each ingredient into its own bowl with a scoop. Set out one bag per kid plus a marker for decorating.
steps: Decorate your bag first: monster face, your name, the works.
Scoop one scoop of each ingredient into your bag - your mix, your rules.
Add the candy corn last - it's the treasure on top.
Seal the bag with a fold and a sticker. Shake it like a maraca.
Monster mix taste test: trade one handful with a neighbor and compare.
activities.tagline: Scoop, mix, bag: every kid builds their own Halloween trail mix.

variations.easier: Teacher pre-portions the ingredients - kids just decorate and shake.
variations.harder: Write the 'recipe' on the bag: ingredient amounts as a real recipe card.

activities.inclusion: Topping bowls labeled; kids with dairy/gluten limits build from the safe bowls - same bar, same fun.

materials.item: toppings: mini chips, sprinkles, crushed pretzels

activities.name: Candy Apple Slices
activities.safety: Only an adult uses a sharp knife - apples are hard and round. Check the allergy list (milk in caramel, gluten in pretzels). Slices are eaten at the party, not saved.
activities.setup: An adult slices the apples into thick wedges just before serving so they stay crisp. Set toppings in bowls with spoons.
steps: Skewer a slice on a popsicle stick - instant handle.
Dip or drizzle with caramel - thin coat sticks best.
Roll the caramel side through your pick of toppings.
Stand slices upright on a plate: a whole candy-apple garden.
Vote: which topping combo wins the class taste test?
activities.tagline: All the caramel-apple joy, none of the whole-apple wrestling: slice bar.

variations.easier: Skip the sticks - apple slices with caramel for dipping, fork-style.
variations.harder: Blind taste test: three apple varieties, sliced - graph the class favorite.

activities.inclusion: Sherbet-free version brews alongside with juice + ginger ale only - same cauldron ritual.
activities.name: Witches' Brew Punch
activities.safety: Check the allergy list (milk in sherbet). One ladle, one server - no hands in the brew, no double-dipping cups.
activities.setup: Chill everything ahead of time. Set the 'cauldron' (punch bowl) where everyone can reach with the ladle.
steps: Pour the cider into the cauldron - two big glugs per kid, taking turns.
Add ginger ale: pour it down the side so it stays fizzy.
Scoop in sherbet - it melts into spooky green-orange swirls.
Stir three times clockwise while everyone chants the magic words.
Ladle into cups, drop in one gummy worm each, and toast the brew.
activities.tagline: No-cook punch mixing: the class brews a cauldron of something delicious.

variations.easier: Teacher mixes; kids do the chanting and the gummy-worm drop.
variations.harder: Potion lab: small cups, three juices, kids invent and name their own brew.

activities.inclusion: Every door's activity has a seated version; the class picks activities everyone can do.
activities.name: Halloween Countdown Calendar
activities.safety: Sticky notes only - no cutting doors for little kids; lift the flap.
activities.setup: Draw a 13-door grid on the poster board (or tape up 13 folded paper 'doors'). Number them 13 down to 1.
steps: Brainstorm as a class: 13 tiny Halloween activities that fit in 10 minutes - a riddle, a drawing, a chant, a stretch.
Write one activity per sticky note and hide it behind each door.
Every day from Oct 19 to Oct 31, open the next door together.
Do the mini-activity on the spot - the calendar IS the plan.
Door 1 (Oct 31): the class votes on the grand finale activity.
activities.tagline: Thirteen doors, thirteen mini-activities: the class counts down to the 31st.

variations.easier: Teacher pre-fills the doors; the class just opens and does.
variations.harder: Each table designs its own 13-day calendar for a different theme.

activities.inclusion: Passing is always fine - and anyone can borrow a monster name instead of their own.
activities.name: Monster Name Alliteration
activities.safety: Keep moves in your own space - no touching other monsters.
activities.setup: None - just a circle and imaginations.
steps: Go around the circle: each kid invents an alliterative monster name - 'Jolly Jack-o'-lantern Jamal,' 'Silly Spider Sofia.'
Say it with a monster move - a stomp, a flap, a wiggle.
The whole circle repeats each name back WITH the move.
Round two: string them into a monster roll-call chant, faster each time.
Finale: the class votes for the most marvelous monster name.
activities.tagline: 'Marvelous Mummy Maya' - alliterative monster names around the circle.

variations.easier: Kids can pick a monster name instead of using their own name.
variations.harder: Write the names on the board as they go - read the roll call tomorrow.

activities.inclusion: Kids without costumes describe an imaginary one - imagination counts the same as fabric.
activities.name: Costume Guess Who
activities.safety: Imaginary costumes count fully - nobody needs a real costume to play.
activities.setup: None. Kids with costumes wear them; kids without describe an imaginary one.
steps: One volunteer stands up front - costume on, or imaginary costume described.
The class asks yes-or-no questions only: 'Are you an animal?' 'Do you fly?'
The volunteer answers truthfully - yes, no, or 'sort of.'
Twenty questions max: then everyone shouts their guess together.
New volunteer, new costume. Keep a tally of stumpers vs. solvers.
activities.tagline: Twenty questions, one costume: can the class guess what you are?

variations.easier: Ten questions max, and the teacher helps phrase the first few.
variations.harder: Mystery guest round: the teacher describes a staff member's costume.

activities.name: Halloween This-or-That
activities.safety: Walking feet between sides - no charging the other team.
activities.setup: None - just room to stand on two sides.
steps: Call out a Halloween either-or: 'Candy corn: love it or leave it?' 'Scary movies or funny costumes?'
Kids move to the LOVE IT side or the LEAVE IT side - no middle.
Each side picks a spokesperson for a 10-second defense.
Switch sides if you got convinced - movers get a cheer.
Rapid round: five quick ones, no defenses, just move.
activities.tagline: Candy corn: love it or leave it? Stand on your side - then defend it.

variations.easier: Kids point instead of moving - whole game from their seats.
variations.harder: Kids write the next five questions; the teacher just reads them.

activities.inclusion: Every pattern has a seated version - stomps become knee pats.
activities.name: Monster Stomp Rhythms
activities.safety: Stomp on the floor, not on feet. Keep the volume neighbor-friendly.
activities.setup: None - bodies are the instruments.
steps: Teach the zombie pattern: STOMP-stomp-clap, STOMP-stomp-clap.
Add the witch pattern: clap-clap-STOMP-stomp - half the group takes each.
Layer them: zombies and witches perform at the same time. Listen for the groove.
Monster solo round: one kid invents a 4-beat pattern, everyone copies.
Finale: the class monster orchestra - every pattern at once, big finish.
activities.tagline: Stomp-clap patterns for every monster: learn it, layer it, perform it.

variations.easier: One pattern only, seated, hands on knees for the stomp.
variations.harder: Compose a full monster symphony: verse, chorus, and a spooky bridge.

activities.why_it_works: Rhythm plus movement in one: patterned stomping gives the wiggles a job, in the under-10-minute format brain-break research (IJRESS) ties to restored focus.

activities.name: Trick-or-Treat Chant Parade
activities.safety: Marching stays in line - no breaking formation near stairs or doors.
activities.setup: None required - voices and feet carry it.
steps: Teach the chant, call-and-response style: 'Trick or treat! (Trick or treat!) Smell my feet! (Smell my feet!)'
Add the march: step-clap-step-clap under the words.
Layer instruments if you have them: shakers on the beat, sticks on the off-beat.
Parade formation: march the hallway or playground chanting in time.
Grand finale: chant it at double speed, then freeze on the last word.
activities.tagline: A marching chant for the big night: rhythm, rhyme, and doorbell timing.

variations.easier: Chant seated in a circle - marching optional.
variations.harder: The class writes verse two: new rhymes for their own neighborhood.

activities.inclusion: Every role has a quiet version - whisperers and shakers matter as much as drummers.
activities.name: Haunted House Soundtrack
activities.safety: Found sounds stay gentle - no sudden screams near sensitive ears. Agree on the scare level first.
activities.setup: Gather instruments and found-sound makers: rice in a bottle (rain), crumpled paper (fire), a ruler on a desk edge (boing).
steps: Storyboard a 2-minute haunted house tour: the creaky gate, the dark hallway, the surprise room.
Assign sounds: each group scores one scene with instruments and voices.
Rehearse the order - scenes must flow without talking in between.
Perform it for another class: they walk the 'tour' (a taped path) while you play.
Audience rates each scene: spooky-fun or needs-more-creak? Revise once.
activities.tagline: Compose the soundscape for a haunted tour: creaks, whispers, and one big scare.

variations.easier: Score one scene instead of three; teacher narrates the tour.
variations.harder: Record the soundtrack and play it over the real haunted hallway build.

activities.inclusion: Every station has a lights-on version; tour guides ask each group's scare comfort level first.
activities.name: Haunted Hallway Build

photo.alt: Futenma Haunted Labyrinth brings service members, Okinawa residents together 150929 M PC671 607
photo.caption: Futenma Haunted Labyrinth brings service members, Okinawa residents together 150929 M PC671 607.
photo.credit: Photo: Cpl. Jessica Collins, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Nothing blocks fire exits or doors - ever. Tape, never nails. An adult checks every station before tours open.
activities.setup: Get permission for the hallway first. Assign each team one 'scare station' along the route, with a clear entrance and exit.
steps: Teams blueprint their station: silly scare, secret passage, marked exit - nothing actually scary.
Build it: black-paper walls, cardboard tunnels, flashlight spotlights.
Safety walk: every builder walks the whole route checking for trip hazards and dead ends.
Open the hallway: other classes tour in small groups with a guide.
Deconstruct together - everything sorted for reuse or recycling.
activities.tagline: Teams transform one hallway into a silly-spooky walkthrough - designed by kids.

variations.easier: One station per team in the classroom instead of a full hallway.
variations.harder: Add a storyteller guide who narrates the tour with a script.

activities.name: Costume Swap Shop
activities.safety: All costumes washed before the swap. Private trying-on space for kids who want it.
activities.setup: A week ahead: invite families to donate clean, outgrown costumes. Sort donations by size on tables.
steps: Tag every costume with its size and a one-line description.
Set up shop zones: trying-on corner, mirror station, checkout table.
Shoppers 'buy' with kindness tokens - everyone gets the same number.
Fitting-room helpers give honest, kind opinions.
Leftovers get bagged for next year or donated onward - nothing wasted.
activities.tagline: Outgrown costumes find new kids: the community swap, run like a real shop.

variations.easier: Classroom-only swap: bring one, take one, no tokens.
variations.harder: Add a repair station: simple fixes (seams, buttons) before costumes go out.

activities.name: Kindness Pumpkins

photo.alt: A big orange pumpkin at a pumpkin patch
photo.caption: A pumpkin picked for decorating and giving away to brighten someone's day.
photo.credit: Photo: inkknife_2000 (7.5 million views +), CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Paint pens, not sharp carving tools - no knives at all. Wash hands after painting; pumpkins are gifts, not snacks.
activities.setup: Cover tables with newspaper. Decide together who gets the pumpkins: neighbors, custodians, the front office.
steps: Paint each pumpkin with a kind message or a cheerful face - no scary faces on these.
Add the giver's first name on the bottom.
Plan the delivery route: pairs, with an adult, during the day.
Deliver with the message: 'Thanks for being part of our neighborhood.'
Back in class: share one reaction story each.
activities.tagline: Paint kindness pumpkins for neighbors and staff - trick-or-treat in reverse.

variations.easier: Paint paper pumpkins instead - same messages, zero cost.
variations.harder: Attach a handwritten thank-you note to every pumpkin.

materials.item: water or sand to weight bottles

activities.name: Pumpkin Bowling

photo.alt: A girl bowling down a hay-bale lane toward gourd pins, her ball rolling ahead of her
photo.caption: Pumpkin bowling on a hay-bale lane: the ball is away and the gourd pins are waiting.
photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

marks.label: The bowler: two rolls a turn
The lane: hay bales or floor tape

activities.safety: Roll, don't throw - pumpkins stay on the floor. Mop up bottle leaks fast so nobody slips.
activities.setup: Fill bottles one-third with water and cap them tight - these are the pins. Tape a lane on the floor, pins in a triangle at the end.
steps: Set the pins: 10 in a triangle, just like real bowling.
Roll (never throw) your pumpkin down the lane - two rolls per turn.
Score it: one point per pin, two turns per frame, five frames.
Reset crew: knocked pins get stood back up by the next bowler.
Championship round: winners bowl left-handed. Or blindfolded. (Not really blindfolded.)
activities.tagline: Mini pumpkins vs. bottle pins: the indoor bowling alley builds itself.

variations.easier: Bowl sitting down, shorter lane, bottles unweighted.
variations.harder: Design trick lanes: a curve of tape, a ramp made of books.

activities.name: Spiderweb Yarn Maze
activities.safety: Yarn stays below shoulder height and off necks - step over or duck under, never around. Clear path to the door stays open.
activities.setup: Pick a hallway or a big room. Tape yarn ends to walls, chairs, and door frames - crisscross at different heights. Leave one clear path per kid.
steps: Study the maze first: where's your route? Plan it before you move.
Crawl, duck, and step through - touching a strand means back to start.
Spotters watch and call 'strand!' - honest spotting keeps it fair.
Everyone who finishes gets a token - no racing, it's a challenge.
Rebuild round: the finishers design a harder maze for the next group.
activities.tagline: Crawl the yarn maze without touching a strand: the quietest challenge indoors.

variations.easier: High strands only - duck under, no crawling needed.
variations.harder: Timed runs for the brave: fastest clean run wins.

activities.inclusion: The lights-on version runs first for anyone who prefers it; passing on any stop is always fine.
activities.name: Haunted Lantern Tour
activities.safety: Warn before dimming - anyone who wants light keeps a buddy lantern. Walk, don't run, in low light; nothing blocking the path.
activities.setup: Before the tour, kids hide sticky-note 'haunts' around the room: a creaky corner, a mysterious stain, a humming vent.
steps: Dim the lights - lanterns on. Warn the group first: lights going low.
The guide leads the tour, stopping at each sticky-note haunt.
At each stop, the hider tells the haunt's silly backstory - one minute max.
Tourists rate each haunt: spooky-fun or needs-more-story?
Lights up. Vote for the best backstory - the winner guides tomorrow.
activities.tagline: Lights low, lanterns up: a guided tour of the room's 'haunted' corners.

variations.easier: Lights stay on; the 'tour' is a walk-and-tell instead.
variations.harder: Tour the whole school after hours (with permission): the ultimate edition.

activities.name: Pumpkin Patch Scavenger Hunt

photo.alt: A pumpkin patch full of ripe orange pumpkins under a cloudy sky with hills behind
photo.caption: The patch itself: something orange, something round, and a whole field to hunt through.
photo.credit: Photo: Visitor7, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Set clear boundaries before anyone moves. Look-don't-touch for webs, mushrooms, and anything unknown.
activities.setup: Write the hunt list on cards: something orange, something round like the moon, a real spider web (look, don't touch), a leaf bigger than your hand, something that crunches, the smallest pumpkin you can find.
steps: Pairs get a card, a pencil, and a bag - and the boundaries.
Find each item: check it off, or collect it if it's loose and allowed.
The spider web is look-only - sketch it instead of taking it.
Back at base: pairs show their finds and tell the story of the hardest one.
Bonus round: who found the funniest-shaped leaf? Group vote.
activities.tagline: Something orange, something round like the moon, one real spider web: go.

variations.easier: Picture cards instead of word cards for the youngest hunters.
variations.harder: Make it a photo hunt: one photo per find, compiled into a class slideshow.

activities.name: Leaf Pile Monster Dig
activities.safety: Check the pile for sticks and sharp bits before digging starts. Gloves for sensitive hands; no throwing leaves at faces.
activities.setup: Rake a big leaf pile (or visit the park's). Hide 20-30 small treasures inside while kids look away.
steps: Monster hands on: dig, toss, and burrow through the leaves.
Found treasure goes in your bucket - count as you go.
No guarding: if you see someone else's treasure spot, digging there is fair game.
Re-hide round: kids bury the treasures for the next group.
Final jump: everyone leaps in together for the group photo.
activities.tagline: Bury treasure in the leaf pile, dig like a monster: the fall sensory classic.

variations.easier: Shallow pile, treasures half-buried and visible.
variations.harder: Treasure map round: draw a map of where you hid yours, trade maps.

activities.name: Ghost Balloon Stomp
activities.safety: Pop means pieces: keep balloons away from mouths, and pick up EVERY popped piece right away - balloon pieces are a choking hazard.
activities.setup: Draw ghost faces on inflated balloons. Tie one to each kid's ankle with a foot of string - two per kid for a second life.
steps: Spread out - stomping needs space.
On GO: try to pop others' ankle ghosts by stomping them.
Guard your own: hop, dodge, hide behind friends.
Popped both? Grab a 'ghost buddy' role - you call out incoming stompers.
Last ghost floating wins the round. New balloons, new round.
activities.tagline: Ghost faces on ankles: stomp others' ghosts while guarding your own.

variations.easier: One balloon each, and stomping is walking-speed only.
variations.harder: Team version: protect your team's ghosts, hunt the other team's.

activities.name: Graveyard Number Dash
activities.safety: Dash in your own lane - no cutting across other runners. Tombstones staked flat so nobody trips.
activities.setup: Number paper tombstones 1-20 and stake them around the field, numbers facing in. Mark a start line with chalk.
steps: Everyone lines up at the start line - tombstones all around.
The caller shouts a math problem: '7 + 5!'
Dash to the tombstone with the answer and tap it - first tap wins the point.
Wrong tombstone? Back to the line, no point - but no elimination.
Caller rotates every 5 problems so everyone gets to call.
activities.tagline: Paper tombstones, called-out math: dash to the right answer.

variations.easier: Tombstones 1-10 only, and walk-dash instead of run-dash.
variations.harder: Two-step problems: 'double 6, minus 2' - dash to 10.

activities.name: Harvest Moon Journal

photo.alt: A bright full moon shining through thin night clouds
photo.caption: The harvest moon behind thin cloud: the sky journal's October subject.
photo.credit: Photo: Schyler at en.wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Moon-watching happens with families at home; in class, sketch from memory or photos. Never stare at the sun looking for the moon.
activities.setup: Draw the 8 moon phases on the board as reference. Each kid gets a journal page: one circle per night for two weeks.
steps: Each night (or each class day), sketch the moon's shape in the next circle.
Note the date and one word about the sky: clear, cloudy, hiding.
After a week, line up your circles: can you see the pattern growing?
Compare with the board chart: which phase are we in today?
Harvest moon night: the class watches together and sketches the big one.
activities.tagline: Watch the October moon change night by night: a real sky journal.

variations.easier: Track just 5 nights instead of 14.
variations.harder: Predict the next full moon's date from your journal - then check.

activities.name: Pumpkin Life Cycle Wheel

photo.alt: Yellow pumpkin flowers open among large green pumpkin vine leaves
photo.caption: The wheel's flower stage: big yellow blooms before the fruit sets.
photo.credit: Photo: Uebersbach8362, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Brass fasteners are pointy - teacher pokes the center holes.
activities.setup: Cut a wedge window out of the top plate. Kids will draw the 5 stages around the bottom plate.
steps: Draw the life cycle around the bottom plate: seed, sprout, vine, flower, green pumpkin, orange pumpkin.
Label each stage in your own words.
Fasten the plates together in the center - spin to reveal each stage through the window.
Quiz a partner: spin to a random stage, name what comes next.
Hang the wheels up: the whole class life cycle, spinning.
activities.tagline: Spin the paper-plate wheel: seed, sprout, vine, flower, pumpkin.

variations.easier: Three stages instead of five: seed, vine, pumpkin.
variations.harder: Add the real timeline: how many days does each stage take?

materials.item: small wooden beads or air-dry clay

activities.name: Acorn Cap Witches

photo.alt: Acorns on a stone surface, with one loose cap beside a small acorn still in its cup
photo.caption: The raw material: acorn caps, ready to become the tiniest witch hats.
photo.credit: Photo: Laitche, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Acorn caps are small - keep them out of mouths for the youngest kids.
activities.setup: Collect acorn caps ahead of time (or buy craft ones). Set out beads for heads and paper triangles for hats.
steps: Glue a bead into an acorn cap - the cap becomes the witch's dress.
Paint a tiny face on the bead: eyes, smile, maybe a wart.
Glue on the black paper triangle hat - every witch needs a hat.
Add a pipe-cleaner broomstick if you're feeling fancy.
Line up the coven: a whole shelf of tiny witches, none taller than your thumb.
activities.tagline: Acorn caps, paint, and pipe cleaners: the tiniest witches in the Vault.

variations.easier: Skip the broomstick; hat and face is plenty.
variations.harder: Build the whole scene: a matchbox house for your witch to haunt.

activities.name: Ornament Geometry Stars
activities.safety: Paper strips only. No scissors needed, which is the point.
activities.setup: Cut paper into 2cm-wide strips, one per kid plus a few spares. Put glue sticks in the middle of each table.
steps: Show the group the finished star first. One strip becomes five points, no cutting.
Fold the strip into a loose pentagon: five equal folds, creasing firmly each time.
Tuck the last fold through the first to close the ring, then pinch each of the five edges outward to pop the points.
Thread a short string through one point and knot it for hanging.
Gallery walk: line the stars up and spot which folds came out most even.
activities.tagline: Fold perfect five-point stars from paper strips. Geometry you can hang on a tree.

variations.easier: Pre-fold the first pentagon so kids copy the pinching step only.
variations.harder: Try seven-point stars (heptagons) or weave two strips for a double star.

materials.item: a drum or box to keep time

activities.name: Jingle Bell Rhythm Band

photo.alt: A set of sleigh bells
photo.caption: Sleigh bells ready to shake, tap, and keep the beat in the rhythm band.
photo.credit: Photo: Richard Wheeler at en.wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Bells are a choking hazard for under-3s. This one starts at 4 for a reason.
activities.setup: Thread 3-4 bells onto a pipe cleaner per kid and twist into a bracelet. Keep one drum (or overturned box) for yourself.
steps: Everyone shakes their bells freely for 30 seconds. Get the wiggles' worth out first.
Teach the core pattern: shake-shake-PAUSE-shake. You drum it, they echo it back.
Split the room: half keeps the pattern, half improvises an answer on the pause.
Build a 4-bar piece: pattern twice, answers twice, everyone together on the last bar.
Final performance for the hallway. One take, no stopping.
activities.tagline: Wristfuls of jingle bells + a call-and-response beat. The loudest quiet-focus breaker there is.

variations.easier: Skip the split; whole group echoes you in unison.
variations.harder: Add foot stomps as the bass line, or notate the pattern with symbols on the board.

activities.name: Christmas Light Circuit Cards
activities.safety: Coin cells are a serious choking/swallowing hazard. Count batteries in and out, and keep spares with the adult.
activities.setup: Pre-cut copper tape into 15cm lengths. Test every LED + battery pair yourself first. Dead bulbs sink the lesson.
steps: Fold a card and draw the front design, leaving the inside blank for the circuit.
Lay two parallel copper-tape tracks inside the card. These are the wires. Leave a small gap in one track.
Bridge the gap with the LED: long leg to the track leading to the battery's + side.
Tape the coin cell at the track ends (+ side up) and press. The bulb should glow.
If it doesn't: flip the battery, then check the LED legs. Debugging IS the lesson.
Sign the card and deliver it, a working circuit beats any store-bought card.
activities.tagline: Paper circuits that actually light up, a greeting card with a working bulb.

variations.easier: Build the circuit on an open card (no folding) with the tracks pre-laid.
variations.harder: Add a paper-clip switch or wire two LEDs in parallel.

activities.name: Candy Cane Olympics

photo.alt: A candy cane hanging on a Christmas tree
photo.caption: A candy cane, the only equipment the Candy Cane Olympics needs.
photo.credit: Photo: Matt Reinbold, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Check for food allergies before anyone eats the equipment. Peppermint is the usual suspect. No eating until the events are done.
activities.setup: Lay out four stations with tape lines: hook-and-carry lane, spoon relay lane, fishing hook line, cane-stack table.
steps: Event 1. Hook and carry: hook a cane through another cane's crook and carry it down the lane without hands touching it.
Event 2, Spoon relay: balance a cane on a spoon, relay-style, down and back.
Event 3, Fishing: dangle a cane on a string and hook a paper fish (or another cane) off the table edge.
Event 4. Stack: how many canes can your team lean into a teepee before it falls?
Score 3-2-1 per event. The canes are the medals. Everyone keeps what they carried.
activities.tagline: Four ridiculous relay events, one box of candy canes as the equipment.

variations.easier: Run two events instead of four, teams of three.
variations.harder: Blindfold the carrier (with a sighted guide) or run the whole thing as a timed bracket.

activities.name: Gumdrop Bridge Build

photo.alt: Hood River students build bridges (8638270382)
photo.caption: Hood River students build bridges (8638270382).
photo.credit: Photo: Oregon Department of Transportation, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Check for food allergies (gelatin, food dyes) before building, and the bridge is load-tested, not lunch.
activities.setup: Set two book stacks 20cm apart as the gorge. Bag 30 gumdrops + 40 toothpicks per team.
steps: The challenge: span the 20cm gorge with only gumdrops and toothpicks. No taping to the books.
Build in triangles. Show one triangle joint, then let them discover why it holds.
Test with pennies, one at a time, placed in the middle. Count the load before collapse.
Redesign round: 10 minutes to rebuild using what the collapse taught you.
Weigh the bridges too. Strongest per gram wins the engineering prize.
activities.tagline: Toothpicks and gumdrops, one span to cross. The tastiest engineering constraint there is.

variations.easier: Shorten the gorge to 12cm and build flat trusses only.
variations.harder: Widen to 30cm, or ban triangles and see what happens.

materials.item: washable block-print ink or thick tempera

activities.name: Holiday Card Print Shop
activities.safety: Washable ink only, block-print ink stains clothes permanently. Smocks or old shirts.
activities.setup: Cut foam into card-sized plates. Pour ink onto trays with rollers ready. Ink management is the whole setup.
steps: Draw the design on the foam with a pencil, pressing hard. The dent is the printing plate.
Roll a thin, even layer of ink onto the foam. Thin beats thick; puddles blur the lines.
Press cardstock onto the inked foam, rub the back firmly, and peel, first print done.
Re-ink and repeat: one plate makes the whole class set. Sign each print in pencil.
Hang the edition to dry and compare: which prints came out cleanest, and why?
activities.tagline: Foam-plate printing: carve once, print a whole stack of cards.

variations.easier: Use pre-cut foam shapes (trees, stars) and print single-color.
variations.harder: Carve two plates and overprint in two colors, or print on folded cards with messages inside.

activities.name: Reindeer Relay Race
activities.setup: Make simple antler headbands (or skip them. Arms work). Mark two relay lanes with cones.
steps: Each team lines up; the first runner dons the antlers and the red nose.
Gallop (yes, gallop) down the lane, circle the cone, and gallop back.
Pass the antlers and nose to the next runner. The handoff is the whole game.
Run it twice: once straight, once with a silly rule (sideways gallop, freeze at the cone).
Winning team leads the victory lap; every team gets a cheer.
activities.tagline: Antler headbands, a red nose, and a relay that rewards silliness over speed.

variations.easier: Shorten the lane and let kids walk-trot instead of gallop.
variations.harder: Add obstacles (crawl under a table = the stable door) or run it as a full bracket.

materials.item: a wall or string to hang them

activities.name: Advent Kindness Envelopes
activities.safety: Keep kindnesses school-appropriate and opt-in. Nobody is assigned someone else's kindness.
activities.setup: Number 25 envelopes 1–25 and hang them on a string. Cut paper slips to fit.
steps: As a group, brainstorm 25 tiny kindnesses that fit a school day: hold a door, thank the custodian, share a pencil.
Write one per slip, seal each in its numbered envelope, and hang them in order.
Each day, the class opens that day's envelope together and commits to the kindness.
Keep a running list on the board of which ones got done. Checkmarks are the advent calendar.
On the last day, open them all and vote for the kindness the class wants to keep year-round.
activities.tagline: Twenty-five sealed envelopes, each hiding one small kindness to do that day.

variations.easier: Do 12 envelopes instead of 25, or let the teacher pre-write the kindnesses.
variations.harder: Each kid makes a personal 7-day set to take home for the break.

activities.name: Dreidel Spin Physics

photo.alt: Woodleywonderworks learning to spin the dreidel
photo.caption: Woodleywonderworks learning to spin the dreidel.
photo.credit: Photo: woodleywonderworks, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Small tops are a choking hazard for under-3s. Keep this one at 7+.
activities.setup: Gather a few dreidels plus tops kids can make. Lay out three test surfaces side by side.
steps: Everyone spins once on the wood surface. Time each spin to the stopwatch. Record the numbers.
Now the question: does the surface matter? Spin the same dreidel on felt, then tile, five spins each.
Average each surface's times. Which surface wins, and by how much?
Test a second variable: spin hard vs spin soft on the same surface. Which matters more. Surface or spin force?
Write the conclusion in one sentence on the board: the longest spin came from ___.
activities.tagline: Whose dreidel spins longest? Friction, weight, and surface, a physics lab in a spinning top.

variations.easier: Spin and time only, skip the averages, just find the longest single spin.
variations.harder: Build DIY dreidels from clay and test whether weight placement changes spin time.

activities.name: Menorah Mosaic Tiles

photo.alt: A lit Hanukkah menorah with nine flames
photo.caption: A lit Hanukkah menorah with nine flames.
photo.credit: Photo: Daniel Dimitrov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Paper scraps only, no glass or ceramic tiles for this age group.
activities.setup: Cut paper into small squares (about 2cm). Draw a simple nine-branch menorah outline on the base, the shamash raised in the middle.
steps: Look at the outline together: nine branches, and the middle one (the shamash) sits higher. It lights the others.
Fill the branches with glued paper tiles, alternating blues and whites. No gaps is the goal.
Add a small yellow or gold flame tile above each branch tip.
Step back: mosaics read best from three steps away. Adjust any bare spots.
Hang it where the light hits. Tile edges catch the light like stained glass.
activities.tagline: Nine branches, hundreds of paper tiles, a mosaic menorah built one square at a time.

variations.easier: Use bigger tiles and fill just three branches as a group.
variations.harder: Design a fully original mosaic pattern inside each branch, or build it as a 9-kid relay (one branch each).

activities.inclusion: Frame it as learning about a real tradition neighbors celebrate, curiosity, not costume. Invite (never require) kids who celebrate to share first.
activities.name: Hanukkah Story Circle
activities.setup: No setup, just a circle. If you want, dim the lights and put one electric candle in the middle.
steps: Sit in a circle. Explain the shape of the story: a small group kept their traditions alive against long odds, and the holiday remembers that endurance.
Tell the story in five short beats, you'll narrate, the circle echoes the key line of each beat back.
Beat by beat: the temple, the small jar of oil, the eight nights, the dreidel game that hid learning in plain sight, the candles lit today.
After the last beat, each kid names one tradition their own family keeps. Any tradition counts.
Close with one quiet minute: everyone thinks of something small that lasted longer than expected.
activities.tagline: The story behind the holiday, told round-robin. Every kid carries one piece of it.

variations.easier: You tell the whole story; the circle just echoes the repeated line.
variations.harder: Kids research one beat each beforehand and teach it to the circle.

activities.name: Gelt Math Market

photo.alt: Chocolate gelt coins in gold foil
photo.caption: Chocolate gelt coins, the currency of the pretend market and its math games.
photo.credit: Photo: Evan-Amos, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Check for food allergies (dairy, nuts) before chocolate changes hands. Paper coins work just as well.
activities.setup: Set up 4-5 'shops' (desks) with price tags: 3 coins, 5 coins, 7 coins. Give every kid 20 coins in a bag.
steps: Everyone starts with 20 coins. The shops sell small treats or trinkets at posted prices.
Round one: buy what you want, but you must get change. Sellers make change from their own stock.
Round two: prices rise by 2 coins everywhere. What changes about what you buy?
Sellers count their takings; buyers count what's left. Who managed their coins best?
Donate one coin per kid to a class jar. The jar funds the next market's stock.
activities.tagline: Chocolate coins, real prices, making change, the sweetest math lesson of the year.

variations.easier: Use paper coins and fixed prices with no change-making.
variations.harder: Add a 10% 'market tax' on round three, or let kids run the shops and set their own prices.
