One jumper at a time. Everyone else stands on the far bank as the welcoming side. The cheer when a jumper lands is half the equipment of this game.
A jumper who steps in the river has not failed anything: the current got them, they climb out, and they jump again from the bank. Rivers at three are for practising on.
When the whole group has crossed twice, move the far rope out by one hand-width. One hand-width is the correct amount of harder, and the group should watch you measure it.
Last crossings are dealer's choice: jump it, or take the stepping-stone version, one big step across, and the group finishes by rolling the river up together.
activities.tagline: Two ropes on the ground make a river. Stand at the bank, jump with two feet, land on the other side.

variations.easier: Narrow the river to a hand-width, or drop the jump entirely: a big step across a tape line is the same game at an earlier page.
variations.harder: Widen the river another hand-width, or cross it backwards. Turn around on the bank, jump, and land facing where you came from.

materials.item: two or three large blankets or sheets
chairs or a low table to drape them over
a small pile of sturdy picture books

activities.name: Blanket Fort Book Nook

photo.alt: Girls in an indoor fort (15075739555)
photo.caption: Girls in an indoor fort (15075739555).
photo.credit: Photo: Personal Creations, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Adults build and clamp; kids never do, and nothing heavy ever goes on top of the blankets. The opening stays wide and uncovered the whole session, an adult can see inside at all times, and the fort is never a hiding place, if a reader cannot be seen, the fort gets rebuilt smaller.
activities.setup: The adult builds the fort, start to finish, before any kid goes in: blankets draped over chairs or a low table, edges clamped, one wide opening that stays open. Test it the way it will be tested, lean on nothing, but tug every edge once; a fort that sags during building gets rebuilt now, not during reading. Line the floor inside with cushions and put the book pile just inside the opening.
steps: Show the fort from outside first and name what it is: a reading nook, a quiet place, three readers at a time. Walk the opening rule: 'In through the door, out through the door. The walls are blankets, and blankets are not doors.'

First readers go in with the adult sitting at the opening. Inside the fort's world, able to see every reader, close enough to hand over books. Pick the first book together and read it at fort volume: the soft voice a small roof asks for.

Between books, readers may swap with the waiting pair at the door. The door swap is part of the ritual, done slowly, book handed over with the swap. Nobody queues long: three short reads inside beat one long sit.

Leave a looking-book round in every visit: one book with no reading at all, just pages turned and pictures pointed at, fort-quiet. Pointing at a picture and naming it is reading at three, and the fort is where it gets taken seriously.

Close the nook properly: books carried out two at a time and stacked, cushions shaken and piled, then the group helps the adult fold the blankets. The fort comes down together, which is the last small job of the session.
activities.tagline: An adult-built blanket fort, a small pile of picture books, and room inside for three readers at a time.

variations.easier: A bigger opening, an adult reader inside for the whole round, and only two readers at a time.
variations.harder: A torch-free 'night reading' round: blankets doubled for dimness (opening still wide and uncovered), and readers retell the book they just heard to the next pair at the door.

activities.inclusion: The signal post is a full job for a kid who would rather not speak in front of the room: a sender by light or by tap talks all session without saying a word, and their messages land exactly like everyone else's. Logging can be marks on paper, tallies, or dots and dashes drawn big. The code does not care how it is written down.

materials.item: a board or big paper for the Morse chart

activities.name: Morse Code Signal Post

photo.alt: Seaman send Morse code signals
photo.caption: Seaman send Morse code signals.
photo.credit: Photo: Tucker M. Yates, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Flashlights point at walls, ceilings, or paper. Never at eyes, and that rule is stated before the first light comes out. Tapping stays on tables, not on each other.
activities.setup: Write the Morse alphabet on the board yourself before the session. A is dot-dash, and the whole alphabet fits in two columns; no printing needed and no handouts to lose. Dimming the room helps the flashlight rounds if your space allows it, but the game works in daylight against a plain wall. Test every flashlight; a dying battery sends a dying signal.
steps: Start with the one message the whole world knows: SOS. S is three dots, O is three dashes, tap it on the table together until the room can send it without looking: dot-dot-dot, dash-dash-dash, dot-dot-dot. It has been the distress call for over a century because it is unmistakable.

Learn the code's one rule: a dot is short, a dash lasts three times as long, and the pause between letters is what keeps a message from becoming soup. Send your first name's first letter across the table by finger-taps, partner logging each mark on paper and decoding it against the board chart.

Initials round: each kid writes their two initials as dots and dashes, practises them until smooth, then pairs up across the room. Sender flashes initials at the wall above their partner's head, never at a face, receiver logs and decodes, then they swap.

Sound post: same game, no lights. A knuckle tap is a dot; a flat-palm thump is a dash. Two sounds different enough to tell apart with your eyes closed. Receivers log by ear only and check against the chart after.

Message relay: split into lines of three or four stations. The first station gets a three-letter word from the word bank (CAT, SUN, MAP, EGG, TOP), sends it by taps station to station, and the last station writes what arrived. Compare the word that landed with the word that left, where it garbled is the real telegraph problem, and the fix is always the same: slower, with honest pauses.

Close in the dimmed room if you have one: the whole group sends SOS by flashlight together on your count, three times, then lights up. A room that can signal together can be quiet together. The stillness after the last round is the proof.
activities.tagline: Dots and dashes sent by flashlight and table-tap. Learn SOS, signal your initials, and run a message post across the room.

variations.easier: Initials only, chart open in front of both partners, and sender and receiver side by side instead of across the room.
variations.harder: Send full words from the bank with no chart for the common letters (E, T, A, O, N, S), or receive the sound round with eyes closed the whole way.

materials.item: one big soft ball (beach-ball size or a soft playground ball)
a wide basket, laundry basket, or big open box

activities.name: Soft Ball New Year Drop
activities.safety: Soft ball only, dropped straight down from a standing hold, never thrown, never dropped off furniture, and nobody stands or sits in the basket. The dropper stands on the taped spot; reaching into the basket waits until the ball has stopped moving.
activities.setup: Put the basket in the middle of the circle and test the drop yourself first: standing, ball held high, dropped straight down. It should land in the basket and stay there. If it bounces out, use a softer ball or a deeper basket; a runaway ball ends the count, not starts a chase.
steps: Teach the count on fingers first, no ball: hold up five fingers, fold one down at a time, five, four, three, two, one, and everybody shouts the last one together. Practise twice; the shout is the payoff the count is building to.
Now the drop. You hold the ball high over the basket. The group counts down on fingers, and on 'one', not before, the ball drops. The rule the kids police for you: the ball only falls on one.
Round two, a kid is the dropper, standing on a taped spot beside the basket with the ball held high in two hands. Dropping is a two-hand job at three; nobody throws, nobody aims from across the room.
Make the wait longer, never the count: hold at 'two' for a long silly pause while the room holds its breath, then fold the last finger. The pause is where the laughing lives.

Finish with the group drop: everyone counts, the dropper drops, and the whole circle does the cheer with both arms up. Then the ball goes in the basket and stays there while you say plainly that the party game is done.
activities.tagline: Count five down to one on your fingers, and the grown-up drops one big soft ball into the basket. That is the whole New Year party at three.

variations.easier: Count down from three instead of five, and the adult drops every round. A shorter wait is still a real drop.
variations.harder: Two baskets and two droppers, counting together: both balls have to land on the same 'one', which takes three or four honest tries.

activities.inclusion: The roll works from a seated position at the top of the slope or from a chair placed at the line. Letting go of an egg needs a hand, not legs. A kid who would rather carry an egg down and roll it on the flat at the bottom is rolling an egg; the slope is the setting, not the test.

materials.item: big plastic eggs (the large fillable kind, one per kid, taped shut by an adult)
a gentle grass slope or a low grassy bank
a starting line: a scarf, rope, or chalk line

activities.name: Big Egg Roll on the Slope

photo.alt: A decorated Easter egg resting in green grass
photo.caption: A decorated egg on the grass, ready to roll down the slope.
photo.credit: Photo: Personal Creations, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Plastic eggs only, taped shut by an adult, and nothing goes in mouths. These are rollers, not snacks. One roller at a time on the line, walking down only: running down a slope carrying eggs is how three-year-olds fall, so the fetch is a walk, every time.
activities.setup: Walk the slope first and pick out anything sharp, and choose the gentlest bank you have. A slope a three-year-old can walk down without leaning is the right one; a slope they slide down is not. Tape every egg shut yourself and shake each one: if it rattles open, it does not go out.
steps: Name the tradition in one sentence, because it is a good one: 'People have rolled eggs down a hill at Easter for a very long time. There is a famous one on the White House lawn, every year since 1878.' Then state the one rule: 'Eggs roll. Hands let go. Feet walk.'
One kid at a time at the starting line: crouch, set the egg on the grass, let go. No pushing contests. A let-go roll is the game, and it stops where it stops.
Everyone walks down together to fetch the eggs. The walk down and back is half the activity at three and none of it is wasted time; the next roller starts when the group is back at the line.

Add the call: before each roll, the roller points at where they think their egg will stop, a bush, a patch of daisies, the bottom. Pointing is the prediction; there is no score and nobody is wrong, eggs have their own ideas.

Last round is the parade roll: the whole group rolls at once, one egg each, and walks down together through the scattered eggs to collect them into the basket. Count them back in out loud, every egg home.
activities.tagline: The old Easter egg roll, sized for three: one big egg, one gentle grass slope, roll it down, walk down, roll it again.

variations.easier: A nearly flat patch and eggs rolled from a crouch two steps away. The roll is short and the fetching is shorter.
variations.harder: A slightly longer slope, or the roller calls their stopping point out loud before letting go and the group checks it together at the bottom.

activities.inclusion: Watching from the dry edge counts in full for the first rounds. A kid in shoes that must stay dry, or one who is not sure about water yet, is the group's ring-counter and stomp-caller from the edge, and the last-round stomp happens close enough to the edge that they can join it in boots borrowed for three stomps or call it for everyone else.

materials.item: rain boots for every kid (their own, or the program's spares)
a towel by the door for the walk back in

activities.name: First Puddle Walk

photo.alt: Innocence (3548064229)
photo.caption: Innocence (3548064229).
photo.credit: Photo: Sean McGrath from Saint John, NB, Canada, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Shallow puddles on flat ground only, boots on every foot, and the walk stays a walk until the stated stomp round, running in wet boots on wet ground is the fall this activity is built to avoid. Puddle water is for boots, never for hands-to-mouths or drinking, and hands wash when the group goes in.
activities.setup: Walk the route yourself after the rain and choose it honestly: puddles no deeper than a boot's foot part, on flat ground with no slope to them, away from the road and away from drains. If you cannot see the bottom of a puddle, it is not on the route. Depth you cannot see is a different outing.
steps: Boots on, and the one rule said out loud where everyone can hear it: 'First we walk. Puddles are for walking through.' Model it: walk the first puddle yourself, slowly, both feet flat, like the water is something you are visiting.
One kid at a time through the first puddle, the group watching from the dry edge. Watching a puddle get walked through, the rings, the small sound, is a real part of this, not waiting.
Chain round: the group walks the whole route together, puddle to puddle, holding the pace of the slowest boots. Between puddles is dry-ground walking; the contrast is the lesson the feet learn.
Stop at the biggest puddle and stand in it together, still. Count the rings when one kid lifts one foot slowly and sets it back down: one lift, one ring spreading. Quiet water, noticed properly.
Last round earns the splash: at the final puddle only, kids may stomp, two feet, in the puddle, three stomps each, then boots off at the door and the towel does its job.
activities.tagline: Boots on, and a slow walk through the shallow puddles after rain, first round walking only, and the splash is saved for last.

variations.easier: One puddle, an adult hand for every crossing, and skip the stomp round entirely. The walk is the activity.
variations.harder: Add the leaf test: float one fallen leaf in a puddle and watch where the stomp-rings push it. Rings move things, and kids can see it happen.

activities.inclusion: A kid can do this whole activity by feel as well as sight: the cup is cold at the start and less cold as it melts, and holding it with two hands at each check tells the same story the marker lines tell. Reports can be a word, a point, or a hand raised or lowered to show the level. The melting does not care how it is reported.

materials.item: clean fresh snow (collected by an adult)

activities.name: Cup of Snow Melting Watch

photo.alt: The same pile of snow photographed as it melts away over several days
photo.caption: One pile of snow, watched day after day as it melts smaller and smaller.
photo.credit: Photo: P K, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Snow is collected by an adult from a clean patch away from roads and salt, and melt water is never drunk. It is looked at, marked, and poured out. Cold hands are part of holding the cup; if a kid says their hands are too cold, the cup goes down and that answer is final.
activities.setup: Collect the snow yourself from a clean patch away from paths, roads and anywhere salt or grit has been spread, if you would not trust it near a kid's mittens, do not scoop it. Fill the clear cup heaped, set it where the whole group can see it, and draw the marker line at the snow's top edge where everyone watches you draw it.
steps: Start with hands behind backs and eyes only: 'What do we think will happen to the snow inside?' Take every answer, smaller, water, gone, and say the plan plainly: 'We are going to watch it happen. Nobody touches the cup. The watching is the job.'

While it melts, go and look at where the snow came from: the same snow, still outside, still white. Coming back to a changed cup after seeing the unchanged patch is what makes the change land at three.

First check after a few minutes: the level has dropped below the marker line. Draw the new line together. The kid with the steadiest hand holds the cup still with two hands while you draw, or you hold and they point at the exact height.

Patience round: name what the water at the bottom used to be. 'That water was the top of the cup.' Say it a few ways; the idea that snow and water are the same thing in two states is the whole science here, and it arrives by looking, not by worksheet.

When the cup is all water, hold it beside a second cup you fill with water to the same mark: same thing, two roads in. The snow cup goes outside to be tipped onto the garden, the water goes home, and the group picks where.
activities.tagline: One clear cup of real snow, brought inside and watched: it goes down, the water comes up, and nobody touches it. Waiting is the activity.

variations.easier: A smaller cup (it melts faster) and just two checks: the first line, and the all-water moment.
variations.harder: Two cups side by side, one by the window in the sun, one in the shade, and the group checks both: same snow, different speeds, and the race needs no winner announced, the lines say it.

materials.item: cushions, mats, or sturdy chairs in a row (one seat per rider)
one big soft block or a beanbag (the ticket)
floor space for a route around the room

activities.name: Cushion Train All Aboard
activities.safety: Seats are sat on, never stood on, and climbing in and out happens on the outside of the row at a walk. The ticket is soft and travels hand to hand at lap height. Nothing is thrown up the train.
activities.setup: Build the train before the group boards: seats in a row close enough that a seated kid can pass the ticket block to the seat behind without standing. The front seat is the driver's and it stays empty until the first driver climbs in. Walk the row and sit in every seat yourself; a seat that tips gets swapped now.
steps: Board in order, back seat first, and state the one rule as they sit: 'The train moves when the driver says go, and the train is pretend, so our feet stay still and the moving is in our voices.' The first sound the train makes, the group invents together and keeps.

Tickets: the last rider holds the big block. On 'all aboard', the block travels hand to hand up the row to the driver. A ticket collected is the train's permission to leave. Dropped tickets are picked up by the nearest hands; the train waits.

Stops are named by the riders: the driver calls 'Next stop…' and a rider names somewhere real to them, grandma's house, the shop with the good bread, the moon, and the whole train says it back as they 'arrive', with a gentle lean-and-stop sway.

Swap the driver every two stops: drivers climb out on the outside of the row, walk up, and the new driver takes the front seat while everyone shuffles one seat back. Shuffling seats without a fuss is a skill this game practises on purpose.
Last stop is the station, your carpet or rug, and the group 'arrives' with the train sound one final time, then helps return the seats to the walls, one cushion carried by two riders.
activities.tagline: A row of cushions and chairs becomes a train: a ticket block to hand the driver, stops the kids name, and everyone rides.

variations.easier: Four seats, the adult as permanent driver, and stops you name, the ticket still travels and the riders still ride.
variations.harder: A second carriage: a second short row behind, with its own ticket, and the driver has to collect both before the train can go.

activities.inclusion: A chair boat counts in full: a kid who rows from a sturdy chair or from their own wheelchair, arms pulling in time with the song while the shore crew counts, is sailing the same crossing. The boat is the rowing and the song, and the cardboard was only ever the costume.

materials.item: one very large sturdy cardboard box (appliance-size, flaps taped down by an adult)

activities.name: Box Boat Row Along
activities.safety: One or two seated kids in the boat, never standing, and climbing in and out is always with an adult hand, box edges fold under a climbing foot. The adult tapes and checks the box; torn or softening cardboard retires the boat that day.
activities.setup: The adult builds the boat: flaps taped flat inside and out, edges checked for staples and sharp folds. Run your hand around every rim before a kid gets in. Set the cushions as the island a short 'row' away, and sit in the box yourself once; a boat that folds under you gets a second box nested inside it or does not sail.
steps: One sailor at a time climbs in (adult hand offered, every time) and sits in the middle of the boat. State the one rule: 'Boats are for sitting in. The rowing is arms, the moving is pretend.'

Teach the row on dry land first, outside the boat: arms reach forward together, pull back together, in time with the slow song you are going to sing. Three practice pulls; the song's pace is the rowing pace.

Sail: you sing the slow song, the sailor rows in the boat, and the boat 'crosses' while the group on the shore counts the pulls out loud. Counting rows is the shore crew's whole job and they take it seriously.

Docking: when the song ends, rowing stops wherever the boat is, and the sailor names the island they reached. The cushions are whatever the sailor says they are. The next sailor's crossing starts from there.

Final crossing is the ferry round: one sailor rows, one passenger sits behind with hands in lap, and the shore crew counts a slower song. Then the boat is 'tied up', turned on its side by the adult with the group's help, until next time.
activities.tagline: One big cardboard box is the boat: sit inside, row with your arms to a slow song, and dock at the cushion island when the song ends.

variations.easier: No passenger round and a shorter song: one sailor, six counted pulls, docked.
variations.harder: Two boats side by side (if you have two big boxes), rowing the same song together and docking on the same last note.

activities.inclusion: The crosser's job can be done entirely by voice: a kid who directs, 'my turn to cross, walk him slow', while a friend's hand walks their toy across is the bridge's engineer that round, and the group counts their traveller in with the rest. Directing is building, said so out loud.

materials.item: one wide flat plank or board (about a metre long, edges smooth)
big blocks or sturdy boxes (for two low stacks)

activities.name: Wide Plank Bridge Crossing
activities.safety: Plank stays low, stacks no higher than two big blocks, and bridges are for toys, never for feet: nobody stands, sits, or crawls on the plank, and that rule is said before the first crossing. Kids' hands stay off the plank while a toy is crossing; a bridge being held is a bridge that cannot be tested.
activities.setup: Build the first bridge yourself where the group can watch: two stacks two blocks high, the plank laid flat across with a hand's width of plank resting on each stack. Walk the soft toy across, then press the middle of the plank with your whole hand, if it tips or slides, shorten the span before any kid builds. Check the plank's edges with your palm; splinters retire it.
steps: Name the parts in plain words as you point: 'Two stacks hold it up. The flat part is the bridge. Bridges are for crossing.' Then take it apart, the group rebuilds what they just saw, which is the building lesson at three.

Kids rebuild in pairs: one stack each, then the plank laid across together, two hands each end. A stack that wobbles gets one block taken off or a wider base, say the fix out loud as it happens, so fixing sounds like building, not failing.

First crossing: the soft toy walks the bridge held by its owner, one slow step at a time, while the group holds its breath theatrically. If the toy 'falls', it falls on carpet, gets picked up, and crosses again. Falling toys are the rehearsal, not the disaster.

Change one thing: move the stacks a little further apart and cross again. The plank sags or feels different. Kids can see the toy dip in the middle. Say what they are seeing: 'Longer bridge, more bend.' That sentence is real engineering at three.

Traveller round: beanbags cross one at a time and stay on the far side, counted as they arrive. Finish by counting the travellers, then the whole bridge comes down block by block. Taking down carefully is the last building job.
activities.tagline: Two low stacks of big blocks, one wide plank across, and a soft toy that walks the bridge, the first bridge a three-year-old can build.

variations.easier: Stacks one block high and close together, adult lays the plank. The crossing is the activity, the building is watched.
variations.harder: Stacks at two different heights so the bridge slopes, and the toy 'walks uphill', then swap the stacks and walk it down.

materials.item: one sturdy blanket or large sheet

activities.name: Blanket Ball Bounce Together
activities.safety: Soft ball only, bounced low, knee height at most, and the blanket never goes higher than the shortest holder's waist. Nobody gets under the blanket, nobody lets go suddenly on purpose, and a dropped edge just gets picked back up; the game pauses, it does not scold.
activities.setup: Spread the blanket and walk around it testing edges: every kid needs a piece of edge they can hold with two hands standing still. Too many kids on one side means a smaller group per round, not a stretch. The ball goes in the middle only when every hand is holding on; test the lift yourself: blanket up to knee height, flat and steady.
steps: State the one rule before the ball exists: 'The ball stays on the blanket. We keep it low and slow. A ball that flies off means we all went too fast together.' Practise one lift and lower with no ball until the blanket rises as one piece.
Ball in. First job is stillness: hold the blanket flat and watch the ball sit in the middle. A group of three-year-olds holding one thing still together has already done the hard part, say so.

Rolling round: on your call, one side lifts a little and the ball rolls slowly toward the low side; then that side lifts and it rolls back. Name the kid the ball is visiting each time: 'It's going to see Maya…'. The rolling has a destination, and the destination is a person.

Small bounce round: tiny lifts together, the ball hopping no higher than the kids' knees. Count the hops out loud as a group; when the ball leaves the blanket (it will), it goes back to the middle and the count starts fresh. Leaving is part of the game, never the end of it.

Finish with the carry: ball resting in the middle, the group carries the blanket together, slow walking, all hands on, to the box or basket and tips the ball in as one team. Blanket folded by its holders, two to an edge.
activities.tagline: Everyone holds the edge of one blanket, one soft ball rolls in the middle, and the whole group's job is the same: keep it on, keep it low.

variations.easier: Fewer holders and a lighter ball, adult on the edge as a permanent holder. The lift is smaller and slower.
variations.harder: Two soft balls, and the group tries to keep both on through the rolling round. Visits get called for both.

materials.item: big animal picture cards, in pairs (adult-drawn or from a chunky picture book set, one pair per two kids, big and clear)

activities.name: Animal Sound Find Your Pair
activities.safety: Wandering is walking. The sounds get loud, the feet do not, and that is said before the deal. Cards are big and stiff; chewed or torn cards retire, and nothing about this game needs running to work.
activities.setup: Make the pairs ahead: big simple animal pictures a three-year-old can name on sight, dog, cow, duck, cat, frog, sheep. Keep the set small (five or six pairs) and leave out anything the room will argue about; a clear duck beats a clever animal every time. Test each card on the youngest kid you know, in your head, honestly.
steps: Show every animal first, whole group, with its sound made together, dog: woof, cow: moo, duck: quack. Making every sound in a crowd first is what makes making yours alone in a minute feel safe.
Deal one card to each kid, face up, at three the card is held and shown, not kept secret. State the one rule: 'Somebody else has your animal. Make your sound and find them.'

Finding round: kids wander slowly, making their sound and listening, holding their card high. When two matching animals find each other they stand together and do their sound once as a pair, the pair call, so the room can hear pairs forming.
Found pairs sit together at the edge as animal couples and keep answering the wandering calls with their pair call. A found pair becomes a landmark the still-searching kids can navigate by.

Regather by animals: call the animals one at a time and each pair comes up, shows both cards, and does their sound for the group. Cards collected by animal, pairs sitting together for whatever comes next, new neighbours, chosen by a cow.
activities.tagline: Deal a big animal card to every kid. Somebody else has your same animal. Make the sound, wander, and find them.

variations.easier: Three pairs only, cards held by adults at first and handed over once the sounds are loud, a smaller field to search.
variations.harder: Add the movement: each animal also has its walk (duck waddle, frog hop in place) and pairs must find each other by sound AND walk.

materials.item: a scarf or flag (the finish marker)

activities.name: Chalk Arrow Trail
activities.safety: The trail stays inside the group's usual safe ground, no road crossings, no car park, and an adult walks the route first that day. Arrows are followed at a walk; a trail is not a race, and the kid standing on an arrow is never hurried off it.
activities.setup: Draw the trail yourself before the group comes out: eight to twelve BIG arrows, each one as long as a kid is tall is not too big, along a safe route with no road crossings, ending at the flag. Walk it back and check every arrow still reads clearly from standing height; a smudged arrow gets redrawn now, not explained later.
steps: Start at the first arrow and teach the one move: stand on the arrow, point the way it points, say 'that way', then walk that way. Pointing before walking is the whole game. The arrow is read first, followed second.

Follow the trail one kid in front, the group behind as the expedition. The leader changes at every arrow: whoever reaches it first stands on it, points, calls 'that way', and the group answers before anyone moves.

Where the trail turns, it turns honestly, around the bench, along the fence, never across planted beds or anywhere the group is not allowed. Following arrows into the wrong place is a trail-drawing fault, not a kid fault, and you redraw on the spot if it happens.

At the flag: the group plants itself around the finish marker and looks back along the whole trail. Name three things the arrows took them past. Remembering the route backwards is the quiet hard part, done as a group.
Walk back along the trail in reverse, following the arrows backwards. They all point the wrong way now, which the group will find hilarious and which teaches more about arrows than the trip out did.
activities.tagline: Big chalk arrows on the ground, one after another, and a whole trail to follow, point where each arrow points, then walk that way.

variations.easier: Five arrows in a nearly straight line with the flag in sight the whole way. The trail is followed, the searching is minimal.
variations.harder: Add one fork drawn by you: two arrows side by side pointing different ways, and the leader chooses, with the group following the choice to a second small flag.

materials.item: no materials, one short song the whole group already knows

activities.name: Loud Quiet Song Switch
activities.safety: Loud means big singing voices, not screaming. Say the difference once, plainly, and keep loud rounds short: 'Loud like singing to the back of the hall, not loud like hurting ears.' If it tips into screaming, hands come down and the song goes quiet mid-line; the switch fixes it without a lecture.
activities.setup: Pick the song with the room, not for it: the one every kid can already sing without being taught, a counting rhyme or the song this group sings at tidying time. Practise the switch signal yourself once: hands high means loud, hands low means quiet, hands halfway means the in-between nobody has to hit exactly.
steps: Sing the song once through plainly, all together, no switching. The group needs one clean run in their ears before the game starts changing it.

Teach the switch on a single line: start the line quiet with hands low, raise your hands mid-line and let the line get loud, bring them down for the end. Then state the one rule: 'My hands tell the song how big to be. Eyes on the hands.'
Full song with switches: two or three changes per verse, never more. A switch every line is a shouting contest, a switch every few lines is listening. Sing with them at their volume, not over them.

Swap the hands job: a kid stands beside you and raises and lowers the hands while the group watches them. The switch-keeper keeps switches slow and clear. Coaching that, kindly, in the moment, is the group's first conducting lesson and nobody calls it that.

Finish with the shrinking song: sing it once more and let your hands sink lower with every line until the last line is a whisper the whole room has to lean in to hear. End quiet on purpose. The next thing the room does starts calmer.
activities.tagline: One song everyone knows, sung whole, but when the grown-up's hands go up it is loud, and when they come down it is quiet.

variations.easier: Two switches in the whole song, telegraphed slowly, hands rising over a full line so everyone sees it coming.
variations.harder: Add the middle: hands halfway, middle voice. The group tries to land the in-between volume on purpose, which is much harder than loud or quiet.

activities.inclusion: Stepping across counts as a crossing in full: a kid who moves pad to pad by stepping, or wheels across the pads laid as a flat path, is doing the course. The landing hold becomes a stop-and-hold at each pad, counted by the group exactly the same way. The skill is stopping on purpose, and every body in the room can practise that.

materials.item: flat foam mats, carpet squares, or big rubber pads (4-6, non-slip)

activities.name: Two Foot Landing Pads
activities.safety: Flat non-slip pads only, spaced for a small hop, never for a leap, and only one kid jumps at a time, with the landing pad clear before they go. If a pad slides in testing, it does not go down; a moving pad is a fall wearing a game costume.
activities.setup: Lay the pads a small hop apart, one short two-foot jump for a three-year-old leg, tested with your own smallest hop, not your comfortable one, and press each pad flat: a pad that slides when you push it with your foot does not go down; on hard floors, carpet squares with grippy backs or pads on a big rug are the honest setup.
steps: Teach the landing before any jumping, standing still: feet apart, knees bent a little, arms out. 'Land like a cat, soft and stuck'. Practise the shape on the spot: small bend, hold, and the group counts one-two-three out loud while everyone holds it.

First hops are step-offs, not jumps: stand on one pad, step off with two feet onto the floor and land in the cat shape, held for the count. Stepping down teaches the landing with nothing to be brave about.

Pad to pad: one kid on the course at a time, two-foot jump, two-foot landing, hold for the group's count of three before the next hop. The count is done by the watchers. Holding a landing while your friends count is the game, and skipping the hold is noticed kindly and redone.

A stuck landing earns the arms-up finish: after the count, arms rise and the pad is 'claimed'. A landing that travels, a step, a hop-forward, hands down, is just information: 'That one rolled. Again?' and the kid tries the same hop once more.

Finish by gathering the pads into one big landing island and taking the final small jump onto it together, one at a time, each landing held while the whole group counts to three, then pads stacked by the course crew, two hands per pad.
activities.tagline: Foam pads on the floor and one job: jump with two feet, land with two feet, and stick it for a count of three.

variations.easier: Pads touching each other, so the 'jump' is a two-foot step across a seam, landing shape only, no air at all.
variations.harder: One pad a little further, or the landing held for a count of five. Longer hold, same hop.

activities.inclusion: A lantern carried on a lap tray, or set on the front of a wheelchair and pushed along the same route, is in the parade in full. The parade is the line, the lights and the slow pace, and every carrier in it is carrying. A kid who would rather be the rug-keeper, holding the row straight as lanterns arrive, has the job the whole parade is walking toward.

materials.item: paper or fabric lanterns with an LED tealight inside (one per kid, adult-assembled)
a rug or blanket (the parade's end)

activities.name: Lantern Carry Parade

photo.alt: Two children in festival dress carrying large paper lanterns in a night parade
photo.caption: Carrying the light: two children in festival dress, each with a big paper lantern, in a night parade.
photo.credit: Photo: Los Angeles Daily News, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: LED tealights only, no real flames, no sparklers, nothing that burns. Carrying is walking, always: a lantern that gets run with comes back to the line's end for one lap carried by the adult, kindly and without a speech. Handles are checked before the walk; a torn handle retires that lantern.
activities.setup: Assemble every lantern yourself before the group arrives: LED tealight inside, top handle taped or tied so it holds a gentle swing, and carry each one across the room yourself. A lantern that tips its light out in your hands gets fixed now, not in a three-year-old's. Set the rug at the far end as the place the parade is walking to.
steps: Name the real custom in one sentence, plainly: 'At the Lantern Festival, at the end of the Lunar New Year celebrations, people carry lanterns outside together. We are doing our small indoor one.' Then state the one rule: 'Two hands on the handle, walking feet. The lantern stays up.'

Hand out lanterns one at a time, lit, and let each kid practise the carry standing still: two hands, lantern held in front, a small sway is fine and a swing is not. Practising still is what makes the walk slow.

The parade walks: one slow line around the room, you at the front setting a pace a lantern can keep up with, the group naming what the lights look like as they go. That naming is the looking this festival is for.

Halfway stop: everyone raises their lantern slowly to shoulder height and holds it while the group counts to five out loud, then lowers it just as slowly. Lifting and lowering a light without swinging it is harder than it looks, and the counting gives it time.

Arrive at the rug: lanterns are set down in a row on the rug, still lit, and the group sits behind them and just looks for a moment. A row of lights you carried yourself is the ending. Lights off one by one as each lantern is collected.
activities.tagline: A made lantern with a safe light inside, carried with two hands on a slow walk around the room, the Lantern Festival, sized for three.

variations.easier: A shorter route, across the room and back, and the adult carries a lantern in the line too, so the pace is set from inside the parade.
variations.harder: A second lap where each carrier chooses one thing in the room to stop and hold their lantern up to, and names it to the group.

materials.item: nine LED tealights or LED candles (eight plus one helper light)
a long tray, board, or taped line on the table (the row)

activities.name: Eight Lights Line Up
activities.safety: LED lights only, never real candles or matches, the record says why in plain words if a kid asks: real flames are a grown-up job away from this table. LED tealights with screw-closed battery covers only; a light with a loose cover is retired on the spot, because button batteries are a serious hazard for this age.
activities.setup: Set the row first: a long tray or a taped line on a low table, with eight marked spots along it, tape crosses work, and count the spots out loud yourself as you mark them. Test every LED light before the group sits down; a light that will not switch on gets swapped now, not discovered by a kid mid-count.
steps: Set the scene in two plain sentences: 'On Hanukkah, families light candles on a holder called a menorah. One more light each night, for eight nights. We are putting our eight lights in a row, all in one go, and counting them as they light.' Put the helper light at the start of the row and switch it on: 'This one is the helper. It is not counted in the eight.'

State the one rule: 'One light at a time. We count it, then the next one.' The first kid places the first light on the first spot, switches it on, and the whole group counts 'one' together. The counting is done by everyone, every time.

Work down the row the same way, a different kid placing each light where they can: place, switch, count up from one together. Recounting from one every time is not inefficiency at three. It is the counting practice this activity is built around.

When all eight are lit, sit back and count the whole row once more, pointing at each light in turn, then name the helper again so the eight stays honest: eight counted lights, one helper, nine lights shining.

Lights-out round, in reverse: the last light placed is the first switched off, counted down, eight, seven, six, by the group, each light carried back to the basket by its placer. The count works both ways and the row ends empty.
activities.tagline: Eight LED lights in a row, put on one at a time and counted as they go. The Hanukkah lights, at a three-year-old's pace.

variations.easier: Four lights instead of eight, with the same one-at-a-time rule and a full recount after each. A shorter row is still a real row.
variations.harder: No marked spots: the placer has to judge the spacing so eight lights fit the tray, and the group helps with 'a bit more room' calls.

materials.item: six to ten long fabric ribbons or strips (adult-tied along a fence, rail, or low branch)
a rug or blanket to sit on

activities.name: Wind Ribbon Watch

photo.alt: An orange and white windsock flying against a blue sky
photo.caption: A windsock stretched out by the wind, a big ribbon that shows which way the air is moving.
photo.credit: Photo: Olaf Oliviero Riemer, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Ribbons are tied by an adult, out of reach of necks and climbing, nobody pulls ribbons down, ties them on themselves, or winds them around hands or wrists. The group stays seated on the rug during watching rounds; gusts are called with voices and fingers, not chased.
activities.setup: Tie the ribbons up yourself before the group comes out: along one fence or rail, spaced out, each tied short enough that it cannot wrap around anything and long enough to stream properly. Waist-height on an adult is about right for a seated group to watch. Tug every knot once; a ribbon that comes away in your hand gets retied now.
steps: Sit the group on the rug facing the ribbons and state the one job: 'The ribbons tell us what the wind is doing. When a gust comes, point at the ribbons and call it.' Model the first call yourself, big and pleased: 'Gust!'. Pointing is the participation, and it starts with you.

Quiet watching round: everyone watches and nobody calls for the first minute. Ribbons hanging still, then stirring, then streaming. Noticing the in-between states is the observation skill here, and it needs a quiet minute to show up.

Calling round: gusts get pointed at and called by whoever spots the movement first, and the group answers the call by looking where the finger points. There is no score; a call everyone checks is a call that worked.

Direction round: when a good gust streams all the ribbons one way, say the plain fact together: 'The wind is pushing them THAT way', and everyone points the way the ribbons lean. Same wind, same direction, said as one group.

Finish with the still test: the group watches for the moment every ribbon hangs completely still, and the kid who calls 'still!' first is believed only when the whole group agrees it is true, then one last gust usually ruins it, which is the correct ending and everyone knows it.
activities.tagline: Ribbons tied along a fence by a grown-up, and one job: watch them, point when a gust comes, and say which way the wind is pushing.

variations.easier: Three ribbons only, tied close together, and the adult calls the first three gusts, a smaller picture to watch.
variations.harder: Two ribbon spots in different places (fence and branch): the group watches one, then the other, and says which spot has more wind today.

activities.inclusion: Prints are prints: wheelchair tracks, a walker frame's marks, or the paired lines of a kid walking with support all write in snow exactly as boots do, and the trail count at the edge counts every track the group made. A kid who watches from the edge is the group's print-spotter. The first to call out when a new set of prints reaches the flag.

materials.item: fresh untrodden snow on flat ground
one scarf or flag (the turnaround point)

activities.name: Boot Print Snow Trail

photo.alt: Hiking boots and foot print in fresh snow
photo.caption: Hiking boots and foot print in fresh snow.
photo.credit: Photo: Th. Voekler, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Flat snow only, a short route, boots on every foot, and the walk stays a walk. Running in snow over unseen ground is how ankles turn. Cold is the limit: when hands or faces say they have had enough, the trail is done, finished or not, and going in is never a punishment.
activities.setup: Pick the patch honestly before the group comes out: flat, shallow fresh snow nobody has walked on yet, well inside the usual safe ground. Push the flag in at the far end yourself, walking around the patch's edge to get there so the middle stays clean. The untrodden snow is the whole point, and your own boots can spoil it before it starts.
steps: Stand the group at the edge and look at the clean snow together first: 'Nobody has walked here. The first prints will be ours.' State the one rule: 'Walk in a line, in my steps or your own, and we all stop at the flag.'

Walk out one kid at a time, or you first, then each kid in your prints or beside them, at a slow walk, all the way to the flag. Fresh prints appearing behind a walker is the sight this activity exists for, and the watchers at the edge get to see it happen.
At the flag, turn around together and look back: a whole line of prints where there was nothing. Say the plain fact out loud: 'We made that. Those are our steps, saved in the snow.'

Walk back in the prints: each kid tries to step in their own prints coming back. Some will fit, some will land beside, and both are fine and funny. Nobody is corrected; prints in snow are allowed to be approximate.

Edge count to finish: from the edge, count the prints you can see in one kid's trail out loud together, pointing at each one. However many it is, that is that kid's number of steps to the flag today. Write nothing down, the snow keeps the record.
activities.tagline: Fresh snow, one short walk, and your own boot prints behind you: walk out, turn around, count your steps back along your own trail.

variations.easier: A shorter patch and the adult's prints only: kids walk in the grown-up's big prints, which is its own game and needs no trail of their own.
variations.harder: Two trails side by side, a kid and the adult walk out together, and at the flag the group compares: whose prints are bigger, whose are closer together.

activities.inclusion: Wheeling across a paper puddle counts as stepping in it in full: a route wide enough for wheels is the setup, not an adaptation, and the counting pass counts those crossings with the rest. A kid can also be the rain, the one who calls 'heavy rain!' to start the stomp round and 'drizzle' to end it, a job with real weather authority.

materials.item: eight to ten big blue paper or card ovals (adult-cut, each bigger than two kid feet)

activities.name: Paper Puddle Stepping

photo.alt: "In April" illustration for "Baby's Lullaby Book ... by Charles Stuart Pratt" showing a young child stepping in puddles on a rainy day in Spring; a young woman is standing at the open LCCN2017650213
photo.caption: "In April" illustration for "Baby's Lullaby Book ... by Charles Stuart Pratt" showing a young child stepping in puddles on a rainy day in Spring; a young woman is standing at the open LCCN2017650213.
photo.credit: Photo: L. Prang & Co., publisher; L. Prang & Co., copyright claimant; Taylor, W, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Puddles are taped flat and tested by an adult first, a sliding paper oval on a hard floor is a fall, and any puddle that tears or lifts gets re-taped or removed on the spot. Stepping and stomping happen on the spot; nobody jumps puddle to puddle.
activities.setup: Cut and tape the puddles down before the group arrives: a wandering route around the room, each puddle flat and taped at the edges, walk the route yourself and stamp on every puddle once; a puddle that slides or curls under your foot gets more tape now, because a skating puddle ends the game early. Leave honest gaps of floor between puddles: the dry parts are part of the route.
steps: Show the route and state the one rule, which is the joy of it: 'Step IN the puddles. Both feet in, every time. The floor between is dry land. The puddles are the part we WANT.' Model one crossing yourself, landing two-footed in a puddle and standing in it proudly.

One kid on the route at a time: step in, stand a moment, step out to dry land, step in the next. The standing-in is not a pause in the game. Standing in a puddle you are allowed to stand in IS the game.
Counting pass: the watchers count the puddles out loud as the walker stands in each one. The walker who hears their biggest number yet has done a longer route, and the group will say so.
Heavy-rain round: the same route, but now each puddle gets two small stomps in it before moving on, indoor rain, paper water, real stomping, and the taped edges are why it works.

Last pass is the flood: everyone walks the route together in a line, puddle to puddle, and the final puddle holds the whole group's feet at once if it can. Count the feet in it together, then puddles are peeled up by their owners and stacked for the next rainy day.
activities.tagline: Big blue paper puddles on the floor indoors, and the rule is the good one: step IN every puddle. Dry feet, wet pretend.

variations.easier: Five puddles in a straight line, close together, with an adult hand available the whole way.
variations.harder: One fork in the route: two puddles side by side, and the walker chooses which one. The route is theirs from the fork on.

materials.item: big easy-squeeze serving tongs (one pair per kid working)
big ice cubes (large moulds or bought big cubes)
two trays or wide bowls per kid (one full, one empty)
a towel (for drips and cold hands)

activities.name: Big Tongs Ice Move

photo.alt: A stack of clear ice cubes
photo.caption: A stack of clear ice cubes.
photo.credit: Photo: Darren Hester, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Ice is for tonging and looking at, not for mouths. Cubes big enough to grip are still a choking hazard if sucked small, so this is a watched table activity and cubes stay on trays. Cold hands get the towel and a break whenever a kid asks; numb fingers drop things, and that is information, not failure.
activities.setup: Freeze big cubes ahead. The biggest moulds you have; a cube that cannot be gripped by the tongs at all will teach nothing but frustration, so test your own pair of tongs on one cube before the group sits down. Set each working spot with a full tray, an empty tray a short carry apart, and the towel in reach: melting is guaranteed, so plan for the drips instead of minding them.
steps: Start with tongs in the air, no ice: open, shut, open, shut, then pick up a soft thing (a big pom-pom or a sponge) and carry it across. The grip has to exist before the slippery version of it is fair to ask for.

State the one rule: 'One cube at a time. The tongs carry it. Hands do not help.' First cube together: grip low on the cube, lift a little, move slowly. A dropped cube goes back on the full tray and gets tried again; dropped is a normal result with ice, say so plainly.

Moving round: each kid moves cubes at their own pace, and every cube that lands in the empty tray gets counted out loud by the mover, or by a counting partner, as it lands. The count is the record of the work.

Melting check, halfway: stop and look at the full tray. The cubes are smaller and the tray has water in it. Say the plain fact: 'The ice is turning into water while we work. The last cubes will be the slipperiest.' They will be, and now the group knows why.

Finish when the full tray holds only water: count the moved cubes one last time in the receiving tray, tip the melt water onto plants or the garden together, and dry the tongs with the towel. Tools get put away dry, even at three.
activities.tagline: Big serving tongs, big ice cubes, one tray to another: grip one, carry it, drop it in, count it. Cold hands, careful work.

variations.easier: Bigger cubes, tongs with a shorter reach, and the two trays touching edge to edge. The carry is one small lift across a seam.
variations.harder: Smaller cubes in the last round, or the receiving tray moved a step further away so the carry is longer and slower.

activities.inclusion: The chooser's job is a full turn done entirely by pointing: a kid who picks the pair, points their prediction, and calls, or signs, or shows, 'down!' when the beam moves has run the test; a partner's hands do the placing to their direction. Directing the test is doing the test, and the group hears it said.

materials.item: a simple two-pan balance scale (sturdy classroom kind)
pairs of big objects to compare (a big stone and a big sponge, a wooden block and a foam block, a full and an empty small bottle)

activities.name: Pan Balance Heavy Light

photo.alt: Children Activities. Children Gardens BAnQ P48S1P06405
photo.caption: Children Activities. Children Gardens BAnQ P48S1P06405.
photo.credit: Photo: Conrad Poirier, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Objects are big, blunt and unbreakable, nothing glass, nothing with edges, nothing small enough to mouth. Hands stay off the balance while it settles: fingers under a dropping pan get pinched, so the hands-off rule is said before the first object and kept kindly. The scale stays on the table; nobody carries it loaded.
activities.setup: Set the balance on a table the group can see over and test it empty first: both pans level, beam swinging free, a balance that sticks or leans on its own gets fixed or swapped now, because a rigged result teaches the wrong lesson. Lay the object pairs out in a row where everyone can see them; every object must be big enough that no mouth is a plausible destination.
steps: Start with the empty balance and the one idea, in plain words: 'Two sides. Put one thing on each side. The side that goes DOWN is carrying the heavier thing.' Do the first test yourself with the most obvious pair you have, stone versus sponge, and let the beam say it.

State the one rule for the testers: 'One thing per side, hands off while it settles.' A kid chooses the next pair, places one object in each pan, with help lifting where needed, and everyone waits with hands behind backs while the beam decides.
Call the result together, every time, in the same sentence shape: 'The stone went down. The stone is heavier.' The sentence is the science report at three, and the repetition is what builds it.

Prediction round: before each new pair is placed, hands go on heads for 'this one will go down', point at the object you back, then the balance settles it. Being wrong is data: 'We thought sponge. The beam says stone. The beam wins.'

Finish with the equal test: the same object on both sides, two matching blocks, and the beam stays level. Say why, plainly: 'Same thing, same heaviness, nobody goes down.' Then objects go back in their row, in pairs, by the testers.
activities.tagline: A two-pan balance and big things to test: one thing per side, watch which side goes down. That side is carrying the heavier one.

variations.easier: The adult places every object and the kids only call the result. Watching and naming is a full turn at this.
variations.harder: Three-object line-up: test pairs until the group can lay three tested objects in a row from heaviest to lightest, using only the beam's results.

activities.inclusion: Pulling is one job on a crew with several: the loader who counts the cargo in, the road-crew checker who tucks it safe, and the unloader who lays the row at the station all deliver the same toys. A kid can pull from a seated position alongside the handle's low end with the wagon moving at their pace. The wagon goes at the crew's pace, and the crew is everybody.

materials.item: a small sturdy wagon with a pull handle (child-size)
soft toys or beanbags (the cargo, six to ten pieces)

activities.name: Toy Wagon Pull Together

photo.alt: Laura Kiehl pulling Miriam Kiehl in an "Iron Clad" wagon, Magnolia Bluff, Seattle, May 27, 1899 (KIEHL 302)
photo.caption: Laura Kiehl pulling Miriam Kiehl in an "Iron Clad" wagon, Magnolia Bluff, Seattle, May 27, 1899 (KIEHL 302).
photo.credit: Photo: H. Ambrose Kiehl, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Walking only, ever. A wagon pulled at a run tips, and tipping wagons land on feet. Hands on the handle only while pulling; nobody rides in the wagon, nobody sits on its edges, and fingers stay out of the wheels. The route keeps clear of slopes the wagon could roll down on its own.
activities.setup: Set the station first: the blanket laid flat across the room or yard, the wagon at the loading end with the cargo in a pile beside it. Test the route yourself with the empty wagon. A route the wagon tips on gets shortened or moved now; the pullers' job is pulling, not rescuing a tipped wagon. Check the handle and wheels roll freely.
steps: Load together: the whole group puts the cargo in the wagon, one piece each in turn, counting the pieces in out loud. State the one rule before anyone pulls: 'The wagon goes slow, and it only goes when BOTH pullers are holding on.'

Two pullers on the handle, side by side, hands on, and the trip is a walk, at the pace of the slower puller, with the rest of the group as the road crew walking alongside, never in front of the wheels.
Halfway stop, on your call: pullers swap sides, road crew checks the cargo. A toy riding near the edge gets tucked back in by its loader. Checking the load is part of delivering it, said out loud.

Arrive at the blanket: the group unloads together, one piece each in turn, laying the toys out on the blanket in a row, and counts them back out. The count in and the count out must match, and finding a missing one in the wagon is the group's detective moment.

Return trip: two new pullers take the empty wagon back the same slow way, road crew alongside. Then new loaders start the next delivery if there is time. Everyone who wants a turn pulling gets one before anyone gets a second.
activities.tagline: A small wagon, a load of soft toys, and a blanket across the room: two pullers, one slow trip, every toy delivered together.

variations.easier: A shorter trip, blanket ten steps away, and one puller plus the adult's hand on the handle beside theirs.
variations.harder: Two deliveries to two blankets: the loaders call which station each load is for, and the road crew has to remember it on arrival.

materials.item: one soft toy or doll per kid (the program's, or their own from home)

activities.name: Teddy Says My Name

photo.alt: Teddy bear that says remote controlled (via smartphone app) sentences
photo.caption: Teddy bear that says remote controlled (via smartphone app) sentences.
photo.credit: Photo: Syced, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Toys are held, never thrown. A thrown teddy sits with the adult until its turn, kindly. Program toys go back in the basket at the end; a kid's own toy from home stays in their own hands throughout if that is what they need, and introducing from inside a hug counts in full.
activities.setup: Gather the toys in a basket in the middle before anyone sits: a mix of bears, dolls and whatever soft things the program owns, enough for a real choice. Choosing your toy is the first minute of this activity and it is not wasted time. Sit the circle first, toys second, so the choosing does not happen over laps.
steps: Each kid picks a toy from the basket and holds it in their lap. Model the whole thing first with your own toy, held up where the circle can see it: 'This is Bruno. Bruno says: my friend's name is Sam, and Sam loves puddles.' Short, plain, a bit silly. Your turn sets the size of theirs.

State the one rule: 'The toy does the talking.' The kid holds the toy up; the toy 'says' the kid's name and one thing they love, in the kid's own voice, a whisper to you that you relay in the toy's voice, or a point at the thing if it is in the room. All three are the toy talking.

Go around the circle with no skipping-pressure: a kid who passes gets a 'teddy will wait' and the circle comes back to them once at the end, by which time they have heard ten examples and the toy has usually found its voice.
Favourites echo: after each introduction, the whole circle says the love back to the toy, 'Puddles! Sam loves puddles!', so every kid hears their thing said gladly by the whole room, once.

Finish with the toys introduced to each other: two neighbouring teddies 'shake hands' (paws touched together by their holders) and the holders say each other's names across the handshake. Toys go back to the basket by name, 'Back you go, Bruno', which the group will insist on doing properly.
activities.tagline: Every kid holds a soft toy, and the toy does the introducing: its name, your name, and one thing you love. Shy voices welcome. Teddies are brave.

variations.easier: Names only, no favourite thing. The toy says the name, the circle echoes the name, done.
variations.harder: Add the toy's own favourite: each toy also 'says' what IT loves (honey, naps, being squeezed), invented entirely by its holder.

activities.inclusion: Standing with the group is the landing however you get there, wheeling in, walking with support, or being the friend everyone gathers at all count exactly the same, and a bright colour on a wheelchair, a frame or a brace is a colour being worn, full stop. A kid who would rather hold the cards with the adult and choose the next colour has the job that runs the game.

materials.item: five or six big colour cards (adult-made from coloured paper or card, big, plain, one colour each)

activities.name: Find a Friend Wearing
activities.safety: Finding is walking. The colours get exciting, the feet do not, and that is said before the first card. Standing groups leave room around them; nobody pulls a friend to a gathering by the arm. You go and stand WITH them, which is the whole social point stated as a safety rule too.
activities.setup: Make the cards ahead from the colours actually in the room: look at what the group wears on a normal day, red tops, blue shoes, yellow hair clips, and cut cards for those colours, big enough to read across the room. A colour nobody is wearing makes a dead round, so the deck is built from the room's real clothes, honestly.
steps: Sit the circle and show every card first, with its colour named by the whole group out loud each time. The naming is the rehearsal, and a kid who can name the colour can play the whole game.

State the one rule: 'I hold up a colour. If YOU are wearing it, stand up. Everyone else: find a friend who is wearing it, go and stand with them, and wave.' Nobody is out; the watchers have the finding job, which is the bigger one.

First rounds are slow on purpose: hold the card high, let the wearing kids stand, then let the finders walk, walking, always, and gather. When every finder has landed, the whole gathered group waves at the circle and the colour gets named once more, together.

Swap the job: the seated kids become the checkers, 'Is everyone standing with the right colour?', and the group checks the gatherings honestly, kindly fixing a wrong-colour landing by walking the finder to the right group together.

Finish with the rainbow round: hold the cards up one after another, fast enough to be funny, and each kid stands when their colour shows and sits when it changes, ending with every card fanned in your hands and the whole circle standing and waving at once.
activities.tagline: The grown-up holds up one big colour card. Somewhere in the circle, somebody is wearing that colour. Go and stand with them, and wave.

variations.easier: Two colours only, and finders walk with an adult to the first gathering. The route is learned before it is trusted.
variations.harder: Two-colour cards: find a friend wearing BOTH colours, somewhere on them, a much harder hunt, and the checkers earn their job.

materials.item: a small watering can (child-size, with a rose head if you have one)
plants in pots or a garden bed that actually need water
a tap, butt, or bucket of water (for refills, adult-managed)

activities.name: Watering Can Plant Round

photo.alt: Child watering plants in a vibrant garden on a sunny day
photo.caption: Child watering plants in a vibrant garden on a sunny day.
photo.credit: Photo: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Half-full cans only, two hands, walking feet. A swinging can of water is heavy enough to pull a small kid off balance. Water goes on soil, never at faces or over other kids, and wet paths get walked around, not through: the round's own spills make the ground slippery behind it. Hands wash after garden work, every time.
activities.setup: Check the round yourself first with the can half full: walk it. A can that drips down your leg at a walk is too full, and a plant route crossing steps or slopes with a carried can is a route to shorten now. Half full is the working amount at three: heavy enough to feel like a job, light enough to arrive. Know which plants actually need water today; watering plants that do not is rehearsal, and kids can tell the difference by the soil. Show them dry soil before you start.
steps: At the first plant, teach the pour yourself: two hands on the can, tip slowly, water landing on the soil at the bottom of the plant, not on its leaves from a height. Say the one rule while you do it: 'Two hands, walking feet, water on the soil.'

First carrier: fill the can half full together, and the kid carries it, two hands, at a walk, to the next plant, with you alongside and the group following as the watering crew. A spill on the way is water landing early, nothing more; it gets named as such and the round continues.

The pour is the carrier's own: they tip, they watch the soil change colour as it drinks, they stop when the can is empty or you call 'that plant has had its drink'. Empty-can shake at the end is traditional and required.

Crew jobs rotate with the can: the next kid refills with the adult, the next carries, and the kid who just poured becomes the soil-checker, finger touched gently to the soil, 'wet now' reported to the group. Every kid on the round has a job on every plant.

Finish at the last plant with the empty can held up: the crew names every plant they watered, in order, pointing back along the round. Then the can is emptied of its last drops onto the driest soil anyone can find, and hung up by its final carrier.
activities.tagline: One small watering can, half full, carried with two hands to the real plants: pour slowly, empty it, and the plants have been watered by you.

variations.easier: Two plants, close to the water source, and the adult carries the can back empty. The pour and one short carry are the round.
variations.harder: A longer round with a halfway refill, and the soil-checker reports 'still dry' or 'wet now' before each pour so the crew decides where the water goes.

materials.item: one soft doll or toy per kid (the program's babies and teddies)
no other materials. One slow song the adult can sing

activities.name: Lullaby Rock and Sway
activities.safety: Dolls are rocked, never swung or thrown. A doll that leaves someone's arms sits the next verse out in the middle, kindly. Sitting spots get elbow room before the music starts; rocking into a neighbour is a spacing problem the adult fixes by moving spots, not a behaviour problem. Quiet voices are kept genuinely quiet. A lullaby at shouting volume is just shouting with a doll.
activities.setup: Pick the song first and keep it slow and known: a lullaby the group has heard at rest time, or any gentle song you can sing without hurrying. The tempo of the song IS the tempo of the rocking, so a rushed song makes rushed rocking. Clear a sitting space where every kid can sit with legs out or crossed and a doll in their arms without an elbow in a neighbour.
steps: Hand out the dolls and let everyone settle theirs in their arms their own way first, cradled, upright, over a shoulder. Then model the rock: side to side, slow, in time with your own humming of the song's first line. State the one rule: 'Rock with the song. When the song stops, the rocking stops. The baby is asleep.'

First verse together: you sing, the group rocks their dolls in time, and you keep your own rock big and visible. Your sway is the metronome the room is following, so make it steady and a little exaggerated.

Quiet verse: the singing drops to a hum and the rocking gets smaller with it, not because anyone said to, but because the room can feel it. Name it afterwards, plainly: 'The humming made the rocking smaller. You did that by listening.'

Swap the singer: a kid who wants to leads the next verse, singing, humming, or la-la-ing it, and the whole group's rocking follows THEIR speed. Following a friend's tempo instead of yours is the musicianship this activity is quietly teaching.

Final verse, the sleep verse: sing it slower and quieter each line, the rocking shrinking with it, until the last line is nearly a whisper and the dolls are still. Hold the stillness for a count of five before anyone moves, a room full of sleeping dolls, rocked to sleep by their people, is the ending and it lands every time.
activities.tagline: A soft doll in your arms and one slow song from the whole group: rock side to side in time, and when the song ends, the baby is asleep.

variations.easier: One verse only, adult singing throughout, and rocking in laps while seated on the floor. The sway can be tiny and still be in time.
variations.harder: Standing rock for the last verse: everyone stands, swaying with their doll, and has to keep the sway as slow standing as it was sitting.

activities.inclusion: The tree's low half belongs to seated decorators: pieces placed from a chair, a lap tray or the floor reach the tree in full, and the counting counts every press the same. A kid who would rather be the basket-keeper, choosing which pieces are offered next, is running the decorating, not watching it.

materials.item: a big felt or flannel tree shape (adult-cut, pinned or taped flat at kid height)
big felt stars, circles and simple shapes (adult-cut, each bigger than a kid's palm)

activities.name: Felt Tree, One by One
activities.safety: Pieces are palm-size or bigger and plain felt, no pins, no hooks, no small ornaments, nothing glass, and nothing with a button battery goes anywhere near this tree. The tree is fixed flat by an adult and checked daily; a peeling corner gets re-taped before a kid finds it with their fingers.
activities.setup: Fix the tree up yourself before the group arrives: flat against a low wall or board, bottom edge at a seated kid's shoulder height, and press every piece onto it yourself once, a piece that slides off in your hand will slide off in theirs, so rough felt or a dot of repositionable glue on the tree fixes it now. Pieces go in the basket beside the tree, all of them, so choosing is part of the activity.
steps: Name the real thing in one plain sentence: 'At Christmas, lots of families decorate a tree, putting one thing on at a time until it is full. This is our tree, and we are decorating it our size.' State the one rule: 'One piece at a time. Press it flat with your whole hand.'

First piece together: a kid chooses from the basket, carries it to the tree in two hands, and presses it on with a whole palm while the group counts the press, 'one!', out loud. The count is the ceremony; a tree decorated one counted piece at a time takes exactly as long as it takes.

Go around the same way, one piece per kid per round, the group counting up after every press: the number the group reaches is the number of pieces on the tree, checked by pointing at each one as it is counted. Counting things you put there yourself is the sturdiest counting there is.

Full-tree moment: when the basket is empty, everyone steps back, or wheels back, and looks. Name what the group can see in plain words: the colours, the star somebody chose for the top, the piece hanging lowest. Looking at finished work together is part of finishing it.

Taking-down is a second activity, not a chore: pieces come off one at a time, counted down by the group, each carried back to the basket by its decorator. The tree ends bare and the basket ends full, ready for the next group to do the whole thing again.
activities.tagline: A big felt tree low on the wall and big soft pieces to press onto it, one kid, one piece, one at a time, a first tree to decorate.

variations.easier: A smaller tree and eight pieces, with the adult's hand over theirs for the press. The choice of WHICH piece is still entirely the kid's.
variations.harder: A pattern round: the adult quietly names a shape, 'the tree needs a star', and the decorator has to find that shape in the basket before the press.

activities.inclusion: Feeling the patches works from any height: a seated kid's hands reach the same sun, and the rug in the shade is placed so wheels and walkers are IN the shade patch, not beside it. A kid who cannot say 'warm' can show it. Hand pressed to the adult's cheek from each patch is a weather report the whole group understands.

materials.item: a sunny patch of ground with a shady patch right beside it (under a tree, an awning, or a building's shadow)
a rug or mat (the shade stop)

activities.name: Sun Patch, Shade Patch
activities.safety: Sun time is short and this activity is why: a minute or two of standing in a sun patch, in hats where the program uses them, and the shade is always the home base. Nobody is left standing in full sun while the group talks. Hot ground is checked with an adult hand first; a patch too hot to stand on in bare legs is a patch for another day.
activities.setup: Scout the patches yourself first, an hour matters: you need sun and shade BESIDE each other at the time the group goes out, with the shade big enough for the whole group to stand in. Stand in both yourself, if your own hands cannot feel the difference today, the weather has not provided this activity and it waits for a better day, honestly.
steps: Gather the group in the shade first and state the one job: 'We are finding out what the sun does. Hands out, palms up. Feel.' Everyone holds their hands out in the shade and names what they feel in whatever words they have, cool, nothing, wind, all answers are weather reports.

Walk the group into the sun patch together and stand still: hands out, palms up, same as before. Give it a real minute. Warmth arrives slowly on skin, and hurrying past it teaches nothing. Then the plain sentence, said together: 'The sun is warm.'

Back to the shade, same still minute, same hands out. The sentence this side: 'The shade is cool.' Two patches, two sentences, felt on the same hands a minute apart. That comparison is the whole science at three, and it is real science.

Choice round: each kid picks their patch, sun or shade, and stands in it while the group calls out where everyone is standing. A kid who keeps swapping patches to feel the change again is doing the activity more, not less.

Finish in the shade with the mat down: sit, hands in laps, and one last call of the two sentences by the whole group, pointing at each patch as it is named. The patches will move by tomorrow. Say so; shadows walking is next year's activity.
activities.tagline: A sunny patch and a shady patch side by side, and one job: stand in each one and feel the difference on your own hands.

variations.easier: Two patches only and the adult's hands as the example: hold one hand in sun and one in shade yourself first, and let each kid feel your warm hand and your cool hand.
variations.harder: Add a middle patch, half sun, half shade across the body, and let kids stand astride the line and report which SIDE of them is warm.

activities.inclusion: Getting to the rug counts however you travel, wheeling, walking with support, or carried steps with an adult all land dry in full, and the rug is big enough that the whole group fits with wheels on it too. A kid who would rather work the weather can hold the rain shaker with the adult and make the rain come, the most powerful job in the room.

materials.item: a rain stick or a sealed shaker with rice or beans inside (the rain sound)
a big rug or mat (the dry place)

activities.name: Rain Call: To the Rug
activities.safety: The umbrella is held by an adult only, opened high and away from faces, and its spokes never come down to kid height. It is a signal, not a shelter, and nobody goes under it. Rain calls are walked, never run: a room of three-year-olds converging on one rug is a pile-up at a run and a pleasure at a walk. The shaker stays sealed; a split shaker is retired, not taped and trusted.
activities.setup: Set the room honestly: the rug goes at one end as the dry place, and the walking space between must be clear enough for excited three-year-olds moving at a walk. Move the chair that will get bumped now, not after. Test your signals: umbrella up high in one hand, rain sound in the other, and practise the two calls yourself so the group learns one signal, not a muddle.
steps: Start with everyone on the rug, the dry place, and teach the weather: umbrella DOWN and no rain sound means sun, and in the sun we walk around the room. Umbrella UP with the rain sound means rain, and the one rule: 'When the rain comes, walk to the rug and crouch down dry.' Model both calls once, slowly, yourself.
