Sun round: umbrella down, the group walks the room, around, not across the rug, while you name the weather like a forecast: 'Still sunny... still sunny...' Walking in the sun is the waiting part, and the waiting is what makes the call exciting.

Rain call: umbrella up, rain sound shaking, and the whole group walks, walking feet, said every time, to the rug and crouches down dry, hands on knees, while the rain sound lasts. When it stops and the umbrella drops: 'Sun's back!' and everyone stands and walks again.

Long-rain round: once, make the rain last. A full slow count of ten of rain sound while the group stays crouched and dry, making small rain pats on their own knees. Staying dry through a long rain, together, is the game's big moment.

Finish with the weather report: the group sits on the rug and you ask what happened, in order, sun, rain, sun, and they will tell it back like a story, because it was one. Umbrella closed and put away by the adult while they watch: signals get retired properly.
activities.tagline: The grown-up raises an umbrella and shakes the rain sound, rain! Everyone walks to the rug and crouches down dry until the sun comes back.

variations.easier: Sun walking in a small circle near the rug and the adult walks the first two rain calls WITH the group, crouching in the middle of the rug like everybody else.
variations.harder: A second signal to tell apart: umbrella up with NO rain sound means drizzle. Walk to the rug but stay standing, because drizzle is not worth crouching for.

materials.item: a window at kid height with real rain running down the outside
a stool or step for shorter kids (adult-placed)
a dry cloth (for wet fingers and fogged spots)

activities.name: Window Raindrop Follow

photo.alt: Large raindrops beading and running on a window pane
photo.caption: Raindrops on the glass, big and clear: pick one and follow it all the way down.
photo.credit: Photo: The Eloquent Peasant, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Fingers stay on the inside glass, flat and gentle, no banging, no leaning body weight on the pane, and stools are placed and held by an adult, never climbed mid-game. The window stays shut whatever the weather is doing; the rain is watched, not let in. If thunder starts, the group leaves the window. Storm watching is not this activity.
activities.setup: This activity cannot be faked and should not be: it needs a rainy day and a window the rain actually hits, low enough for a three-year-old to reach the top of the glass. Stand there yourself first and watch one drop make the whole trip, if the rain is too light to run today, say so and save the activity; a window of still drops is a different, shorter look, not this.
steps: Gather the group at the window and watch together for a moment before any fingers go up: drops landing, sitting, then suddenly sliding. Say the plain fact the whole activity hangs on: 'A drop slides when it gets heavy enough. Watch. It will take other drops with it.'

State the one job: 'Pick a drop near the top. Finger BESIDE it, on our side of the glass. Follow your drop down.' Model it once with your own finger riding beside a sliding drop, slow enough for the group to track.

Following round: each kid picks a drop and rides a finger down beside it. Drops will merge mid-slide, when yours joins a bigger drop, say so out loud: 'My drop got bigger!', because merging is not losing your drop, it is what rain does, and the group will report every merge like news.

Race-that-isn't round: two kids pick two drops side by side and follow both. One will win; nobody chose the weather, so the result belongs to the rain. Name that plainly, because this is the rare race where the loser did nothing wrong and everyone can see it.

Finish when the rain eases or the window runs dry of runners: count together how many drops the group followed all the way to the bottom, the number is whatever it is, then the cloth wipes the fingerprints off the glass, because the next rainy day deserves a clean window.
activities.tagline: Real rain on a real window: pick one drop at the top, put your finger beside it on the glass, and follow it all the way down.

variations.easier: The adult picks the drop and every finger follows the SAME one together. One shared drop, no choosing, still a full follow when it slides.
variations.harder: Follow a drop with your eyes only, hands in laps, and call 'now!' at the exact moment it starts to slide. Watching for the start is the harder skill.

activities.inclusion: Sorting is a full test done by direction: a kid who points at a tray while a partner lifts has called the result, and calling it is the science. The wand can be worked two-handed, rested on the table edge, or moved along a lap tray. The tray set-up travels to the tester, never the other way round.

materials.item: big encased magnet wands (one per kid, the chunky classroom kind, magnet sealed inside)
big smooth metal jar lids and lids from big cans (adult-checked, no sharp rims)
big non-metal things to test (a wooden block, a big plastic lid, a sponge, a fabric scrap)

activities.name: Big Magnet Wand: It Sticks
activities.safety: Encased classroom wands only. The magnet is sealed inside the plastic and can never come out. Loose small magnets of any kind never appear at this table, ever: they are a genuine emergency if swallowed, and this record says so in plain words so no substitute improvises with fridge magnets. Lids are big, smooth-rimmed and adult-checked; wand work stays on the table, and wands are never put in mouths.
activities.setup: Check every test object with your own wand before the group sits down: the metal lids must actually stick (some lids are aluminium and will not. An all-fails tray teaches the wrong lesson), and every rim gets a thumb run around it for sharpness; a lid that fails either check does not reach the table. Set each place with a mixed handful, some that stick, some that don't, because a tray that all sticks is a demo, not a test.
steps: Start with the wand alone in the air: wave it, turn it over, look at it together. Say the one plain fact that frames everything: 'This wand is a magnet. Magnets stick to SOME things. Our job is finding out which.' No more theory than that. The table is the theory now.

State the one rule: 'One thing at a time. Touch it with the wand. If it sticks, it rides to the sticks tray. If it doesn't, it goes to the other tray.' First test together, slowly: touch a big lid, lift. It comes with the wand, and the whole group says it: 'It sticks!'

Testing round: each kid works through their handful at their own pace, touch, lift or not, sort, with the two sentences running constantly. 'It sticks!' / 'It doesn't.' The sentences are the data at three, and the trays filling up are the graph.

Surprise check, halfway: hold up the two trays and look together. The sticks tray is all lids; the other tray is wood, plastic, sponge, cloth. Say the pattern in the plainest words: 'The sticking ones are all metal lids. The magnet is choosing the metal.' That sentence is earned by their own hands by now.

Finish with the wand trick that never fails: a lid stuck UNDER the table, held through it, sliding along as the wand moves on top. Do it once yourself, then let each tester try while the group watches the lid travel by itself. Trays tipped back into the basket by their testers; wands collected and counted.
activities.tagline: One big magnet wand and a tray of big things: touch each one and find out. It sticks, or it doesn't. Your hand is the lab.

variations.easier: Four objects only, two that stick and two that don't, and the adult does the lifting while the kid points at the right tray. Choosing the tray is the test result.
variations.harder: Hide-and-stick round: the adult hides three lids under a cloth and the tester fishes with the wand alone, if it comes up stuck to the wand, it was metal, sight unseen.

activities.inclusion: The crew is bigger than the corners: the hush-crew chief who raises the stop hand, the loader who lays Teddy down, and the tucker-in who finishes the job all carry Teddy to bed. A carrier can hold a corner seated at the route's middle station for the blanket's halfway rest, a real stop the carry genuinely needs, so the blanket visits them on its way.

materials.item: a cushion or folded mat across the room (the bed)

activities.name: Blanket Carry: Teddy to Bed
activities.safety: Walking only, and the blanket stays LOW, a dropped teddy from knee height onto a mat is a story point, a raised blanket is how carriers trip. Nobody rides on the blanket and nobody is carried, ever: Teddy is the only passenger, and the rule is said before the first load, kindly and once. Routes are cleared before loading, not during.
activities.setup: Walk the route yourself first carrying one corner of the blanket: it should be short, flat and clear, a carried blanket hangs low between two small carriers, so anything on the floor is a trip and anything sticking out is a snag. Lay the bed out properly at the far end, pillow on it, so arriving looks like arriving. Teddy starts the activity sitting up by the blanket, wide awake, and the group will fix that.
steps: Tell the one small story that runs the whole activity: 'Teddy is very nearly asleep. He cannot walk to bed. Two carriers can take him, on the blanket, slowly, without waking him.' State the one rule: 'The blanket stays low and level, and we walk. If Teddy wakes, we have gone too fast.'

Load together: two carriers hold the blanket's near corners, two more, or the adult, hold the far ones, blanket stretched low between them, and Teddy is laid in the middle by the whole group, one hand each where hands are offered. A four-corner carry at three is a crew job, and crewing it is the teamwork.

The carry: walking feet, blanket low, eyes on Teddy. The non-carriers walk alongside as the hush-crew, one finger on lips, making the corridor quiet. Their job is real: a woken Teddy is a group result, and so is a sleeping one.

Arrive: at the bed, the carriers lower the blanket slowly together, 'down, down, down' said by the hush-crew as the count, until Teddy rests on the cushion, then the blanket slides out from under him one corner at a time. A carrier does the tuck: pillow under his head, blanket folded over him from the stretcher itself.

Report and rotate: the group gathers round the bed and the hush-crew reports, in whispers, 'He's asleep.' Then new carriers take the blanket, Teddy is 'woken' gently by the adult and carried back the same slow way. Everyone who wants a carry gets one before anyone gets a second.
activities.tagline: Two carriers, one small blanket held low, and a big teddy who is very nearly asleep: walk him to his bed without waking him.

variations.easier: Two carriers only, short route, the adult holding the two far corners. The level blanket is demonstrated by doing it alongside them.
variations.harder: A second passenger joins mid-route: the hush-crew chief stops the carry with a raised hand, a doll is laid beside Teddy without a jiggle, and the carry continues heavier and slower.

materials.item: no materials, voices and hands only

activities.name: Name Echo, Two Claps
activities.safety: Echoes copy names kindly or not at all: a name is said the way its owner said it, never funnier, never louder-then-laughed-at. The rule is stated once, plainly, before the first name, because names are the one thing in the room that belongs entirely to the kid who carries it. Claps stay at talking volume; this is a hello, not a drum line.
activities.setup: No set-up beyond a real circle: everyone seated where they can see the speaker, knees in, hands free. Say the size of the thing before it starts. This takes five minutes and that is its virtue: it is a first-days activity for a room where nobody knows anybody's name yet, adults included, so the adult goes first and goes honestly.
steps: Model the whole game with your own name, start to finish: stand or sit tall, say 'My name is ___' once, clearly, at a three-year-old's pace. The circle's job, taught now, before anyone is on the spot, is to say the name right back, the same way, then clap twice together: clap, clap.

State the one rule: 'One name at a time, and the echo says it JUST like the speaker.' Go around the circle in order, no volunteering order, no spotlight roulette: the order is the seat order, known in advance, which is what makes it safe to take a turn.

Every echo counts, every way it arrives: a kid who says their name gets it echoed; a kid who whispers it to the adult gets it said by the adult and echoed just the same; a kid who only points at themselves gets their name spoken by the adult with the same ceremony, the circle echoes all three identically, and the claps land the same.

Middle round, once the names are warm: the speaker says their name in a chosen voice, tiny voice, big voice, slow voice, and the echo has to copy the VOICE as well as the name. Copying a friend's tiny voice exactly is the listening this game is quietly training.

Finish with the all-names wave: you point around the circle fast, and the group echoes each name with its two claps in one flowing round, by the last name the room knows itself, which was the entire point, and it took five minutes.
activities.tagline: Say your name. The whole circle says it right back, just like you said it, then two claps, together, like a small drum answering.

variations.easier: Adult names only for round one, the kids spend a whole round as the echo, which is a full turn, before any kid is a speaker.
variations.harder: Add a favourite sound after the name, 'Sam!' clap clap 'Vroom!', and the echo copies name, claps and sound in order.

materials.item: ripe dandelion clocks (the fluffy seed heads) growing on untreated grass
no other materials, lungs and eyes only

activities.name: Dandelion Clock Blow Walk

photo.alt: A young child blowing a dandelion clock, its seeds scattering in the sunlight
photo.caption: One dandelion clock, one big blow: the seeds are already away.
photo.credit: Photo: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Untreated grass only, no exceptions. A lawn whose spray history is unknown is not used, and the adult, not the patch, decides. Blowing is always away from faces and eyes; a kid who wants to watch from a step back is watching in full. Seeds and stems are not eaten, hands get washed back inside, and clocks near pathsides where dogs are walked are looked at, not picked.
activities.setup: Walk the patch yourself before the group comes out, this activity exists only where it honestly can: grass you KNOW is untreated (no sprays, no weed killer, ever, if you do not know, the walk finds something else that day), with ripe clocks actually standing. Count them roughly: a patch with three clocks and twelve kids is a sharing lesson, not a blowing walk, so find the good patch first.
steps: Tell the group the old game in one plain breath, named as the tradition it is: 'Long ago, people played a game with these: you blow the seeds off and count your blows. That number was your pretend time. They called it a dandelion clock.' Pretend time, said as pretend. The counting is real, the clock is a game people have played for a very long time.

Finding round: walk slowly and spot clocks, a kid who finds one points and calls 'Clock!' and the group gathers. The finder holds the stem low, with an adult hand steadying it if the ground is uneven, because a clock that gets knocked loses its seeds to the wind instead of the game.

State the one rule before the first blow: 'Blow AWAY from faces, and the clock stays on its stem until it is bare.' The finder blows: one puff, seeds lifting off and floating. The group watches where they go before the next puff, because watching the seeds travel is most of the activity.

Count the puffs together, out loud, one number per blow, until the head is bare or only the stubborn seeds are left: 'Seven puffs. Seven o'clock!' by the group's pretend clock. The number belongs to the blower and gets said with ceremony; every blower's time is different and that is correct.

Finish down low: get eyes at seed height and look at the bare head and the seeds landed around it, and say the plain true thing: 'Those seeds are trying to grow new dandelions. Some of them will.' Then the walk goes on. There may be one more clock, and everyone knows how to read it now.
activities.tagline: A slow walk to find a ripe dandelion clock: hold it low, blow, and count your puffs while the seeds float away like tiny parachutes.

variations.easier: One shared clock for the whole group, puffs taken in turns around it. The count still builds blow by blow, and the clock is read together.
variations.harder: Two clocks side by side: two blowers, two counts, and the group compares the pretend times, earlier clock, later clock, with no faster-or-slower judgement attached.

materials.item: one big tambourine (sturdy, adult-checked, no loose jingles)

activities.name: One Shake, Pass It Around
activities.safety: The tambourine is passed, never thrown, and never snatched: a pass that gets grabbed is redone slowly, kindly, because the passing is half the instrument. Jingles are checked before every use. A loose jingle on the floor is picked up by an adult immediately; small metal discs and small hands are a combination this activity simply designs out.
activities.setup: Check the tambourine yourself first: shake it hard over your own hand and look, every jingle fixed, no cracks, nothing that a determined three-year-old could work loose. Sit the circle close enough that the tambourine passes hand to hand without anyone leaning across a lap: passing distance is the set-up, and a circle that is too wide makes droppers of everyone.
steps: Start with the tambourine in your own hands and model the whole turn in four beats: receive it in two hands, ONE shake, wrist up, a proper ring, say nothing, pass it two-handed to the next person. State the one rule: 'One shake when it comes to you. Then it travels.'

First round is slow on purpose and that is the music of it: shake, pass, shake, pass, the circle finds the rhythm of the PASSING itself, and you name it when it settles: 'Listen, shake, wait, shake, wait. We are playing the silences too.'

Name round: as the tambourine arrives, the receiver says their name first, then shakes once. Name, ring, pass. A name said into a listening circle and answered by an instrument is a performance a three-year-old can actually hold, and each one gets the circle's whole attention.

Growing round: the LAST kid in the circle earns the double, two shakes to close the song, and the group counts them: 'One... two!' Then the tambourine starts a fresh round the other way around the circle, which at three is a genuinely new journey.

Finish by putting the tambourine to sleep in the middle: the final receiver carries it in two hands to the centre, lays it down flat, and the whole circle puts one finger on their lips over it. An instrument resting is an instrument respected, and a quiet circle of three-year-olds, achieved by music, is worth sitting in for a moment.
activities.tagline: One tambourine for the whole circle. When it reaches you: one shake, a real one, then pass it on. The music is taking turns.

variations.easier: The adult passes hand-over-hand with each receiver. The shake is still the kid's own, the pass is shared until hands learn it.
variations.harder: Choice round: the receiver may shake once OR tap the skin once. Choosing your sound is arranging, and the circle hears two instruments in one.

activities.inclusion: The bottom third of the window is the seated artists' section by design, not by leftovers: it catches the same light, and pieces pressed from a chair or a lap tray are in the picture in full. A kid can also work as the piece-keeper, holding the basket and handing each artist their chosen shape. Handing over the right piece, by name, is gallery work.

materials.item: clear contact paper / sticky-back film (adult-taped to a low window or smooth board, sticky side OUT)
big shapes to stick: tissue-paper pieces, fabric scraps, big leaves, felt shapes (all adult-cut, palm-size or bigger)
a tray or basket for the pieces

activities.name: Sticky Window Big Shapes
activities.safety: The film's edges are taped by an adult and checked each session: peeled-up film corners are the one real hazard here (sticky film over a face is no joke) and a lifting edge retires the window until it is re-taped. Pieces are palm-size or bigger, no glitter, no sequins, nothing small and shiny at this table. Pressing is done with hands only; nobody leans their weight or their forehead on the glass behind the film.
activities.setup: Mount the film yourself and take your time over it: sticky side out, edges taped down ALL the way round so no small fingers can peel the film itself up, at a height where a standing kid's palm reaches the middle and a seated kid's palm reaches the bottom third. Test it with the biggest, softest piece you have. Tissue that will not hold gets swapped for fabric before the group arrives, because a piece that falls teaches the window is broken.
steps: Show the window working before anyone is handed a piece: press one big shape on yourself with a flat palm, hold, let go. It stays. Then peel it off and press it somewhere else. Say the plain wonder of it out loud: 'It sticks, and it UN-sticks. You can move your picture all day. Nothing here can be put in the wrong place.'

State the one rule: 'Press with your whole hand, flat.' First pieces go up one kid at a time so everyone sees a palm-press work, a fingertip poke crumples tissue, a palm lays it flat, and the difference is visible across the room.

Making round: pieces travel from basket to window at each kid's own pace, pressed, looked at, peeled, moved. Overlaps are fine and get named kindly, 'Your leaf is sleeping on the red one', because a shared window is a group picture whether anyone planned it that way or not.

Step-back round, halfway: everyone takes two steps back, or wheels back, and just looks at the window together, light coming through the tissue pieces. Naming what you can see in it (a sun, a fish, nothing at all yet) is looking practice, and the light does half the showing.

Finish open-ended on purpose: the window STAYS UP. Pieces can be moved at any free moment for the rest of the day, and the last job, whenever the film finally comes down, is the group peeling their own pieces off into the basket, because an un-sticking round is as satisfying as the sticking one and the pieces keep for next time.
activities.tagline: Clear sticky film on a low window, sticky side out, and big shapes to press on with a whole palm. A picture you can move all day.

variations.easier: Three big fabric pieces only, on the lowest third of the film, with the adult holding the basket at elbow height. Choosing and pressing is the whole craft.
variations.harder: A loose theme offered, never set: 'The window is hungry for green things today', and the basket quietly holds mostly leaves and green pieces for kids who want a brief.

activities.inclusion: Rolling takes many shapes at the bottom of the same hill: a seated log-roll across a flat mat with an adult's hands guiding each turn is rolling in full, at the speed that body rolls. The bottom-caller with the flag runs the safety of the whole hill, nothing moves without their 'Clear!', and a kid who never rolls can hold that job for every single run.

materials.item: a gentle grass slope (adult-walked and checked)
a cone, scarf or flag at the bottom (the stop line)
a clear side path back up the hill

activities.name: Grass Hill Roll Down

photo.alt: A smooth green grass hill under a grey sky
photo.caption: A smooth green grass hill under a grey sky.
photo.credit: Photo: Bill Boaden, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Checked, gentle, grass-only slope; one roller at a time; the lane and the walking-back path never cross. Arms stay hugged and chins stay tucked. No head-first rolling, no standing starts, no pushing a roller faster. A dizzy kid sits at the bottom with an adult until the world settles. Rolling stops the moment any kid says stop, mid-hill included, and getting up slowly is taught as part of the roll, not an afterthought.
activities.setup: Walk the slope yourself before the group comes out, properly, on foot, top to bottom: you are looking for stones, holes, sticks, bare hard patches and anything the grass is hiding, and you roll it once yourself if the group's adults will allow the dignity hit, because your body finds what your eyes missed. The slope must be GENTLE: a hill a nervous kid walks down without using their hands. If the only slope fails any of this, the activity waits. A roll down a bad hill is not a braver version, it is a different and worse one.
steps: Gather at the top and teach the roll standing still, on the flat: arms crossed over the chest in a self-hug, chin a little down. Say the plain shape of it: 'Hug yourself, lie on your side, and the hill does the rolling. You just stay hugged.' Practise the hug until every kid can find it without thinking. The hug is the seatbelt.

State the one rule: 'One roller at a time, and the next hug starts only when the bottom is clear.' The bottom-caller, an adult or a kid with the flag, stands at the stop line and calls 'Clear!' The call is a real job and the roller does not start without it.

First rolls: the adult walks the first roller down the side path, lies them on their side at the top with the hug on, and gives the gentlest start. Rolling sideways is strange the first time, some kids unroll flat and stop, some need a second setting of the hug, all of it is learning the skill, at whatever speed knees and grass agree on.

Going round: each roller stands up at the bottom, slowly, the world is wobbly, that is normal and funny, waves at the top, and walks back up the SIDE path, never up the rolling lane. Waiting kids at the top watch the whole roll; watching a friend roll well is how the next hug gets braver.

Finish with a group count of the day's rolls and one last look at the hill: grass flattened in winding lines where the rolling happened. The hill keeps the score for an hour. Then everyone walks down the side path together, upright, like people who have somewhere to be.
activities.tagline: A gentle grass slope, arms hugged tight, and the oldest ride there is: lie down sideways at the top and roll, all the way to the bottom.

variations.easier: Half-hill starts: the roller begins halfway down where the slope is gentlest, with an adult's hands setting the hug and the first turn. The bottom arrives sooner and the skill is the same.
variations.harder: A paired roll for the confident: two rollers side by side at the top, hugs on, starting on the same 'Clear!', keeping your own line while a friend rolls beside you is the advanced class.

activities.inclusion: Holding is half the job: a partner who holds a pot steady with both hands while the matcher tries lids has matched that pot. The shake test at the end is done together and the success belongs to both sets of hands. Pots and lids work just as well on a lap tray or a low table edge, and the try-wobble-fit feedback is all in the hands, exactly where this activity lives.

materials.item: four to six big plastic pots, tubs and containers (adult-checked, all palm-size or bigger)
their real lids, plus one or two lids that fit NOTHING in the basket (the honest decoys)
a basket or tray (everything lives on it)

activities.name: Big Lid Match Basket
activities.safety: Big and plastic only. Every lid is palm-size or bigger, every container too large to mouth, and anything cracked or sharp-edged is retired by the adult on sight. Lids are pressed and twisted, never forced with body weight and never pried with teeth; a stuck lid goes to the adult, whose stronger hands are a tool of the room, not a defeat.
activities.setup: Build the basket yourself and test every pairing with your own hands: each container's lid must genuinely fit, press or twist, firmly enough to pass the gentle shake test in your hand, and the decoy lids must genuinely fit nothing, because a rigged basket teaches that trying is pointless. Everything is big and plastic: lids a whole palm covers, containers too large to be interesting to a mouth, no glass anywhere in the basket.
steps: Empty the basket onto the tray together and look at the jumble for a moment: pots without lids, lids without pots. Say the plain job: 'Every pot has a lid that fits it. Not every lid fits every pot. Our job is matching them, by trying.'

State the one rule: 'Try it gently. If it doesn't fit, that's the lid telling you something, put it back and try another.' First match together, slowly: a lid tried on a wrong pot wobbles and sits crooked, show the wobble. Then on its own pot it sits flat, and a press or twist makes it hold. The difference is felt in the hands before it is understood in words.

Matching round: each kid works their own pot or shares a basket between two, trying, wobbling, rejecting, fitting. Quietly, because the work itself is quiet. A finished pot gets the gentle shake test beside an ear: no rattle of a loose lid, a small satisfying nothing. Then it joins the finished row.

Decoy moment: sooner or later someone wrestles a lid that fits nothing. Name it like a discovery, not an error: 'That one is the trick lid. It doesn't belong to any pot today.' Finding the decoy is a result the whole table will want announced, and it proves the trying was real.

Finish with the full row: every pot covered, decoys back in the basket, and the group runs one finger along the row counting covered pots out loud. Then lids come OFF to finish, popped and twisted back into the basket by their matchers, because a basket that resets itself gets used again tomorrow.
activities.tagline: A basket of big lids and the pots they belong to: try a lid, feel if it fits, twist or press. A covered pot is a finished job.

variations.easier: Three containers with three lids and no decoys, lids rested ON TOP beside their pots. The fit is found by looking first and confirmed by the press.
variations.harder: Lids only, sorted by sound: matchers close their eyes while the adult taps each lid. Find the lid that SOUNDS like the one in your hand. Ears do the matching; the shake test confirms it.

activities.inclusion: A delivery counts however it travels: a carrier can wheel their heart on a lap tray, carry it seated-to-seated along a row, or hand it to the adult as a co-carrier who walks it the last step with them. The hand-over, hand-to-hand, is the delivery, and it happens in full every way. A kid who would rather not carry can be the name-caller with the adult, reading the room one delivery at a time. The list-keeper runs the valentines.

materials.item: big card or foam hearts (adult-cut, each bigger than two kid hands, one per kid plus spares)
a tray or mat at each seat (the delivery spots)

activities.name: Big Heart Hand Delivery
activities.safety: Hearts are big, plain card. Nothing small, shiny or stuck-on goes on them, because a valentine at three gets hugged, waved and occasionally tasted. Deliveries are walked, one carrier moving at a time: a room of three-year-olds all carrying at once is a collision arranged in advance. Names are said kindly and hearts are handed over, never snatched back. A heart given stays given.
activities.setup: Cut the hearts yourself beforehand, palm-and-a-half size, plain card, no glitter, no small stickers, and keep your own delivery list where only you can see it: who hands a heart to whom, arranged so every kid gives exactly one and receives exactly one. That list is the whole fairness system of this activity, and it lives with the adult so no three-year-old has to hold it. Hearts wait in the basket; trays wait at seats.
steps: Name the real thing in one plain sentence: 'On Valentine's Day, people give cards to people they are glad to know. Ours are big, and we deliver them by hand.' State the one rule: 'Two hands on your heart, walking feet, and you hand it over. Never throw it, never drop it in a lap and run.'

First delivery together, yours: take a heart in two hands, walk it slowly to its person, hold it out at their height, and wait until their two hands have it before yours let go. Say the whole sentence out loud, 'This heart is for you', because the words are the delivery as much as the card is.

Deliveries round: one carrier at a time, name called by you from the list, heart carried in two hands, handed over hand to hand, thank-you said back. One at a time is not slow. It is what makes each delivery an event the whole room watches, and watching a friend receive theirs is half of receiving your own.

Received hearts go flat on the receiver's tray, where they stay visible for the rest of the session: a room slowly filling with one heart at every seat is the picture this activity is making, and kids will keep checking that theirs is still there. Let them.

Finish with the full-room look: everyone seated behind their heart, and you name what the list already knows, every person in this room gave one heart and every person got one. Then hearts go home in bags or stay on trays for pickup time, carrier's choice, because a delivered valentine belongs to its receiver now.
activities.tagline: One big paper heart, carried in two hands across the room and handed to one named friend, a valentine delivered by hand, at walking pace.

variations.easier: Short route only: the receiver sits two seats away, and the adult walks the first delivery beside the carrier, hands ready underneath the heart without touching it.
variations.harder: A return round: each receiver carries their heart BACK to its giver with a thank-you said in their own words. Delivering and returning are two different walks and both count.

activities.inclusion: The count comes to every counter: a fallen twig with buds, or a low branch the adult holds gently down at seated height, puts real buds under a seated kid's fingertip, and their numbers join the branch count in full. A kid who counts by pointing while a partner touches has counted. The number said out loud is the count, whichever hand did the touching.

materials.item: one low branch on a tree or shrub the adult has checked (buds at kid height, nothing thorny, nothing sprayed)
no other materials, one finger per counter

activities.name: One Branch Bud Count

photo.alt: Cherry blossom buds clustered along a branch against a blue sky
photo.caption: Cherry blossom buds clustered along a branch against a blue sky.
photo.credit: Photo: W.carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The adult picks the plant and the branch. Nothing thorny, nothing with berries or leaves a three-year-old should be handling, and nothing recently sprayed; if the plant cannot be named, it is looked at, not touched. Buds are touched, never picked or twisted: a picked bud is next month's missing leaf, and the rule is said as care, not as scolding. Hands wash back inside, as after any plant handling.
activities.setup: Choose the branch yourself before the group comes out, and choose it like it matters: low enough for a standing three-year-old to reach the buds, on a plant you can name, with no thorns, no berries at mouth height, and a bud count a small group can actually finish. Eight to fifteen is a morning's honest work. Touch every bud yourself first; a branch that will not hold still for your hand will not hold still for theirs.
steps: Gather the group at the branch and say the plain spring fact the whole activity hangs on: 'This branch was bare all winter. These bumps are buds. Leaves and flowers folded up small, waiting. We are going to count how many are waiting on THIS branch.'

State the one rule: 'One finger, one bud, one number. Touch it soft. The bud stays on the branch.' Model the first three yourself: fingertip lands, number said, finger lifts. The touch is how a three-year-old keeps count, eyes alone lose buds, a finger remembers where it has been.

Counting round: the group counts the branch together, one counter's finger leading while everyone says the numbers, or one kid per stretch of branch, handing the count over: 'You left off at six...' However it is shared, the count goes bud by bud to the end of the branch and stops at the real number.

Look-closer round: with the count done, get eyes near one bud, with permission of the branch, hands behind backs this time, and name what a bud actually looks like up close: the colour, the scales, the tiny point. Counting told the group how many; looking tells them what one is.

Finish with the promise said out loud, because it is checkable: 'When we come back to this branch, some of these buds will be leaves.' Write the number down back inside where the group can see it. A count that gets revisited is data, and this branch now belongs to the room.
activities.tagline: One low branch in spring, and its buds counted one by one with a fingertip, touch a bud, say a number, because the buds are counting on growing.

variations.easier: A short twiggy offcut or a potted plant with five big buds, counted on a lap tray at the table, the same one-finger-one-number rule, at seated height.
variations.harder: Count a second branch on the same tree and compare the two numbers: which branch is carrying more spring, and can the group say by how much, in handfuls if not in numbers?

activities.inclusion: Every cook cooks: the spoon can be stirred two-handed, rested against the pot's edge for leverage, or held with an adult's hand under the cook's. The five circles are still theirs. A cook who names their ingredient by pointing at a picture, a sign, or the adult's offered choices has named it in full, and a pot-holder whose two hands keep the whole kitchen steady is cooking with both of them.

materials.item: one big sturdy pot or mixing bowl (empty, clean, too big to tip)
nothing else. The ingredients are pretend

activities.name: Big Pot Stir-Together
activities.safety: Nothing real goes in the pot and nothing is tasted, at any point. The rule is said at the start and holds when a helpful cook offers an actual snack from their pocket. The pot is stirred from a seated position only, spoon moving in circles inside it: a spoon waved standing up is a spoon at face height for the cook beside you. Hot is never part of the pretend. The soup is warm in the story and the pot is cold in the hand, and the record says so in case a substitute asks.
activities.setup: Set the pot where the whole group can reach it, middle of a low table or on the floor rug with everyone seated round it, and test it yourself: it must sit dead steady when stirred hard by an enthusiastic cook, because a pot that walks across the table teaches chasing, not stirring. The spoon is long enough that a stirring hand stays clear of the pot's rim. Nothing goes in the pot. That is not a shortage; it is the recipe.
steps: Tell the group the situation plainly: 'It is raining, we are inside, and we are making soup. Our soup is pretend soup. Nothing real goes in the pot, and nobody tastes it. What goes in is ideas, one per cook.' State the one rule: 'The spoon travels hand to hand. Only the cook holding the spoon stirs.'

First stir together, yours: name your ingredient out loud. 'I am putting in... a carrot', mime dropping it in, then stir five slow circles while the group counts the circles with you: the count is how the room knows a stir is finished, and five is a stir a three-year-old can complete without the pot becoming a drum.

Cooks' round: the spoon passes, each cook names one thing going in, real foods, silly foods, one memorable dinosaur, drops it in by mime, and stirs their five counted circles. A named ingredient is never corrected: dinosaur soup is a legitimate soup in this kitchen, and the group will defend that position.

Halfway taste-check, performed entirely in mime: you lift the spoon, blow on it, pretend-sip, and deliver the verdict, 'Needs one more thing', and let the group shout suggestions before the next cook chooses. The verdict is always nearly there; a soup that is finished ends the stirring, and nobody wants that.

Finish when every cook has stirred: the last cook gives five final circles, the spoon is laid across the pot like a lid, and the group names the soup by its most famous ingredient. The name gets said with ceremony, because they cooked it. Pot and spoon are washed by the adult where the group can see: pretend kitchens clean up too.
activities.tagline: One big empty pot, one long spoon passed hand to hand: everyone adds one pretend thing and stirs it in. Rainy-day soup, made of turns.

variations.easier: Two cooks at a time sharing the spoon. One holds the pot steady with both hands (a real job the pot genuinely needs) while the other stirs, then they swap.
variations.harder: Counting up: later cooks stir as many circles as their turn number, cook three stirs three, cook six stirs six, with the group counting every circle out loud.

activities.inclusion: A pot played in any way that makes its sound counts in full: flat palm, fingertips, the back of a hand, or a pot resting on a lap tray at the drummer's own height. The weather-caller job, holding up the drizzle or downpour picture in your own hands at the right moment, runs the whole storm, and a caller who never drums has still made the rain happen.

materials.item: several sturdy pots, pans or big bowls, upturned (adult-checked: stable, no sharp rims)
no sticks, hands and fingers only

activities.name: Rain Drums on Pots
activities.safety: Hands only, never sticks or utensils, a pot played with fingers cannot be drummed into anyone's fingers beside it, and the volume stays at a level set by palms, not hardware. Pots are adult-checked for sharp rims and dead stability before the group sits; a pot that tips is retired mid-session without discussion. The downpour is five counted seconds, not a free-for-all: ears at three are close to the drums, and the storm ending on the call is part of the weather.
activities.setup: Set the drums yourself before the group sits: pots upturned on a low table or the floor, each one rocked by your hand first. A pot that wobbles will tip mid-downpour and end the weather. Mix sizes on purpose: the biggest pot is the deep sound, the smallest is the bright one, and the group will hear the difference before you name it. Best on a genuinely rainy day, when the real sound is at the window for comparison.
steps: Start by listening, not playing: hands in laps, ears on the window if it is really raining. Say the plain framing: 'Rain makes a sound landing on things. Pots make a sound too. We are going to make the rain's sound, our size.' One demonstration pat from you, flat palm, once, so the group hears how quiet a pot can be played.

State the one rule: 'Fingers and soft palms only, and only when your pot is called.' Teach the two weathers with your hands in the air first: DRIZZLE is fingertips, light and slow, pat-pat-pat; DOWNPOUR is flat palms, busy and low. The group practises both in the air before any pot is touched.

Weather round, one pot at a time: you call the weather, 'Drizzle over the garden...', one drummer plays it on their pot while everyone else listens, then the call moves on. Hearing your own pot do weather, alone, is the listening this activity exists for.

Storm round, the big moment, once: weather builds over the whole shelf, drizzle on the small pots, growing, until you raise both hands and call 'DOWNPOUR!' and every pot plays at once for a slow count of five, then your hands fall: '...and the rain stops.' Silence after a downpour, in a room of three-year-olds, is a sound worth sitting in.

Finish by matching the window: if real rain is still falling, the group plays ALONG with it for a moment, at its volume, whatever that is. Then pots are turned right-side up and stacked by their drummers, weather over, kitchen restored.
activities.tagline: Upturned pots and fingertips: drizzle is a patter, a downpour is a rumble, the rain outside, played on the kitchen shelf.

variations.easier: One big pot for the whole group, drummers taking turns around it, the adult's hand keeping the weather calls slow and far apart.
variations.harder: Add the in-between weather: RAIN (steady palms, medium) between drizzle and downpour. Three weathers to tell apart by ear before a hand moves.

activities.inclusion: The pour is the pourer's at any height: the whole tray station works on a lap tray or a low table edge, the cup can be tipped two-handed or with its handle braced on the funnel's rim, and an adult pouring at a kid's direction, 'pour... keep pouring... stop!'. Is a full experiment where the director called every variable. The level-checker job, finger on the glass calling the count, is the measurement itself.

materials.item: one big wide-mouth funnel per pourer (adult-checked, smooth rim)
a clear bottle or jar with the funnel seated in it
dry sand in a big pouring cup
a deep tray under everything (the sand's whole world)

activities.name: Big Funnel Sand Pour
activities.safety: Sand stays on the tray and in the station, never thrown, never blown, and hands that have been in sand stay away from faces until they are washed; sand in an eye is the one real accident this activity can have, and the tray rule is what prevents it. Pouring is done seated or standing still at the tray, never carried around the room. The bottle is plastic or the adult's hands move it, always: glass and sand and small pourers meet only through an adult.
activities.setup: Build the station on the tray and test it with your own pour first: the funnel must sit steady in the bottle's mouth without being held. A funnel that needs a holding hand leaves the pourer one-handed, so wedge or choose until it stands alone. Sand is dry and clean, the cup is small enough that a pour finishes, and the whole station lives on the tray: sand that reaches the tray has not escaped, it has arrived.
steps: Show the empty bottle first and say the plain question the whole activity answers: 'The sand is in the cup. The bottle's mouth is little. How does the sand get in? Slowly, through the funnel. Watch where it lands.' Hold the funnel up alone once: wide top, narrow bottom, one hole. The shape is the explanation.

State the one rule: 'Pour slow, over the funnel, and stop when I say the cup is empty, then we LOOK before anyone pours again.' First pour together: sand goes in a thin stream, and the group watches the pile inside the bottle start at the bottom and build, 'The bottle fills from the bottom up. The top fills last.'

Pouring round: each pourer tips their own cup, at their own pace, keeping the stream inside the funnel's wide mouth. A stream that misses teaches aim better than any correction, the tray catches the evidence and the next pour adjusts itself. Between pours, the group checks the level: finger on the glass at the sand line, number of cups counted out loud.

Full-and-finish moment: when the sand reaches the funnel's neck and slows to a stop, leave it there a moment and look, the bottle full, the funnel holding the last of the stream back. Say the earned sentence: 'The funnel let it in a little at a time. That is the funnel's whole job.'

Reset is the second half of the science and the group does it: the adult lifts the bottle, the pourers hold the big cup, sand comes back out, faster upside down than it went in, which somebody will notice, and the noticing is the lesson landing twice. Tray sand is scooped back into the cup by hand, every grain accounted for by small fingers.
activities.tagline: A big funnel in a bottle, a cup of dry sand, and a stream that pours, narrows and fills, watch the level climb from the bottom up.

variations.easier: A bigger funnel and a measuring jug instead of a bottle, three cups only, with the adult's hand steadying nothing but staying under the funnel as a safety net that never touches.
variations.harder: Two funnels, two bottles, two sands of different colours poured side by side: same cups, and the group judges which bottle's level climbed faster, and argues about why, which is the point.

activities.inclusion: The banner visits every carrier: a seated carrier's hand-span can be at the route's halfway station, where the banner's edge is carried TO their hands for the stop-and-hold. The halfway hold the carry genuinely needs a crew member stationed to do. A carrier can also walk their span wheeling with one hand on the edge, the paper light enough that the grip is the whole job, and the banner arrives exactly as flat.

materials.item: one long banner (a roll of paper or joined sheets, adult-made, with a welcome word or the group's own marks on it)
a clear straight route across the room
tape or clips at the far wall (adult's, for hanging)

activities.name: Long Banner Carry-Together
activities.safety: Walking only, and the pace is the slowest carrier's. A banner carried at a run tears, and the tear is the lesson nobody needs twice. Grips are gentle and edges are never yanked from another carrier's hands; a dropped edge is re-gripped on the stop call, not grabbed at mid-stride. The hanging is the adult's job at adult height: carriers hold, the adult tapes, and nobody climbs to reach the wall.
activities.setup: Make the banner before the group gathers. Long enough to need at least six hands, light enough that a three-year-old's grip is real, and already decorated or carrying one big word, so what is being carried visibly matters. Walk the route yourself carrying one edge: it must be straight, flat and boring, because the carrying is the event and the route should contribute nothing. Mark the hanging spot at the far end at adult height; the arrival has a destination the crew can see.
steps: Show the banner laid flat on the floor and say the plain truth of it: 'This banner is too long for two hands. It needs a hand every little while along its edge. That is us. If we all walk together, it stays flat. If one of us hurries, it folds and tears.' State the one rule: 'Two hands or one hand on the edge, walking feet, and we start and stop on the call.'

Crewing round: the group spreads along one side, and the bigger kids of the crew along both sides if numbers allow, each carrier finding their own hand-span of edge and gripping it gently, paper held, not pulled. You call the lift: 'Hands on... lift', and the banner comes off the floor as one thing, which the group will feel happen in their own hands.

The carry: walking feet, your pace set at the front, the banner travelling flat across the room. Call one stop halfway, 'Stop', and let the crew feel the banner hang still and level between them: holding a thing still together is harder than moving it together, and three-year-olds can feel that fact without a word of explanation.

Arrive: at the far wall the crew holds the banner up and steady, arms at whatever height their grip reaches, while you tape or clip the top edge. Their holding IS the hanging; a banner that goes up while its crew holds it has been installed by the crew, and everyone present knows it.

Finish with the step-back: whole crew behind you, looking at the banner on the wall, flat because they walked it flat. Name the crew's work in one plain sentence, 'Every hand on that edge is why it is up there whole', then the banner stays up for the day, and carriers will point their hand-span out to anyone who visits.
activities.tagline: A long paper banner and a hand every few steps along its edge: the whole crew walks it across the room flat, or it does not arrive at all.

variations.easier: A shorter banner and a crew of four, the adult carrying the middle span where the sag lives. The crew still feels the banner need every hand it has.
variations.harder: A corner to turn: the route bends once around a table, and the crew discovers the outside of the bend must walk further than the inside, called, practised, and carried at a shuffle.

activities.inclusion: Every way of arriving is already in the room: wheels are a first-class movement here, shown by the kid who travels that way and copied by everyone, exactly as shown. The teller is the group's expert on their own journey. A teller can show their movement with one hand, with their head, or by choosing the adult's demonstration of it and nodding it correct. Directing your own movement's copy is telling in full.

materials.item: no materials, voices and bodies only

activities.name: How I Got Here Moves
activities.safety: Movements are copied kindly and exactly. Never bigger-funny, never with sound effects at a teller's expense; the rule is stated once, plainly, before the first turn. All movement happens in place in the circle: marching feet stay on one spot, because twenty three-year-olds actually marching is a parade leaving the activity behind. A teller's real travel is never corrected, if they say the bus and you know it was a car, the bus is what the room copies; this is their telling, not a transport audit.
activities.setup: No set-up beyond a circle with room to move in place. Think about your own group before you start: you need the travel kinds your kids actually use, walking, car, bus, bike seat, stroller, wheelchair, and every single one gets a movement the whole group can copy with respect and pleasure. Your own travel goes first, told honestly, so the telling is modelled before anyone small is asked to do it.
steps: Model the whole turn with your own journey: 'I got here in a car. I steered like this', hands on an invisible wheel, gentle turns, 'Now everybody drive my car with me.' The whole group steers together for a few beats. That copying is the welcome: your way of arriving just got driven by the entire room.

State the one rule: 'One teller at a time, and we copy EVERY way of getting here the same, because every way got somebody here.' Go in seat order, known in advance, so nobody wonders when their turn is coming or whether it is.

Tellers' round: each kid names their travel, in words, by pointing at themselves and miming it, or by choosing between two the adult offers out loud, then shows the movement: marching feet for walking, a bounce in the seat for the bus, pedalling legs for a bike, smooth rolling hands for wheels. The group copies it together, properly, for a real few seconds.

The copying is the point and it is never a joke at the teller's expense: movements are copied the way the teller showed them, at the teller's size. If a movement is big, the room does it big; if it is small and careful, the room does it small. Matching a friend exactly is the friendship being practised.

Finish with the whole journey home: you call the group's travels back in order, 'First we marched with ___, then we steered with ___', and the room replays every movement once, fast, like a film of the morning. Every way of getting here is in the film, because every kid in the room is.
activities.tagline: Tell the group how you travel, feet, wheels, bus, car, and everyone copies the movement: marching feet, steering hands, a gentle bus bounce.

variations.easier: Adult offers two choices to each teller, 'Did your feet bring you, or did wheels?', and a point is a complete answer that earns the group's full copy.
variations.harder: Add the middle of the journey: 'What did you see on the way?', one thing per teller, named or mimed, and the group copies the looking as well as the travelling.

activities.inclusion: Holding on works from any height and any hand: two palms, one palm, a forearm rested on the bark, or a lap tray's edge against the trunk with the kid's hand over it. The tree does not grade the hold. The listening is the activity's heart and it asks nothing of hands at all: a kid who only listens, and reports their sound by making it, has done the whole thing. The report-by-sound option is stated up front so it is a choice, not a fallback.

materials.item: one big tree the adult has checked (sound trunk, no hives, no low dead branches, room all round it)
no other materials, arms and ears only

activities.name: Big Tree Hug and Listen

photo.alt: Child hugging tree at Peravoor (1)
photo.caption: Child hugging tree at Peravoor (1).
photo.credit: Photo: Vinayaraj, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The adult's tree check is the safety: no hives or active nests, no ant highways, no dead branches overhead, and the group never gathers under a tree in wind strong enough to be dropping twigs. Hugging is offered, never assigned, palms flat, one hand, or standing at the trunk with hands in pockets and ears open are all full participation, and bark never goes in mouths. The group stays at the trunk: no climbing, no root-stepping races, and the quiet minute happens where the adult can see every holder-on at once.
activities.setup: Choose and check the tree yourself before the group comes out. Properly: trunk sound and rough-barked enough to feel, no wasp or bee activity anywhere on it, no ants in a highway up the bark, nothing dead overhead, and space all the way round for the whole group to stand at the trunk together. Put your own arms round it. If the tree fails any of this, another tree gets the hug; the activity is portable and trees are not interchangeable only in the details.
steps: Gather the group at the trunk and say the plain framing: 'This tree is alive and it is older than everybody here. We are going to say hello the tree way, by holding on and listening.' First contact is palms flat on the bark, all round the trunk at once, feeling it before anyone wraps an arm.

State the one rule: 'Hands on the tree, feet on the ground, and when the listening starts, our voices rest.' Show the hug properly, arms round as far as they reach, cheek nowhere near bark, a hold that can be let go of at any moment by its owner. Nobody has to hug: palms flat is holding on in full.

The listening minute: you say 'Listening...' and the group holds on in quiet for a real minute, at three, a minute of held quiet outdoors is a long, rich time, and sounds will arrive: leaves, birds, wind in the branches overhead, the tree's own creaks. Your job in the minute is only to keep it: one gentle 'listening...' if voices start, nothing more.

Report round, hands still on the tree: each kid names one thing they heard, in words, by pointing at their ear and then at the sound's direction, or by making the sound themselves. Every report is received as a hearing: if two kids heard the same bird, the bird gets named twice, proudly.

Finish with the thank-you and the fact: hands pat the trunk twice, together, pat, pat, 'Thank you, tree.' Then the plain true sentence on the walk back: 'The tree will be making those sounds all day. We just stopped long enough to hear them.' A tree the group has listened at gets greeted on every future walk past it; that is a side effect, not a rule.
activities.tagline: One big tree, arms around it or palms flat on the bark, and a whole quiet minute of listening to what a tree's place sounds like.

variations.easier: A small group and a half-minute: palms flat only, the adult's hands on the trunk too, and the reports taken during the quiet in whispers rather than after it.
variations.harder: A second tree, a second minute, and the comparison: which tree's place was louder, and what was the biggest sound at each. The group votes by walking to stand at the tree they mean.

activities.inclusion: An echo counts in every voice it comes back in: sung, hummed with the mouth closed, signed along while a neighbour sings, or tapped on knees in the line's rhythm while the group carries the words, the line came back, and coming back is the game. A small singer can also conduct their line: they point at the group at their moment and the room sings it for them, which is a solo performed by direction.

materials.item: no materials, voices only, and songs the group already knows

activities.name: Sing It Back: Echo Lines
activities.safety: Voices only and voices at singing size: an echo game that becomes a shouting match has left the activity, and the adult's own line is always sung at the size the echoes should be. The group will copy the volume they are given. Singers sing by volunteering or by known seat order, never by surprise nomination; a passed turn is passed without comment and the line goes to the group instead. Songs are the group's own known songs, nothing with words a three-year-old should not be carrying around gets introduced by this game.
activities.setup: No set-up beyond choosing your songs before the group sits, and the choosing is the set-up: two or three songs this group genuinely knows (the ones they already join in on), with lines short enough to hold whole: one line, four to eight words, a tune a three-year-old's ear can keep. Test your lines on your own voice: if you cannot sing it back to yourself exactly, it is too long, and a shorter line from the same song is waiting.
steps: Start inside a song the group owns: sing the whole first verse together the normal way, so the echo game grows out of real singing and not out of an instruction. Then say the plain shape of the game: 'Now I sing ONE line by myself, and you sing it back to me, just like I sang it. The song, answering.'

State the one rule: 'Wait for my line to finish. Then sing it back, the same words, the same tune.' First echo easy on purpose: the best-known line of the best-known song, sung by you at the group's own pace, and answered by everybody at once. A room singing a line back together is a choir that did not need forming.

Line-by-line round: work through one song a line at a time, you singing each line into the quiet and the group returning it. Lines they stumble on get sung by you twice, hearing it twice is not a failure, it is how the line moves in, and the echo that lands gets named: 'That one came back whole.'

Small-voices round, the heart of it: one singer per line when singers want it, a volunteer or the next seat in a known order, never a spotlight ambush, sings a line alone and the GROUP echoes the small singer, at the small singer's size. Being echoed by the whole room is a three-year-old's first solo, with the room as their instrument.

Finish by singing the whole song straight through, no echoes, all together, and the group will hear it differently now, line by line, because they have held each piece of it separately. End seated, voices down on the last line, the way songs in this room end.
activities.tagline: The grown-up sings one short line of a song everybody knows, and the whole group sings it right back, same tune, like the song answering itself.

variations.easier: Two-word echoes only: the ends of lines ('...twinkle star' becomes you singing the line and the group answering just 'twinkle star'). Holding the tail of a line is a full echo at its smallest honest size.
variations.harder: Echo with a change the group must catch and copy: you sing a known line SLOW, or tiny-voiced, or with one word swapped for a silly one, and the echo has to return it exactly as sung, swap included.

activities.inclusion: Every wall has a low country: the bottom panels of all four walls are painters' territory at seated height, catching the same light and the same commentary as any panel, and the groundsheet is laid so wheels roll onto it and up to the wall. A painter can also work the inside from the doorway in a chair placed in the opening, in the house, painting the house. The colour-caller job, choosing which colour goes to which wall and calling the swaps, is art direction, and the house bears the caller's decisions all day.

materials.item: one very large sturdy cardboard box (appliance-size, adult-prepared: door and windows cut by the adult beforehand)
big brushes and sponge dabbers (one per painter)
a groundsheet or flattened cardboard under the whole house

activities.name: Paint the Big Box House
activities.safety: Washable paint only, and the pots are wide and low so a reached-for colour does not become a tipped one. The box is cut, trimmed and taped by adults before painting starts and never cut during it, no blades at a painting session, at any height, for any touch-up. One painter inside the house at a time with the doorway always clear, and the whole box is checked by an adult before play use: a softened, paint-soaked panel that sags gets retired, because the house's job after today is being a building.
activities.setup: Build the house before the painters arrive, and build it like a building: door and window holes cut by an adult's hands only, flaps taped down flat inside and out, the box set on its groundsheet where it will stay for the day. A painted house does not get carried. Stand inside it yourself for one second if it fits you, or crouch-test the door: if the doorway snags an adult's shoulder it will snag a painted three-year-old's, and it gets trimmed now, not mid-session.
steps: Walk the group round their house first, paint still closed: name its parts in plain words, walls, door, windows, roof edge, and say the job straight: 'This is our house and it is made of cardboard and it is BROWN. Houses get painted. Today the painters are us.' State the one rule: 'Paint goes on the house. Brushes stay at the house.'

First strokes together: pots open, each painter chooses a wall section at their own height and makes the first mark, a stripe, a splodge, a whole panel of one colour, and you name what is happening in builder's words: 'The front wall is going red. The door wall is starting blue.' Painting WITH commentary is how a coat of paint becomes a project.

Painting round: painters work their sections at their own pace, pots shared by carrying them two-handed or calling for a colour swap. Overlaps where two sections meet are the house's style, named as such on sight. The inside walls are paintable too, one painter in the house at a time, doorway kept clear. A painted-inside house is a different country and the group will know it.

Step-back inspection, halfway: brushes down, whole group two steps back, or wheeled back, looking at the house like inspectors. What is still brown? Which wall needs a painter? Inspectors assign themselves; an unpainted patch spotted by the group gets a volunteer before you can suggest one.

Finish when the group calls it painted: brushes washed in the bucket by their painters, pots lidded by the adult, and the house left OPEN to dry where it stands. Then it is not a craft project any more, it is the room's new building, and it stays in use for days: a house the group painted themselves, entered through a door they watched being a doorway while it was still brown.
activities.tagline: A cardboard box big enough to stand inside, washable paint and brushes as big as your hand: the group paints its house, outside and in, then lives in it.

variations.easier: One wall only, three painters, the house pre-primed by the adult in one pale colour so every mark shows at full strength from the first stroke.
variations.harder: A second coat day: patterns over the base, handprints along the door wall, stripes on the roof edge, planned by the inspectors from the first session before a pot opens.

activities.inclusion: A step is a step at every size it honestly comes in: a wheel's roll of one big push is a giant step, a short roll is a baby step, and the caller calls the same sizes to the whole line, wheels and feet travelling in one row, arriving in one row. A traveller can also be the caller for a stretch: calling the sizes IS playing the game at full stretch, and a caller who watches the line take their call learns the sizes by eye the way the line learns them by leg.

materials.item: a start line and a finish line (tape, a rug edge, the garden gate itself)

activities.name: Giant Steps, Baby Steps
activities.safety: Everybody moves on every call and nobody is ever sent back or out. That is not a softening of this game, it is the game, and a caller who suggests sending someone back is gently reminded of the promise made on the start line. Giant steps are stretches, not leaps: feet stay in contact with the ground's story, one foot down before the other leaves, because a line of leaping three-year-olds lands on each other. The lane is adult-cleared, the group travels in a wide line rather than a bunch, and a fallen traveller stops the calls until they are up and brushed off, the gate waits, it always waits.
activities.setup: Mark the two lines yourself and walk the distance at a baby step before the group lines up: the whole trip should take a mixed bag of calls, eight to twelve steps in total, because a journey of thirty calls loses its travellers and a journey of three never becomes one. Clear the lane as you walk it: at three, looking at your own feet is the game, so the floor owes the group a clear view and nothing to trip over.
steps: Teach the steps standing on the start line, before any travelling: a GIANT step is the biggest stretch a leg can honestly make; a baby step is heel-to-toe tiny, a foot-length and no more; a marching step is knees up, in the middle, and proud. The group practises all three on the line until the sizes are in their legs. Sizes are the vocabulary of this game and the travelling makes no sense without them.

State the one rule, whole: 'The caller calls a step. EVERYBODY takes that step together. Nobody is ever out, nobody is sent back, and we all reach the gate.' That last part is the design, said out loud at the start so the group hears the promise the game keeps.

Travelling round: you call, 'GIANT step!', and the whole line stretches one giant step together and freezes in the stretch a moment, marvelling at the distance; 'Baby step, baby step', two tiny ones, heel to toe; 'Marching steps, one, two, three!' The calls vary the sizes on purpose: after two giants, a run of babies makes the gate feel far again, and the group will groan happily, because the distance changing size IS the game.

Last-step ceremony: when the group is one call from the gate, stop and look at the gap together and let the group choose the final step by vote of voices. It will be a giant, and it should be: the whole line takes it together and lands at the gate in one stretched, laughing row, exactly as promised at the start line.

Finish at the gate with the journey told back in sizes: 'Two giants got us started. Then the babies made us wait. Then we MARCHED.' Kids will re-walk the journey in the telling, feet remembering the sizes without a call. Then the whole group turns round, because the gate is also a start line, and the way back is the same game in the other direction, if legs are willing.
activities.tagline: The caller names a step, a GIANT step, a baby step, a marching step, and the whole group takes it together, all the way to the garden gate.

variations.easier: Three calls only over a short lane, the adult walking each call INSIDE the line with the group, taking the same size step. A model in the middle is worth ten from the front.
variations.harder: New sizes join the vocabulary: a twirling step (one slow turn as you travel), a sideways crab step, a tiptoe step, each taught on the line first, then callable, and inventors of a step get it called by their name once: 'A ___ step!'

activities.inclusion: Matching is done by eyes and announcement as much as by hands: a matcher who spots a pair from where they sit and calls 'Those two!' while a partner gathers them has matched that pair in full. The calling eye is the skill this activity trains. The whole pile works spread on a lap tray in a single layer, and holding a found sock up high for its partner to be spotted gives the holder the room's best job: being searched for.

materials.item: a basket of big clean odd socks (adult socks work best, long, bright, clearly patterned; every sock in the basket has its true pair in there too)
a finished-pairs tray or second basket

activities.name: Sock Pair Match Basket
activities.safety: Socks are clean laundry, full stop. This basket is washed, adult-supplied stock, never the group's own worn socks gathered up, and it goes back through the wash when it has been mouthed, as socks at three occasionally are. Socks are matched held in hands, never worn during the activity and never put over faces or heads, even in triumph. Small socks stay out of the basket: everything here is big, soft, and interesting to nobody's mouth for long.
activities.setup: Build the basket yourself and audit it like it matters, because it does: every sock's real pair must genuinely be in the basket. Count them in pairs as you load it, since a basket with an unmatchable sock teaches that looking carefully does not pay. Use big socks with bold differences, stripes against spots, long against short, loud against plain, and nothing small or baby-sized: at three, the matching should be hard enough to need looking and easy enough that looking wins.
steps: Tip the basket out together and look at the muddle for a moment: socks everywhere, no two together. Say the plain job: 'Every sock in this pile has its other half hiding in here. Socks live in pairs. Our job is putting the pairs back together, by looking.' That last phrase is the method and it gets said before a hand moves.

State the one rule: 'Pick up ONE sock. Hold it where you can see it. Find the one that matches it, same colour, same pattern, same size.' First pair together, slowly: a sock held up, the pile searched with eyes first and hands second, its pair lifted out and the two laid side by side and CHECKED, toe to toe, stripe to stripe, because a near-match held up to the light is this activity's favourite discovery.

Matching round: each matcher works their own socks at their own pace. Hold, search, check, and when a pair is proven, roll it into a ball (one sock tucked into the other, the way real drawers keep them) and set the ball on the finished tray. Rolling the ball is the period at the end of the pair's sentence, and matchers will not skip it.

Near-match moment: sooner or later two socks that almost agree, same stripes, different size, get held up together. Name what the eyes just did, out loud, as a skill: 'Those two fooled us for a second. Looking closer caught it.' A basket that cannot fool you teaches nothing; this one can, briefly, and being caught by it is the looking getting stronger.

Finish with the empty pile and the full tray: every sock balled with its pair, and the group counts the balls along the tray in a row. The count is the laundry done. Then, if the room wants it, the adult unballs them back into the basket for tomorrow: a job that resets itself to be done again is a job a quiet corner can hold all year.
activities.tagline: A basket of big clean odd socks: find the two that match, same colour, same stripes, same size, and roll each pair into a ball. Real laundry, real quiet.

variations.easier: Six pairs only, all wildly different, socks spread face-up in a single layer so the searching is done with eyes alone before hands are needed.
variations.harder: A memory layer: pairs are matched with half the socks face-down. A sock's pair must be recognised from a cuff and a stripe of heel, and a wrong guess is turned back over and remembered, not regretted.

activities.inclusion: A lamp's placing counts however it travels: a carrier can carry theirs on a lap tray wheeled along the path's edge, place it seated-to-seated from the row's end, or direct the adult as co-carrier. 'There... down... light it', with the setting-down and the switching done at their word. The door-end lookout job, calling 'the welcome is growing!' as each light lands, belongs to whoever holds it and runs the whole ceremony.

materials.item: big paper diya lamps (adult-made: stiff card folded into a shallow boat shape, palm-and-a-half wide, one per kid plus spares)
battery tea lights (adult-handled, screwed-shut battery covers, one per lamp)
a clear floor path from the door to a rug or reading corner (the welcome route)

activities.name: Paper Diya Welcome Row
activities.safety: Battery tea lights only, no real flame, no oil, nothing hot exists in this activity at any point. Battery covers stay screwed shut and lights are switched and handled by the adult; a tea light is never a toy and never goes in a mouth, and the lamps are carried, never the lights alone. Carriers walk one at a time along a clear path: a room of three-year-olds all carrying lamps at once is a collision arranged in advance, and stepping over a placed lamp is not a route. The path's edge is.
activities.setup: Make the diyas yourself beforehand, big, stiff, and plain, with a flat spot in the middle where a tea light sits without wobbling when a lamp is set down by small hands; test-carry each one across the room yourself. Say the real thing plainly in your own head before the group hears it: Diwali is the festival of lights, and clay diya lamps are lit and set out to welcome guests and good fortune into a home. Tea lights are battery ones, screwed shut, and they are switched on by adult hands only, at the moment each lamp is placed. The light arriving is the adult's half of the job; the carrying and placing are the kids'.
steps: Name the festival in one plain sentence: 'Diwali is a festival of lights. Families light small lamps called diyas and set them where guests come in, to welcome them. We are making a welcome row of lamps along our path.' State the one rule: 'Two hands carry the lamp. Walking feet. You set it down gently where the path is waiting.'

First lamp together, yours: carry a diya in two hands down the path at walking pace, set it down at the path's start with both hands still on it, and switch its light on only once it is placed, then step back with the group and look at one light, alone, doing its job. One lamp is a light; the row is the welcome, and the group should see the difference coming.

Placing round: one carrier at a time, lamp carried in two hands, set down at the next spot along the path. The spots close enough that the lights read as a row, far enough that each placing is its own walk. The carrier walks back empty-handed along the path's edge, never through the lamps. Lit lamps are never picked up again; a lamp that has landed has arrived.

Halfway look: stop the carrying, gather at the door end, and look down the path together. Half light, half waiting. Name what is happening in the plainest words: 'The welcome is half built.' Three-year-olds who can SEE the job half done will finish it like builders.

Finish at the last lamp: the final carrier places theirs, the light goes on, and the whole group walks the finished row once, slowly, guest-style, from the door to the rug. Arriving the way the lamps were lit to welcome. Then lights off, lamps collected in two hands by their makers, and the row exists in the room's memory at full brightness.
activities.tagline: Big paper diya lamps carried in two hands and set along a floor path, each one lit as it lands. A welcome written in light, one lamp at a time.

variations.easier: A short path of four lamps to the rug only, the adult walking each carry beside the carrier with a hand under the lamp without touching it.
variations.harder: A second row on the path's other side, placed by the returning carriers, the group judges whether the two rows match lamp for lamp, and a missing lamp is a discovery, not a mistake.
