activities.inclusion: Every roller rolls: the ball's lane passes a seated roller stationed at its edge, whose push, with a hand, a forearm, or a tray edge leaned into it, counts in the turning exactly as any push does, and the escort job, riding alongside calling 'grass!' at the thin patches, is the roll's navigation. The final shared heave includes every hand that wants in, at whatever height the ball offers a side.

materials.item: real snow on the ground, deep and soft enough to pack (the adult has tested it)
mittens or gloves for every roller
one marked rolling lane (a path the adult has walked first: flat, clear, no ice)

activities.name: Roll It Bigger Snowball

photo.alt: Children rolling two large snowballs through the snow, in Bertha Lum's print Snow balls
photo.caption: Children rolling snowballs bigger and bigger through the snow.
photo.credit: Photo: Bertha Lum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Snowballs are rolled, never thrown, at three, the rule is absolute and said first, because a ball this activity grows heavy is a ball nobody lifts at all: if it cannot be rolled by its crew, it is finished, not carried. Mittens stay on for every push; cold hands end a roller's turn without debate. The lane is adult-walked and ice-free, and eyes stay on the ball, not on faces. No snow goes near anyone's face, in play or in triumph, ever.
activities.setup: The set-up is the snow itself, and the adult checks it like equipment: it must pack, a handful squeezed must hold together, because powder that will not pack teaches only frustration, and a day of wet snow is this activity's whole season. Walk the rolling lane first: flat, clear of ice and sticks, ending somewhere the finished snowball can stay as the group's work. Start the first core ball yourself, fist-sized and packed hard: a soft core falls apart under new rollers and the growing never starts.
steps: Show the core ball and say the plain snow fact the whole activity hangs on: 'Snow sticks to snow. If we roll this little ball along the ground, it picks up more snow and gets bigger. Watch my hands. We push it, we never throw it.' State the one rule: 'Mittens on, hands push together, and the ball stays on the ground.'

First roll together: everyone who can reach kneels or stands round the ball and pushes it one slow turn along the lane, hands flat on its sides. Stop after a few turns and LOOK: the ball is wearing a new coat of snow and its shape is already less round. That first visible growth is the lesson landing. Name it: 'It grew. The rolling did that.'

Rolling round: the ball travels the lane with rollers swapping in as it grows, and it will need swapping, because a bigger ball is a heavier push, and two fresh mittens on each side is how it keeps moving. Rollers who are not pushing walk beside it as the escort, watching for the thin patches where the ball picks up grass instead of snow, and calling the turn-around.

Heavy moment, planned for: somewhere down the lane the ball gets too heavy for its current crew, and that is a ceremony, not a failure. Everyone gathers, hands go flat on it together, and the group pushes it its last turns in one shared heave. A three-year-old who has felt a thing outgrow their own strength, safely, with help arriving, has learned the snowball's second lesson.

Finish where the lane ends: hands off, step back, and look at what the lane made, a ball that started in one adult fist. Compare it honestly with body words: 'It is as big as a pumpkin. As big as somebody's tummy.' It stays where it finished for the day, the group's work on display, melting on its own schedule like everything made of snow.
activities.tagline: One small snowball, rolled along the snow by many mittens: it picks up snow as it goes and grows. Everybody can feel it getting heavier.

variations.easier: A table-top version at a tray of shaved ice or a short lane of three turns only, the ball finished at handful size and compared with the core the adult kept back.
variations.harder: Two balls, two short lanes, rolled side by side: which grew bigger over the same ground, and can the group say why. Wetter snow, more turns, more mittens?

activities.inclusion: A road reaches every driver: one road is laid straight to a seated driver's place and along their tray edge if needed, so their car sets out from home like everyone else's. Driving a car by pushing it with a palm, a fist, or a pusher stick taped chunky at the grip is driving in full. The town planner job, choosing where the next road goes and pointing its line while the layers lay it, builds the town as surely as tape does.

materials.item: big chunky toy cars and trucks (too big to be a mouth worry, one per driver plus spares)
a smooth floor space big enough for two or three roads

activities.name: Big Tape Roads Car Town
activities.safety: Tape is low-tack and floor-only, never on skin, hair, or faces, and peeled-up tape is balled by the adult straight into the bin, because a loose tape ball is a mouth-sized curiosity. Cars are big and chunky with no small detachable parts, checked before the town opens. Driving happens crouched or seated at the road's edge; nobody walks ON a road while cars are moving. Feet use the paths, which is the town's rule and the room's safety in one sentence.
activities.setup: Build the town's skeleton before the drivers arrive: one long straight tape road across the floor, pressed down by your own palm along its whole length, edges flat. Tape that lifts trips feet and stops cars, and neither is the activity. Leave the roll and pre-torn lengths where the group can build with you: the second and third roads are theirs to lay, with your hands smoothing. A road needs a destination a three-year-old can name: the rug is the park, a taped square is the shop, the bookshelf is home.
steps: Show the first road and say the plain job: 'This is a road. Cars drive ON roads. We are going to build a car town, first the roads, then the driving.' State the one rule: 'Cars stay on the roads, and feet walk around them.' Model one drive yourself, slowly, down the whole first road, stopping at its end and naming the place you have arrived at.

Building round: the group lays the next roads with you, a length of tape carried flat in two hands, set down along a line the adult points, pressed smooth by every palm that reaches it. Roads can join the first road or run beside it; a road that wanders gets named for where it ends up, because at three the town plans itself around the building.

Driving round: one car per driver, driven by a hand on its roof at walking-hand pace. Drivers call their destinations as they set out, 'Going to the shop!', and the town answers when they arrive. Two cars meeting on one road is traffic, handled the town way: one waits, one passes slowly, nobody lifts a car over another.

Rush moment, once, on purpose: you call 'Lots of cars today!' and every driver drives at the same time, slowly, on their own roads. The town holding a whole group's traffic at once, cars on roads, feet on the paths between them, is the picture this activity was built to reach, and the calm inside it is the skill.

Finish with the town at rest: cars parked in the taped square, drivers standing back to look at the whole map they built and drove. Tape roads can stay down for the day, a town on the floor gets visited again, and peeling them up at tidy time, slowly, in whole lengths, is a job the builders will queue for.
activities.tagline: Painter's tape roads laid straight across the floor, and big chunky cars to drive them: the town is built first, then driven, stop by stop.

variations.easier: One road only and two big cars, the adult driving the second car as traffic company for the whole session.
variations.harder: Add one taped STOP square mid-road: cars that reach it must stop, count to three with the group, then drive on. The town's first traffic rule, invented by its builders.

activities.inclusion: The window comes down to every artist: a low pane, a glass door's bottom section, or a hand mirror misted on a tray all hold fog and a finger line equally well, and the drawing counts in full whatever glass it clears from. An artist can also direct a drawing, 'a sun... with a face... there', while the adult's finger draws exactly what is directed, which is authorship by the oldest method there is.

materials.item: one big window or glass door the group can reach the bottom half of (adult-checked: sound glass, low sill)
a spray bottle of plain water (adult's hands only)
no other materials, one finger per artist

activities.name: Fog Window Finger Drawing
activities.safety: The spray bottle lives in adult hands, filled with plain water only, and is never pointed at a face. It mists glass, full stop. The glass is adult-checked, sound, and never leaned on: drawing fingers press as lightly as writing on a cloud requires, which the fog itself teaches in one smudged line. Wet drips below the window are wiped as they come. A wet floor under standing artists is the one real hazard in a weather activity, and it is managed with a cloth, not a lecture.
activities.setup: Choose the glass like it matters: a low window the group already gathers at, sound and clean, with the bottom panes at standing three-year-old height. Test your fog before the group arrives, a fine mist, wiped hands, and one test drawing of your own: the fog must hold a finger line long enough to finish a sun, and if the room is too warm and dry for fog to hold, a cold day or a breathed-on pane is the honest version and the session waits for its weather.
steps: Gather at the window and say the plain wonder of it straight: 'Watch. I am going to make weather on the window.' Mist the pane in front of the group, the fog arriving IS the opening ceremony, 'Now the window is foggy, like a cloud sat on it. And a finger can draw in a cloud.' Draw your own sun first, one finger, slowly, so the line appearing is watched, not just the sun.

State the one rule: 'One finger draws. The fog does the rest, and when it fades, the drawing goes home with it. Nothing in this picture can be wrong, because the window keeps nothing.' That promise is the activity: a first drawing medium with no wrong marks in it, and three-year-olds who have been corrected at paper will test the promise and find it true.

Artists' round: each artist gets a fresh-misted stretch of pane, re-misted by you between artists, and draws whatever one finger draws: suns, faces, spirals, a line that is honestly a line. Drawings are named by their makers if they want naming; a spiral called 'my dog' is a dog, and the window agrees with every artist.

Fading watch, the quiet middle: when several drawings share the glass, stop misting and watch together as the fog thins, edges softening, lines going pale, the window clearing itself. 'The sun is drying our cloud.' A room of three-year-olds watching a picture disappear on purpose, unhurried, is practising something most media never teach: a thing can be finished by ending.

Finish with one group drawing: a fresh mist across the whole pane, every artist adding one mark each in turn, a stripe of sun, a dot, a door, until the window holds the whole group's one picture. Then stand back and let this one fade together too, while everyone is watching, because the fading is the frame this gallery hangs on every piece.
activities.tagline: The grown-up mists the window until it fogs, and one finger draws a sun, a face, a wobbly house. Then the fog fades and takes every mark with it.

variations.easier: One small pane and three artists, the adult misting smaller and oftener, drawings limited to one shape each: a circle is a complete picture here.
variations.harder: Drawing pairs: one artist draws, and their partner must guess what it is BEFORE it fades. The fading sets an honest clock no timer has to enforce.

activities.inclusion: Directing is the activity, and it runs on any signal a director has: a word, a point toward or away from the light, a big-arms gesture for GROW and hands-close for shrink. Every director's call moves the shape the same distance. A director can also hold the SECOND shape at the wall end, still, as the size the moving shadow must match, the fixed point the whole experiment leans on, held by its most patient scientist.

materials.item: one big cardboard shape (adult-cut: a star, a fish, a hand, bigger than two kid hands, held on a stick or by its edge)
one lamp or bright torch on a stable stand (adult-positioned, shining at a clear wall)
a room that can be dimmed a little

activities.name: Big Shadow Grow and Shrink
activities.safety: The lamp is the adult's, positioned once and never carried, aimed at a wall and never at eyes. Its brightness is respected the way this archive respects every bright thing, by looking at what it lights, not at it. The shape travels in the adult's hands only, so no small body ever crosses between a hot or bright lamp and the wall. Directors direct from their seats; the floor between seats and wall stays empty, because a shadow stage with a toddler wandering it teaches collisions, not optics.
activities.setup: Set the stage before the group sits: lamp steady and adult-height-handled, wall clear, shape tested through its whole journey, from right against the wall to right against the light, so you know the shadow stays on the wall and the shape never has to touch anything hot or bright. The shape is plain and bold: a three-year-old reads a shadow by its outline, and a shape with ears, points or a tail gives the group something to watch change size. Nobody carries the lamp but you; that is fixed before the first shadow appears.
steps: Darken the room a little, switch the lamp on, and make the first shadow yourself without a word of explanation: shape against the wall, a small neat shadow. Then walk it slowly toward the light and let the group watch the shadow swell across the wall. Their reaction IS the introduction. Then say the plain sentence it all hangs on: 'The shadow does what the shape does, but bigger, when the shape goes nearer the light.'

State the one rule: 'Only the grown-up holds the light and the shape. Everybody else is a director. You tell it: nearer... further... stop.' Directors' hands stay in laps or pointing; pointing is a director's whole toolkit and it is enough.

Directing round: the group directs the shape's journey in chorus and by turns, 'NEARER!' as it creeps toward the lamp and the shadow climbs the wall, 'further...' as it shrinks back down. Call the sizes as they pass: 'As big as the door! As big as a cat!'. Naming a shadow's size against real things is measurement in the only units this room needs.

Freeze moments: on a director's 'STOP!', the shape freezes and everyone looks hard at the shadow's edges. Fuzzy when the shape is near the light, sharper when it is near the wall. Say only what eyes can check: 'Near the light, the shadow is big and soft at the edges. Near the wall, small and sharp.' Two facts, both visible, both theirs now.

Finish with the biggest possible shadow: the group directs the shape as near the light as it safely goes, the shadow fills the wall, and every director puts their own hands up into the light's edge from their seats to see their hand-shadows join it, a wall full of shadow, made by the whole room, before the lamp goes off and the ordinary wall comes back.
activities.tagline: One big cardboard shape, one lamp, one wall: move the shape nearer the light and its shadow grows, the group directs, the shadow obeys.

variations.easier: Two positions only, marked on the floor: BIG (near the light) and SMALL (near the wall). Directors call just the two words and the shape travels between them.
variations.harder: A second shape joins: the group directs two shadows to the same size, one near, one far, matched by eye, and argues about whether they truly match, which is the point.

activities.inclusion: A seated line counts in full. This archive has said it before and the sponge proves it again: hands at chair height pass a sponge exactly as standing hands do, and a pass that travels palm to palm across a lap tray has travelled. The end-hands job, the squeeze over the pot, counted by the whole line, can be held by any hands the team sends the sponge to, including hands the adult steadies from underneath while the squeezing stays theirs.

materials.item: one big soft sponge (adult-sized, the drippier the better)
a bucket of water at the line's start (adult's station)
a pot or clear jug at the line's end (the fill target. A mark on its side is the goal)
a tray or mat under the whole line (the drips' home)

activities.name: Sponge Pass: Fill the Pot
activities.safety: Water stays on the tray's country: the line stands or sits on a dry edge of it, and drips that escape are the adult's cloth's job between rounds, a wet floor under a standing line is a slip arranged in advance. The sponge is squeezed only over the pot, never at a neighbour; water play at three stays kind or it stops. Bucket water is clean, changed if it gets grubby, and never drunk. A line thirsty from watching water is offered the drinking kind, from a cup, away from the game.
activities.setup: Set the line's country before the team does: tray down the middle of where the line will stand or sit, bucket at one end with you, pot at the other with its goal mark where everyone can see it. Test the sponge yourself. It should be big enough that a squeeze visibly matters and drippy enough that passing it hand to hand is an event, not a formality. The distance matters: the line must be long enough that the pass is a journey, short enough that the sponge arrives still worth squeezing.
steps: Show the dry pot and its mark and say the plain job: 'This pot needs filling, and the water bucket is way over there. Our water travels in this sponge, hand to hand, down the whole line. The last hands squeeze it into the pot. Then we do it again, until the water reaches the mark.' State the one rule: 'The sponge travels hand to hand. Nobody carries it. Nobody squeezes until the end.'

First pass together, slow: you soak the sponge, it travels down the line hand to hand, every pair of hands holding it a moment, feeling the weight and the drip, to the end hands, who squeeze it over the pot while the whole line counts the squeeze: 'One... two... three.' The first squeeze's water lands visibly short of the mark, which is the best possible news: the line can see exactly how much journey is left.

Passing rounds: the sponge returns UP the line dry-side, carried back by the adult or passed back hand to hand, the group will have opinions, gets re-soaked, and travels again. Round by round the pot climbs: call the level at every squeeze, in handful words first and mark words as it nears: 'Halfway to the mark. One squeeze from the mark...'

Careful-hands discovery, somewhere mid-game: the line will notice on its own that a gentle pass arrives wetter than a hurried one. When it is noticed, name it as the team's own finding: 'Slow hands keep the water.' No adult announced that rule, the sponge taught it, and a rule a team discovers is a rule the team keeps.

Finish at the mark: the squeeze that reaches it gets the full count and the full ceremony. The whole line looks into the pot together, and the number of journeys gets told back: 'Six trips the sponge made. Every hand in this line carried the water.' The pot's water waters a plant or washes the tray down, poured by the end hands: the fill was never the point; it also always has a use.
activities.tagline: One soaked sponge passed hand to hand down the whole line, and a squeeze over the pot at the end: the line's job is measured in what arrives still wet.

variations.easier: A short line of four, the pot a small jug with a low mark: two journeys fill it, and the team finishes while the discovery is still fresh.
variations.harder: Two sponges travelling: a second sponge starts when the first is halfway home. The line must keep two journeys straight, and the squeeze count doubles at the pot.

activities.inclusion: Three arrives by every road: folded with a thumb, held down by the other hand, spread wide and counted, or shown on a hand resting on a tray with fingers lifted one by one while the circle counts them standing. A shower who directs the adult's hand. 'That one down... that one up... THREE'. Has built the sign in full, and the circle copies the directed three exactly as proudly as any other.

materials.item: no materials, hands only, ten fingers per expert

activities.name: Show Me Three Fingers
activities.safety: Hands only, at hand height: a showing hand never goes in another kid's face, and copies are made looking at your own hand, not grabbing a neighbour's fingers to arrange them. Fingers get folded by their owner or their owner's other hand, nobody else's. A hand that does not want to show rests, and its owner directs a copy from the adult's hand instead; the circle copies that one with the same respect, because directing your sign is showing it.
activities.setup: No set-up beyond knowing your room: this is the three-year-old room's own party trick, and it only works because everyone in it shares the number. Practise your own three first with the hand you will model with. Thumb holding the little finger down is the classic route, but fingers that arrive at three by any honest road are the point of the session, and your model should be the achievable kind, wobble included.
steps: Hold your hand up and say the plain boast that starts it: 'I am going to tell you something about this whole room. Every single person here is THREE. And three has a sign. Watch.' Make your three slowly, folding the little finger down, holding it with your thumb, and count the standing fingers out loud: 'One, two, THREE. That is us.'

State the one rule: 'One shower at a time, and the whole circle copies their three. Exactly their three, wobbles and all.' Go in seat order, known in advance, so every shower knows their moment is coming and nobody's hand is a surprise.

Showers' round: each kid raises their three any way their hand can manage it, the classic fold, fingers spread wide, a three built with the other hand's help, a three held for one second before the fingers spring back. The circle copies it faithfully: spread for spread, wobble for wobble, and counts the copy together, 'One, two, THREE', because the count is the room agreeing the sign is real.

Hard-finger honesty: somewhere in the round, a little finger will refuse to stay down, and it gets named kindly as the room's shared enemy: 'That little finger has its own ideas. Everybody's does.' A hand helped by its partner hand is not a failed three. It is the standard three at this age, and the circle copying the helped version says so without a speech.

Finish with the whole room's sign at once: 'Show me three!', every hand up, every version of three the room owns, held for a count of three, counted by everyone. Photograph it in your memory if not in fact: eighteen different threes, all correct, is the three-year-old room's group portrait.
activities.tagline: Everybody in this room is three, so everybody learns the hard, proud trick of holding up three fingers, and the whole circle copies yours.

variations.easier: Two fingers first as a warm-up sign ('show me two, the easy cousin'), then three: the room feels its own hands level up inside one session.
variations.harder: Signs grow: thumbs-up for 'yes', a wave for 'hello', a flat palm for 'stop'. The circle builds its first three-sign language, every sign copied the shower's way.

activities.inclusion: Counting is done by voice and pointing from wherever a counter is stationed: a counter watching from the path's edge, whose 'there. One more!' is called out and chalked into the group count by the adult, has counted that worm in full. The step-wide is done at every wheel's width too. The route is walked first by the adult precisely so its residents and its careful lines suit every traveller who will take it.

materials.item: a paved path or playground edge on a morning just after rain (the adult has walked it first and found worms to count)
no other materials, eyes and careful feet only

activities.name: After-Rain Worm Count

photo.alt: Worms in balls after rain
photo.caption: Worms in balls after rain.
photo.credit: Photo: LlamaJoe96, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Nobody touches a worm, ever. The rule is the activity's spine, stated as the worm's need, not the children's fault: worm skin is delicate and dry hands harm it, full stop. Feet step wide and eyes watch the ground; the adult walks the route first so no worm is a surprise under a running foot, and walking, only walking, is the pace, because this path has residents. Hands that never touched a worm still wash back inside, as after any outdoor work; the path after rain holds more than worms, and the washing is routine, not alarm.
activities.setup: The set-up is timing and scouting, and both are the adult's: worms come onto hard ground after rain, so this is a morning-after activity, taken when the weather offers it, not scheduled against it. Walk the path yourself first: there must be worms actually there to count, a wormless path is a walk, not a count, and note where they are thickest, so the group's careful feet are planned around real residents, not hoped-for ones. Soft ground beside the path is the stepping-aside place; check it is not a swamp.
steps: Gather at the path's edge and say the plain true framing: 'Last night it rained. When it rains, worms come up out of the wet ground and onto the path. We are going to count how many came up on OUR path. And the rule that matters most. ' State it whole: 'We count with our eyes. Nobody touches a worm. Their skin is their breathing, and hands are too rough and too dry for them.' Said once, plainly, as care rather than warning.

First worm together: walk the group to the first one you scouted, everyone stops a full step back, and the group looks properly, its length against a leaf, its slow way of moving, which end is going where, argued about with real interest. The count starts: 'One.' A worm counted is a worm greeted: 'Hello, worm one.' Three-year-olds who greet a resident do not step on it.

Counting walk: the group moves along the path at worm pace, which is to say barely, stopping at every worm, 'Two... three...', with pointers counting from a step back and steppers stepping WIDE around every counted resident. A worm lying across the whole path stops the walk entirely: the group watches it cross, or the adult moves it gently on a wet leaf if it is truly stuck in harm's way, and the moving is watched as the skilled, kind exception it is.

Thick-patch moment: where the worms are many, the count slows and the looking deepens, big ones, small ones, one coiled, one stretched to its full surprising length. Compare honestly in body words: 'That one is longer than my finger. That tiny one is a baby-sized worm.' Nobody's measure needs a ruler; the path is the chart.

Finish at the path's end with the number told back whole: 'Eleven worms came up on our path after the rain.' Then the group leaves the path the way it came, stepping round the same residents, and the last word is the plain cycle said out loud: 'When the ground dries, they will go back down where it is safe and wet. The path is theirs until then.' A count that gets retold at lunch is data at this age, and it will be.
activities.tagline: After rain, the worms come up onto the path: the group counts them where they lie, steps carefully round them, and touches not one.

variations.easier: A three-worm path and a very small group: the whole count at one crouch, with the step-wide practised once around a worm the adult found first.
variations.harder: Count a second surface, the grass edge as well as the path: which ground had more worms after the same rain, and can the counters say by how many, in fingers if not in words?

activities.inclusion: The drum is found at every position: marching can be feet stamping seated, arms pumping, or wheels rocking, the beat quickens for effort of any kind, and the hand that feels it can rest on a chest directly or over the adult's hand placed there at the feeler's direction. A tapper whose tapping is one finger on a tray plays their tempo as truly as any knees in the room; the beat is the music, never the limb that plays it.

materials.item: no materials, hands, chests and knees only
a rug or clear floor space for marching in place

activities.name: Feel the Beat: Heart Tap
activities.safety: Hands on your own chest only. The rule is stated before the first march and holds absolutely; nobody feels, taps, or thumps anybody else's chest, in play or in curiosity. Marching is twenty seconds in place and stops on the word; a kid who feels dizzy or done sits straight down and rests with the resting group early. Resting is a full part in this activity, never an exit from it. The record makes no health claims and reads no one's beat aloud for comment: every heart in the room is described as doing its job, because that is the whole of what is claimed.
activities.setup: No set-up beyond clear floor and your own rehearsal: put your hand flat on your own chest first and march in place for twenty seconds. You must be able to feel your own beat clearly enough to describe it, because at three the whole activity is 'can you find it on yourself', and a teacher who has just found theirs teaches it in half the words. Plan the rest as carefully as the marching: this activity is a fast half and a slow half, and the slow half is where the music is.
steps: Start still: everyone standing or seated, one hand flat on their own chest, quiet for a moment. Say the plain body fact: 'Inside you, your heart is beating, all the time, like a drum that never stops. Sometimes it is hard to feel. We are going to make it easy to feel, and then play it.' A few kids will find a beat just from the stillness; let them announce it. Most will need the march, which is coming.

State the one rule: 'Your hand stays on YOUR chest. Your beat is yours, we never feel anybody else's.' Marching round: the whole group marches in place together, twenty honest seconds, knees up, arms swinging, then 'Stop. Hand on your heart. FEEL it.' The room goes still with hands on chests, and the finding happens in faces before it happens in words: there it is, thumping away, fast.

Tapping round, fast: hands move to knees and tap the beat they just felt, tap-tap-tap at marching speed, the group tapping its own hearts' tempo together, roughly and gloriously not in unison. Say the earned sentence over the tapping: 'That is your heart's song right now. It is fast because you marched.'

Resting round, the turn: everyone sits, hands back on chests, and the group breathes and waits while the drum inside slows, give it real time, a slow count of twenty, then hands find the beat again: 'Feel it now? Slower.' Knees tap the second tempo, gentle where the first was busy, and the difference between the two tappings is the whole lesson, played by every musician on their own body.

Finish by naming the instrument properly: 'Your heart is a drum you carry everywhere. Fast when you run, slow when you rest, and it never, ever stops playing.' One last still moment, hands on chests, feeling the resting beat together. The quietest ensemble this room will ever be part of, and every player in it is the instrument.
activities.tagline: March in place until your heart goes fast, hand flat on your chest to feel it, then tap that beat on your knees, and tap it again slower after the rest.

variations.easier: Seated beats only: stamp feet in place instead of marching, twenty stamps, then feel and tap. The fast beat arrives the same, at table height.
variations.harder: A third tempo joins: after a slow sway to a lullaby the group knows, feel and tap the swaying beat, three speeds of the same drum, told back in order at the end.

activities.inclusion: A print lands from any height the sheet is met at: the mural runs along a low table edge and the floor alike, and a sponge pressed with a palm, a fist, or two hands stacked prints exactly as boldly. The caller job, naming which shape goes next and where along the sheet it belongs, is the mural's composition done aloud, and a caller who never touches a sponge has still arranged the whole picture.

materials.item: chunky sponge shapes (adult-cut from thick sponges: circles, stars, houses. Each bigger than a kid's whole hand)
one very long sheet of paper, taped down flat (the mural)
washable paint in wide shallow trays (one per colour)

activities.name: Big Sponge Stamp Mural
activities.safety: Washable paint only, in shallow trays that cannot tip into a lap when a sponge presses them. Sponges are big and single-piece, no small cut-offs anywhere near the table, because a painty sponge piece is a mouth magnet at three. Pressing happens seated or standing still at the sheet's edge; nobody reaches ACROSS wet prints to print further in. The sheet is walked around, because a sleeve dragged through a garden of prints is a mural redrawn by accident.
activities.setup: Build the mural's country before the painters sit: the long sheet taped at every corner and along its edges, a sheet that slides under a pressing hand teaches chasing, not printing, and trays shallow enough that a sponge dips its face, not its whole body. Cut the sponges yourself and test each one: a shape that prints as a blob gets recut now, because the first time a star prints as a star is the moment this activity explains itself to the whole table at once.
steps: Show the empty mural and the dry sponges and say the plain job: 'This long paper is going to become a picture of everybody's printing. A sponge shape gets paint on its face, presses down on the paper, and lifts straight up, and leaves its shape behind.' Demonstrate the whole move yourself, slowly: dip, press, count one-two, lift straight, 'The lifting is the printing. Pull sideways and it smears; lift straight and it stays a star.'

State the one rule: 'Dip, press, lift straight. One shape, one print, then look at it before you print again.' First prints together: each painter's first print lands on the mural's near end with the group watching each lift, star, circle, house, because a print appearing out of a lift is a small magic trick the whole table needs to see land before the printing spreads out.

Printing round: painters work along the sheet at their own stations, shapes shared by calling for them by name, 'Pass the house!', and waiting for the pass. Prints can row up in lines, crowd into gardens, or stand one per child with space around; the mural takes every arrangement as its style, and a print that lands pale gets named honestly: 'That one needs more paint on its face', a fixable fact, not a failed star.

Smear moment, planned for kindly: sooner or later a lift goes sideways and a star becomes a comet. Name it as the mural's first comet, because it is one, and let its maker decide: it stays as the comet it became, or one clean print goes beside it as its star. Both choices stay on the mural; the smear rule was physics, not judgement, and the mural proves it.

Finish when the sheet is printed to its far end: cloths down, hands washed by painters in turn, and the whole group walks the mural's length slowly, reading it like a story. Who printed the garden, where the comet lives, whose house stands by whose star. It dries flat where it lies and goes up whole: a wall built of lifts, every print in it the shape it meant to be, or better.
activities.tagline: Chunky sponge shapes dipped in paint and pressed straight down on one long shared sheet: print, lift, look, a mural built one honest print at a time.

variations.easier: Three painters, three shapes, one short sheet: one print each per colour, and the mural finished inside ten minutes at full quality.
variations.harder: Pattern printing: prints must alternate, star, circle, star, circle, down one whole row, called along the row by the group before each press, so the pattern is planned aloud and printed by hands.

activities.inclusion: Kicking is a leg's job at every height it works: a ball struck by a footplate, a swung lower leg from a standing frame's support, or a strong arm-push from the spot, renamed honestly as that kicker's kick, swung at their call, sends the same ball to the same wall and earns the same 'Wall!' from the room. The caller job, naming each kicker and calling the wall arrivals, runs the whole lane and belongs to whoever holds it by voice or by pointing the name card the adult flips.

materials.item: one big light ball (beach-ball sized, soft, slow. The adult has tested its roll)
a clear wall stretch with a taped target patch at kick height
a start mat a few steps from the wall (the kicking spot)

activities.name: Big Ball Kick to the Wall
activities.safety: One kicker in the lane, ever. The rule is the activity's whole safety system, and the waiting line sits behind the spot where no swing or rolling ball can reach it. The ball is big, light and slow by design: nothing in this game flies, and a ball kicked at a face height is a ball that was too hard or too small, retired by the adult on the spot. Fetching is walking, kicking is from a standstill beside a still ball, no running kicks at three, because a leg swung at speed by a body still learning balance lands its owner as often as its ball.
activities.setup: Set the lane like a promise: ball tested first, big enough that a swinging foot cannot miss it entirely and light enough that a full three-year-old swing sends it rolling, not flying. The wall stretch is bare and hard-wearing, the target patch taped at the height a rolled ball actually arrives, and the kicking spot marked a distance a small kick can honestly cover: success at three is the ball REACHING the wall, so the wall starts close and only ever moves by the group's own growing legs. Waiting space sits behind the kicking spot, out of the lane entirely.
steps: Show the whole movement yourself, in teacher time: walk to the ball, stop beside it, plant one foot, swing the other. The ball rolls to the wall, bumps it, and rolls gently back. Say the plain framing: 'Kicking is your foot's turn to play the ball. One kicker at a time, everybody watches, and the wall is the goalie. The ball just has to REACH it.' State the one rule: 'Only the kicker is in the lane. Feet kick the ball, nobody dives, nobody throws.'

Kickers' round begins with the group behind the line and the first kicker walking the lane alone. The walk-up matters: arrive, stop, look at the target, plant, swing. A kick that tops the ball and dribbles it halfway is a kick, the kicker fetches it at a walk, brings it back to the spot, and kicks the rest of the journey, because a ball re-kicked is a turn finished honestly, not a turn failed.

Wall arrivals get their due: when a ball bumps the wall, and the bump is audible, which the group will treat as applause, the kicker calls 'Wall!' and the room answers it. The target patch earns its own call when a ball lands on it: not better than the wall, just a different address on it, said that way every time so reaching stays the achievement and the patch stays a decoration on it.

Fetching is part of the turn, at a walk, always: the kicker collects their ball from the wall and carries it back in two arms to the next kicker, handing over the turn with the ball itself. A lane where the worker fetches is a lane that never has two bodies moving toward each other. The safety is built into the ceremony and the ceremony is built into the game.

Finish with a full-room final: every kicker takes one last kick in order, the wall getting bumpier in the group's ears with practice, and the tell-back at the end counts something true: 'Every leg in this line reached the wall today.' The ball gets parked against the wall it worked against, and legs that have kicked walk out slower and taller than legs that waited. Which is why the waiting line rotates fast and fair, called by name, in the open.
activities.tagline: One big light ball, one kicker at a time, one wall: walk up, plant your feet, swing your leg, and the wall stops it and sends the next turn back.

variations.easier: The wall comes closer: two steps only between spot and wall, and a bigger ball. A turn built so the newest legs in the room reach the wall on their first swing.
variations.harder: Two target patches, high-ankle and knee height on the wall's stretch: kickers call their patch before they swing, and the room calls whether the ball visited the called address or another. Both are celebrated, only one is counted as a call landed.

activities.inclusion: The zip works at lap height, table height, or held upright by the adult at exactly the angle its worker directs. The board travels, the skill doesn't change. A pull can be gripped by a fist through the ribbon, pushed with a palm heel along its track on a board laid flat, or directed, 'up... stop... down', while a partner's hand pulls at the director's pace: the pacing, which is the skill's heart, belongs to the director in full.

materials.item: one zip board (adult-made: a chunky jacket zip sewn or firmly fixed on stiff fabric over board, the pull tab big enough for a whole fist. A ribbon loop through the pull helps)
a lap or low table to rest the board on

activities.name: Big Zip Up-and-Down Board
activities.safety: Zips pinch: the rule is in the method. Fingers live on the pull and its ribbon, never on the teeth's path, and a pull stops the instant anything (fabric, skin, thread) is in the track. The board is the only zip practised on: nobody practises on a worn coat, theirs or anyone's, where a pinch lands on a body instead of a board. Boards are adult-checked before every session, a detached pull or a tooth out of line retires the board until it is repaired, no exceptions negotiated by enthusiasm.
activities.setup: Make or check the board like the tool it is: the zip must run SMOOTHLY. A zip that snags teaches yanking, so work it up and down twenty times yourself first, free its teeth of threads, and retire any zip that catches, because the board's whole lesson is that slow and steady is what works. The pull gets a ribbon loop a whole fist can hold. The fabric sits taut on the board so the zip's path never wrinkles under a pull; a slack path is a snag built in advance.
steps: Show the board closed and say the plain job: 'Coats have zips. Zips are a two-direction job: up joins the two sides together, down lets them apart. This board is where hands practise, so no coat ever has to wait on a zip again.' Work the zip once yourself, both ways, SLOWLY, letting the group hear the teeth join and part: the zip's sound is its own progress report.

State the one rule: 'Slow pulls only. If it stops, your hand stops. A zip is never forced, because a forced zip is a broken zip.' First pull together: a kid's fist through the ribbon loop, your hand under theirs not pulling, just present, and the zip travels up at the pace the teeth allow. The stop-and-back-off moment gets rehearsed on purpose: meet a snag, stop, back half a tooth, go again. Named out loud as the expert move it is.

Up-and-down rounds: each worker takes the board on their lap or the low table and runs the zip its whole journey, up, pause at the top, the two sides one side now, and down, the sides parting like a road opening. The full trip is the unit: nobody rushes to finish, because the quiet in this activity is the sound of a job being done at the speed it asks for.

Two-hand discovery, arriving on its own schedule: workers will find that one hand must hold the board's bottom still while the other pulls, the zip pulls the board otherwise. Name it when it lands: 'One hand holds, one hand works. That is every zip, on every coat, for everybody.' A board that teaches its own two-handedness has taught the dressing skill whole.

Finish with the board zipped up and passed hand to hand for one last look at the joined seam, a straight, closed line made by slow hands. Boards live in the quiet corner after today, available at coat time's hardest moments and calm ones alike: a skill practised in quiet gets used in weather, which is the entire reason it exists.
activities.tagline: One chunky zip on a sturdy board: grip the big pull, slide it up slow, slide it down slow. A coat's hardest job, practised where no coat is waiting.

variations.easier: Half-trips only: the adult starts every zip halfway, workers finish the up or the down; the journey is halved and the expert stop-and-back-off still gets its rehearsal.
variations.harder: A second board joins with its zip running the other way, or a bigger-toothed camping zip: workers must read a new zip's pace before pulling, same rule, new teeth, and the comparison is the lesson repeated with interest.

activities.inclusion: A coin's carry counts however it travels: on a lap tray wheeled along the path's edge, held against a chest in two hands from a seated carry-position at the pot's side, or directed. 'Carry it... drop it NOW', while the adult's hands do exactly what the director's words say. The pot-side listener job, calling 'CLINK, one more in!' at every landing, belongs to whoever holds it and is the pot's official scorekeeper.

materials.item: big pretend gold coins (adult-made: stiff gold card discs, wider than a kid's palm, edges smooth, one per kid plus spares)
one big pot (a sturdy bucket or plastic cauldron) at the path's end
a short clear carrying path from the coin basket to the pot

activities.name: Big Gold Coin Pot Carry

photo.alt: A gold five franc coin from 1857
photo.caption: A big gold coin, the treasure everyone carries carefully to the pot.
photo.credit: Photo: Jacques-Jean Barre, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Coins are big stiff card, far too wide for a mouth and with nothing peelable or detachable on them. A coin that gets chewed or starts to delaminate retires on the spot. The pot is sturdy and stays where the adult put it; nobody climbs in, sits in, or reaches deep inside it while others are dropping. Drops happen over the rim, at arm's length, one carrier at a time. Carrying is walking, always: a running carrier holding a coin at face height with both hands has no hand free to fall on, and the rule exists for exactly that reason.
activities.setup: Make the coins yourself beforehand, big, stiff, and honestly pretend: gold card, palm-and-a-half wide, no foil small enough to peel. Say the framing plainly in your own head before the group hears it: St. Patrick's Day is a real celebration, and the pot of gold at the rainbow's end is a pretend story people tell with it. The record keeps those two things separate and so does the session. Test the pot's clink yourself: the coin landing must be HEARD, because the sound is the receipt each carrier is carrying toward.
steps: Name the day and the story in two plain sentences: 'Today is for St. Patrick's Day. People tell a pretend story about a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow. It is a story, not a real thing, and stories are for playing. We are playing it big.' State the one rule: 'Two hands carry the coin. Walking feet. The coin goes in the pot, and only in the pot.'

First coin together, yours: carry a coin in two hands down the path at walking pace, hold it over the pot, and let it drop, CLINK, while the group listens. Say what just happened in the smallest words: 'One coin, carried all the way, in the pot.' Then look in together: one coin looks lonely in a big pot, which is exactly the problem this group is about to solve together.

Carrying round: one carrier at a time, coin in two hands, walking feet, the drop done by the carrier's own hands over the pot. Carriers walk back empty-handed along the path's edge. A dropped coin on the way is picked up by its own carrier and the carry simply continues, the path forgives, the pot waits, and nobody's carry is ever re-done by anyone else.

Halfway listen: stop the carrying, gather round the pot, and have the last carrier drop a coin in while everyone stays quiet for the clink and the rattle of the coins already there. Name the change out loud: 'The pot sounds different already. Fuller.' Three-year-olds who can HEAR the job half done will finish it like savers.

Finish when every coin is in: the final carrier drops theirs, the group counts the pot's coins by lifting them out one at a time back into the basket, the count is the second game hiding inside the first, and the tell-back is plain: 'Every coin in this pot got here in two hands, at walking pace, one carrier at a time.' Coins away, pot away, story closed as a story.
activities.tagline: Palm-sized pretend gold coins carried in two hands, one at a time, and dropped into the big pot with a clink. The whole group's carrying, collected.

variations.easier: A four-coin pot only and a path of six steps, the adult walking each carry beside the carrier with a hand hovering under the coin without touching it.
variations.harder: Two pots and a sorted carry: gold coins to the big pot, plain card coins to the small one. Carriers must read their coin before they set out and walk to the right pot.

activities.inclusion: Counting light is already everybody's game: a counter stationed at the blanket's edge in any seat they use has the same grass, the same sky, and the same vote on whether that blink counted. Calls can be a word, a point, or a hand raised fast. Every call is checked by the group the same way, and a blink only one counter saw still enters the count on their word, because at dusk, on a blanket, everybody's eyes are instruments.

materials.item: a grassy spot the group knows, at dusk in firefly season (the adult has checked the same week that fireflies are actually out there)
a blanket or mat to sit on together
no other materials. Eyes only, and staying together is the equipment

activities.name: First Firefly Blink Count

photo.alt: Fireflies tracing glowing trails over a dark stream
photo.caption: Fireflies tracing glowing trails over a dark stream.
photo.credit: Photo: T.Kiya さん https://www.flickr.com/photos/cq-biker/, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The group stays on the blanket, together, for the whole count. Dusk is not the hour for a three-year-old to wander toward something interesting, and the counting works precisely because the counters stay still and the fireflies come past. Catch nothing, jar nothing, touch nothing that lands: a firefly's light is its own business, and hands stay on laps or the blanket. The adult checks the grass spot in daylight first, no holes, no nests, no surprises, and everybody is up and moving back inside while there is still light enough to walk by.
activities.setup: The set-up is season, hour, and honesty, and all three are the adult's: fireflies come out at dusk in the warm months, so this is an evening activity taken when the summer offers it, not scheduled against it. Check the spot yourself the same week, fireflies actually blinking over that grass, because a firefly count with no fireflies is just sitting outside, and the record refuses to promise insects it has not met. The blanket goes where the group can see open grass and sky without wandering: the fireflies come to the counters, never the other way round.
steps: Settle on the blanket while there is still a little light and say the plain true framing: 'When summer nights come, tiny beetles called fireflies fly over the grass and blink a light from their tails, on, off, on, off. Tonight we are counting the blinks.' State the one rule whole: 'We count with our eyes. We catch nothing and we jar nothing. The fireflies stay free, and so does their light.'

First blink together: everyone watches the grass quietly, and the first blink anyone sees gets called, 'THERE!', and counted out loud by the whole group: 'One.' A blink argued over ('that was a plane') is settled kindly by waiting for the next one: fireflies blink again, planes do not blink like that, and the grass itself provides the evidence within the minute.

Counting stretch: the group counts blinks as they come, in chorus, at firefly pace. Which means long quiet watches between numbers, and the quiet is not a gap in the activity, it IS the activity. The adult keeps the running total on fingers where counters can see it grow, and recounts it at every tenth blink: 'Ten blinks over our grass.' Nobody has to count past what they can. Hearing the count grow is counting, at three.

Blink-pattern moment, if the evening offers it: two fireflies blinking near each other, 'That one answered that one!', and the group watches whether the pattern repeats. Say only what eyes can check: sometimes they do seem to answer, and watching for it is the oldest firefly science there is. A firefly that lands on the blanket's edge is looked at, not touched, and takes off on its own schedule to general respect.

Finish as the dark settles and the blinking thickens: one last minute of counting, the total told back whole, 'Twenty-three blinks we counted, and hundreds we didn't', and the plain cycle said out loud: 'The fireflies will blink all night without us. Tomorrow night they will be here again.' The group leaves the grass to its owners, blanket carried between them, at walking pace, in the near-dark they have all just practised seeing in.
activities.tagline: Out at dusk on a summer evening: fireflies blink over the grass and the group counts the blinks together. Catching nothing, just counting light.

variations.easier: A porch or window version: counters watch from behind a screen door or window, the blinking grass beyond it, the count kept in whispers as a bedtime game.
variations.harder: Blink-map round: the adult sketches the grass patch on a big sheet as blinks land, a dot per blink where it appeared, so the group can see WHERE the fireflies gathered by the end of the evening.

activities.inclusion: The mountain has a route at every height: a low summit annex, one wide cushion at the mountain's side, same up-and-over shape at a tenth of the height, belongs to the same climb and earns the same summit sit and the same cheering. A climber can also serve as the mountain's official tester: seated at the top by the adult's lift for the summit moment alone, having directed the whole inspection, 'press that one... that one wobbles... rebuild it'. Which is the mountaineer's oldest job, reading the mountain.

materials.item: big pillows and cushions (the biggest and firmest the room has. Sofa cushions are perfect)
a mat or rug under the whole mountain (the mountain's ground)
a clear floor space the adult has fenced with the room itself: mountain in the middle, waiting line at its foot

activities.name: Big Pillow Mountain Climb
activities.safety: One climber on the mountain at a time, ever. The rule is the activity's whole safety system, and the waiting line stands at the foot, behind the descent side, where no descending climber can land on a watcher. The mountain is adult-built, adult-tested, and adult-rebuilt the moment it shifts; jumping off the top is not a descent, ever. Down is hands and knees, like up, said first and held kindly. Climbers climb in bare feet or grippy socks on a mat that does not slide: a mountain on a skating rug is a fairground ride, and this is mountaineering.
activities.setup: Build the mountain yourself before the climbers arrive, and build it like it will be climbed on, because it will: biggest, firmest cushions at the bottom, each layer pressed down by your own knees and weight first, a mountain that shifts under the adult will shift under a child, and a shifting mountain is retired and rebuilt, not apologised for. Test the whole route yourself on hands and knees: up, the top flat enough to sit on for a real moment, down the far side to the mat. One route, obvious, with the way down as built as the way up.
steps: Show the mountain and climb it yourself first, slowly, narrating nothing but the plain job: 'This is our mountain. Mountains are climbed UP one side, and DOWN the other. Watch my hands, hands and knees, the whole way.' State the one rule: 'One climber on the mountain. Everybody else waits at the bottom, and the next climber starts when the mountain is empty.'

First climbs, close up: the first climbers go with you right beside the mountain, a hand hovering, not holding, near each climber, ready for a wobble that mostly does not come. Hands and knees up, and coach the top out loud: 'You are nearly there... hands on the top pillow...' The summit sit gets its full moment: every climber sits at the top, looks at the room from the mountain's height, and is seen by the whole waiting line. Being beheld from above is half the climb's pay.

Climbing round: climbers rotate in line order, known in advance, the descent finished and feet on the mat before the next climber's hands touch the first pillow. A climber who wants the summit twice waits for a second turn like everyone. The mountain keeps, and its queue is fair. Cheering from the line is the line's whole job and they will invent its forms themselves; all forms are traditional from the first climb onward.

Wobble moment, planned for kindly: a pillow will shift mid-climb for someone, sooner or later. The climber stops, you steady the mountain with your hands, the climber backs down or climbs on. Their call, made from stillness, never from a slide. Then the mountain gets its repair in front of everyone: pressed down, tested, declared rebuilt. A mountain that gets mended openly teaches more trust than one that pretends to be rock.

Finish with a full-group summit photo that exists only in memory if need be: the last climber sits at the top, the line gathers at the foot, and the tell-back counts something true: 'Every climber in this room went up one side and down the other, on their own hands and knees.' Then the mountain comes down the builders' way, cushions carried back one at a time, in two arms, by the climbers themselves: unbuilding is mountaineering too.
activities.tagline: A mountain of big soft pillows built by the grown-up: hands and knees up one side, a sit at the top, hands and knees down the other, one climber at a time.

variations.easier: A foothill version: one layer of cushions only, a climb of two steps up and over, summited and descended in under a minute per climber.
variations.harder: A flag for the summit: each climber carries a big soft flag up in one hand (three points of contact becoming the honest challenge) and plants it beside them for the length of their summit sit.

activities.inclusion: The sled comes to every rider: a rider can be seated on the blanket in the position that suits their body, cross-legged, side-seated, or reclined against a cushion backrest the adult wedges safely behind them, and the pull stays the same slow pull, because the ride is the glide, not the posture. A rider who prefers to direct can stand with the adult as co-horse in name: they call 'walk on... and... stop' and the sled obeys their voice exactly, which is driving in full by the oldest method on any farm.

materials.item: one big sturdy blanket (thick, no fringe or tassels, big enough for a seated kid plus a pulling flap at the front)
a smooth floor run (the adult has walked it: long, straight, clear at both ends)
no other materials. The rider's two hands on the blanket's edges are the harness

activities.name: Blanket Sled Slow Pull
activities.safety: The blanket is pulled by the grown-up only, at walking pace or slower, in a straight line. No swings, no spins, no sudden stops: a sled that lurches pitches its rider, and the start and stop are both creeps for that reason. Riders sit, always, a standing rider on a moving blanket is a fall already happening, and hands hold the blanket's edges, never a wrist, rope, or another person. The run is walked and cleared by the adult first and kept clear during rides: a loose toy on a sled run is a brake made of surprise, and there are no surprises on this floor.
activities.setup: Choose the blanket and the run like equipment, because they are: the blanket must be sturdy enough to take a seated rider's weight sliding, with a front flap long enough for your two hands and no fringe a finger could wind into. The run is walked first by you, smooth floor, no thresholds, no rug edges to catch, a clear stopping space at each end, and nothing at rider height along the sides. Test-pull it yourself with a cushion rider: the blanket should glide, not lurch, and the start must be a creep, not a jerk. You will practise the start until it is boring, because the riders deserve boring starts.
steps: Lay the blanket at the run's start and say the plain framing: 'This blanket is a sled, and this floor is its snow. A sled rider sits in the middle, holds the edges, and the sled goes SLOW. I am the pulling horse, and horses in this room walk.' State the one rule: 'The rider sits and holds on. Only the grown-up pulls. Nobody stands on the sled, ever.'

First ride together, shortest version: the first rider sits cross-legged in the blanket's middle, hands gripping the edges beside their hips, and you pull the run at half length and walking pace while the waiting group watches the method. Start slow, pull straight, stop slower. The rider's review is taken seriously and out loud: 'Too fast? Too wobbly?', and the pulling adjusts to the review, in front of everyone, so every rider knows their review will steer their ride too.

Riding round: riders take turns in line order, full run, there and back counting as one ride. The turn-around at the far end is done stopped: rider stays seated, you walk the blanket round in a wide slow arc, and the return begins only when the rider calls 'Ready!' A rider who never calls ready simply waits, enjoying the far end, for exactly as long as they like. The sled departs on the rider's word, and that is written on the activity, not improvised.

Cargo variant once the riders are seasoned: a rider may carry one big soft passenger, a teddy or cushion, held in their lap with both arms, which changes the ride honestly: hands busy with cargo cannot hold edges, so this version goes at half pace again and half length. The first cargo ride gets the first-rider review treatment all over again, because a new version deserves new consent.

Finish with the blanket's own ceremony: the last rider rides to the middle of the run, stops there, and the whole group gathers on and around the blanket for the tell-back. 'Every rider sat, held on, and was pulled slow.' Then riders help fold the blanket in half, and half again, hand over hand along its edges: the sled becomes a blanket again by the hands that rode it, which is the right way for a magic floor to end.
activities.tagline: One big blanket on a smooth floor, one seated rider holding its edges, and the grown-up pulling slow and straight, an indoor sled ride at walking pace.

variations.easier: A half-length run at creep pace with the adult pulling on knees beside the blanket's front corner, one hand on the blanket and one near the rider, for the newest riders in the room.
variations.harder: A two-stop route: the run passes a marked 'station' (a taped line), where the sled stops, the rider names a place they are travelling to, and only then does the pull continue, a journey with geography.

activities.inclusion: A report arrives in any form a nose can file it: a word, a point at the matching picture card, a thumbs-up or a screwed-up face that the adult translates faithfully and checks. 'Sour face means the coffee? Then coffee it is, found by your nose.' The jar is brought to each sniffer's chin at the height and distance the sniffer directs, and a sniffer who directs the jar's tour for the whole group, choosing the order, calling each nose forward, has run the laboratory in full.

materials.item: big wide-mouth jars with lids (adult-prepared, one smell per jar: orange peel, a cinnamon stick, fresh mint leaves, a piece of vanilla pod or a few coffee beans, foods and plant things only)
a tray the jars travel on
big picture cards of each smell's source (adult-drawn or printed BIG. The matching is by nose first, card second)

activities.name: Big Smell Jar: Sniff and Say
activities.safety: Foods and plant things only. Nothing perfumed, chemical, or sharp ever goes in a smell jar, and essential oils are banned from this activity outright: concentrated is the opposite of what a three-year-old's nose is for. The group's allergy list is checked against every jar before the tray comes out, and jars are held by the adult at chin height, never pressed to a face or passed hand to hand. Nothing is tasted and nothing is touched: a sniffer who feels sneezy or done turns their head away and their turn is complete, because a nose's 'enough' is a full scientific report.
activities.setup: Prepare the jars yourself and check every one with your own nose first: each smell must be findable in one honest sniff. Too faint teaches nothing, and anything sharp, perfumed, or chemical has no place in these jars at all, ever. Foods and plant things only, and you have checked the group's allergy list against every jar before the tray comes out: a jar whose smell belongs to a food a child in the room is allergic to simply does not exist today. Labels live on the lids' undersides for your eyes only; the jars themselves stay mystery jars until a nose reports.
steps: Bring the tray in covered and say the plain framing: 'Your nose knows things your eyes cannot see. In these jars are smells, real smells of real things. We are going to sniff, and say what our noses find.' State the one rule: 'One sniff at a time, jar held by the grown-up, and nothing in a jar is ever tasted or touched. Noses only.' Demonstrate on yourself: lid off, jar below your chin, never pressed to a face, one sniff, and your own report said like a scientist: 'That smells warm and spicy. I think it is cinnamon.'

Sniffing round: the first jar travels the group on its tray, each sniffer in turn, jar held by you at chin height, one good sniff, a second if wanted, and the report is theirs to phrase: a name, a description ('like oranges!'), a feeling ('smells like Grandma's kitchen'), or an honest 'I don't know,' which gets the picture cards brought out and the smell matched to its source by looking and sniffing together. Every report is written into the air the same way: 'Orange peel. Found by Maya's nose.'

Compare round, once all jars have travelled: two jars side by side, sniffed in turn by volunteers, 'Which one is the mint?', noses voting by pointing at the jar, the lids flipped to show the labels as the verdict. Getting it wrong here is data, said that way: 'Your nose said orange for the mint. Mint can trick a nose. Sniff again.' A nose learning its own tricks is the science, and it only arrives through the misses.

Favourite-smell vote, the quiet middle: each sniffer names the jar they'd take home, and the adult stacks those jars at the tray's front in vote order. The group's official ranking, built by noses. Expect the orange to win and the coffee to start arguments; both outcomes get reported in the tell-back as the findings they are.

Finish with the sources revealed properly: each jar opened beside its real source, the actual orange, the actual mint sprig, and one last sniff of jar and source together, so noses leave knowing the smell has an address. Jars are lidded, tray carried out by you, and the last plain sentence is the method itself: 'We found out what was in the jars without looking. The nose did that.'
activities.tagline: Big jars with one honest smell each, orange peel, cinnamon, fresh mint: lid off, one sniff, and say what your nose found. Nothing to guess, nothing to win.

variations.easier: Two jars only, with smells a world apart (orange and mint), and every sniffer guaranteed a findable difference inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A mystery fifth jar joins, unknown even in ranking, prepared by another adult, and the group must place it by sniffing: a new smell, or one of today's four wearing a different jar? Noses argue, then the lid decides.

activities.inclusion: Every square travels however its builder travels: on a lap tray to the board's edge, pressed on from a seated position at the board's low side, the board's lowest row is reserved, by the crew's own law, for builders who place from sitting height, or placed high by a builder directing the adult's hands as their stepladder: 'there... left a bit... PRESS.' The gap-watcher job, stationed at the board calling windows as they appear, is the build's chief engineer and never touches a square at all.

materials.item: big felt squares (adult-cut: a hand-and-a-half across, in four or five colours, one per builder plus spares)
a big flannel or felt wall board at kid height (felt sticks to felt, test yours)
a basket of squares at the room's other end (the quilt's supply depot)

activities.name: Big Felt Quilt Wall Build
activities.safety: Felt squares are big, single-piece, and plain, no buttons, pins, beads, or sewn-on anything exists on a square at this age, because a quilt square at three is a thing that will be carried against chests and occasionally faces. The board is fixed so it cannot tip or rock under pressing hands, and builders press with flat palms, not body weight leaned through the board into a wall fixings' mercy. Carrying happens one builder at a time along a clear lane: a roomful of square-carriers crossing paths at once is a quilting bee held in a corridor, and the lane exists so nobody has to dodge with both hands full.
activities.setup: Test the sticking before the builders arrive, because the whole activity stands on it: a felt square pressed flat with a whole palm onto your board must STAY. Ones that curl or slide get retired now, not mid-build, and the board itself is fixed to the wall or a stand so it cannot rock under a pressing hand. Mark nothing on the board: no grid, no outline. The quilt's pattern belongs to the crew, and a builder arriving at a blank board with a square in hand is facing the real job quilters face, where does MY piece belong?
steps: Show the empty board and one square and say the plain job: 'Quilters sew quilts out of squares. Ours sticks instead of sewing. Every square in that basket has to travel here and find its place on the board, edge touching edge, no gaps where we can help it. When the board is full, the quilt is built.' State the one rule: 'One square carried at a time, two hands, and you press your own square on yourself.' Press yours on first, alone in the board's middle-top, with a full flat palm: 'The first square is the hardest to place. It has no neighbours yet.'

Building round: builders travel one at a time, square chosen from the basket by its own builder, carried in two hands, placed where that builder decides, with the single craft taught as it is needed: 'Press the corners. A square sticks by its corners.' Neighbours get named as they arrive: 'You put the red one beside the blue one. They are touching all along that edge. That is a quilt seam.' Placing is never corrected; a square placed crooked is placed, and the next builder's square negotiates with it, which is how real quilts and real crews both work.

Gap watch, the build's middle: when the board is half covered, stop the carrying and look together. Gaps show themselves, felt-board showing through in quilt-shaped holes. 'The quilt has windows. Who is carrying a square that could close a window?' Builders choose squares FOR the gaps now, judging size and fit with their eyes before they travel, and a square that fills a window exactly gets the crew's full appreciation, because fitting is the builder's highest skill and everyone just saw it.

Last-square ceremony: when one space remains, the crew chooses its final builder by the fairest method the room owns. The builder who has carried fewest squares carries the last. It is pressed on with the whole crew watching and the count done aloud: 'Square number twenty-four... ON.' A board covered edge to edge, built by a line of two-handed carries, is looked at in silence for one breath before anyone speaks. Quilts deserve the breath.

Finish with the quilt's story told back along its rows: who carried the corner squares, where the window was, which two colours kept ending up neighbours. The quilt stays up for the day, it is the room's now, and comes down at tidy time square by square into the basket, peeled slowly by their own builders, which every builder will tell you is somehow the best part.
activities.tagline: Hand-sized felt squares carried one at a time to a big wall board and pressed edge to edge. A quilt the whole crew builds standing up, square by square.

variations.easier: A half board: twelve squares fill a smaller board completely, so a small crew gets the whole arc, first square, gap watch, last square, inside fifteen minutes.
variations.harder: A pattern promise: the crew agrees a pattern first (red in every corner, say) and builds to keep it, corners claimed and defended by planning, the quilt's first design meeting.

activities.inclusion: The hat's circle includes every seat as it stands: it travels lap to lap and tray to tray as faithfully as hand to hand, and its stopping-place is wherever it stops, honoured identically. An introduction arrives by voice, by sign, by a picture card held up for the favourite thing, or by the adult voicing what the wearer indicates. The hat's two questions answered in any language the circle can receive. The song-keeper job, choosing which song the hat travels to, belongs to whoever holds it and programs the whole session.

materials.item: one big soft hat (floppy, clean, big enough to sit loosely on any head in the room, the sillier the better, and it belongs to the group, not to a costume box's depths)
no other materials. The grown-up's singing voice is the music

activities.name: Big Hat Pass and Say
activities.safety: The hat is soft, group-owned, and washed before its first circle and between groups, a hat that travels head to head is laundry with a job, and it is treated that way. It is passed hand to hand, never thrown: a thrown hat at three is followed by thrown everything, and the hat's dignity is the circle's. Wearing is always by the wearer's own hands at the song's stop; nobody places the hat on another person's head, and a holder who does not want to wear it may hold it on their lap and introduce themselves to the hat instead, which counts completely.
activities.setup: Know your hat before the circle does: it must be soft all through (no stiff brim edge at face height), clean enough to pass head to head, it gets a wash before its first circle and between groups as a matter of course, and big enough that wearing it is never a squeeze. Rehearse your stopping song too: any song the group knows, sung by you, that you can end mid-line without apology, because the stop is the mechanism and it must be allowed to arrive anywhere.
steps: Hold the hat up and say the plain bargain: 'This is the talking hat. While I sing, the hat travels, hand to hand, round the circle. When my song STOPS, the hands holding the hat keep it, and that person puts it on and tells us two things: their name, and one favourite thing. Then the singing starts again.' State the one rule: 'The hat travels hand to hand. It is never thrown, and it only goes on a head when the song stops.'

First stop together, rigged kindly: sing, pass the hat hand to hand yourself with the first holders, and stop the song with the hat in YOUR hands. On it goes, and you model the whole introduction at full size: 'My name is Teacher Sam, and my favourite thing is puddles.' Two sentences, said proudly, by a person wearing a ridiculous hat, the room now knows exactly what courage is required, and exactly how small it is.

Passing rounds: the song restarts, the hat travels, sometimes three hands, sometimes right round the circle, and every stop produces one wearer and one introduction, received by the circle with the group's own growing ceremony (a clap, a cheer, the name said back: all traditional by the third stop). A wearer may pass on the favourite and give only their name; the hat accepts, the circle accepts, and the record notes that a name alone, said aloud in a big hat, is a complete introduction at three.

Hat-respect moment, arriving on schedule: the hat will be grabbed for, worn mid-song, or worn by three heads at once in a pile-up of enthusiasm, usually by week two of knowing it. The rule is restated as hat law, kindly: 'The hat is one person's at a time, and its person is chosen by the song stopping. The hat is patient. We are learning to be patient like the hat.' It lands, because by then the hat has a personality and the room is fond of it.

Finish when the hat has been worn by everyone who wants a turn, want being the operative word, checked honestly round the circle, with a final all-group photograph taken in memory: every introduced name said back in order round the circle by the group, as the hat makes one last slow lap held high. Then the hat goes to its hook, where it lives between circles: furniture now, not a prop, and rooms treat it accordingly.
activities.tagline: One big soft hat travels hand to hand while the grown-up sings; when the song stops, whoever holds it puts it on and says their name and one favourite thing.

variations.easier: A small circle of five and a short song: the hat completes the whole circle inside ten minutes and every intro gets its full ceremony.
variations.harder: Favourite-thing themes: today's hat asks for a favourite FOOD, tomorrow's a favourite ANIMAL. The introduction grows a category, and returning wearers must reach for a new answer.

activities.inclusion: The path is walked at every height it is met: a walker whose feet travel by wheel is offered the same four textures under HANDS on a parallel table path, grass in a tray, smooth mat, sand, towel, reported in hand words with identical ceremony, because the sense is the activity, not the limb. A walker can also serve as the path's announcer, stationed at its end, receiving each walker's reports and declaring them to the group in full voice. The path's official record-keeper, through whom every feeling enters the record.

materials.item: big texture panels laid as a path (a patch of real grass, one smooth mat, one wide shallow tray of clean play sand, one thick soft towel, each at least two kid-feet wide)
a bucket of water and a towel at the path's end (the foot-washing station)
the path laid somewhere flat and familiar (the adult has walked every panel in bare feet first)

activities.name: Big Texture Feet Path Walk
activities.safety: The path is walked first, barefoot, by the adult, every session, feet find what eyes miss, and a panel with a sharp surprise in it is removed whole, never walked around. One walker at a time, walking only: the panels include a sand tray with edges, and a running foot meeting a tray rim is the path's one real hazard, designed out by pace. Feet are washed at the end without exception. The grass patch is chosen untreated and dog-free, and the washing is still total, because paths hold more than textures and clean feet are how this activity closes its books.
activities.setup: Walk the whole path yourself in bare feet before any small foot touches it. Every panel, at a three-year-old's pace, feeling for the stone, the stick, the tray edge, the one rough corner: your feet are the inspection, and anything they find that argues gets removed, not explained.
