Practise your own launch until the feather LEAVES your hand floating, not falling: a soft upward toss with a puff under it. The launch is the game's heartbeat and it is yours every time. A feather that falls straight down teaches the circle to lunge, and lunging is not this game.
steps: Hold the feather up and say the plain framing: 'This feather wants to float. Feathers fall slower than anything, but they DO fall, unless somebody blows underneath them. When it drifts over YOUR spot, your breath is what keeps it in the sky. When it is over somebody else, your job is watching, and being ready.' State the one rule whole: 'We blow at the feather. We never touch it, grab it, or catch it. Hands stay home. Only breath works up there.' Launch it yourself over the circle's middle with a founding puff, and let the first float simply be watched for a breath before anyone blows: floating deserves a moment of plain looking.

First rescues together: as the feather sinks toward a sector of the circle, coach the blowers under it, 'Under it... blow UP at it, gentle...', and let the group feel a real rescue land: the feather stalls, wobbles, climbs a hand's height. Name it precisely: 'The feather was FALLING and your breath said no.' Blowers blow from where they sit or stand, at whatever strength their lungs honestly have. A small puff that moves the feather one inch is a complete rescue, said so in front of everyone, because it is true.

Floating round: the feather travels as the blows take it, and it will take itself on unplanned journeys across the circle, stalling over empty middle (where the adult's ground-crew puff, delivered sparingly, returns it to play) and hovering over the same lucky blower three times running. A blower it visits repeatedly simply blows repeatedly; a blower it has not visited watches, ready, in the game's real discipline: paying full attention to a sky that has not needed you YET. The adult names watchers' readiness aloud as the skill it is: 'Ready eyes on this side, the feather knows.'

Slow-motion moment, the game's heart: sooner or later the feather will hang for one long moment almost still over the middle, turning slowly, while the whole circle holds a collective breath nobody called for. Do not break it. When it finally chooses a side and sinks to its rescue, the group will exhale like one animal, and the adult says the true thing: 'For a second there, nobody in this room breathed, and the feather floated on the quiet too.'

Finish with the landing ceremony the rules promised: when the session's last float ends, the feather is caught, by the adult's two hands, as the circle was told at the start it would be, and held up for its applause: 'Caught by the ground crew, as agreed.' The tell-back honours the whole sky: 'The feather floated for all of that time and touched nothing but air and breath. Every blower here kept it up at least once, and every watcher kept ready, which is the same job from further away.' The feather goes back in its box, washed before its next flight like the travelling equipment it is.
activities.tagline: One big feather over the circle, kept in the air by breath alone: blow when it drifts to you, watch when it doesn't, a whole game at floating speed.

variations.easier: A two-blower version: the feather floats back and forth over one rug between two seated blowers and the adult, a whole game of rescues inside ten minutes for the newest room.
variations.harder: A journey version: the circle agrees a destination. The feather must be blown, blower to blower, all the way round the circle and back to the adult's hands without one ground-crew puff, a circumnavigation at floating speed.

activities.inclusion: The drop works at every station: the box can sit on a table edge, a lap board, or the floor at its worker's exact height, and the button can be held in a full palm, between two hands, or released from a palm the worker tips at their own angle. Flatness is judged by the slot, identically, whoever presents the button. A worker can also direct the drops: choosing each button from the store by colour and calling the release, 'flat?... FLAT... drop it', while a partner's hand hovers and lets go at the director's word; the box fills by the director's decisions, and the shake-count at the end sounds exactly the same.

materials.item: a sturdy box with a lid the grown-up has cut one wide slot in (slot edges sanded or taped smooth, wide enough for a button held FLAT and nothing else)
big buttons, palm-sized (adult-sourced: the biggest coat buttons or button-shaped wooden discs, one colour each, far too big for a mouth, checked, no cracks, no loose shanks)
a bowl the buttons start in (the button store)

activities.name: Big Button Slot Drop Box
activities.safety: Buttons are palm-sized, single-piece, and audited one by one before every session: at three, a button is exactly the size of thing the record treats with ceremony, so anything cracked, small, sharp-edged, or carrying a loose part is out of the store permanently, no exceptions argued. The slot's edges are sanded or taped smooth and checked with the adult's own fingertip. A slot that can scratch teaches flinching, not flatness. Dropping happens seated with the box still on the table or floor: a carried box sheds buttons from a moving slot at face height, so the box travels only in the adult's hands, lid held, when the workers are elsewhere.
activities.setup: Cut and finish the slot yourself, then test it with your own hand until it teaches the right lesson: a button held flat must pass with a small, satisfying resistance, and a button held edge-first must NOT pass at all. That one refusal is the activity's whole curriculum, and a slot too wide deletes it. Tape or sand every cut edge until your own fingertip finds nothing sharp, then audit the buttons the same way: palm-sized, single-piece, no cracked rims, no shank that could come away. Count the buttons and write the number on the box's underside for yourself. The closing shake-count check depends on you knowing the true total without ever saying it early.
steps: Show the box, the slot, and one button, and say the plain job: 'This box is hungry for buttons, but it only eats them FLAT. Hold your button flat over the slot, hover... and let go. Then LISTEN, the box tells you it landed.' Work one button yourself at full ceremony: flat in your palm, hovered, released, the soft clatter from inside the box is the activity's whole reward structure arriving in its first minute. State the one rule: 'Flat buttons only, one at a time, and your other hand waits. If it will not go, the button is telling you something. Turn it flatter.'

First drops together: each worker takes one button from the store and the group's first drops happen in chorus at your count, hover... let go, and the box answers with a small chorus of landings. A button that will not go gets the coached fix, in words, on the worker's own button, your hands staying off it: 'Turn it... flatter... there.' The moment a refused button rotates flat and DROPS is the biggest sound in the session, and it is celebrated at exactly that size: 'The box took it. You turned it flat. That was the whole job and you did it.'

Quiet working stretch, the activity's middle: workers draw buttons from the store one at a time and drop at their own pace, the box filling by ones, the room's sound narrowing to the drop-rhythm, hover, release, clatter, reach, that is this shelf's definition of concentration. The adult sits as a fellow worker with a button of their own, dropping in the same rhythm, available for a flatness consultation that is always given in words and a demonstration on the adult's button, never by hands on the worker's: a box filled by the wrong hands is a photograph of help, not a record of skill.

Store-emptying moment: when the store runs low, the pace changes. Workers can hear the box is filling (each new landing lands on BUTTONS now, a softer, richer clatter than the first drops on bare box) and the last buttons get a ceremony: the final button is hovered by its worker while the whole group listens in complete quiet for its landing, the last word the box says in its empty-box-to-full-box sentence.

Finish with the shake-count, the activity's closing instrument: lid held down by you, the box shaken ONCE, firmly, beside the workers' ears, 'That is the sound of ALL your buttons together', and the count verified properly: buttons tipped out onto the tray and counted back into the store by the workers, one flat palmful at a time, reaching the true number you wrote underneath. Lid back on, box back on its shelf with the store beside it, and the ledge of the room holds a hungry box, fed completely, by flat hands only.
activities.tagline: Palm-sized buttons, one wide slot in a box lid: hold flat, hover, let go, and listen for the landing. Then shake the box and hear how many you made.

variations.easier: A six-button version: a small store and a short count, the whole arc, refusal, fix, chorus, shake-count, inside ten minutes for one or two workers.
variations.harder: A colour-order version: the worker declares an order first, 'red, then blue, then red', and must hunt the store and drop to keep the promise, the box judged at shake-time by nobody but its maker's memory, kindly.

activities.inclusion: The dream needs no particular voice: a dreamer can say their dream in words, in a sign, in one word plus a point at the card's sun, or by choosing which earlier dream the circle echoes again for them. Every form is echoed back by the whole circle identically, because the echo, not the phrasing, is the ceremony. The card-holder job and the first-echo job (starting the circle's echo on the adult's cue) are real roles that belong to whoever holds them, from any seat in the circle.

materials.item: one big dream card, adult-drawn (a simple sun rising over a hill, drawn bold. The circle's talking piece, held by whoever is dreaming)
no other materials. Voices are the instruments

activities.name: Big Dream Echo Circle
activities.safety: The constitution, every dream is a right dream, is enforced exactly like the feelings cards' law in this archive: no dream is laughed at, corrected, ranked, or topped, and the adult's protection of a small dream is instant, warm, and public, because the circle is learning what this room does with hopes. Nothing is promised: dreams are said, echoed, and honoured, and the adult never tells a dreamer their dream will come true. The record's claim is only that saying it out loud, and hearing it said back kindly, is itself worth doing. The card is big, plain, and blunt-cornered; the circle is seated for the whole session.
activities.setup: Draw the card big and plain, and learn your framing sentences before the circle sits down, because this record lives or dies on the adult saying the day's name and meaning plainly, at three-year-old size, without a lecture growing out of it. Practise the first dream sentence yourself until it is short enough to echo whole. Six words is the honest ceiling at three ('I dream of friends for everyone'). A sentence the circle cannot echo back entire is a speech, and speeches belong to another shelf.
steps: Gather the circle and say the plain framing, in full: 'Today is Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s day. He was a man who worked so that everybody would be treated fairly, and he told the whole country his dream out loud. A dream you say out loud is one other people can help with. So today we say ours.' Hold up the dream card. State the one rule: 'The dreamer holds the card and says the dream. Everybody else echoes it back, whole, in our kindest voices. Every dream is a right dream.'

First dream together, yours: hold the card, say your short dream slowly, 'I dream of friends for everyone', and let the circle echo it back at you, whole. It will come back ragged, overlapping, and too loud at the end; that is a complete first echo at three, and it gets the full review: 'You said my whole dream back to me. Now it is not only mine.' The echo is the activity's engine and its meaning, and it is named the first time it runs.

Dreaming round: the card travels hand to hand round the circle in order. Each dreamer may say a dream of their own, one short sentence, any size ('I dream of a big slide', 'I dream of my grandma'), or may choose to re-say the dream before theirs, which counts in full: repeating a friend's dream kindly is a complete turn, never a failed one. The circle echoes every dream whole, at the dreamer's own volume, before the card moves on.

Growing moment, offered once and never pressed: after several dreams, the adult wonders aloud whether two dreams can ride together, 'Maya dreams of a big slide. Jonah dreams of friends for everyone. Can a slide have friends on it?', and the circle tries the joined dream as one echo. Some joins are silliness and get laughed WITH, never at; the joining is a game laid over the ceremony, and the ceremony, card held, dream said, dream echoed, never changes shape underneath it.

Finish with the whole circle's dreams held up together: the card is placed in the middle where everyone can see the sun on it, the adult says the closing plainly, 'Dr. King said his dream to the whole country. We said ours to the whole circle. That is how dreams start travelling', and the first dream is echoed one last time, all together, as the session's last sound.
activities.tagline: One short dream sentence, said by the grown-up and echoed whole by the circle: on Dr. King's day, everybody's dream gets said out loud.

variations.easier: A three-dream circle: a small group, the adult's dream and two more, the whole ceremony complete inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A dream-for-someone-else round: each dreamer dreams a dream FOR the neighbour on their right, 'I dream of a puppy for Sam', and the echo carries it to its owner, who may say thank you in any form at all.

activities.inclusion: Palms are the instrument, so the reading is open at every station: a holder can hold both stones on a lap tray at their exact height, report by pointing at the sun card or the shade card the adult holds up, or direct a partner's hands. 'That one... in the sun hand', while the choice of which stone is which stays the director's reading entirely. Palm-words can be single words, signs, sounds, or a chosen comparison object fetched by the adult; every report enters the day's collection in the same shape.

materials.item: big smooth stones, adult-gathered (palm-sized or bigger, washed, checked, no sharp edges, no cracks; at least two full pairs: one pair warming in full sun, one pair resting in full shade)
a shady sitting spot the adult has chosen in advance, close to both stone stations (the reporting circle)
a small towel under each stone station (the stones' addresses, so warm stays warm and cool stays cool)

activities.name: Big Warm Stone Hold and Tell
activities.safety: Stones are palm-sized or bigger, smooth, washed, and checked one by one before every session: anything cracked, sharp-edged, or small enough to be interesting to a mouth is out of the set permanently. Stones are carried low in two hands, one at a time, and never thrown, tapped together, or held over another child's lap. A dropped big stone is the session's one real hazard, so holders are seated for every hold and standing carries happen over grass, slowly, in the adult's sight. Sun stones are sun-WARM, checked against the adult's own inner wrist first: a stone too warm for the wrist's skin never reaches a small palm, and on a fierce day the sun station moves to gentler sun and the record says why.
activities.setup: Gather and wash the stones well ahead, and set the stations at least half an hour before the session: sun stones on their towel in the fiercest sun you have, shade stones on theirs in the deepest shade, because the whole activity is a temperature difference the palms must be able to READ, and a half-hearted sun gives a lesson nobody can feel. Test with your own palms first: if you cannot tell the pair apart blind, the stations need more time or stronger spots, the record refuses to schedule a difference that is not there. On a cool or cloudy day this activity honestly waits for a better one, announced as such.
steps: Gather the group at the reporting circle and say the plain framing: 'Summer does something you can hold. The sun has been working on some stones all morning, and the shade has been keeping others cool. Your hands are going to find out which is which, no peeking at the towels until your palms have reported.' State the one rule: 'One stone in each hand, held still. Hands do not swap stones, drop stones, or tap stones together. Heavy hands stay low, over laps.'

First hold together, yours: an adult demonstration at full ceremony, one stone from each station, eyes honestly closed, a real pause while the palms read, then the report in the session's official shape: 'My LEFT hand is holding summer. This one is the sun's.' Open your eyes, carry both stones low to their towels to show where each truly came from, and let the group check your palms' report against the stations. A report the stations confirm gets celebrated as an instrument working: 'My hands read the day correctly.'

Holding round: holders take turns in known order, one holder, two stones, eyes closed or honestly averted, and every holder's report is taken in the same shape and checked the same way, carried (by the holder, low, two hands per stone, one at a time) back to the station each stone claims. Reports that come back wrong are never wrong children: 'Your hands said cool, and the stone came from the sun towel. This one had lost its warm in the carrying. Hands read what is TRUE at the moment they read it.' The science stays honest even when the answer surprises.

Telling stretch, the activity's second half: once the reports are practised, holders must TELL the difference, not just name it. One palm-word each: 'This one feels like bath water. This one feels like the fridge door.' The group collects the day's palm-words and argues kindly about the best ones; a word the group loves gets repeated by all, hands miming the hold. Language for a feeling only palms can check is being built here, out loud, at three.

Finish with the stones retired properly, because instruments get put away: all stones carried low, one at a time, two hands each, to one gathering towel, warm and cool mixed now, their work done, and the tell-back reads the day off the towels: 'The sun heated four stones, the shade kept four cool, and every pair of hands in this circle read the day and reported it. Next hot day, the stones go back to work.'
activities.tagline: Two big smooth stones, one sun-warmed and one shade-cool, held one in each hand: which hand is holding summer? Palms report, words follow.

variations.easier: A one-pair version: a single pair of stones passed holder to holder, every report on the same two instruments, inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A three-station version (high summer only): a third pair in half-shade, SUN, IN-BETWEEN, SHADE, and holders must rank all three by palm, the archive's first three-point scale.

activities.inclusion: Every job on the route exists at more than one height: the driver's chair takes any driver, the conductor's prompting works in words, signs, or a tapped order card, and a rider can travel the whole route from a seat that is already theirs, placed in the row like any other seat, paying and alighting by the same calls. A rider who communicates their stop by holding up its picture sign has called it in full; the driver answers every form of 'that's mine' identically. The token can be paid hand to hand, slid across the driver's tray, or dropped in the driver's tin. The fare is the handing over, in whatever form the hand offers.

materials.item: sturdy chairs in one row with an aisle (the bus. One seat per rider plus the driver's chair at the front, turned to face the row)
one big steering wheel for the driver (a big plastic plate or a cardboard wheel the adult has made. Blunt, light, unbreakable)
big ride tokens, one per rider per ride (palm-sized wooden discs or big bottle-top-free counters, audited, nothing small, nothing cracked)
three or four big stop signs, adult-drawn (a star stop, a tree stop, a fish stop, a moon stop, big simple pictures on card, stood along the aisle)

activities.name: Big Bus Stop Ride-Along

photo.alt: A bus full of children, faces at every window, about to ride in 1927
photo.caption: A busload of children, every window full: the ride-along, 1927 style.
photo.credit: Photo: Webster & Stevens, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The bus never moves and neither do its seats: chairs are checked steady before every run, riders sit fully while travelling is being called, and all walking happens in the clear aisle at walking pace, a running rider on a chair-row bus is the session's one real hazard, so the driver's calls pace the whole game and a route pauses kindly if feet hurry. Tokens are palm-sized, single-piece, and audited before every session; anything small, cracked, or coin-shaped enough to invite a mouth leaves the tin permanently. The wheel is light and blunt, held in two hands, and stays in the driver's chair: it is never carried round the room.
activities.setup: Build the bus yourself and sit in every seat before the riders arrive: chairs steady, close enough to feel like a bus, far enough that small knees are not pressed into the seat ahead, with a clear aisle a token-carrying three-year-old can walk without squeezing past a single knee. Stand the stop signs along the aisle in an order you can call without thinking, and audit the tokens like the safety equipment they are: palm-sized, single-piece, boring to a mouth. The driver's wheel must be light enough that a dropped wheel is a noise, never an injury.
steps: Point at the bus and say the plain framing: 'This bus goes on a very particular route. It stops at the star, the tree, the fish, and the moon, and it never, ever moves. WE do the travelling: getting on, paying our token, riding, and getting off at our stop.' State the route's laws whole: 'Riders sit while the bus is travelling. Tokens are paid to the driver, one each, in a flat open hand. Getting off happens only at YOUR stop, when the driver calls it.' Take the driver's chair for the first run yourself.

First boarding together: riders line up at the bus door (the aisle's front) holding one token each, and board one at a time. Token into the driver's flat hand, 'One ride, please' in any words or none, then walk the aisle and choose a seat. Boarding IS the first curriculum: paying, choosing, sitting, in a line that waits. When every rider is seated, the driver makes the travelling noise (a low hum the riders may join) and calls the first stop: 'STAR STOP. Star riders, this is your getting-off place.'

The ride round: before each run, every rider has quietly been given a stop by the driver, whispered, or shown the matching small sign, and the game's whole delicious tension is listening for YOUR stop while other stops are called and other riders rise, walk the aisle forward, hand the driver a 'thank you' in any form, and step off onto the pavement chairs to watch the rest of the route. A rider who rises at the wrong stop gets the driver's kindest line, which is also the rule restated: 'Not yet. That's the FISH stop. Your moon is coming. The bus will wait.' Sitting back down is a complete, respected move, never a failure.

Driver's turn, the round everyone waits for: a rider becomes the driver. Wheel in hands, the hum to make, the stops to call in order with the adult beside them as the conductor, whose whole job is supplying the next stop's name quietly and applauding the calls publicly. Calling a full route clearly, in order, for passengers who are depending on you, is public speaking at its smallest true size, and the record treats it with that respect.

Finish with the bus parked for the day: the last route ends at the MOON STOP for everybody. 'End of the line. Everybody off. The bus sleeps here tonight'. Tokens are counted back into their tin by the riders one at a time (the count said aloud to its true number), the wheel is hung on its peg by the driver, and the chairs go back to being chairs one rider at a time, carried or pushed in the adult's company. The tell-back: 'Four stops, three drivers, and not one rider left riding forever.'
activities.tagline: A row of chairs is the bus and it never moves an inch: the driver calls the stops, riders pay one big token, ride, and get off at their stop.

variations.easier: A two-stop bus: star stop and moon stop only, a short route, new riders, the whole arc, pay, ride, listen, alight, inside fifteen minutes.
variations.harder: A request-stop version: riders may ring for their stop by raising a hand and saying 'stop, please' as the bus 'approaches'. The driver must watch the whole bus, not just the route.

activities.inclusion: The tunnel is built of whoever is there: a wall can be any standing or seated position at the road's edge, a keeper seated in a chair with the road passing beside them is a wall in full, and their redirecting hands work from exactly that station. The roller can roll from a kneel, a chair at the gate, or a standing bend, and can direct a partner's rolling hands, 'lower... slower... NOW', while the aim and the moment stay the director's. The corner-keeper and cheer-gate catcher jobs, the tunnel's two honours, rotate by list, so every keeper's name is thanked by gate name across a session.

materials.item: one big soft ball, the biggest that still rolls true (a foam or soft playground ball, adult-checked, no hard seams, no valve nub a palm can find)
a clear straight run of floor, wall to wall if possible (the tunnel's road. Swept by the adult's eyes for anything a rolling ball or a small foot could meet)
two cones or cushions (the tunnel's two gates. Start gate and cheer gate)

activities.name: Big Leg Tunnel Ball Roll
activities.safety: Feet are walls and walls do not move: the planted-feet law is the safety system as well as the game, because a child stepping into the road meets a rolling ball at ankle height and another wall-keeper's legs at the same moment, so the ball is rolled only from a kneel, two hands, at true rolling pace, and any ball that starts travelling fast ends the journey: it is caught by the adult and the roll restarts from the gate, kindly, without a lecture. The road is walked and cleared by the adult before every session, wall-keepers stand a full arm from the rows opposite them, and nobody lies, sits, or crawls in the road at any time, for any reason. The tunnel is walked around, always, by everyone, the roller included.
activities.setup: Walk the road yourself first, ball in hand, and roll it the full length at the speed the game will use: it must travel straight, slowly, and stop kindly against the far cushion, a ball that veers hard or bounces high will teach the tunnel to lunge, and lunging is not this game. Check the ball like equipment: soft all over, seams flat, and big enough that no roller is tempted to kick it back into line, because feet are this record's walls, not its tools, and that only works if hands can always do the job.
steps: Line the group up in two facing rows, legs comfortably wide, and say the plain framing: 'Look what you have built: a tunnel, made of people. This ball is going to travel the whole tunnel, rolled in at this gate, caught at that gate, and the tunnel's job is to let it through home.' State the laws whole: 'Feet stay planted like tunnel walls. Nobody steps into the road. The roller rolls from a kneel, two hands, gently. A roll, never a throw.' Demonstrate the whole journey yourself with an adult-sized gap first if another grown-up is near, so the group sees a complete trip before anyone's legs are walls.

First roll together: the first roller kneels at the start gate, the tunnel goes quiet, tunnel quiet is a real, learnable thing, and the ball rolls in. It will bump a wall. It will bump several. Every bump is the tunnel doing its job out loud ('The tunnel caught it. Roll on!'), the ball nudged forward ONLY by the roller walking (outside the rows) to its stopping place and rolling it on from there, or by the nearest wall-keeper's gentle two-hand redirect from exactly where they stand. Nobody dives, nobody kicks; the ball's journey, however bumped, is a success the whole way down.

Cheer-gate moment: when the ball finally rolls out of the cheer gate into the catcher's two waiting hands, the tunnel gets its ceremony, both rows raise their arms into a roof for one held breath ('The tunnel salutes the traveller!'), then walls reform. That roof is the game's trophy: brief, enormous, and earned by a ball that travelled maybe six feet. Take it at full size anyway; at three, six feet of tunnel IS a journey.

Building stretch: once one tunnel runs, the group builds, a LONGER tunnel (every wall-keeper steps one pace outward, the road grows), then, for the steadiest groups, a BENT tunnel: one corner, marked by a cushion, where the roller must roll to the corner-keeper, who becomes the second roller for the home leg. A corner is advanced engineering at three and is introduced as exactly that: 'Engineers, we are bending the tunnel. Nobody has done this in this room before.'

Finish with the tunnel driven one last full journey at the group's best length, the roof raised and held a breath longer, and the tunnel demolished kindly: wall-keepers step out in order from the cheer gate, each thanked by gate name ('Thank you, wall three'), the ball carried by the last roller to its basket, and the tell-back said on the empty road: 'The ball travelled the whole tunnel, the walls never moved, and nobody chased it. The tunnel did that.'
activities.tagline: The group stands in two facing lines, legs wide: a tunnel made of people. One big ball rolls its whole length, in one end, out the other, to cheers.

variations.easier: A short-tunnel version: four wall-keepers, a four-foot road, and three complete journeys inside ten minutes. Length is not the achievement; arrival is.
variations.harder: A silent-tunnel version: the whole journey in complete quiet, walls and roller alike, the roof raised in silence too. The group's own held breath is the loudest cheer of all.

activities.inclusion: The scale adapts to its scientist: objects can be weighed on a lap tray the adult tips very slightly at the weigher's direction. 'Left is sinking... read it', while the judgement, the call, and the report remain the weigher's own. Reports arrive as the official sentence, a pointed sinking-side hand, a sign, or a chosen heavy/light card pair the adult holds; every channel enters the results identically. The shelf-keeper job, bringing each pair to its weigher and retiring it after, in order, is the laboratory's official hands and belongs to whoever holds it.

materials.item: big object pairs, adult-built (matched-looking pairs that differ honestly in weight: two same-size soft bags, one filled with fabric and one with dry rice, sewn shut and labelled by feel only to the adult; a big sponge and a same-size smooth stone; a feather-light scarf ball and a bean-filled ball)
a low table or mat the pairs wait on (the instrument shelf)
no scale of any kind. That absence is the lesson

activities.name: Big Heavy-Light Hand Balance
activities.safety: Objects live over the mat, on open palms, at arm's length and waist height: a dropped stone lands on the mat, which is why the mat is there and why weighing never happens standing over hard floor or another child's feet. Pairs are palm-sized or bigger, smooth, sealed, and audited before every session, a leaking filled bag retires on the spot, because its contents at three become a floor hazard and a mouth question in the same minute. Arms tire honestly at three: a weigher whose scale is shaking from effort is rested without comment. The adult takes the pair, the weigher shakes out, and a tired instrument's readings are never argued with.
activities.setup: Build the pairs yourself and test every one in your own two hands, eyes closed, until each pair's difference is honest and readable: a difference only an adult's hands can feel teaches a three-year-old that their hands are broken, and these hands are not. The rice bag and its fabric twin must LOOK like siblings, the whole discovery is that eyes cannot weigh, so fill, sew, and check them as a pair. Stone pairs are smooth, washed, and palm-sized or bigger; anything cracked or sharp leaves the shelf permanently, because these objects live at face height on outstretched arms.
steps: Bring the group to the instrument shelf and say the plain framing: 'Your hands can weigh things. Hold one thing in this hand and one in that hand, arms out, and one hand will SINK a little. The sinking hand is holding the heavy one. Your body is the scale.' State the one rule: 'Objects are held OUT, over the mat, in open palms, never gripped over the floor, never swapped mid-weigh, never dropped on purpose. The scale reads, then the objects go back on the shelf.' Demonstrate on the first pair yourself, arms wide, and let the group SEE your heavy hand sink.

First weigh together, yours at full ceremony: eyes open, one twin in each hand, arms out, a real pause while the scale settles, then the report in the session's official shape: 'THIS hand sank. This bag is the heavy one.' Carry both back to the shelf, swap them between your hands, and weigh again in front of everyone: the same hand does NOT sink twice, the WEIGHT sank, not the hand, and that check, done early and plainly, is the moment the room understands it is an instrument being read, not a trick being watched.

Weighing round: weighers take turns in known order, one pair at a time, with the same ceremony, palms open, objects placed by the adult or lifted from the shelf's edge, arms out, settle, report ('This hand sank, HEAVY. This hand floated. LIGHT'), and the pair returned to the shelf by its weigher before the next pair exists. A report the adult's hands privately dispute is re-weighed TOGETHER, four hands, kindly: 'Let's read it again, slower.' Scales that disagree get read again; that is what scales are for, and nobody's hand is ever declared wrong. Only re-read.

Twin-discovery moment: bring out the matched-looking twins mid-round, after the weighers have grown confident, and let the room predict by EYE first. Hands must vote before they weigh. The vote will be a guess dressed as certainty, and then the palms read what the eyes could not: same size, same look, different sink. The record's line is ready and true: 'Eyes cannot weigh. Hands can. That is why scientists pick things UP.'

Finish with the shelf read back like results: 'The stone: heavy. The sponge: light, though it is just as big. The rice bag fooled every eye in the room and no hands at all.' Pairs are returned to the shelf in their places by their weighers, palms are shaken out together, scales rest too, and the last word belongs to the instrument: 'Your hands knew. They will keep knowing. You can weigh anything you are allowed to pick up, for the rest of your life, for free.'
activities.tagline: One object in each hand, arms out like a scale: which hand sinks? The body's own balance reports heavy and light, no scale required.

variations.easier: A two-pair version: stone-and-sponge, twins, three weighs, two discoveries, inside ten minutes for the newest scientists.
variations.harder: A shopping version: the weigher must find 'the heavy one' for a pretend recipe from a shelf of three, two lights and one heavy, weighing pairs until their hands identify it, a search conducted entirely by sinking.

activities.inclusion: Every statue needs parts at every height, and the design round assigns them as honours, not accommodations: the star's base point, the bridge's grounded side, the tree's roots, a part performed from any seated or supported position is a load-bearing part of the design, discussed and placed like any other. A builder can also hold the architect's job for a whole statue: standing outside it with the adult, placing pieces by direction. 'You, tall, at the edge... you, crouched, in the middle', and calling STATUE and MELT for the group; the architect's statue is theirs in full, and the museum guide describes it by their name.

materials.item: one big statue card, adult-drawn (a bold simple statue to aim at first, a star, a tree, a bridge, one card per session is plenty)
a clear statue ground (a rug or mat big enough for the whole group to stand on together)
no other materials. The group IS the material

activities.name: Big One Statue, Many Bodies
activities.safety: Every part holds ITSELF up: that law is the session's safety system, stated first and enforced gently throughout, no child leans their weight on, hangs from, climbs onto, or is held up by another child, ever, and statue designs that need it are redesigned on the spot by the adult acting as the group's safety engineer: 'A statue whose top needs holding is a statue asking for a different top.' Freezes are short (a count of five growing to ten) and melts are always available: any statue piece may melt themselves out at any moment, no reason needed, and the statue stands one part smaller with the room's respect intact. Building happens at walking pace on the clear rug; a fallen piece is helped up by the adult, checked, and offered a ground-level part if they want back in.
activities.setup: Draw the first statue card big and genuinely buildable at three: a star is five points, five children standing tall with arms up, close together, is a star a room can actually make; a 'dragon' is not a first statue, it is an argument with scales. Practise the freeze yourself, honestly: statues at three hold for a count of ten on a good day, and the session's timings are built on that truth. A statue asked to hold for thirty is a statue designed to melt, and melting gets blamed on the wrong people.
steps: Spread the statue card where everyone can see it and say the plain job: 'A statue is usually ONE person standing very still. Ours is going to be ALL of us. Each person is one part of it, and it only stands when everybody is in it.' State the laws whole: 'We build it piece by piece, walking. When I say STATUE, everybody freezes, feet, hands, faces. Frozen people do not poke, lean on, or hold up anybody else. Your part holds YOU up; the statue holds together because everyone does their own part.' Build the star together first, piece by piece, you placing yourself as one of its points.

First freeze together: pieces in place, the call, 'STATUE', and the group freezes for a count of five, counted by the adult out loud, slowly, like a small ceremony. At five: 'MELT', and everyone melts down into a cheerful puddle on the rug, shaking arms out. The melt is not the statue failing; it is the statue's second half, and it is taught in the same breath as the freeze, because a freeze with no kind ending is a trap, not a game. Name the achievement whole: 'Five people. One star. It stood.'

Building stretch: the group designs its OWN statue now. The adult scribes, hands stay the materials. Ideas arrive as poses, tested one at a time: 'A bridge needs two tall sides and a top, who is the top?' (Answer, found by trying: two tall sides and a third person standing between them with arms stretched to touch both, a bridge with a person as its span, held by nobody.) Pieces are placed by the builders walking, negotiating in statue language: 'I'm the star's point. I need to be at the EDGE.' A statue that keeps falling gets redesigned by its own builders, kindly: changing the design is the engineering, and the record says so.

Audience moment: once a statue stands for a full count of ten, it earns a viewing. Any other adult, class, or the adult's own slow walk around it, describing it like a museum guide at full respect: 'Note the star's tallest point. Note how the bridge's span connects BOTH sides.' Being LOOKED at, properly, while holding still together, is the deepest freeze of the session, and the guide's seriousness is what makes it delicious rather than silly.

Finish with the group's favourite statue rebuilt one last time, frozen for its best count yet, melted with ceremony, and the tell-back naming the parts as a roster: 'The star had five points and every point was a person. The bridge stood because its sides stood. Nobody held anybody up, and the whole thing stood anyway. That is the trick this room now knows.'
activities.tagline: The whole group builds ONE statue together, an arm here, a crouch there, then everybody freezes at once and the statue stands, breathing quietly.

variations.easier: A pairs version: two-person statues only (a table, one crouched, one flat-backed beside; a tree and its apple), the whole curriculum of freeze-together inside ten minutes for the smallest crews.
variations.harder: A silhouette version (bright day, big wall): the statue is built against a sunlit wall so the group can see its own shadow-shape standing. Building for the shadow is a second design problem laid over the first.

activities.inclusion: The smile travels by whatever road a face offers: it can be passed by a full turn, a head turned partway, a smile shown to the whole circle that the next neighbour collects. Every route is the route, and the circle's direction flexes around its members without a word of explanation, because a smile's journey is measured in faces visited, not degrees turned. The smile-starter job, sending the first smile of a journey out under the adult's narration, and the home-keeper job (announcing 'IT'S HOME' when it returns) are the circle's two honours and rotate by list.

materials.item: no materials at all. One smile, which the grown-up starts, and the circle's own faces

activities.name: Big Pass the Smile Circle
activities.safety: The smile is offered, never extracted: a passer whose smile comes out small, sideways, or as a serious look has passed a true face, and it is received and passed on with identical honour, coaching a child to perform a bigger feeling is the one move this record forbids outright, kindly and instantly, because the game's entire safety is that faces in this circle are believed. Equally: a receiver may pass the smile on with eyes lowered or turned slightly aside if direct face-to-face is too much today; the smile still counts as received, the journey still counts as whole, and nobody's route round the circle is ever commented on. Nobody touches anyone's face, and passing distances are ordinary circle distances, set once and kept.
activities.setup: There is nothing to set up, and that is precisely what to prepare: practise your own starting smile until it is a real one, because the smile this circle passes will be calibrated on yours. A performed, teeth-only smile gets passed back as a performed, teeth-only smile, faithfully, all the way round. Decide the circle's direction before you sit down and keep it all session: a smile passed back and forth across the same two neighbours is a smile that never travels, and travelling is the whole game.
steps: Sit the circle close and say the plain framing: 'I have a smile. It is a good one, and I am going to give it away. Watch: I turn to the person next to me, and I SMILE at them, a real one. Then THEY have it, and they turn and give it to the next person. We are going to pass this one smile all the way round the circle and back to me.' State the laws whole: 'A smile is passed face to face, one neighbour at a time. Nobody grabs it early, nobody passes it backwards, and a smile you receive is yours to pass at YOUR size, big, small, shy, all true.'

First pass together: you turn to your neighbour with full ceremony, shoulders, face, the real smile, held a full second, and coach their receiving out loud, kindly: 'You have it now. Show me... there it is. Now turn, slowly, and give it on.' The first three passes are narrated step by step, because the mechanics (turn, receive, turn, give) are a four-part skill wearing a smile. Then let it travel unwatched by your voice for as many faces as it can: a smile crossing a room under its own power is this archive's quietest spectacle.

Full-circle moment: when the smile comes home to you, changed, as everything that travels is changed, receive it like the treasure it is and tell the circle what it did: 'It left as my smile. It has been on EVERY face in this circle. Look at it now.' Expect the report to be true: the returning smile at three is usually bigger, wobblier, and funnier than the one that left, and saying so, accurately and with wonder, is the activity's whole thesis in one sentence.

Second-journey stretch: the smile travels again, and the circle learns the game's one refinement, the RECEIVING pause. Each receiver must hold the smile for one full breath before passing it, so every face gets its moment of actually being smiled with, not just smiled past. A circle that can slow its kindest game down on purpose has learned something most grown-up rooms have not, and the adult says exactly that, at full size, because it is true.

Finish with the smile retired properly: it comes home, the whole circle smiles AT ONCE at nobody in particular for one breath, 'Everyone keep theirs this time', and the tell-back closes the loop: 'One smile, every face, nobody left out of its journey. If you ever need one, this circle knows how to send one round.' Seats are un-crossed, faces are shaken out together, and the session ends with every smile back in its owner's keeping.
activities.tagline: One smile, passed neighbour to neighbour round the whole circle: turn, smile at the next face, and watch your smile travel all the way home.

variations.easier: A half-circle version: the smile travels down a line of four and back again, a journey and a return inside ten minutes for the newest circles.
variations.harder: A wink-and-wave variation (older threes, late in the year): the smile travels with a small wave riding on it. The receiver must catch BOTH and pass both on, a two-part parcel for practised faces.

activities.inclusion: Looking is the whole instrument, so every looker reads the same picture: the puddle's best vantage, its low, flat side, is where the front row forms by need, without comment, and the find list is built from calls in any form: a word, a point, a sound the group learns means 'THERE, in the water'. The face moment adapts identically: a looker can find their face with the adult holding the lean, or watch their waving HAND's reflection arrive in the sky first and their face join it. The ripple-spotter job, calling 'ripples... settling... STILL' for the whole group. Is the expedition's official voice and belongs to whoever holds it.

materials.item: one good puddle, found by the grown-up in advance (still, unbroken, on flat ground the group can gather round without standing in it, a puddle with a picture in it, checked the same day)
a gathering line round the puddle (the adult's own pacing decides it: close enough to see the picture, far enough that no foot is in the water)
no other materials, the sky provides the picture and the puddle holds it

activities.name: Big Puddle Sky Mirror Look
activities.safety: The gathering line is absolute and it is the adult who holds it: feet stay out of the water for the whole looking, because a foot in the puddle is a fall risk on slick ground as well as the picture's end, lookers lean from the waist at the edge with the adult beside the leaning spot, and nobody kneels in mud or lies across the puddle's edge. The puddle itself is scouted plain and unglamorous: on flat ground away from traffic, drains, and anything a car has washed into it, a puddle near a road or a bin is looked at by nobody, and hands that have been near any puddle are washed back inside, because the looking is eyes-only precisely so the rest stays simple. Slippery edges are named, walked round slowly, and the expedition moves at the pace of the steadiest looker.
activities.setup: Scout the puddle the same day, at the same hour if you can: a puddle's picture depends on stillness, light, and nobody having splashed through it yet, and a puddle that was a mirror at nine may be a ripple at ten. You are looking for a puddle on truly flat ground, big enough for the whole group to gather round one side of, with the sky in it when YOU bend over it. If the day's puddles are all rippled, trafficked, or mud-soup, the honest move is to announce the expedition waits for a better puddle, the record refuses to promise a picture that is not there, and waiting for weather is an outdoor skill in itself.
steps: Lead the group to the gathering line, settle everyone, and say the plain framing: 'Rain left something behind. This puddle is holding a picture, not painted, not printed: the SKY, fallen into the water and lying there flat. We are going to look at a picture that only exists while nobody touches it.' State the laws whole: 'Feet stay OUT. Hands stay OUT. The picture lives in still water, and still is the puddle's whole job and ours.' Let the first look happen in silence, unled: bend, look, and give the group a full ten seconds to find the sky by themselves.

Finding round, the picture read together: the adult names what the puddle is holding, one find at a time, and pointers hover ABOVE the water, never in it, 'A cloud. A white one, moving. Look, it is crossing the puddle.' (It is: cloud drift in a puddle mirror is real motion in a small sky, and it stops a group of three-year-olds like a spell.) 'The blue between the clouds. And at the edge, upside-down TREES.' Each finder points, a second looker confirms, and the find joins the picture's official list, read back as it grows.

Faces moment, the expedition's treasure: one looker at a time leans carefully over the edge, feet behind the line, lean from the waist, the adult's hand near but not holding, and finds their own face in the puddle, upside down, wearing the sky. What happens next is unscriptable and always happens: the face in the water gets a wave, a tongue, a enormous grin, and the puddle wears them all. Each looker gets the same unhurried moment; a face found in a puddle and waved at is a self-portrait in the world's oldest mirror, and the record treats it with that full respect.

Stillness stretch: the group practises the picture's price, thirty seconds of complete stillness and quiet round the puddle, while a cloud crosses or a leaf's shadow drifts through the frame. Any ripple (a drip from a leaf, a far-off step's tremor) is watched spreading and SETTLING, narrated by whoever spots it: 'Ripples... going... going... still.' The group learns the puddle's own tempo: pictures in water are always returning, never ruined. They just need their moment, which is a lesson with a longer reach than the puddle.

Finish with the picture closed properly, together: on the count of three, ONE looker, chosen by rota, announced in advance, dips one toe at the puddle's very edge, once. The group watches the sky break into rings, spread, and slowly, slowly re-form: 'The picture broke, and the puddle is already mending it.' The group leaves backwards from the line, the puddle is left holding whatever sky is next, and the tell-back is the find list, read as a portrait: 'Our puddle held two clouds, the blue, upside-down trees, and every face in this group, and it is still holding them now.'
activities.tagline: A still puddle after rain is holding a picture of the sky. The group gathers round its edge and looks IN, clouds, blue, and their own faces, upside down.

variations.easier: A one-cloud version: a small puddle, a short sky, three finders, the whole expedition inside ten minutes on a just-rained morning.
variations.harder: A leaf-boat picture version: ONE leaf, placed (not dropped) at the puddle's edge by the adult, floats into the picture and becomes the only boat on an upside-down sea, the group narrates its voyage across the sky until it grounds.

activities.inclusion: Listening is the circle's main instrument and it is equally open to every ear, from the rug's best hearing spot, chosen by its listener, arranged by the group without comment. The tipping can be done with two hands of any grip, with the stick's low end resting on the rug for leverage, or by a holder directing the adult's hands degree by degree. 'Start... slower... THERE, hold it', while the judgement of slowness, the session's whole skill, stays the director's. Forecasts can be called in words, signs, or by holding up the sun or cloud card, and the last-grain call belongs to any ear that catches it, in any form.

materials.item: one big rainstick, adult-checked (a long, sealed rainstick the adult has tipped a hundred times: contents settled, ends firm, nothing rattling loose, the slower it pours, the better it serves)
a listening rug the circle sits on (the weather station)
no other materials. Ears are the instruments

activities.name: Big Rainstick Tip and Listen
activities.safety: The stick is the adult-audited instrument and its seal is the safety system: ends firm, body uncracked, and a stick that sheds one grain is out of the circle on the spot and out of the room's set permanently, because its contents are exactly the size this archive treats with most respect. The stick is held in two hands over the rug and tipped from a seated position only, a long stick raised and tipped from standing puts its high end over neighbours' heads, so all weather is made sitting down, and the stick travels (rarely, and by the adult) held low and horizontal. Listening quiet is a pleasure here, never a discipline: a listener who whispers into the rain is answered with the record's one line, 'The rain is quiet, so we are', said warmly, once, and the rain continues.
activities.setup: Know your stick before the circle does: tip it alone, slowly, and time its rain. A stick that dumps its rain in three seconds is a rattle in a costume. This record needs a stick whose filling falls for twenty seconds or more at a slow tip, because the listening IS the duration. Check the ends and the body like equipment: a rainstick that leaks a single grain has a crack, and a crack at three, mid-circle, is a spill of a thousand tiny pieces. A stick with any damage is retired before the session, entirely, no tape repairs trusted under small hands.
steps: Hold the rainstick upright in the middle of the circle and say the plain framing: 'Inside this stick there is rain, waiting. It is not real rain. It is tiny hard seeds, and when the stick tips, they fall through a maze inside, a few at a time, and it SOUNDS like rain coming through trees. One person tips it. Everybody else has the other job.' State the laws whole: 'The stick is tipped SLOWLY, slower than you think. It is held in two hands, over the rug, always. And while the rain is falling, the circle is QUIET: the rain is quiet, so we are.'

First rain together, yours at full slowness: raise the stick, let the circle watch your hands begin a tip so gradual the first grains are heard before the stick has visibly moved. That threshold moment, sound arriving ahead of sight, stills a room of three-year-olds like a hand on a shoulder. Tip it the whole way over the course of its full rain, then hold the silence the rain leaves behind for a count of three before anyone speaks. Name what the room just did: 'That was one rain. It took as long as it took, and every ear here stayed with it to the last grain.'

Tipping round: holders take the stick in known order, in the middle's seat, and tip their rain while the circle listens. The adult's coaching is one word, offered early and quietly, and it is always the same: 'Slower...' A holder who tips fast gets no correction beyond a second rain, offered on the spot as the real curriculum: 'Again, and this time, tip it like you are pouring the rain for a sleeping garden.' Two tries is the design, not a penalty; slowness is a physical skill and it is being learned in the hands, in public, kindly.

Weather stretch, the activity's deepening: once slow tipping is owned, holders may make WEATHER, a drizzle tip (barely begun, a handful of grains, held, returned upright), a long rain (the full tip), and the beloved third forecast: the rain that STOPS MID-FALL, tipped to halfway, the stick frozen vertical... no, held at its angle, grains settling, and the circle must call the moment the rain truly ends, in whispers, agreeing on the last grain's sound. Calling the exact end of a quiet thing, together, is listening at concert level, and the record names it as such.

Finish with the stick retired like the instrument it is: the last holder tips the day's final rain at the group's slowest yet, the silence after it is held longest of all, and the stick is laid in its place by two hands, horizontal, at rest: 'The rain is back inside, waiting. It will keep until the next day this room needs weather.' The tell-back is the count of rains, said plainly: 'Seven rains fell in this room today, and not one of them was hurried.'
activities.tagline: One big rainstick, tipped so slowly the rain inside takes a whole minute to fall: the holder tips, the whole circle listens to weather only hands can make.

variations.easier: A three-rain version: the adult's rain and two holders', the whole curriculum, slow, slower, call the end, inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A weather-map version: holders draw straws of sky, a big sun card means drizzle, a cloud card means the long rain, and the circle must identify which weather fell by ear alone before the card is shown.

activities.inclusion: The press works at every station: the board can be held steady by the adult at the printer's exact table height, the painted sheet laid and lifted by a partner's hands following the printer's calls, 'down... press... now LIFT', while the colour, the page, and the moment of the lift stay the printer's decisions entirely; the print that comes up is theirs. A printer can press with a flat palm, two palms, or a full forearm laid gently across the board. The field reads pressure, not anatomy, and every true press prints. Choosing which of their pages joins the gallery walk is each printer's own curatorial call, respected in full.

materials.item: sheets of BIG-bubble wrap, adult-prepared (bubbles at least a thumb wide, one sheet per printer, edges taped to a stiff board so the sheet works like a stamp, not a toy, checked: no torn bubbles, no loose flaps)
washable tempera in wide shallow trays (two or three colours. Paint the adult has read the ingredient list of first)
big paper sheets, one per printer plus spares (the print bed, taped flat to the table)
a washing bowl, soap, and towels at the table's end (the printers' station)

activities.name: Big Bubble Wrap Print Painting
activities.safety: Paint is washable tempera whose ingredient list the adult has read before the session, checked against the room's known sensitivities, and sleeves are rolled before paint, not rescued after. The wrap's law, flat palms, gentle press, NEVER popped, is a safety rule as well as a craft one: pounding a mounted sheet on a board invites the board to skid and hands to slide into paint trays, so presses happen seated or standing still at a table at the printer's own height, and any sheet that pops a bubble despite everything is retired to be examined by the adult, not squeezed further by anyone. Mounted boards have taped, splinter-free edges, checked with the adult's own palm; the washing bowl is used after every print, because painted palms travel exactly as far as the drying line and no further.
activities.setup: Mount every wrap sheet on its board yourself and press-test the set before the printers arrive: a sheet stamps WELL when a flat palm press, lifted straight, leaves a full field of rings, if your test print is patchy, the board is bowing or the bubbles are too small, and the printers deserve a press that works before their technique is ever judged. The law of this record is set in the setup: the wrap must NOT pop. Popping is for feet and another activity entirely; here the bubbles are the printing surface, their air is the press's spring, and a popped bubble stamps a flat dead spot, so boards are stiff, presses are flat-palmed, and the setup's whole job is making not-popping the easy way to print.
steps: Spread the first printed page, yours, made in setup, and say the plain framing: 'These circles were not drawn. They were PRINTED, by this', hold up the mounted wrap, 'which is full of little air pillows. Paint goes on the pillows, the sheet lies down flat on the paper, hands press, flat, gently, and when it lifts, the circles stay.' State the press's two laws whole: 'Flat palms, gentle press. We do not POUND the pillows, and we never pop them. And the lift is STRAIGHT UP, slow, like the sheet is waking up.'

First print together, yours at full ceremony: brush or dab the paint across the bubbles (a wide brush dragged lightly, or the sheet pressed once into its tray, either way, paint on the BUBBLE TOPS, not flooded between them), lay it paint-down on a fresh page, press with two flat palms in a slow count of three, and lift straight up by the board's edges. The field of rings gets its true review, in front of everyone: 'Every pillow left its circle. That is a print.' A patch in the field is pointed at and named aloud, kindly, as press-craft: 'This corner got a shy press. It needs a flatter palm next time.'

Printing round: printers work one at a time at the press, in known order, choosing their colour and their page. Each print has the full liturgy, paint, lay, press to three, lift straight, and each printer's field is laid to dry on the drying line where the whole room can watch the gallery grow. A printer whose lift slides sideways gets the press's mercy, identical in spirit to every record on this shelf: the smear is a WEATHER print, it stays, it is named kindly ('this one printed in a wind'), and the printer may pull one more page if the spares allow. No print is ever binned by anyone but its own printer, and printers at three rarely bin.

Two-colour moment, for steady pressers: a second colour, dabbed only on HALF the sheet, printed over a dried first field at a slight turn. Rings inside rings, two colours deep. It is introduced as the press's advanced work, because it is: alignment by eye, a turn judged by hands, and a field that can fail beautifully. Success is celebrated exactly; failure is named a storm print and joins the line. The drying line's democracy is total, and every printer can see that it is.

Finish with the gallery walked properly: pages dry, the group processes slowly along the line while the adult reads the fields like weather reports, 'Circles all the way. A windy one. A two-colour storm, printed by its maker on purpose.' Each printer takes their own page down by its corners at the very end, the wrap sheets are wiped gently (flat palm, no scrubbing, the presses retire unpopped, ready to print another day), boards are stacked, and hands go to the washing bowl in printing order.
activities.tagline: A sheet of big-bubble wrap is the printing press: painted, pressed flat onto big paper, lifted straight, a page of circles, stamped by the sheet itself.

variations.easier: A one-colour, one-page version: a small crew, every printer pulling two pages inside fifteen minutes, the full liturgy intact.
variations.harder: A giant-field version: one enormous shared page on the floor, every printer pressing one field onto it in turn, a group print, signed at the corner by every flat palm in paint, once each.

activities.inclusion: Rolling is gloriously adaptable: a roller can travel the road by rolling with a partner log rolling in arm's reach beside them for company, by rolling a shorter road that ends at their own finish cushion placed mid-mat with the same ceremony, or by being the road's official starter. Lying at the start line to demonstrate the tuck, calling 'LOG AWAY' for each traveller, and standing at the finish to give the forest salute first. A participant who directs rolls, choosing each log's line, calling veers in the group's own language ('two hands off the line!'), is the road's engineer for the session, in full.

materials.item: one long gym mat (or two mats joined flat, seams taped, the rolling road, walked and pressed by the adult for any lump, gap, or slide)
one straight tape line down the mat's middle (the log's road map)
a soft finish cushion at the far end (the rolling's destination. Logs stop against something kind)

activities.name: Big Log Roll Down the Mat
activities.safety: One log on the mat at a time, enforced by the queue and the adult's roadside post: a second body on the road is a collision between the two softest and least steerable vehicles there are. Arms stay tucked. The law is safety before style, because a hand posted out sideways mid-roll takes the roller's weight on a wrist at exactly the wrong angle; rollers who cannot yet keep arms in roll with arms crossed on the chest and hands holding their own shoulders, which gives every hand a job it can keep. The mat's surface is the adult's inspection, done on knees before the session; jewellery, hair clips that dig, and anything in a pocket come off before rolling, and a roller who feels dizzy stops, sits at the roadside with the adult, and watches the forest until the world is still. Rejoining is theirs to choose, never expected.
activities.setup: Walk the mat like an engineer before anyone rolls on it: press every join with your own knee, looking for the one thing that ruins a roll and frightens a roller, a sudden lump, a gap that grabs a shoulder, a mat that slides on the floor mid-turn. Tape joins flat, wedge the mat against a wall if it travels, and roll it YOURSELF once, full length, arms in: if your own roll veers off the line twice, the mat is too short, too narrow, or too bumpy for honest rolling at three, and the setup changes before the rollers are ever blamed. The finish cushion is placed and its softness believed in.
steps: Stand the group at the mat's end and say the plain framing: 'Logs do not walk. Logs do not crawl. A log ROLLS. It lies down, tucks its branches in, and turns over and over until it arrives. Today everybody travels this mat the log way: down at this end, roll, roll, roll, and stand up at THAT end, where the cushion is.' State the log laws whole: 'Arms stay IN, tucked to your chest or straight along your body, no pushing with hands. Legs stay together and straight-ish. One log on the mat at a time, and the log that has arrived clears the cushion for the next log.'

First roll together, yours at full ceremony, and at three, the adult rolling is not a demonstration, it is an EVENT: lie down, tuck in, and roll the whole length slowly, narrating nothing (logs are quiet), then stand at the finish with genuine ceremony: 'The log has arrived.' The group will want to roll immediately and all at once; the queue forms at the mat's end in order, and waiting rollers sit where they can watch the road, because watching a log arrive is how the next log learns the route.

Rolling round: one log at a time, each rolled at their own honest pace. Some logs barrel down in six turns, some take twelve with long pauses lying flat mid-road, and both are complete logs. A log that veers off the line gets the record's re-route, delivered kindly from the roadside: 'Log, you are rolling toward the forest. Lie still... turn your nose toward the cushion... roll on.' Sitting up mid-roll to fix direction is allowed and is never cheating: logs are re-aimed by pausing, and the pause is part of rolling. A log may also stop, rest, and declare the roll finished from wherever they are. Arrival is the cushion's honour, but a roll ended by its own log is a roll completed.

Straight-line stretch: once plain rolling is owned, the tape line becomes the challenge. Roll the whole road and finish ON the line's end, the log unspooling straight as a ruler. Introduce it as the craft it is: 'Any log can roll. A log that arrives ON THE LINE has rolled like it was sawn.' Veers now get measured in the group's new language, 'two hands off the line!', and improvement is tracked out loud across a roller's turns, because a log whose second roll lands closer than its first has demonstrably grown at a skill, in public, in one session.

Finish with a whole-forest moment: the group's last rolls are taken back to back, each log's arrival met by the forest's salute, arms raised straight like standing trees, held until the log stands, and the tell-back rolls the session home: 'Every log in this forest travelled the whole mat without walking one step. Some rolled straight, some rolled wandering, and every single one arrived lying down and stood up a tree.' Mats are walked back to their place by the adult; logs carry only the small things.
activities.tagline: One long mat, one straight line: lie down at the end, arms in like a log, and roll the whole length without once sitting up. Rolling IS the travelling.

variations.easier: A half-mat version: the road is one mat long, rolls are four turns each, and every roller gets three journeys inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A passenger version: a steady log rolls the road carrying one soft toy balanced on their tummy, tucked arms and all, if the passenger arrives riding, the forest salutes twice.

activities.inclusion: The threading works at every station: the lace can be held in a full fist, pushed with a palm-rock, or worked with the bead held in a table clamp the adult has placed, so the stringer's hands do only the aiming and pushing that are theirs today. A stringer can direct a whole string, choosing every bead by colour from the store, calling each push, 'that one... hole up... PUSH', while a partner's hands follow the direction exactly; the finished string, its pattern, and its length are the director's work, and it is worn by its director. Pattern-reading at the end, calling a finished string's colours bead by bead for the room, is the jeweller's official voice and belongs to whoever holds it.

materials.item: big wooden beads, adult-audited (the biggest craft beads, too big for a mouth by a wide margin, holes wide and smooth, no cracks, no splinters, colours honest and few)
stiff laces, one per stringer (thick cord or a shoelace with its end taped into a firm point. The needle that is not a needle; the other end knotted with ONE bead fixed as the stopper)
a bowl the beads start in (the bead store)

activities.name: Big Wooden Bead Stringing

photo.alt: A pile of colorful beads with holes for stringing
photo.caption: Beads with big holes, ready for small hands to thread onto a string.
photo.credit: Photo: https://pixabay.com/fr/users/khfalk-36012/, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Beads are big, smooth, single-piece, and audited one by one before every session, at three, the store's rule has no exceptions argued: anything small, cracked, splintered, sharp at the hole's rim, or losing its colour is out permanently. Stringing happens seated with the bowl still on the table: beads roll, and a rolled bead is retrieved by the adult at a walk, because beads on a floor under small feet are marbles' treacherous cousins. Laces are thick, soft-ended by tape, and never worn round a neck by the child themselves. Finished strings worn over the head are tied by the adult with a breakaway loose knot, worn supervised, and are the session's, coming off before any running, climbing, or leaving the room.
activities.setup: Audit the beads one by one like the safety equipment they are, because at three a bead is exactly the size of thing this archive treats with most ceremony: every bead passes the adult's own checks, too big for a mouth by a wide margin, hole rims smooth to a fingertip, no crack, no splinter, no flaking paint, and any bead that fails leaves the store permanently, no debate. Test the laces the same way: the taped point must be firm enough to aim and soft enough to bend against a palm without a point that matters, and the stopper bead must be truly fixed. A string whose stopper escapes teaches gravity where you wanted threading. Count the beads into the store and know the number; the closing count-in depends on it.
steps: Tip a few beads onto the table and say the plain job: 'A bead has a hole through its middle. The lace goes in one side and out the other, and the bead slides down and STAYS. Enough beads, and you have made a string, a thing that did not exist this morning.' Work one bead yourself at full ceremony, slowly, where every eye can see the whole skill: choose, hold the bead hole-up in finger and thumb, aim the lace's point at the hole, push, let the group see the point appear on the other side, pinch it, pull, and slide the bead down to the stopper with a small, satisfying knock. State the one rule: 'One bead at a time, and the lace's point does the travelling. If it will not go, the bead is telling you something. Turn the bead until its hole faces the point.'

First stringings together: each stringer takes a lace and three beads to start, and the room's sound changes into this shelf's definition of concentration, the small knock of a bead arriving home, again and again, at six different paces. The adult strings alongside, a fellow worker with a lace of their own, available for the one consultation that matters (holding a bead steady, hole-up, while its stringer's point finds the way. Help given to the BEAD, never hands taking over the lace: a string threaded by the wrong hands is a photograph of help, not a record of skill).

Pattern stretch, offered to steady stringers: a string with an ORDER in it, red, blue, red, blue, chosen by its stringer before the beads are touched, and kept, bead by bead, against the temptation of the bowl's other colours. Keeping a promise to a pattern across eight beads, with the wrong colour sitting right there in the store looking beautiful, is executive function wearing its working clothes, and the record honours finished patterns by reading them aloud, bead by bead, like necklaces in a jeweller's window.

Wearing moment: when a string reaches its stringer's chosen length, and the length is the stringer's call, from three beads to the lace's whole capacity, it is tied off by the adult with a loose, easy knot and WORN for the rest of the session: over the head, on a wrist, carried as treasure. A made thing being worn by its maker changes the room's weather; later stringers work in the presence of finished strings, which is how craft traditions actually transmit, and the record protects the wearing as part of the activity, not a reward after it.

Finish with the count-in, the activity's closing instrument: worn strings are admired once more, then unthreaded by their own makers back into the store, the reverse journey, bead by bead, which is its own quiet skill, while the count is kept aloud to the true number the adult knows. Laces are coiled, stoppers checked, and the tell-back is said over the full bowl: 'Every bead is home. This room made four strings today out of a bowl and some string, and took them apart again with its own hands, and the bowl cannot tell the difference, but the hands can.'
activities.tagline: Big wooden beads and one stiff lace with a taped end: find a bead, aim the lace at its hole, push it home. A string that grows one bead at a time.

variations.easier: A three-bead version: one lace, three beads, the whole arc, aim, push, knock, wear, inside ten minutes for one or two stringers.
variations.harder: A longest-string challenge (for a veteran stringer): how many beads before the lace runs out?, strung in full, counted in full, worn in full, and unthreaded in full, a complete expedition on one lace.

activities.inclusion: Holding the stone asks nothing of a voice: a holder can add their true thing in words, in a sign, in one word plus a point out the window toward the place itself, or by tapping the stone twice to ask the circle to say the people's name together for them. Every form closes with the same line, said by all. The stone can travel on a lap tray between neighbours for any holder whose hands are busy elsewhere; the turn, the timing, and the honour are identical. The closing-line caller, the voice that leads 'That is a true story, and it is still true', is the circle's official honour and rotates by list.

materials.item: one big smooth story stone, adult-chosen (palm-sized or bigger, washed, no sharp edges, no cracks. The circle's talking piece, held by whoever is telling or listening hardest)
no other materials. The story is carried in words

activities.name: Big Story Stone, First People
activities.safety: The stone is palm-sized or bigger, smooth, washed, and checked before every session; anything cracked or sharp-edged leaves the set permanently. It travels low, lap to lap, in two hands, and is never tossed or handed over another child's head. The adult's hands shadow the pass for the youngest holders. The content rule is the record's other safety: only true, plain things are told, no invented ceremonies, no costumes, no 'playing' at being the people being honoured, ever; this record teaches about real neighbours with respect, and the adult corrects a drift toward pretend instantly and kindly.
activities.setup: Choose and wash the stone ahead, and, this is the real preparation, learn whose land your classroom actually stands on before the circle sits down: the name of the Indigenous people of your place, said correctly, and two or three true, plain things about them that a three-year-old can hold (they lived here first; many are still here, our neighbours now; they cared for this land a very long time). If you do not know, find out from your library or your district's own land statement before this record runs. The record refuses to be run on a guess, because a story told wrong at three gets remembered wrong at thirty. Practise saying the people's name aloud until it is ordinary in your mouth.
steps: Gather the circle, hold the stone in both hands, and say the plain framing in full: 'This land had people on it before there were towns, before there were schools, before there was us. The first people here were the [name, said plainly and correctly]. They are still here. They are our neighbours. Today is a day for saying their name properly and hearing one true story about them.' State the one rule: 'The stone is held in two hands, in a lap. When the stone is with you, you may hold it quietly or add one true-sized thing. The stone is never thrown, tapped, or passed over anybody's head.'

First telling together, yours: with the stone in your lap, tell the short true story you prepared, three or four sentences, no more: who the people are, one thing they made or did on this land ('they fished this river'), one thing that is still true now ('their children go to school in our town'). Keep it at story size, not lesson size: names, a river, a neighbour. When your telling is done, say the closing line of every turn, which the circle will learn to say with you: 'That is a true story, and it is still true.'

Stone round: the stone travels hand to hand round the circle in order, low, two hands to two hands. Each holder may add ONE small true thing, something from the story retold in their own words, something true about this place ('the river is near our park'), or simply the people's name said carefully, which counts in full and is honoured at full size: a name said right by a three-year-old is this record's whole curriculum arriving.
