Directing the adult's carrying hands by description ('behind the BIG cushion... the ear OUT') while the choice, the nerve, and the clue-giving stay the director's; the spotter's freeze-and-point can be a freeze-and-call, a freeze-and-stamp, or a held-up hand the pack has agreed means FOUND IT, and every form stops the hunt with the same authority. The clue-giver, keeper of the honours paid to good hiding, and the bear-carrier, who brings the rescued sailor home at full ceremony, rotate by list from any seat. A seeker who hunts better sitting still, watching the room's edges from the middle while the pack circuits, is posted as the room's lighthouse at full membership: spotting is spotting, and the lighthouse's bear is cheered like any other.

materials.item: one big soft bear (the hider, big enough that a good hiding place still leaves a paw, an ear, or a hopeful nose showing; soft, washed, and famous: this bear has a name and the room knows it)
the whole room, arranged as the hunting ground (its ordinary furniture, with the adult's one addition: nothing is hidden IN anything that closes, locks, or tips)

activities.name: Big Hide the Bear, Seek Together
activities.safety: The laws are the safety: the bear hides, children do not. Nobody is ever hidden, enclosed, or left alone in this record, and the adult says so in the framing so the room's expectation is set before the first count. Hiding places live inside four fences: nothing that closes (no cupboards, boxes with lids, or doors that latch), nothing that tips or is climbed for, nothing with cords, and nothing at height. The bear is found by eyes at three-year-old altitude, standing on a floor that stays under every seeker. Eye-covering lasts one count of ten with bottoms on the floor; a child who will not cover is the count-keeper's partner at full honour, watching the adult's back instead. Seeking is walking, in the adult's company, as one pack: a search that scatters is re-gathered kindly at the bear's last known dignity, 'hunters together', because running searches in furnished rooms are how seekers meet chair legs. The bear itself is soft, washed, and seam-checked; a found bear is carried, never thrown back in triumph.
activities.setup: Prepare the room, not the bear: walk the hunting ground with a hider's eye and pre-decide the session's three or four honest hiding places, behind the cushion with an ear out, under the low table wearing the rug's shadow, in the book basket with one paw over the edge, places a three-year-old's eye can actually reach, because this record's difficulty lives in the LOOKING, not the hiding, and a bear hidden beyond the room's eyes teaches only waiting. Check each place for the session's one law: the bear is never inside anything that closes, anything heavy, anything with a cord, or anything a seeker must climb to search. Then brief the hider's assistant, you, first, on the ceremony's timing: the group hides its eyes for the count of ten, no more, because at three the covering of eyes is itself an act of faith that must be kept short and kept safe.
steps: Gather the group in the room's middle, the bear held up where everyone can greet it, and say the plain framing: 'It is raining, we are inside, and [the bear] would like to play hiding. The bear will hide. Somewhere in this room, where eyes can find it. Nobody hides THEMSELVES: the whole group seeks, together, holding the same search in twenty hands. When somebody spots the bear, they do not grab, they FREEZE, and they point, and the whole group gets the finding.' State the laws whole: 'While the bear hides, our eyes are covered and our bottoms are on the floor, the hiding is a trust, and we keep it. Seeking is walking: hunters walk, in a bunch, where the adult walks. A found bear is lifted by the spotter and carried back like a rescued sailor, at full ceremony.'

First hiding, yours: the group covers its eyes (hands, or faces in laps, every covering is honest), and the adult counts aloud to ten at ceremony pace while hiding the bear in the session's kindest place, an ear and a paw showing, findable by the door-side seekers first. 'Ready or not, eyes open, the bear is... somewhere.' The first search is conducted at the record's official manner: the whole pack moves together, slowly, the adult narrating the search like weather: 'Not behind the door... the bear is not a door bear. The cushions have not been ASKED yet...'. Until the first spot lands (a freeze, a point, a noise like a struck bell) and the room converges on one visible ear: 'FOUND. Mina's eyes found it. Everybody's search found it. The bear was in the cushions, showing one ear the whole time, bravely.' The bear is carried back by its spotter, held high, unhurt by fame.

Seeking round: the hiding passes to its keepers, a child, with the adult as their ladder-free, door-holding assistant, chooses the hiding place from the room's known places (or invents one inside the laws, approved by the adult's eye before the eyes close) while the group covers and counts, the count now given to the circle's steadiest counter. Searches grow craftier in the open: the pack learns to ask places in order, to look LOW (bears are low creatures), to return to the place a paw showed last time, and the adult protects the round's constitution throughout: a bear unfound after one full circuit is not failed but 'winning', and the hider earns the record's highest honour early, revealing it by degrees: 'I will give the room ONE clue, because this hiding was masterly: the bear can see the window from where it is.' Clues are honours paid to good hiding, never penalties for slow seeking.

Hard-hiding stretch, for a room whose eyes have grown sharp: the bear hides with only ONE sign showing, the very tip of a nose at a cushion's edge, one paw's worth of shadow under the table, and the pack, told plainly that this hiding is the day's hardest, searches at its most ceremonious: two circuits, a clue, and the adult's looking-glass held in reserve. A finding at this level is celebrated at festival size, and the record says why while it happens: 'You found a NOSE. Rooms full of grown-ups walk past noses. This room hunts better than weather.' If the stretch's bear outlasts two clues, its hider reveals it standing beside the place like a lighthouse keeper, to applause: the bear was hidden by a master, and the record files the day accordingly.

Finish with the bear's retirement: it is hidden one final time by the whole group together (eyes open, placing it in its favourite found-place, tucked with ceremony) and left there 'sleeping off the hunt' while the group files past it quietly. Then the tell-back, said at the door of the hunting ground: 'The bear hid five times. It was found five times, once by a nose. Nobody hid alone, nobody sought alone, and the finding belonged to everybody every time. That is how this room hunts: together, at walking pace, cheering.' On the next rainy day the bear will be found already hiding, because somebody, the adult, before breakfast, will have kept the game's promise overnight.
activities.tagline: One big soft bear hides somewhere in the room, not too well. The whole group seeks together, and the finding belongs to everybody.

variations.easier: A two-hiding version: two places, two searches, the whole ceremony inside ten minutes for the newest hunting packs.
variations.harder: A torch version (a dim afternoon, a willing room): seekers carry one big torch between two hands, adult-led, and the bear is found by its lit ear in the gloom. The hunting ground's furniture pre-walked in the light, twice.

activities.inclusion: Building is turns, and every turn has shapes: a brick can be carried in two arms, pushed along the floor by a builder who travels differently (a pushed brick arrives as built as a carried one), or placed by direction, 'flat... a little toward me... THERE, hands off soft', with a partner's hands serving as the crane while the placement, the pause, and the report stay the director's. The line-keeper's job, standing at the builders' line, giving the room's progress reports and calling CLEAR at the adult's word, is the site's official voice and belongs to whoever holds it, from any position behind the line. A builder whose whole contribution is the foundation course, laid first and never bettered, is named in the final report exactly so: foundations are credited in this record's tell-back by name, because the record means it.

materials.item: big cardboard bricks, a wall's worth (large light boxes, taped shut and adult-tested. Each must be lift-able in a three-year-old's two arms and soft-edged all over; a brick that hurts a shin in the adult's test is retired)
a clear stretch of floor with a line marked at standing distance (the builders' line. Behind it, the wall is watched; in front of it, the wall is built)

one cushion city at the wall's fall-side (the soft landing the adult has arranged in the wall's most likely falling direction, because walls fall toward their audiences unless an adult plans otherwise)

activities.name: Big Cardboard Brick Wall Build
activities.safety: Bricks are light by law and proven on the adult's own foot before the session; a wall of them falling is a rustle, never an injury, and the room is arranged so that even the rustle lands kindly: the fall-side is cushioned, the builders' line stands a full wall-height back, and the CLEAR call is rehearsed in the first minute (called once in fun, obeyed in a beat) before any brick rises. One builder at the wall at a time; carrying is two-armed and walked; nobody climbs, stands on, or leans against bricks at any height, finished or fallen. A brick under a climbing foot is a skate, and the record retires the idea on sight. The adult watches leans the way sailors watch weather: a wall leaning beyond its reading is unloaded course by course from the top by its builders, behind the line between each brick, before it can choose its own moment. Demolition is by invitation, counted, and aimed at the cushions, never toward a person, a window, or next door's nap.
activities.setup: Make the bricks like a builder who will be audited by toddlers: every box taped shut along every seam, every flap end checked by a run palm, and the whole set dropped once from waist height onto the adult's own foot, if it smarts, it is not a brick for this wall. Count the bricks and agree the wall's ambition with yourself: chin-high on a three-year-old is about six bricks per stack two wide, and a plan beyond the bricks is a disappointment scheduled in advance. Walk the floor and choose the wall's ground with a founder's care, flat, clear, away from anything a falling wall's draught could ruffle, and set the builders' line a full wall-height away from where the wall will stand: the geometry of this record is that excitement pulls children toward tall things, and the line, not the adult's voice, is what holds the geometry kindly.
steps: Spread the bricks where the builders can reach them and say the plain framing: 'Bricks build walls when they are stacked flat, steady, and one at a time. Our wall has one job: to stand as high as your chins. When it stands, we will report on it. If it falls, walls fall, it is nearly their favourite thing, the fall is part of the building, and we will report that too, and build it again different.' State the laws whole: 'Bricks are carried in two arms, one at a time, at walking pace. Builders build one at a time at the wall; everybody else watches from behind the line. Nobody touches a standing wall except the builder placing the next brick. When the adult calls CLEAR, everybody steps behind the line. Clear means clear, at once, like a fire drill with better news.'

First courses together: the foundation is laid as a public work, two bricks side by side, flat, butted true, with the record's building law spoken into the first layer: 'A wall is only ever as steady as its bottom. Flat bricks, all the way down, no wobbles forgiven early.' Builders take their turns in known order, one brick each, carried at ceremony and placed with two hands and a pause, THE PAUSE, named as a tool: place, hands still ON, one breath, hands off soft. The room watches each placing from the line with the builder's report collected as the wall grows, in the session's official shape: 'Three bricks. STILL STANDING.'. A progress report the room gives together, like a crew.

Rising round: the wall climbs course by course, and the building gets honest about its difficulties in the open. A brick that rocks is lifted off and re-seated by its own builder, never patted into obedience ('A rocked brick is a wall asking for a second chance. Builders listen'); a course that leans gets the adult's reading aloud: 'The wall is leaning toward the window. Leaning is information. The next brick goes on the OTHER side, and we shall see if the wall agrees.' Chins are the measure and the record uses them: at the height of the smallest builder's chin the room pauses behind the line for the wall's portrait moment. Builders standing beside (never against) their work, the report given in full: 'The wall is at CHIN height. It leans a little toward the window. It is STILL STANDING.'

One-more-brick stretch, the engineer's temptation run honestly: past chin height, the wall may take ONE more brick, placed by the day's steadiest builder, if, and the record's law is stated before, not after, the wall beneath is standing true: no lean, no rock, all courses flat. If the wall takes it, the room has beaten its own ambition and the report is a festival. If the wall answers with a fall, the fall is met with the record's standing response, delivered at full size because it is the whole point: 'DOWN SHE COMES, and look, nobody is surprised and nobody is sorry: the fall told us where the wall stopped agreeing. That is the last piece of information this wall had, and it gave it to us free.' The fallen wall is read before it is cleared: which course went first, which way it chose, where the honest bricks lie, three-year-old forensic engineering, conducted with respect.

Finish with the rebuild-that-is-different, because the record does not end on a fall or a stand but on a revision: the wall is built once more, faster now (hands have learned the pause), with ONE change the builders choose from the fall's evidence, wider bottom, shorter ambition, bricks turned the long way, and the final report, whatever it is, is given by the whole room in the official shape and received as the day's result: 'THIS wall stands at chin height and does not lean. We built it twice. The second one knew more.' Bricks are then demolished by invitation only, builders push their own wall over together on the count, into its cushion city, if demolition is the room's wish, and carried back to their corner two arms at a time, counted aloud to their true number.
activities.tagline: Bricks as big as pillows, light as boxes: build a wall as high as your chin, report on it honestly, and when it falls, that is data too.

variations.easier: A three-course version: a low wall, waist-high, two reports, the whole engineering cycle inside fifteen minutes for the newest builders.
variations.harder: A doorway version: the wall is built across the room's play doorway at knee height, and the afternoon's traffic steps OVER the record's result, carefully, all day, engineering with a public.

activities.inclusion: Every job in the laundry has a shape for every worker: a cloth can be carried by two standing carriers, by one carrier and one seated holder at the line's end who receives and steadies it, or across a lap on the way, the corner held, the pace kept, the peg placed by its owner's hand or at its owner's word: 'open... THERE... let go.' Pegging adapts without shrinking: two-hand squeezes, a peg braced against the line itself while the carrier presses, or the adult's strength closing a peg the carrier has placed and aimed. Placing and aiming are the skill; strength is just the weather. The chant-keepers, the crew's voice while a pair travels, hold the round's rhythm from any seat, and the line-caller, who reads the wash's count at the inspection ('nine cloths... NINE'), is the laundry's official voice and rotates by list.

materials.item: big soft cloths, one per trip (towels, pillowcases, tea towels grown large, freshly washed, soft, and big enough that two carriers each hold a real share)
one low line strung where the adult set it (a rope or cord tied between two sturdy chair backs or hooks at the carriers' chest height. Sagging kindly, tested to take the adult's hard tug)
big pegs in a basket at the line (spring pegs big enough for small hands to squeeze with a whole-hand grip. The adult has tested every one: a peg that fights back is retired)

activities.name: Big Laundry Line, Helping Hands
activities.safety: The line is the record's one piece of infrastructure and it is over-built: tied to fixed points or furniture too heavy to travel, tug-tested at adult weight, strung at chest height so no neck ever meets it, and never, not once, not as a joke the room invents, wrapped, swung on, or used to pull anything but air and cloths. A line that comes down mid-session ends the round kindly: carriers step back, the adult re-ties or retires it, and the wash waits in the basket like washing does. Pegs are big, whole-hand pegs, squeeze-tested; a peg is opened AWAY from fingers and faces, and a peg that bites wood too hard for its carrier is worked by the carrier's direction with the adult's strength. The placement and the credit stay the carrier's. Cloths travel off the floor at washing pace; a dropped cloth on a walked floor is re-carried, not re-hung, because floors are honest about what they add to washing.
activities.setup: String the line and lean on it before the crew is called: hang your full weight off its middle for three seconds, tie it again if it sighs, and check what it is tied TO, a line that pulls a chair over mid-hang turns a laundry day into a furniture day. Wash the cloths (real washing, real soap): this record's pretend rests on the pegs and the line being honestly ready, and a cloth that smells of the cupboard teaches the wrong job. Test every peg with your own whole-hand squeeze, because at three a peg is a two-hand, whole-arm event. Pegs that need fingertip strength will strand cloths and carriers alike. Set the basket of dry cloths at the room's far end: the carrying distance, about ten small steps, is the record's working length.
steps: Gather the crew and say the plain framing: 'All this washing needs hanging, and hanging is a two-person job. Two carriers take ONE cloth, one holds this end, one holds that end, walk it to the line together, and peg it up together: one peg each, one corner each. When the line is full, the whole wash waves, and this room did that.' State the laws whole: 'A cloth is carried between two people, held at its corners, off the floor. Dragging ends the trip and the cloth goes back to be carried again, kindly. Pegs squeeze OPEN, place, let go: fingers never go where a peg can bite. The line takes one hanging pair at a time; the next pair waits at the basket, holding their cloth ready.'

First hanging together, yours: take a partner from the crew, choose the biggest cloth with ceremony, take your corners, and walk it to the line at the carriers' official pace, 'Washing pace. The wash is in no hurry, and neither are we', then hang it as a public demonstration: shake it once (the laundry snap, small version), corners up, pegs squeezed open in whole-hand grips, placed, released, and the pair's report said in the session's official shape: 'HUNG. Two corners, two pegs, one cloth.' Step back with your partner and admire it at full size: 'That cloth is up because FOUR hands did it. No pair of hands in this room could have hurried it, and none needed to.'

Hanging round: pairs take their trips in known order, choose a cloth, corners, the ten-step carry at washing pace, the hang, while the waiting crew holds the session's rhythm with the clothesline chant the record keeps for exactly this: quiet, in carrier-time, 'Two hands here, two hands there, hang the washing in the air'. Said only while a pair is travelling, falling silent at the hang so the pegs' two clicks can be heard like punctuation. A peg that drops is retrieved by its own pair and re-squeezed; a cloth that lands half-hung is read honestly and re-hung by the same hands: 'One corner is waving and one is weeping. Carriers. Mend your cloth.' The mending is the job, and the record honours it over speed every time.

Full-line stretch, as the line fills: the adult names the geography of the growing wash in the open, 'Four cloths waving. The line is halfway to full', and the last empty stretch of line becomes the room's shared horizon. Pairs hanging late in the round place their cloths in the gaps with a stepladder's care (no stepladder: the line is at chest height by design, and gaps are chosen by eye from the floor). Shaking each cloth once before hanging, the snap, is now performed by the pairs themselves, taught hand over hand in the early trips, because a crew that shakes its own washing has stopped being helped and started working.

Finish with the line full and the whole crew standing back from it in a row. The wash's official inspection. The tell-back is read along the line like a banner: 'Nine cloths up. Nine trips. Eighteen corners pegged by the hands that carried them. The wash is waving because this room hung it together, two hands here, two hands there.' The cloths stay up through the day as the room's bunting, and come down in the late-day mirror of the round: pairs again, one cloth each, pegs back in the basket, cloths folded in four hands, badly, kindly, together.
activities.tagline: The room's pretend washing needs doing: pairs of carriers take one big cloth at a time to the low line and peg it up together until the whole wash waves.

variations.easier: A four-cloth version: four pairs, the basket close to the line, the whole job inside ten minutes for the smallest crews.
variations.harder: A wash-day version (a warm room, a real need simplified): the cloths are the room's OWN painting aprons and hand towels from the morning, genuinely damp, genuinely needing the line, the record at full employment.

activities.inclusion: Copying works across every distance the room contains: a mirror can copy from a seat beside the maker rather than opposite (some faces read better from the side), a face can be made by direction, 'cheeks OUT... eyes WIDE', with a partner's face following the words while the composition stays the director's, and a copy can be answered in any register the copyist owns, including a described copy ('I am doing the fish, my mouth is the O') which the maker accepts or tops up, in words. The gallery-keeper's job, the room's recognition called out loud, is one of the session's two honours and belongs to whoever holds it, and the final face's maker is chosen by the circle's acclamation, never by the adult's favour.

materials.item: no materials at all. The group's own faces are the entire equipment, which is the record's first lesson: you brought everything you need

activities.name: Big Mirror Face, Copy My Face
activities.safety: Faces are made of faces only: no hands on anybody's face, no pulled cheeks or held eyelids. A face that needs hands to make it is retired and replaced, kindly, because the game's whole dignity is that the copying partner must be able to copy safely too. Pairs sit knee to knee and stay seated: leaning in is done by faces growing in view, not bodies tipping, and a pair that migrates closer and closer in its enthusiasm is re-seated once, kindly, at mirror distance. Any child may take the whole session as the room's gallery-keeper, watching pairs, calling the recognitions ('THERE it is!'), at full honour; a face that wants to be watched by the room but not copied by one partner is accommodated by the keeper's role, not negotiated away. Two breaths is the holding limit the adult keeps: a face held to the point of aching cheeks is melted by the adult's own melt, in solidarity, on sight.
activities.setup: There is nothing to fetch and everything to decide: the pairs. Set them before the circle sits, a confident face-maker with a shy one, a still child with a wriggly one, and seat each pair knee to knee at a distance where faces are BIG in each other's view, because at three a face a room away is a rumour. Rehearse your own demonstration face until it is readably one thing, the adult's first face teaches the game's size: not a subtle eyebrow (a rumour) but a whole event, cheeks puffed, eyes wide, mouth a round O, a face that survives being copied by a three-year-old and comes back recognisable. The record is taught by a face, or it is not taught at all.
steps: Sit the pairs down and say the plain framing: 'Your face can do things. Watch mine, ' (make the demonstration face, hold it, let it melt) ', that was my Surprised Fish. Now: one of you makes a face, any face, and your partner copies it, like a mirror. Mirrors in this room are kind: they copy what they see as best they can, and a copy that comes out different is not wrong, it is a NEW face, and new faces get copied back.' State the laws whole: 'Faces are made of faces only, no touching anybody's face, ever. A face is held while your partner looks: two whole breaths. Either partner can say 'new face' and the making passes over, no reason needed.'

First copying together, yours: take a partner from the circle, make the Surprised Fish at full ceremony, hold it for two breaths while your partner studies it like weather, and let them build their copy piece by piece in the open, 'Cheeks out... eyes BIG... mouth like an O', naming the pieces as coaching, never as correction, until the pair of you sit face to face, two fish, regarding each other gravely. Hold the moment one breath longer than feels necessary, then melt together, and say the record's line over the melt: 'Your face knew mine. That is what faces are FOR, it turns out.'

Copying round: pairs take the making in turns round the circle, the maker composes a face (the record's gallery grows in the open: Sleepy Bear, with heavy lids and a yawn held hostage; Pop-Eyes; the Long Face, chin down, everything mournful; the Cheek-Puff Champion), holds it two breaths, and the mirror builds the copy while the room, watching each pair in turn, witnesses without scoring: the only verdict the room gives is recognition, called out when it lands: 'THERE it is, two Sleepy Bears!' A copy that wanders into its own invention is received under the record's constitution: 'Your mirror made a new face. Maker, copy THAT one back.' And the round becomes a conversation faces have with each other, which is what it always was.

Fast-mirror stretch, offered to the pairs whose copying has grown certain: the maker changes faces slowly, fish, bear, pop-eyes, with a breath between each, and the mirror follows a half-breath behind, like a pond catching up. Nobody speeds past the following: the stretch is not quickness, it is TOGETHERNESS, and the record names it while it happens: 'You are not behind. A mirror is always a moment behind. That is how you know it is a mirror and not a photograph.' Pairs that wobble into giggling have not failed the stretch; the giggle is a face, and it will be copied too.

Finish with the whole-circle mirror: one maker, the day's steadiest, stands where every face can see them, makes the group's final face (chosen by acclamation from the day's gallery), and the WHOLE circle builds it at once: twenty Surprised Fish, melting together on the maker's melt, the room regarding itself. Faces rest, and the tell-back is said plainly: 'Every face in this room was looked at properly today, and every face was copied by a friend. Being copied is what being known feels like at three. It feels like that later too. It just gets quieter.'
activities.tagline: Two partners sit face to face. One makes a face, any face at all. The other copies it, like a mirror that is also a friend.

variations.easier: A one-pair version: a single pair, four faces, the full ceremony inside ten minutes for the newest groups or a single new friendship being built on purpose.
variations.harder: A family-faces version: the gallery is built from home, a face somebody's grandmother makes, the dog's face, a baby sibling's face, each made, copied, and honoured with its story in one sentence.

activities.inclusion: Naming is the record's door and it stands open at every height: a namer can name from the blanket, from a chair at its edge with the same sky overhead, or from a lap, and can name by pointing a whole arm, by describing ('the one over the fence corner, the LONG one'), or by choosing among the adult's offered sightings ('your cloud, is it the one being a ship?') with the name itself still the namer's own word, kept exact. The pointer-reader job, repeating each name at full size so the whole blanket hears it land, is the session's official voice and belongs to whoever holds it, including a namer who reads for others between their own turns. A name signed, tapped out on a friend's arm in agreed rhythm, or sung is a name; the record's gallery collects them all in the same frame.

materials.item: one big blanket or old sheet, grass-sized (the lying blanket, spread by the adult on grass checked by hand and by eye: dry-ish, flat, and free of anything a back should not meet)
a sky with clouds in it (the session's whole gallery. The adult has looked up before gathering anyone: a cloudless sky postpones the record, honestly, and the group is told why)

activities.name: Big Cloud Lying, Picture Names
activities.safety: Eyes are the record's instruments and the sun is its one hazard: the blanket is laid where faces look up into cloud country away from the sun, the adult checks the sun's arc before the session and moves the blanket rather than arguing with it, and any face that finds glare turns to the blanket's shade end or takes a hat's brim as its instrument. Looking is done lying down, nobody walks with their eyes up, nobody stands on the blanket, and the sitting-up at the end is slow by instruction because a sky-watched head is a dizzy head for ten honest seconds. The grass patch is adult-checked for stones, sticks, and stingers' country before the blanket lands; anyone may be a watcher from a chair at the blanket's edge at full honour if the ground is not for them today. The session is short by design: fifteen minutes of sky is a feast at three, and the record ends while the looking is still sweet.
activities.setup: Do the looking first, alone, standing where the blanket will go: if the sky is one clean blue, this record waits for a cloudier morning and says so, a gallery with no pictures in it teaches pointing at nothing, and the sky provides so often that honesty costs a day at most. Check the grass the way a back would meet it: walk the blanket's patch in your own socks if you doubt it, feeling for stones, sticks, and the wet that soaks through in a minute. Lie down yourself for ten seconds in the middle of the session's future and look up: you are checking sightlines (the group must see sky, not the fence's top) and the sun's position. The lying spot is chosen so the sun is never in a lying face, because the record's one gaze goes UP.
steps: Spread the blanket, walk the group out around it, and say the plain framing: 'Clouds are not just clouds. Look up long enough and every one of them is being SOMETHING, a ship, a sheep, a sleeping dog, and today we are lying down to catch them at it. Each person names what one cloud is being, in their own words, and the whole group looks where the naming points.' State the laws whole: 'We lie on the blanket, on our backs, and we stay lying while the naming goes on. Sitting up ends your looking, kindly understood. Pointing is done with a whole arm, slowly: the sky is big and a fast point loses everybody. The sun is never looked at. Our clouds live away from it today, and a face that finds the sun in its view turns to the blanket's shadier end.'

First naming together, yours: lie down in the middle of the blanket with the group settling round you like petals, take a full breath of just looking, the record insists on the breath, because a sky named too fast is a sky unseen, and give the first name in the session's official shape, pointing the whole arm up at one honest cloud: 'That one is being... a WHALE. There is its back. There is its tail, going.' Narrate only what the cloud truly offers; a name that needs five invented features is a name the cloud didn't earn, and the room can tell. The group looks where you point until heads nod: seeing what a namer sees, together, is the skill, and it arrives in this minute or it doesn't arrive at all.

Naming round: namers take the sky in known order, each choosing one cloud, by pointing the whole arm and holding it until the group's eyes arrive, and naming what it is being, in the official shape, with the adult as the room's pointer-reader: 'Mina's cloud, up from her hand, past the tree, THERE, the long one. A TRAIN, she says. I can see its carriages.' A name received is repeated by the adult exactly as given, never improved: 'a boat with a hat' stands in the record as said, because it is almost certainly true. Clouds nobody claims are named by the sky itself, via the adult's wondering aloud: 'And that small one, all alone. Nobody's named it. It might be being a secret.'

Cloud-changing stretch, for a group whose looking lasts: return to the FIRST cloud named, the whale, and look at what it is being NOW: 'It was a whale. Its tail has gone somewhere. Now its back is longer and its head has... melted into a hill.' The lesson lands in the open, at the record's own pace: clouds do not hold their shapes for anybody, a name is true for the minute it is said in, and watching a picture un-become is as much looking as watching it arrive. A namer whose cloud dissolves entirely mid-round is honoured, not pitied: 'Your cloud finished being a bear and went back to being weather. You caught the whole of it. Nobody else can say that.'

Finish with one whole-group cloud, chosen by the adult's slow arm sweeping to the biggest cloud in reach of everybody's eyes, named by the circle in chorus, three names offered, the group settling on one by the ancient method of which feels most true said together, and one full breath of looking at it, all together, in quiet. Then the sitting-up, done slowly (the sky spins a little after long looking; the record knows, and says so: 'Up slowly. The ground has to catch up with your eyes'), the blanket shaken out by many hands, and the tell-back said under the sky that hosted it: 'Seven clouds were something today, and we caught them being it. They have all gone back to being weather now. The sky will make more. It always does.'
activities.tagline: One big blanket on the grass, the whole group on its back, eyes up: every cloud is being something today, and the group's job is to say what.

variations.easier: A three-cloud version: three namers, three clouds, the breath and the pointing whole, inside ten minutes on a busy morning.
variations.harder: A window version (a wet week, a room with big glass): the same lying, naming, and pointing done on rugs at the window's base, heads on cushions. The gallery is the same sky, the frame is glass.

activities.inclusion: The fence takes every painter at their own height: low stretches belong to seated painters and are worked as seriously as the high ones (the record's gallery is read top to bottom, all of it), a stroke can be painted by direction, 'a LONG one... up... stop, THAT is my door', with a partner's arm laying the water while the picture, its place, and its finishing stay the director's, and a painter working from a chair paints on the canvas the adult has brought to them if the fence stands too far: a board or a stone slab, wetted and honest, hung at their reach. The fading-rescue job, patrolling the fence with a wet brush, re-wetting any stroke whose painter calls 'keep mine shining!', is the gallery's official keeper role, and it belongs to whoever holds the bucket.

materials.item: big brushes, one per painter (the widest, softest brushes the store cupboard owns. House-painting brushes are perfect and make a three-year-old's stroke read at fence distance)
buckets of plain water, one between two painters (filled low, set on the ground where a kick cannot reach them, the paint)
a fence, wall, or stretch of paving the water can darken (the canvas, chosen by the adult for its honest response: a surface that goes satisfyingly dark when wet and pale again as it dries)

activities.name: Big Water Painting, Fence Picture
activities.safety: The paint is water and the craft is a brush, and the record keeps both honest: brushes are soft and wide, never flicked, a flicked brush throws water in eyes and ends its painter's turn for one picture while the rule is re-met kindly, and buckets sit on the ground outside the walking line, because a kicked bucket is the session's only flood and it is prevented by geography. The canvas is chosen with a ladder nowhere in it: every painter paints what they can reach standing on the ground, and high ambitions are met by the adult painting the top stroke at the painter's direction, never by climbing. Sun and wet ground are the morning's ordinary weather rules. The session is short, hats belong to the day's practice, and a painter who is wet through rather than damp is changed before the circle sits again. Brushes are counted back in, washed, and stood to dry: a brush left in a bucket sours, and the record's tools are kept the way the record teaches pictures are kept, properly, while they last.
activities.setup: Test the canvas before the painters are called: take a brush and a cup of water out alone and paint one bold stroke on the fence, the wall, the paving, wherever the session will live, and watch it. The stroke must arrive DARK and certain (a pale ghost of a picture teaches painters that their work doesn't show) and it must fade inside ten minutes (a canvas that holds the morning's first picture all day is a wall being slowly ruined, and a canvas that never fades can't offer the record's whole gift: again). Adjust the surface, not the story: sunlit wood and warm stone are the reliable canvases. Check the brushes in your own fist, a brush too heavy to hold up at fence height for twenty strokes will paint the ground instead, and set the buckets where small feet are not.
steps: Bring the painters to the canvas and say the plain framing: 'Today our paint is water and our picture place is the fence. Watch, ' (one bold stroke, laid on in the open, dark and shining) ', a real picture, made of water. It will stay while it is wet. Then the sun will drink it, slowly, and it will disappear, and that is not the picture breaking. That is the fence giving it back so you can paint again.' State the laws whole: 'Brushes paint the FENCE, never people, never clothes on purpose, never faces. Water stays in the buckets and on the canvas: no throwing, no tipping. A painter's stretch of fence is theirs while they work it; sharing a stretch is by invitation.'

First strokes together: every painter dips, brushes in, a real soak, the drip given one shake over the bucket, and makes their first mark on the canvas in the same breath, the adult painting alongside at full size: a sun, a house, a long, serious line. Name the sensation in the open because it is the craft: 'The brush is HEAVY with water. The fence goes dark where you have BEEN. Look behind your brush. There is your picture, arriving.' Early pictures are strokes and splashes and one bold circle that took everything the painter had; the record receives them all as pictures, because the canvas does.

Whole-picture round: painters settle to real compositions at three-year-old scale, the house gains a door, the sun gains rays one wet stroke at a time, somebody paints the dog (a dark patch with intentions), while the sun works the other end of the session: the earliest strokes are drying, paling, going. The adult watches for the record's central moment and names it when it comes, kindly, before any painter can read it as loss: 'Look. Amara's sun is LEAVING. The dry part is the fence again. The wet part is still her sun. A picture can be half here and half gone, and both halves are true.' Painters who want to rescue a fading stroke re-wet it on sight. The record's first lesson in maintenance, learned with a brush in hand.

Painting-over stretch, the disappearing turned into a door: a fully faded stretch of fence is offered back to its painter. 'Your canvas is back. It kept nothing, so it can hold anything', and the second picture is painted over the ghost of the first, bolder now (second pictures at three are where the ambition lives: the house gets a CHIMNEY). Neighbours' dry stretches can be adopted by invitation, and the fence by mid-session holds pictures in every state of being, arriving, shining, half-gone, returned, which the adult reads aloud like a gallery wall: 'This whole fence is pictures at different times of their lives.'

Finish when the buckets are low and the strokes are paling faster than painting can chase them. The sun winning is the session's true clock, and the record says so: 'The sun is drinking faster than we can paint now. That is its win, and it is allowed one.' Last strokes are laid on together, brushes are washed in the last of the bucket water (a painting session ends with clean brushes, even when the paint was water), shaken out, and stood handle-down to dry. The tell-back is said in front of the fence, over pictures in every stage of leaving: 'We painted the whole fence and kept none of it, and it was still painting. The doing was the picture, the whole time it shone. Tomorrow the fence will be empty and ready, and it will owe every one of those pictures to us.'
activities.tagline: Big brushes, buckets of plain water, the fence for a canvas: paint any picture. It shines dark, dries, disappears, and the fence is ready again.

variations.easier: A one-bucket version: two painters, one stretch of wall, strokes and one shared sun, the whole craft inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A paving-letters version (a name in the group is short): the day's picture is one enormous letter or shape painted together, stroke by assigned stroke, re-wet as it fades until the group's verdict: finished.

activities.inclusion: The circle is a court that fits its players: seats can be chairs, cushions, or a bench, spaced so the ball's road reaches everybody, and the adult, who serves each new flight, serves it toward whoever's turn for a visit the air hasn't chosen lately, because inclusion in this record is partly the server's quiet craft. A tap can be made with flat hands, with one hand, with a forearm, or with a foam paddle held in both hands for a player whose reach needs extending. The ball cannot tell the difference and neither can the score, because the count belongs to the circle. A player can hold the session's second honour, the counter's job. Calling the flight's taps aloud at nap-volume commentary, 'three... FOUR...', from any seat, and the final flight's count is always given to two voices together.

materials.item: one big beach ball, well blown up (the biggest, softest ball the cupboard owns. It must fall SLOWLY and land like a rumour; the adult has tossed it at their own face, kindly, and been unhurt and unbothered)
a circle of seated players with room to lean (the court. Chairs or floor spots set close enough that the ball always has a next pair of hands)

activities.name: Big Beach Ball, Keep It Floating

photo.alt: Children reaching up to keep a beach ball in the air
photo.caption: Children reaching up to keep a beach ball in the air.
photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Kerryl Cacho, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The ball is the record's whole apparatus and it is soft by law: beach-ball weight, beach-ball air, a ball that stings a palm or startles a face at arm's length is deflated and replaced before the circle sits. Taps are flat-handed and upward, always: a downward spike or a thrown ball is rested in the adult's hands for one flight while the law is re-met kindly, because a ball driven at a seated player's face is the session's one real unpleasantness and it is designed out by the tapping rule, not by hope. Players stay seated and reach from their seats, leaning, yes; lunging across a neighbour, no, and the floor inside the circle is clear, so a landed ball is retrieved at arm's length, not crawled for under chairs. Balls are never sat on, lain on, or stood on between flights: a beach ball under a body is a fall with a soundtrack.
activities.setup: Blow the ball up properly and judge it like equipment: under-blown it flops and dies mid-air (the session's rhythm dies with it), over-blown it stings a palm and startles the circle out of its gentleness. Drop it from head height onto the floor in front of you: it should bounce once, softly, and come to rest thinking about it. Then test the falling, toss it high and time its descent against your own breathing: a beach ball's whole virtue at three is that it gives the room TIME, and a ball that dives is just a ball, and gets swapped before the circle ever sits down. Set the court: seats close, a clear floor inside the circle for the ball's landings, and nothing behind the players that a leaning reach can pull down.
steps: Seat the circle, ball in your hands in the middle, and say the plain framing: 'This ball is light and slow and it LIKES being up. Our job, all of us together, is to keep it floating: when it comes to you, tap it, gently, UP, with flat hands, and send it on its travels. It will come down sometimes. Down is not losing. Down is where it rests, and then we lift it and it flies again.' State the laws whole: 'Taps are gentle and upward, no hitting down, no grabbing and holding, no throwing at anybody. Players stay seated: the ball travels, we don't. Hands that miss are not wrong hands, the ball chose its road.'

First flight together, yours: tap the ball up from the circle's middle, high and slow, straight into the air above the seats, and narrate its falling honestly while twenty eyes track it: 'Up it goes... it is thinking... it is coming down to... JONAH'S side, flat hands, Jonah, TAP.' The first successful return tap gets the record's full celebration, out of proportion and meant: 'IT STAYED UP. The circle did that. One tap is all it takes and the tap has to come from whoever it visits. That is the whole game, and you are already playing it.' A first flight that lands on the floor inside three taps is equally the curriculum: 'Down. It rested. We lift it, and it flies.' The record's line is said NOW, early, so no landing later can surprise the room.

Floating round: the ball travels the circle in the air's own order, tapped up by whoever it visits, drifting across the middle on the room's draughts, sometimes visiting two players in a row, sometimes resting on the floor for a breath before the nearest hands lift it back into weather. The adult keeps the session's one statistic, said aloud like sports commentary at nap volume: the count of taps before a landing, kept honestly and celebrated at whatever size it grows: 'That flight had SIX taps. Six times somebody's hands were ready.' Counting the flight, never scoring the players, is this record's constitution: the number belongs to the circle, and every hand in it owns a share.

Two-ball stretch, offered only to a circle whose one ball is truly flying: a second beach ball joins the air, 'TWO weathers at once', and the circle's job doubles in the only way it can: more eyes up, more readiness, and landings twice as forgiven, because two balls resting is twice the lifting and the record's line scales without changing: 'Down is where they rest. Up is where this circle sends them.' The stretch is withdrawn the moment it stops being gentle, the adult's call, made kindly and final, and one ball is retired to applause like a player leaving the field.

Finish with the longest flight the circle can give the ball together, taps counted in chorus now, the room's voice rising with the number, and when it lands, it lands: the ball is gathered into the middle, held up once for the room's regard, and deflated another day (today it retires blown up, to the cupboard's top, where floating things live). The tell-back is said over the resting ball: 'It went up forty times and came down forty times and it was a game BOTH ways, because this circle knows how to send a thing back up. The ball is resting now. It earned it. So did your hands.'
activities.tagline: The whole circle sits down, hands up: one big soft beach ball is tapped gently into the air, and the circle's one job is to not let it come home to the floor.

variations.easier: A four-player version: a small circle, a medium ball, taps counted to ten and celebrated there, the whole record inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A standing-garden version (a settled group, a calm day): the circle stands, the ball travels slower and higher, and a gentle step toward the ball is allowed. Walking feet only, because the ball is never worth a collision.

activities.inclusion: The watch fits every watcher: the buddy can ride a belly, a chest, or a tray resting across a seated watcher's lap, and it can be watched from lying, from reclining against cushions, or from a chair where the adult's own buddy performs the riding at narration distance. The in-and-up belongs to whoever's breath is watched or whoever is watching, and both are full citizenship. A watcher can run the session's one instrument, the narrating voice for the first rides ('In... up it rides'), which is the quiet-room honour and rotates by list across the week's sessions. Reports arrive as the tiny sentences, a slow hand rising and falling in imitation, the room's favourite report of all, a sign, or a buddy held up and tipped in demonstration; every report joins the tell-back in the same shape.

materials.item: one small soft buddy per watcher (a palm-sized soft toy or bean-filled animal. Light enough to ride a belly, big enough to see riding; buddies are chosen by their watchers, because a buddy is a relationship)
mats or a carpet soft enough for lying (the shore of the session. One per watcher, with a body's worth of space on every side)

activities.name: Big Belly Buddy Breathing Watch
activities.safety: Nothing in this record is medical and nothing is promised: it is watching your own breath move a soft toy, described as exactly that, and any child who finds lying still uncomfortable, for any reason, named or not, sits up, takes a chair at the mats' edge, and watches a buddy ride on the adult's belly at full honour, because the watching is the record and it works from a chair. Buddies are palm-sized, soft, and light, checked for loose seams and fillings before the session, because a buddy will be hugged, dropped, and investigated; anything small enough to mouth never joins the cast. Mats are spaced so no rolling watcher meets a neighbour, buddies are never thrown across the room (a thrown buddy ends its flight in the adult's hands and rejoins at the next session), and the sitting-up at the end is slow by spoken instruction. Dreamy heads and fast standing are a wobble the record designs out. The room's door stays open and the session is short: quiet that is chosen, bounded, and endable by sitting up is the only kind this record keeps.
activities.setup: Choose the buddies like casting: each must be light (a heavy buddy argues with a small breath and the breath loses), soft (it will be handled, hugged, and occasionally dropped on a face, kindly), and just big enough that its riding shows from the watcher's own chin-down view. That view, down one's own front, is the session's whole cinema, and the adult tests it lying on a mat with the day's heaviest candidate before anyone else lies down. Breathe, once, and watch your own buddy ride: if you cannot see it move, the room's smaller breathers cannot either, and the buddy is recast. Lay the mats with honest space between them. A breathing room is a room where nobody's elbow is in anybody else's weather.
steps: Lay the watchers down, one mat each, buddies held, and say the plain framing: 'Your breath is moving all day and you never get to watch it. Today you do. Lie back. Put your buddy on your belly. There. Now just breathe like you always breathe, and watch: when the breath comes IN, your belly lifts, and your buddy rides UP. When the breath goes OUT, down it comes. Your only job is watching. The breathing does itself.' State the laws whole: 'Buddies ride bellies. They are not thrown, and they do not visit anybody else's belly. Hands rest beside you or hold your buddy steady at the start; then hands rest too. Anybody may sit up and be finished, any time, quietly. Resting is allowed to end.'

First ride together, everyone's at once: the adult lies on the middle mat where the room can glance sideways and copy, buddy placed, and breathes at honest size, no performance breath, no great heaving, narrating the first two rides in the session's official shape, quiet as snowfall: 'In... up it rides. Out... down it comes. In... up. Out... down. That is my breath, doing what it does all day, and my buddy is showing me.' Then the narration stops, and the room watches its own buddies in the first true quiet of the session, which the adult protects by doing the session's hardest work: nothing, visibly, at full length.

Slow-bell stretch, once the riding is familiar: the adult's voice returns, once, to offer the session's one deepening: 'See if your buddy can ride SLOWER. Not bigger, slower. The breath can take its time going out, like a lift coming down gently.' Slow rides spread round the room the way yawns do, honestly and by contagion, and the reports, when the sitting-up comes, collect in the session's tiny official shape: 'Mine went slow at the end.' 'Mine fell off twice and I put it back.' A fallen buddy is the record's expected guest, never an error: it is replaced by its own watcher, without sitting up if they can manage it, with sitting up if they can't, and the watch resumes. The replacing is part of the watching, and the record says so if a face falls with the buddy.

Sleeping-buddy finish, the session's close: the adult tells the room the buddies are tired from all their riding and are going to be rocked the last of the way, watchers slow their watching to the session's final minute, breaths at whatever size they have honestly become, buddies riding small and steady, and the adult's closing words come at the volume of the room itself by then: 'Still riding. Up... and down. Your breath carried your buddy the whole watch and never once asked your help. It will carry you all day, too. It is doing it now.' Watchers sit up SLOWLY (a watched breath makes a dreamy head; the record knows and says so), buddies hugged once and retired to the buddy basket by their own watchers.

Tell-back, said over the basket before the room stands: 'Nineteen buddies rode, and every rider was a breath nobody had to be taught. Slow at the end, all of them. Your breath can do that whenever the day gets loud. You know where it lives now, and your buddy can show you any time you lie down together.' Mats are rolled by their watchers, two hands and a knee, badly and proudly, because the session's calm survives the tidying and should.
activities.tagline: Lie down, set one small soft buddy on your belly, and watch it ride: up when the breath comes in, down when the breath goes out. That is the whole watch.

variations.easier: A five-minute version: mats, buddies, three narrated rides and a quiet minute, the whole watch, pocket-sized, for a loud moment in a long day.
variations.harder: A story-buddy version: the buddy that rides is the class's story bear, passed mat to mat across the week, every watcher rides the SAME buddy, and its week's worth of rides is the class's shared weather report.

activities.inclusion: Answering asks for one hit, and one hit has many bodies: a flat palm, the back of a hand, a forearm roll, a drum steadied by the adult while its owner strikes it at their own angle, or a whole drum answered by direction, 'on my word... HIT', with a partner's hand landing as called while the call, the timing, and the size stay the director's. Keeping the call is equally open: the leader drum can be struck by its keeper's strongest motion, tapped with one finger for the soft-call examination (the circle's answering ceremony is identical at any volume), or raised silent for the zero call, which keepers of every kind of hand can give perfectly. The palm-on-the-skin finish, feeling the last hit hum home, belongs to every player at once and needs no hit at all to have played the whole game.

materials.item: one big drum or deep-voiced box per answering pair, or hand-drums all round (the answering voices, chosen for kindness: a drum that BOOMS gently beats a drum that cracks, and the adult has hit every one at full session strength and lived in its sound)
one leader drum for the adult (the calling voice. A tone the circle can tell from its own, so the echo always knows its caller)

activities.name: Big Echo Drum, One Hit Back
activities.safety: Volume is this record's material and it is governed like material: the calling drum is chosen for a kind voice, sessions begin at kindness volume and BIG calls are earned and brief, and any ear in the room is protected without negotiation. A player may cover their ears for any call and still answer (a hit given with covered ears' honesty about its size is a better echo, not a worse one), and a player who wants the whole session at arm's length takes the circle's outer seat with a drum of their own, at full membership. Drums are hit with flat open hands only: no sticks, sticks being the record's one retired technology at this age, and no drum is ever hit while another player's hand is on it. The leader's restraint is a safety instrument too, calls are single and separated, so the room's sound never builds into the wall that makes small ears and small tempers fray, and the session ends on a soft call, always, so the room it returns is a quieter one than it found.
activities.setup: Choose and test every drum the way you would tune a room: hit each one the way a three-year-old will, open palm, full enthusiasm, at lap height, and listen for the two failures: harsh (a thin crack that will wear ears out in four minutes) and dead (a thud that gives a hitter nothing back). Keep the kind ones. Practise your own calling craft alone until it is boring in its reliability: ONE hit, clean, at reading volume, then hands OFF the drum and into your lap where the circle can see their stillness. The leader's restraint is the instrument the whole record is played on, and it is learned before the session or faked during it, and three-year-olds can always tell. Set the drums at laps in the circle's final shape before anyone sits: drums that arrive after children become furniture to climb in the imagination.
steps: Gather the circle, drums resting at laps, and say the plain framing: 'A drum is a voice that answers. Here is the whole game: I hit my drum ONE time, ' (one hit, hands to lap, the sound dying in full before you speak again) ', and you hit yours ONE time back, all together, like an echo. An echo does not add anything. An echo does not rush. The listening between my hit and yours is part of the music.' State the laws whole: 'One hit means one hit: hands rest on laps between hits, and a hand in the air is a hand that has not hit yet. Drums are hit with open hands, flat, no sticks, no fists, no feet. Loud is allowed when the game calls for it; wild is never the same as loud.'

First echo together: one call, at kindness volume, and let the answer come at whatever togetherness the first try owns (it will be a scatter, near-unison with stragglers, and it will be received at full size): 'AN ECHO. Nineteen drums answered one drum. Listen to what happens if we all WAIT for the sound to finish before ours starts.' Call again; answer again; and by the third call the record's miracle assembles itself in the open. The circle's hit lands as one drum with many hands, and the adult names it with genuine respect: 'That was ONE sound. Bands made of grown-ups take months to land one sound together. This circle took three tries.'

Echo round: the calls vary in the record's three honest dimensions, one at a time and named as they come, the SOFT call ('an echo of a whisper of a drum, answer me as soft'), the BIG call ('all the drum you have, and the answer is allowed to be everything'), and the SLOW echo, the record's favourite: the call is given, and the circle must wait one full breath of silence, hands visibly resting. Before answering, so the gap itself becomes the music's longest note. Variations combine only when each has landed alone: a soft call with a slow echo is the session's examination piece, and the circle will pass it like a choir. Wrong-ness does not exist in this record except one kind: the extra hit, the hit-and-a-half, which is met with the record's standing grace. 'That drum had two things to say. It happens to echoes near mountains. Once more, all together.'

Leader round, the record's honour distributed: the calling drum passes. Keepers take it in turn, one call each, at whatever size is truly theirs, and the circle answers the smallest call with the same ceremony as the biggest. A keeper may call with a hit, a hit-and-a-pause double (the record's one allowed pattern, and only in this round, and the circle answers it whole: two hits, together, because an echo answers what it heard), or by holding their drum up silent, the zero call, which the circle answers with a held silence of its own, the hardest echo of all, and the keeper's masterpiece. The adult guards the round's dignity: every call is answered in full ceremony, because being echoed by a room is a serious honour at three and the record treats it as one.

Finish with the last echo given to the whole circle calling together (all drums, one hit, unled) and the adult alone answering on the leader drum, the echo reversed, the room hearing itself called, then drums are rested, palms flat on their skins for one breath ('feel that? the drum is still hum-humming from the last hit. That is its voice going home'), and turned over or lapped quiet for the tell-back: 'We made one sound out of twenty drums, we echoed whispers and thunderstorms, and the silences were music too. An echo answers exactly what it hears. This circle answered kindly, every time.'
activities.tagline: One big drum voice at a time: the adult hits the drum ONCE, and the whole circle hits once back, an echo with hands, and the listening in between.

variations.easier: A four-drum version: four answerers, one caller, soft and big calls only, the whole instrument inside ten minutes.
variations.harder: A hands-only version (a room between drums): the echo is played on thighs and table-tops, calls and answers in palm-slaps, quieter, and the listening identical.

activities.inclusion: Humming has more doors than singing ever offered: a closed-mouth hum, a hand-on-throat hum felt rather than heard, an 'mmm' on one note while the tune moves round the room, or rocking-only membership. The circle's cradle needs rockers as truly as voices, and a silent rocker's part is named in the tell-back with the voices, unsplit. The keeper's honours divide the ceremony for every kind of participant: holding the patient, drawing the blanket, saying the small goodnight, and conducting the rocking tempo with one raised hand slowing like a metronome settling. Each is a whole job and none requires a voice. The solo phrase can be hummed, signed along the tune's shape in the air (the circle knows it well enough by then to follow a hand), or given by the session's official hummer-by-direction, the soloist conducting their own phrase while a partner's voice carries it.

materials.item: one very sleepy bear (a soft toy with a face that can be watched settling. The session's whole patient; chosen for its sleepiness credentials and carried in like someone already half-asleep)

one soft tune the adult knows in their bones (the lullaby, wordless by design: a simple hum-able melody the adult has hummed alone, start to finish, until it runs without thinking; an old folk tune or one the room has adopted as its own)
a small blanket or cloth (the bear's bed-cover. Being tucked in is the ceremony's second act)

activities.name: Big Humming Lullaby, Bear Sleep
activities.safety: The session's whole action is humming and rocking in seats, and its safety is the safety of quiet rooms: rocking stays IN the seat, small and slow, a rock that grows into bouncing ends its rocker's round kindly (the bear needs the cradle calm, and the record says so as the reason, because it is true), and the rising at the end is done in the sleeping-room manner the session itself teaches, chairs eased back by the adult's circuit. The bear and its blanket are soft, washed, and seam-checked like anything that lives at face height in a circle of three-year-olds, and the blanket is drawn to the bear's chin by ceremony, never over any child's face in play afterwards, the record models the rule so the room can keep it. Volume is governed by the lullaby itself: humming cannot shout by design, which is half of why the record chose it, and any child may hum with a hand resting on their own throat feeling the buzz, the session's small science, instead of voicing at all, at full membership.
activities.setup: Learn the tune the way the room will need it: hum it alone, walking, until your mouth knows it the way feet know stairs, because you will be conducting, tucking, and watching a circle while humming it, and a tune the adult must think about is a tune the room will lose. Keep it SHORT (four phrases is a whole lullaby at this size), keep it LOW (a hum lives lower than a song and a circle of three-year-olds hums exactly where the adult starts, so start where their voices live), and decide its official ending now: the last phrase slows, always, like something arriving at sleep. The slowing is the ceremony's signature and it must be identical every time, because rituals are how three-year-olds know a thing is real. Choose the bear's sleeping place, a chair, a cushion, a small box-bed, in the circle's middle where every eye can watch a face settle.
steps: Carry the bear in slowly, cradled, with the face of someone transporting sleep itself, and say the plain framing: 'This bear has had a very long day, and bears cannot sleep without their lullaby. Ours has no words. Lullabies for bears don't need them. We HUM it, all together, soft, and we rock a little in our seats, and the bear listens with its whole self. When the tune finishes, slowly, the way it always finishes, the bear will be asleep, and we will KNOW, because this room will be the quietest it has ever been.' State the laws whole: 'Humming mouths are closed mouths. The sound comes through, the words stay home. Rocking is in your seat, small and slow: we are the cradle, not the storm. When the bear is asleep the quiet after is part of the lullaby, nobody spends it.'

First hum together: the adult hums the first phrase ALONE at full ceremony, one hand rocking an imaginary edge, eyes on the bear, and the circle joins from the second phrase like a tide coming in, at whatever raggedness a first tide owns. The tune is short and it repeats: second time round, the humming is already a choir finding itself, and the adult's only conducting is a hand rocking slower as the bear's head (the adult's other hand, confessing nothing) settles by degrees toward its rest. When the tune's slow ending arrives, the bear is arranged, gently, in view, into sleeping position, the blanket drawn up to its chin by two fingers' care, and the room sits inside the finished quiet for one full breath before anyone names it: 'Asleep. You hummed a bear to sleep. That is a real thing that just happened in this room.'

Second-bear round: the lullaby's work is not done, a second patient is produced (a rabbit, a doll, the class's second-most-sleepy resident) OR the bear, ceremonially, has a younger sibling in the same box-bed, and the circle runs the whole ceremony again, ownership visible now: a keeper holds the patient, the circle's humming starts together this time (the adult's hum arrives a half-phrase late, on purpose, and nobody notices, which is the point), and the rocking is the room's own tempo. A hummer who hums LOUDER with love rather than softer is coached by the record's only direction, given to the whole room so it singles out nobody: 'Softer, the bear is nearly there, let the tune get small enough to fit under a blanket.'

Solo-phrase stretch, offered when the circle's humming is truly together: one phrase of the tune is given to one voice, the day's steadiest hummer, chosen by the adult's list, not by volume, humming their phrase while the circle rocks in silence, then the choir rejoins for the rest. A phrase carried alone over a patient bear, with sixteen friends rocking quietly round it, is the biggest stage this record owns, and it is billed exactly so: 'That phrase was all yours, and the bear slept through it the way bears sleep through the parts they trust.' The honour rotates across sessions by list; today's soloist is next session's first tuck-in.

Finish with the last lullaby given to whoever still stirs, nobody, usually; the patients are asleep, plural now, and the tuck-in completed by the day's keeper: blanket smoothed, the small goodnight said in the record's official words, barely voiced: 'Sleep well. The humming room is right here.' Then the circle rises in the particular quiet of people leaving a sleeping room, chairs eased, feet soft, and the tell-back is said OUTSIDE the bear's hearing, at the door, in ordinary voices, which is itself the joke and the proof: 'Two bears asleep, one tune with no words, and a room that made itself quiet enough to rock in. Any room that can do that can do anything gently. Ours can.'
activities.tagline: One very sleepy bear, one soft tune with no words: the whole circle hums it together, rocking gently, until the bear is, officially, ceremonially, asleep.

variations.easier: A one-bear version: one patient, two full lullabies, the whole ceremony inside ten minutes for the newest humming rooms.
variations.harder: A rest-time version: the lullaby opens the room's own rest. Children lying down as the bear is tucked, the tune hummed twice through by the adult and the still-awake, ending in the room's own quiet, on purpose.

activities.inclusion: Checking works from any position the patch allows: a seated checker checks from a chair set in the sunny place, a shadow keeps no opinions about the height it is cast from, and a checker's wave can be a raised hand, a turned head, or a held-up scarf, each answered by the shadow identically and reported at the same size. The reports are the record's honours and they come in every register the room owns: spoken, signed, stamped on the floor with one foot for SHADOW OUT, or given by the checker pointing at the group's two big report cards, which the adult holds up one at a time. The groundhog's carrier, walking beside the adult as the tenant travels to the checking place, hands ready under it, is the morning's official second honour and rotates by list.

materials.item: one soft toy groundhog (or a brown sock puppet with two ears sewn or tied on. A groundhog the room can greet by name; soft, washed, and big enough to see across a circle)
one big cardboard burrow box (a box with a round door cut by the adult, big enough for the groundhog to peek from and for nobody to climb into, its door faces the group)

one sunny patch of ground or floor by a window (the shadow-checking place, found by the adult that same morning; on a grey morning, a bright torch shone across the floor is the honest stand-in and is named as one)

activities.name: Big Groundhog Shadow Morning Look

photo.alt: A groundhog resting on gravel beside its burrow
photo.caption: A groundhog resting on gravel beside its burrow.
photo.credit: Photo: Cephas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Eyes look down, always: nobody looks at the sun in this record, and the adult says it in the framing and watches for it in the round, a child who tips their face up is brought back to the evidence kindly ('the shadow is down HERE, with us'). The checking patch is walked by the adult that morning for ice, puddles hiding ice, and anything the ground is keeping; standing still is the game's whole motion, and it is done on ground the adult would stand on in socks. The burrow box is adult-cut, tape-smoothed, and furniture, not a toy: nobody climbs in, on, or through it, and a box that softens or tips is retired to the recycling with the groundhog's thanks. The torch stand-in is an adult-held lamp, never passed hand to hand, and its light is shone across the floor, at the ground, like the sun's job requires, never into anybody's eyes.
activities.setup: Cut the burrow door yourself and check the box the way this record checks everything: by trying it. The box must stand steady when the groundhog is pushed through its door a dozen times, and its edges must be tape-smooth, a burrow that collapses on its tenant teaches slapstick, not February. That morning, not the day before, stand in the shadow-checking place yourself and learn what kind of morning it is: if the sun is out, your own shadow will be standing there to meet you, and the record will run on the real thing; if the sky is grey wall to wall, set the torch across the floorboards instead and plan to name it honestly in the framing ('the sun is behind the clouds today, so our lamp will hold the sun's job'). Knowing which morning you have before the circle gathers is the whole preparation.
steps: Gather the group where every eye can see the burrow box and say the plain framing: 'Today is the second of February, and people tell a story about this day. That a groundhog comes out of its burrow, and if it sees its shadow, winter stays a while longer. It is a story people love. It is not a weather report. A groundhog cannot call the spring, and neither can we. But the story is ABOUT something real, and we can check the real thing ourselves: shadows. When the sun is out, shadows come out. When the clouds cover the sun, they do not. Today we check.' State the laws whole: 'The groundhog lives in the adult's hands or in its burrow. It is greeted, never grabbed. Shadow-checking is standing still and looking DOWN: eyes look at the ground, never up at the sun, ever. Reports are given in the day's two words, and both words are good news.'

First peeking together: the burrow door faces the group, the adult's hand goes in slow, and the groundhog comes out the way the story says, nose first, then ears, then the whole round body, blinking at the room. The group greets it by name, and then the record's real question is put to it at full ceremony: 'Groundhog. The story says you look for your shadow. We will help you look, because looking is a job this room is good at.' The groundhog is carried to the shadow-checking place by the adult, held low where a groundhog lives, and the group watches the ground beneath it like a jury: is there a groundhog-shaped shadow on the ground, or is there not?

Shadow-checking round: whatever the groundhog's report, the children check their own, one at a time, standing in the patch at full stillness, feet planted, arms a little out, eyes DOWN at the evidence, while the room calls the finding in the session's official shape: 'SHADOW OUT' (a dark self standing on the ground, waving when its owner waves, which the owner is invited to test exactly once) or 'NO SHADOW' (the ground bare of any second self, the light flat, the clouds holding the whole sky). Both reports are received at identical size, and the record says why while it happens: 'A no-shadow morning is not a broken morning. It is a cloudy one. The groundhog's story works on cloudy mornings too. That is most of why people kept telling it.'

Story stretch, once every checker has a report: the adult tells the last piece plainly, because this record does not let a story borrow science's coat: 'In the story, a shadow means six more weeks of winter. In the real world, the one we just checked with our own eyes, a shadow means the sun is out RIGHT NOW, on this patch of ground. It says nothing about next week. Next week will bring its own mornings, and we will check those too.' Then the group's own morning is named and filed in the day's official sentence, said together: 'On OUR February the second, the report was: SHADOW OUT' (or NO SHADOW) ', seen with our own eyes, on our own ground.'

Finish with the groundhog returned to its burrow at full ceremony, backwards in, the way groundhogs in stories go, to sleep until the story needs it again, and the tell-back said over the closed door: 'The story said a groundhog would look. We looked WITH it, and then we looked for ourselves, every one of us, eyes down, standing still. Whatever the morning was, we know what it was, because we checked. That is worth more than the story, and the story is worth quite a lot.' The burrow box lives on the shelf until spring, and on any sunny morning before then, any child may point at a shadow and file the report again: it stays official all season.
activities.tagline: February the second: a soft groundhog peeks out of its burrow box, and the whole group checks the sunny patch. Is anybody's shadow out today?

variations.easier: A two-checker version: the groundhog and one volunteer check, the group reports, the whole ceremony inside ten minutes for the newest circles.
variations.harder: A torch version (a grey week, no sun at all): the checking place is a dark corner and a big torch, every child checks by lamplight across several mornings, and the day the real sun finally does the job is celebrated as the record's true February the second, whatever the calendar says.

activities.inclusion: Guiding divides cleanly into jobs at every distance: the pointer points, the namer names, the carrier carries the guest, the pace-setter walks first and sets the guest's pace, and a guide who travels the room differently still points from their own position, because the three places can be shown from a seat at each stop as truly as from a stance beside them. Naming arrives in any register the room owns: spoken, signed, tapped on the place itself, or given by the guide holding up the room's picture of the place while the adult speaks the name the guide has chosen. The credit for the showing stays the guide's in the tell-back, by name. The guest's honours are sized to the guest: a real new child who says nothing all tour and then chooses the quiet corner has taken the tour at its deepest, and the record receives it that way.

materials.item: the group's own room, as it stands (the tour's whole territory, its cup shelf, its coat hooks, its quiet corner, in the room's ordinary state, not tidied into a show home)

one soft friend to be the guest when no real new child is visiting (the class bear or another famous soft resident, carried by a rotating carrier, greeted by name, treated exactly as a guest is treated)

activities.name: Big New Friend Room Tour
