activities.safety: The tour stays inside the group's own room, on the route the adult walked at child height first: no toilets, no staff areas, no other rooms, and no door in the route is opened by a child's hands. Doors on the way are the adult's, held, every time. Pointing hands point at things, never into faces, and other children's belongings on the route, the cups and coats of the room's own people, are looked at and named, never handled, rearranged, or tried on: a tour that disturbs the room teaches the opposite of welcome, and the adult restores anything touched without comment and without blame. A real guest child is never the tour's exhibit: they walk it, watch it from a lap, or leave it halfway, all at full honour, and the group's excitement is coached in the framing. A new person is shown the room, not surrounded by it.
activities.setup: Decide the tour's three places before the group gathers, and decide them the way a three-year-old's first day actually runs: where my cup lives (and whose hands may fetch it), where my coat hangs (and which hook could be mine), and where the quiet is (the corner a person goes to when the room is too much, shown with the same pride as the other two, because knowing where the quiet is, is belonging). Walk the route yourself at child height and child pace: it should take about forty small steps with no squeezing past furniture, no doors the adult must fight, and nothing on the way that a pointing hand could knock into a face. If a real new child is the guest, brief nobody and rehearse nothing: the tour is offered, and watching the whole thing from a safe lap counts as taking it. That rule is set before the guest arrives, not negotiated after.
steps: Gather the group by the door, the room's threshold, where every arrival stands, and say the plain framing: 'When somebody is new in a room, everything in it is a question. Where does my cup go? Where does my coat hang? Where is the quiet, if I need it? Today we practise answering, the way this room answers: by showing. Our guest, ' (the guest is named: the real new child, welcomed at full size, or the bear, presented with identical ceremony) ', will be shown three places by the people who live here. You.' State the laws whole: 'Tours walk. Guides point and name. Hands stay kind and off other people's things: we point AT the cup shelf, we do not rearrange it. The guest may look as long as looking takes. Nobody is quizzed at the end: showing is the whole job, and it ends when the showing is done.'

First place together, the cups: the whole tour walks the forty steps at the guest's pace, which is set by the slowest walker without comment, and gathers where the guest can see the shelf properly. Two guides, chosen by list, do the showing in the session's official shape: one points, one names: 'THIS is where the cups live. Yours would go HERE, ' (the pointing hand shows the honest spare space, not a space invented for the day) ', and the water is THERE, and an adult helps, always.' If the guest is real and reaches for a cup, the reach is honoured as the tour working, and the adult quietly makes the cup theirs: naming a cup is lovely, but handing it over is the room meaning it.

Second place, the coats, and third, the quiet: the route continues at the same unhurried pace, with the pointing-and-naming passing to fresh guides at each stop so the honours spread around the room, at the hooks: 'Coats hang HERE. This hook is spare. It could be yours in one minute, if you wanted it to be', and at the quiet corner, the tour's most important stop, the guides say the record's plainest line at full size: 'And THIS is where the quiet is. Anybody may come here. You do not have to ask, and nobody follows you in. It is part of the room, like the cups.' The guest is shown how the corner works, its cushion, its soft thing, its boundary, by a guide sitting in it for three breaths, demonstrating that the corner is used by the room's own people, not reserved for its saddest ones.

Guest's-choice stretch, the tour's heart: the route walked, the guest chooses the place they liked best, and the whole tour goes back to it together. A teddy guest's choice is made by its carrier, at the carrier's own honest preference, and a real guest's choice can also be the door, the window, or nowhere yet, and every one of those is received as a complete answer: 'The door is a good favourite. It is where the room begins.' At the chosen place the group settles for one minute of simply being there together, drinking the pretend tea of arrival, saying nothing that needs saying, because a tour that ends by USING the room together teaches more than the pointing did.

Finish back at the threshold, where tours end: the guest is thanked for visiting ('You let us show you our room. Showing it made it more ours, not less') and the guides are thanked by name for the specific thing each one showed. 'You showed where the quiet is. A new person will remember that longest.' The tell-back is said at the door: 'Three places: where the cups live, where the coats hang, and where the quiet is. Shown by the people who live here, at walking pace, with pointing hands. Whoever arrives in this room next gets this tour, because now this room knows how to give it.' The bear, if it was the guest, keeps a place of honour by the door for the week: the room's greeter, on duty.
activities.tagline: A new friend needs three places first: where the cups live, where the coats hang, and where the quiet is. The group shows all three, pointing and naming.

variations.easier: A one-place version: only the quiet corner is shown, with full ceremony, the whole record inside ten minutes, for a day when one place is what a real arrival needs.
variations.harder: A photograph version (a real arrival expected next week): the guides pose at each of the three places, the adult photographs the pointing and the naming, and the three pictures wait by the door for the guest who has not come yet, a tour that travels ahead of its guest.

activities.inclusion: Every stage of building has a shape for every builder: the scoop can be two-handed, the pat can be done with a flat palm or the back of a scoop, the turn can be powered by a partner's hands under the direction of the tower's own builder. 'Turn... LIFT, slow', with the tower, and the report, staying the director's. The wetting crew and the decoration tray are full building jobs, not consolation ones: a builder whose whole morning is keeping the sand at building dampness has held the castle's foundation in their hands all session, and the tell-back names it so. Counting can be called from the counting place by the room's counter in any register, spoken, signed, or held up on fingers one tower at a time, and the hush before the lift belongs to everybody equally, from every position around the sand.

materials.item: a sand place with sand that can be wetted (a sandbox, sandpit, or a stretch of beach sand the adult has checked, plus a bucket of water and a small watering can for keeping it at building dampness)
big buckets, one per builder at a time (sturdy, smooth-rimmed, big enough that a tower made from one is worth decorating)
big scoops for filling (short-handled, blunt, a scoop that bends under wet sand is retired before it teaches frustration)
found decorations (shells, smooth pebbles, sticks and fallen leaves gathered from the sand place itself. Adult-checked, nothing sharp, nothing that was living in it)

activities.name: Big Sandcastle, One Bucket Towers

photo.alt: Sandcastle Competition on West Beach geograph.org.uk
photo.caption: Sandcastle Competition on West Beach geograph.org.uk.
photo.credit: Photo: Colin Smith, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Sand stays low, by law, from the first minute: thrown sand ends a builder's turn kindly and immediately, because sand in eyes is this record's one real injury and it is designed out by the rule, not by luck. The sand place is adult-raked before the session for glass, sharp shell, and buried rubbish, and re-checked after any break, and the decorations pass the same adult hand: shells washed and edge-checked, sticks smooth and short, nothing that was living in a shell comes to the building ground at all. Summer rules stand around the record: shade or morning hours for the building ground, hats by the house's ordinary law, water for drinking kept apart from water for wetting. The can is for the sand, the cups are for the builders, and the two never swap jobs. Hands are washed with soap when the building ends; sand under nails is a souvenir the record does not send home in mouths.
activities.setup: Wet the sand yourself before anyone is called and learn its temper with your own hands: pack a bucket, turn it, lift, if the tower comes out whole, the sand is at building dampness; if it slumps, add water a can at a time and test again, because at three the difference between a castle and a disappointment is a watering can nobody used in time. Check the whole sand place the way the season demands: rake through it with the scoop for anything buried that small hands should not find (glass, sharp shells, the leavings of other people's picnics), and check its temperature with the back of your hand. Summer sand in full noon sun can be too hot for the knees that will kneel in it, and a shaded corner or a morning hour is this record's honest fix. Set the water bucket where its spills do the sand good, not the path.
steps: Gather the builders at the sand's edge and say the plain framing: 'Summer gives us sand and water, and together they do a trick. Dry sand, watch, ' (let a handful run through your fingers, all of it, to the last grain) '. Runs away. It cannot stand. But wet sand, ' (pack the bucket as the group's first lesson, pat-pat, turn, lift: a tower) ', STANDS. That is the whole trick, and it is a real one: the water holds the grains together, like tiny hands. Today we build towers out of the holding kind.' State the laws whole: 'Sand stays LOW: it is scooped, carried low, and built with. It is never thrown, and a handful that rises above waist height is set down and the building starts again. Water goes on the SAND, from the can, at the adult's end of the sand place. Castles are built in the building ground, where knees and towers have room. Nobody builds in the walking way.'

First tower together, yours: fill the big bucket at full ceremony, scoop, scoop, scoop, with the room counting the scoops because filling is the record's rhythm section, then pat the top flat with two flat hands (pat-pat, all over, the tower's roof being made level before it exists), choose the tower's ground together, turn the bucket over in one honest motion, pat its bottom twice, the tower-maker's knock, and lift straight up, slow, while the room holds the hush the moment deserves. Whether it stands whole or slumps at one corner, the report is given in the session's official shape: 'ONE tower standing', or 'One tower SLUMPED, its sand was too dry at the corner. The corner told us. We shall wet it and build it again, exactly there.' A first slump, read kindly, teaches more than a first success; the record does not arrange either, it reads both.

Building round: builders take the bucket in known order, one tower each, along the building ground, fill, pat, turn, knock, lift, while the waiting builders keep the sand at building dampness with the can (a job with its own ceremony: 'Wetting crew, the corner by the standing tower looks thirsty') and the room counts the castle as it grows: 'THREE towers standing.' A tower that falls to its own builder's lift is that builder's to rebuild on the spot with wetter sand and the room's full patience; a tower that stands gets its flag moment, a stick stood in its top by its own builder, at whatever angle the sand allows, so the skyline of finished work is visible from the counting place.

Decorating stretch, once the towers stand in their row or their ring: the found decorations come out in the adult's flat tray, and builders dress their own towers, a shell pressed flat into the wall like a window, a pebble path laid grain by grain to the door that isn't there, a leaf flying from the flag-stick, while the record's decorating law holds kindly: 'A decoration is PRESSED in, gently. Pressing hard is building backwards.' Towers dressed, the builders walk the counting place view together, the castle from the front, at adult-knee height, in silence for three breaths, because looking at finished work properly is part of building it, and summer afternoons are long enough for both.

Finish with the record's honest ending, said before it happens so it lands as knowledge, not loss: 'Castles are for today. The sand was here before the castle and it will be here after, the towers go back to being a sand place, and everything we learned stays standing in US.' The builders may knock their own towers down, by their own hands, tower by tower, at the count, or leave them standing for the next group to find, and the choice is the builders' and is recorded either way in the tell-back: 'Five towers stood today, because wet sand holds and this room learned how wet. The sand is sand again. The builders are builders for good.' Hands and knees are brushed down at the sand's edge, shoes shaken out over the grass, and the water bucket's last can goes on the building ground. Keeping it ready, kindly, for whoever builds tomorrow.
activities.tagline: Wet sand, one big bucket, pat-pat-turn: a tower stands. Dry sand runs through your fingers. Wet sand stands up. That is the whole summer science, built.

variations.easier: A two-tower version: the adult's tower and one builder's, the full ceremony of fill-pat-turn inside fifteen minutes for the newest builders.
variations.harder: A sand-table version (no outdoor sand place): a deep tray of sand on a table, wetted the same way, towers built small-bucket size. The same science, the same reports, at standing height indoors.

activities.inclusion: The filing office honours every kind of ear: a clerk who hears with their hands holds each jar against their own flat palm, or lets a partner shake it while both their hands rest on it, and files by the jar's travel, which the loud jars give generously and the soft ones give as a pour; both are real evidence and the final count treats them so. Filing can be done by direction ('the feather mat, THERE'), by pointing at the drum or feather card the adult holds up one at a time, or by the room's signing at the count, and the appeal shake, the office's great dignity, belongs to any clerk on request, requested in any register. The hush-keeper, the clerk whose held-up hand calls the room to listening before each shake, holds the office's official silence and rotates by list from any seat.

materials.item: big sound jars, a filing set of six to eight (big opaque jars with lids the adult has filled, sealed, and tape-locked, the loud ones carrying a few big bells or wooden beads, the soft ones carrying rice or dried lentils; every jar shaken by the adult first, at arm's length, against their own ear)
two big filing mats (the LOUD mat and the SOFT mat. Two floor cards the adult has marked big and clear: a drum drawn on one, a feather on the other; the room learns them before the first jar appears)

activities.name: Big Sound Jar, Loud or Soft
activities.safety: The jars are sealed by the adult, tape-locked, and audited before the session and after it: a lid that turns, cracks, or weeps a single grain retires its jar from the set instantly and permanently. The fillings (bells, beads, rice, lentils) are choking hazards the record keeps behind a sealed lid as its first law, and no jar is ever opened in the room, by anyone, for any verdict; the final count argues with shakes, not with evidence. Shaking happens at the shaker's own chest, one shake at a time: never beside ears, anybody's, including the shaker's, and never thrown, dropped on purpose, or rolled across the floor; a jar is carried in two hands between shakings like the instrument it is. Jars are big, light when dropped by accident, and plastic or well-padded: glass has no place in a filing office run by three-year-olds, and the adult's set uses none.
activities.setup: Make the jars like an instrument-maker who will be audited by toddlers: fill them in two honest families, loud (two or three big bells, or four wooden beads, in a jar with room to travel) and soft (rice or lentils, a third full, so the sound pours rather than rattles), then seal every lid, tape it round, and shake each jar yourself at arm's length. Any jar whose sound sits between the families, the maybes, is refilled or retired: at three, the record's filing must be honestly fileable, and a jar that argues with the ears teaches arguing, not listening. Line the jars up in a mixed order you have written down (your own answer key, for the final count), set the two mats a body's width apart on the floor, and learn the drum card and the feather card by heart so you can introduce them without a flicker of doubt: drum is LOUD, feather is SOFT.
steps: Set the two mats where the whole circle can see them, hold up the cards' meaning first ('This drum means LOUD. A sound that fills the room. This feather means SOFT, a sound that lands like this, ' and let a feather of paper fall, if you have one, in the hush) ', and today your ears are the filing clerks.' Say the plain framing: 'These jars are sealed, and they stay sealed, what is inside them is not the lesson, and nobody will open one to check. Inside, some jars carry LOUD sounds and some carry SOFT ones. One shake tells your ears which. Your job: shake once, listen properly, and file the jar on its mat. The jar will not be offended. Jars are professional.' State the laws whole: 'One shake per jar, a good shake, at your chest, never beside anybody's ears, never beside your own. While a jar shakes, the room is quiet: listening is everybody's job, not just the shaker's. A filed jar stays filed until the final count. Ears may argue later, at the count, kindly.'

First filing together, yours: take the first jar, hold it where every eye can see it, and shake it once at full ceremony, one shake, no more, while the room does the listening at full size, which at three looks like hands going still and mouths closing by themselves. Give your own ears their moment in the open ('I hear it landing heavy and bright... my ears say LOUD') and file the jar on the drum mat with the session's official report, said whole: 'Jar one: LOUD. Filed.' Then the record's honesty is established in the open, because it governs everything after: 'If your ears heard it differently, keep your hearing. At the final count we may argue, kindly, with shakes, and the jars will be re-heard by the whole room. Filing is not finished until the count.'

Filing round: shakers take the jars in known order, one each, shake held at the chest, ONE shake, while the room listens in the official hush and the shaker files the jar on the mat their own ears choose, giving the report in the official shape: 'Jar four: SOFT, filed.' A shaker who cannot decide shakes once more, the record allows exactly one appeal shake, announced as such ('An appeal, ONE more'), because listening again is a scientific act, and then files by their best hearing. The adult guards only the constitution: jars shaken at chests, hush kept kindly ('Clerks, the jar is speaking'), and never, not once, a hint from the adult's face about which mat is right, the adult's face in this record is a sealed jar too.

Borderline stretch, for a room whose ears have grown sharp: the last jar in the set is the adult's planted puzzle, a jar filled to sit nearer the border than its brothers (beads in a fuller jar, their rattle muffled), introduced honestly as such before it is shaken: 'This last jar is the difficult file. Grown-up clerks argue about jars like this one. Shake it twice, it has earned two, and file it where your ears truly say, and know that the count may move it, and moving it will be the room learning, not the shaker failing.' The argument at its filing is the lesson's summit and is given its time: two hearings, two opinions stated with their evidence ('It landed heavy, but SMALL'), and a filing by the shaker's own final call.

Finish with the final count, the record's audit, conducted like a ceremony because it is one: the jars on each mat are counted aloud. 'The LOUD mat holds four. The SOFT mat holds three', and then each jar is re-shaken once by its own filer while the whole room confirms or appeals its file with a show of the drum-feather hands (flat palm down for drum, fingers floating down for feather, the room's own signing). A jar the room moves is moved by its filer, with the record's line said over it at full size: 'The room heard it again, and the room knows more than it did. That is not a mistake being fixed. That is ears, working.' The tell-back closes the files: 'Seven jars, shaken once each, filed by ear, loud on the drum, soft on the feather, and one difficult file argued like professionals. Nobody opened a thing. The ears did all of it.' The jars return to their shelf unopened, where their mystery keeps, filed, and faintly audible whenever the shelf is bumped, which the room will notice for weeks.
activities.tagline: Big sealed jars, one shake each: some jars are LOUD and some are SOFT, and the ears of the room file every one on its right mat.

variations.easier: A four-jar version: two loud, two soft, the whole filing office inside ten minutes for the newest clerks.
variations.harder: A matching version (a room that has filed before): twin jars hide in the set, two jars with the same sound, and after the filing, shakers hunt the pair by ear alone, the mats' work done, the office become a detective agency.

activities.inclusion: Choosing is done with the feet when the feet are willing, and at the same size by every other road: a chooser can be carried to their colour by the room's ordinary way of travelling, point at the colour card the adult holds up and be walked the choice by a partner's company, or hold their colour's small card in the middle while the corner waves to THEM, the wave travels both directions in this record, and a corner's people can be counted around a seated chooser exactly as around a standing one. Reasons arrive in any register, a word, a point at something in the room wearing the colour ('blue, like THAT cup'), a held-up card, and changers are honoured identically however the change is announced, including by simply arriving. The corner-callers, who give the room's counts in the official shape, rotate by list and may call from inside their own colour, which is where the authority comes from anyway.

materials.item: four big colour mats, one per corner of the room (red, blue, yellow, green, mats or big cards laid flat and weighted or taped at their corners so no edge can curl under a small foot; the colours are the whole equipment)

activities.name: Big Choose Your Colour Corner
activities.safety: Choosing is walking, enforced kindly from the first crossing: four directions of travel at once is a small traffic system, and its only rule that matters is pace. A child whose excitement runs is walked back to the middle by the adult's company and sent again at walking pace, without loss of colour or dignity. The mats lie dead flat, corners weighted or taped, edges checked by the adult's own sliding foot before the group gathers: a mat that can skate is a card on the floor or nothing. Corners are furniture-cleared with standing room and a clear wall behind them. No corner sits beside a door that opens into it, a shelf that can be pulled, or the room's traffic lane to the toilet. Nobody is ever left standing alone in a corner as a spectacle: the adult's first choosing plants an adult visibly content in a corner of one, and if the round still produces a corner of one child, the corner-caller's report names it 'a whole corner' before any other size is mentioned.
activities.setup: Lay the four corners before the group gathers and then walk them yourself, slowly, at three-year-old eye height: each colour must read clearly across the room (a yellow card on a pale floor in bright window light can wash into a rumour, move it into shade or back it with something dark), each corner must have standing room for more children than you expect to choose it, because a colour everybody loves is a crowd, and a crowd in a corner needs its ground planned, not discovered, and the walking lanes between the middle and every corner must be clear of the furniture that migrates into rooms like this. Learn the record's one kindness in advance: you will not balance the corners. If eleven children choose blue, blue holds eleven, and the corner's size is reported as joy, not corrected as a problem.
steps: Gather the group in the room's middle and say the plain framing: 'Look at the corners. This room is wearing four colours today, red there, blue there, yellow there, green there. In a moment, each of you will walk to ONE colour: the one you like best TODAY. Not forever. Not for a team. Just the colour your eyes are happiest standing in this morning. You will stand with your colour, and your colour's people will stand with you, and we will see what this room likes today.' State the laws whole: 'Choosing is walking. Nobody runs to a colour; a colour is worth walking to. Colours are not teams: nobody recruits, nobody persuades, nobody says a colour is wrong. A colour cannot be wrong; it can only be somebody's favourite, or not yours. Changing your mind is allowed, in the second round, anybody may walk to a new colour, and the room will be glad to watch them go.'

First choosing together, yours: name your own colour at full ceremony and walk to it at the record's official pace, talking your choosing out loud the way the room will need to hear choosing done: 'My eyes keep going to the yellow. Yellow is standing in the sun over there and it looks like morning. I am choosing yellow, today. Yesterday I might have chosen blue. Tomorrow is tomorrow's business.' Stand in your corner and be counted there, visibly, an adult alone in a colour with nobody yet beside you, because the room must see that a corner of one is a complete corner before anyone is asked to risk being one.

Choosing round: the group chooses at the adult's word, walking, in all directions at once, the room briefly a slow weather of small people crossing to their colours, and settles. Then the corners are greeted in the session's official ceremony: each corner, in turn, WAVES to the other three and calls its colour ('BLUE corner. Here we are!'), and the other corners wave back, because the record's whole sociology is in that wave: different colours, one room, everybody visible to everybody. The counts are taken by the corner-callers and given in the official shape. 'Blue holds five. Red holds two. Yellow holds three. Green holds ONE, and one is a whole corner', the smallest corner named at exactly the same size as the largest, by design, every time.

Second choosing stretch, the record's heart: after a minute of standing in colour, the adult opens the floor's one great permission: 'Second choosing. Your feet may keep your colour, or they may take you somewhere new, if your eyes have changed their minds while standing here. Changing is not cheating. Changing is looking twice.' Whoever walks, walks at the same unhurried pace, received by their new corner with the wave, and whoever stays is named kindly too ('Some colours hold their people. Staying is also a choice, and the room can see it'). The new counts are taken and the CHANGES are reported as the day's real news, ahead of the numbers: 'Two people changed. One went from red to green because, ' (the changer, if they wish, gives their reason in any size: 'Green looked quieter' is a complete philosophy) ', and the room is glad to know it.'

Finish with the whole group walking back to the middle together, colours dissolving kindly into the room again, and the tell-back said in the middle where it started: 'This room, today: blue five, yellow three, red two, green one, and two changers, whose eyes looked twice. Nobody was wrong, nobody was recruited, and every corner was waved at by every other. When somebody new joins this room, the colours will be the first thing we show them: choose one, stand in it, be waved at. It is the quickest way we know to be a person in a new room.' The mats stay down through the day as the room's quiet geography. Children will drift to their colours at odd moments, and the record lets them: a corner chosen in the morning is a place to stand in all day.
activities.tagline: Four big colours, one in each corner. Walk to the colour you like best today, stand with your colour, and wave to the other corners. Tomorrow may differ.

variations.easier: A two-colour version: red and blue only, two corners, the whole record inside ten minutes for the very newest groups. Choosing between two is already choosing.
variations.harder: A family version: the colours are chosen for somebody else first, 'walk to the colour your grandmother would like', and the room hears the reasons, which arrive as small stories about people who are not in the room.

activities.inclusion: The bakery's jobs stand open at every reach: stirring can be two-handed, one-handed with the bowl steadied by a partner, or done by direction, 'stir... slower... the groove, THERE, stop', with the thickness judged by the director's eyes on the spoon's mark, which is the skill itself. The jug-keeper holds the morning's most trusted honour (water decides everything in a bakery) and pours at the mixer's word from any position at the counter. Decorating is placing, at any scale of movement, including placing by description while a partner's fingers press. The design, the ring of petals, stays the designer's. Serving can be done seated at the serving place as the bakery's host, receiving customers, taking orders by description, giving the official compliment, a job with no carrying in it at all and the whole parade passing through it. The customer chair, rotated by list, belongs to everybody, and an order given in any register, a point at the petal-ring pie, is taken at full ceremony.

materials.item: clean garden soil in two big bowls (soil from a bed the adult dug and picked through themselves that morning, no glass, no sharp stones, no animal mess, nothing sprayed; this is the bakery's flour and it is chosen like it)
a jug of water for the mixing (the bakery's milk, poured by the adult or under the adult's hand, a little at a time)
big spoons and big pie tins (sturdy spoons that can stir real mud without bending, and a tin per baker, muffin tins, pie dishes, big jar lids)
fallen decorations (petals, leaves, and small smooth pebbles gathered from the ground that morning, fallen only, adult-checked; nothing picked off a living plant, nothing sharp)

activities.name: Big Mud Pie Bakery Morning
activities.safety: The first law is the record's whole food safety, said in the framing and kept by the adult's eye all morning: mud is never eaten, licked, or tasted, hands that have stirred go to mouths exactly never, and the adult stations themself where the counter's mouths are visible; a baker who needs their hands near their face is walked to the washing station kindly, washed, and welcomed back, the law has no shame in it, only soap. The soil itself is the adult's audit: dug or bagged from a known-clean source, hand-picked for glass, shards, sharp stone and any animal mess, and a bed with any doubt about it is simply not the bakery's bed. Broken skin on a baker's hands is covered before the mixing starts, or that baker takes the jug, the tray, and the serving honours for the morning, at full size. Washing at the end is with soap, to the elbow, checked by the adult the way the soil was: by looking, carefully, at every hand.
activities.setup: Dig the soil yourself, that morning, from a bed you know: pick it through with your own hands, stone by stone and shard by shard, because what a three-year-old's hands will stir for twenty minutes must first have passed through the adult's. Choose the ground the way the record's honesty requires: a bed that is soil and only soil. No animal fouling (if the neighbourhood's cats use your beds, choose another bed or a bought bag of plain topsoil, and let the bakery's flour come from the bag without apology; the pies do not care, and the bakers must not be asked to). Set the bakery on a table or a big board at the garden's edge, bowls, jug, spoons, tins in a row like a real counter, and put the washing station (a basin of soapy water and a towel, or the hose at a trickle) where the bakers can see it from the counter: in this record, the washing-up is visible from the first minute, as part of the bakery, not as its punishment.
steps: Open the bakery at full ceremony and say the plain framing: 'The bakery is open. Today we bake mud pies, real mud, mixed by real bakers, in real tins. Mud pies are for LOOKING at, for carrying carefully, for serving on a leaf to a customer who pretends beautifully. They are never, not a crumb, not a lick, not a dare, for eating. Mud is not food. That is the bakery's first law, and it is older than everyone here.' State the remaining laws whole: 'Bakers stir their own bowls and help at the big bowl when asked. Decorations are the fallen ones in the tray. We do not pick the garden; the garden has already dropped what it can spare. Pies travel on their tins, at walking pace, like pies in a good bakery always travel.'

First mixing together, at the big bowl: the adult puts the first spoonfuls of soil in and the bakers take the spoon in turn, while the water goes in a little at a time from the jug, the adult's hand on it or guiding, and the record's one piece of bakery science is taught by the spoon itself: 'Too dry. It crumbles. It will not hold a pie. More water... now watch, TOO wet, it pours like soup. A pie must hold the spoon's mark, ' (draw the spoon through and show the groove staying) ', THERE. Pie-thickness. The groove stays. That is how bakers know, in every bakery there is: the mixture tells you, if you watch it.' Every baker stirs the big bowl at pie-thickness at least once, feeling the exact heaviness through the spoon, because the morning's whole skill lives in that groove.

Baking round: bakers fill their own tins from the big bowl, spoon, spoon, pat flat with the spoon's back, while the adult walks the counter the way bakers' teachers do, naming the work at full size: 'That pie is filled to the rim and patted smooth, a bakery pie.' A tin that will not hold its mixture gets the counter's remedy, not a verdict: back to the big bowl, a spoon of dry soil or a splash of water, stir, and fill again, the record's line for it said in the open: 'Bakers fix mixtures. Mixtures are allowed to need fixing.' When every tin is filled and patted, the decorating tray comes down the counter and the pies are dressed: petals pressed flat in a ring, a pebble stood in the middle like a cherry. Pressed IN, gently, because pressing hard is mixing again.

Serving stretch, the bakery's parade: the finished pies are carried, on their tins, two hands, walking pace, to the serving log or step at the garden's edge, and laid on leaf plates the bakers choose from the fallen tray's biggest leaves. Customers are received at the serving place in the room's best pretend: the adult first, ordering gravely ('One mud pie, please. The one with the petal ring'), being served with ceremony, admiring it at length, and returning it uneaten with the bakery's official compliment: 'A beautiful pie. My eyes are full.' Children take the customer chair in turn, ordering by describing ('the pie with the STONE in the middle') so the bakers must read their own work to find it, and every pie is served at least once, because a pie unserved is a pie unfinished, and the bakers keep the tally on their fingers.

Finish with the bakery's closing, which is the record's last lesson and is taught as one: 'Bakeries close. The pies go back to the garden, they were the garden all along, wearing tin hats, ' (each baker tips their own pie back onto the bed it came from, tin by tin, with a small ceremony the record does not hurry) ', the tins are washed by their bakers, ' (the washing station, soapy water, real scrubbing, adult hands helping with the stubborn corners) ', and the bakers are washed to the elbow, because that is what bakers do before they touch anything else.' The tell-back is said at the empty counter: 'The bakery opened, the mixture reached pie-thickness and told us so, every pie was dressed and served and admired, and not one bite was taken, by law and by pride. The garden has its soil back. The bakers keep everything else.'
activities.tagline: Real mud, big tins, fallen petals for decoration: the bakery opens, the pies are mixed to pie-thickness, served on leaf plates, and never, ever eaten.

variations.easier: A two-baker version: the big bowl and two tins, mixing and one serving inside fifteen minutes, the whole bakery at its smallest honest size.
variations.harder: A rainy-morning version (a covered porch or awning): the bakery sets up under cover with the soil already dug, and the rain, watched from the dry counter, is received as the bakery's weather, bakers like weather.

activities.inclusion: Custodianship divides into jobs at every reach: the tape is read by one pair of hands and called aloud by another; the photograph can be directed from the fixed point by a custodian who frames the shot in words while a partner works the camera; the log itself welcomes every register. A phenology entry can be written, dictated to the visit's scribe, drawn to scale, or given as the spoken 'first seen by' report the scribe records verbatim with the spotter's name attached. The fixed point and the gathering ground are chosen at setup for step-free access, and a custodian who cannot make a given month's visit still signs its page: long-keeping is the job, and the log has a line, kept honestly all year, for custodians present in the record when they could not be present at the trunk.

materials.item: one adoptable tree on the site (a tree the group can reach weekly without crossing any boundary the adults set. Its name, species if known, and story are the year's first research job)
the year log itself (a hardback notebook that lives with the adults between visits, weatherproofed in a sealed bag, because a log that dissolves in October teaches nothing about November)
a long tape measure that can pass around a trunk (or a length of string and a ruler. The string method is older than the tape and just as honest)
a camera or one volunteer's phone for the fixed-point photograph (the same marked standing spot every visit, so the year's change is comparable, frame to frame)

activities.name: Adopt-a-Tree Year Log

photo.alt: 9th JROTC BN first to participate in the USAG Ansbach Adopt A Tree Program (5782104)
photo.caption: 9th JROTC BN first to participate in the USAG Ansbach Adopt A Tree Program (5782104).
photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Army USAGA by Amy Stork, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The tree is never climbed, not to measure, not to photograph, not for the closing ceremony: every measurement in this record is designed to be taken from the ground, and a custodian who wants a higher view gets the fixed-point photograph's honest answer, which is that some things are recorded as 'not seen', in ink. Visits run in ordinary daylight and ordinary weather; a thunderstorm, ice underfoot, or a wind strong enough to move big branches cancels the visit, and the log records the cancellation as data ('January visit lost to storm, the tree kept its own counsel'). The root zone is walked on gently and never dug; nothing is nailed, screwed, or tied tight to the tree. The ribbon is loose, checked monthly, and removed the moment it marks the bark. Hands are washed after visits; anything the tree drops is looked at, logged, and left. Nothing from the tree is eaten, ever, identified or not.
activities.setup: Choose the tree before the group is offered the adoption, and choose it like a custodian, not a romantic: reachable in all weathers, on ground the group is allowed to stand on, with a clear fixed point for the photograph and room around the trunk for the whole group to gather without trampling the root zone into mud. Learn its name if it has one, a plaque, a groundskeeper, an older student who remembers, and if its species is uncertain, leave the question open in the log's first page rather than guessing: an honest 'not yet known' is this record's founding entry. Mark the photograph spot with something that survives (a paving edge, a painted stone set by permission), and walk the first visit yourself: you are checking sightlines, footing after rain, and whether the tape can pass around the trunk without anyone reaching through branches at face height.
steps: First visit, the adoption itself: the group walks to the tree and the record's framing is said under it, plainly: 'This tree was here before this group arrived, and it will be here after this group leaves. We are not planting it and we are not studying it for a week. We are adopting it for a year: we will come back every month, we will measure what can be measured, we will write down what we actually see, and at the end of the year we will hand its log to next year's group, who will know this tree's year because we kept it honestly. Custodians, not owners. The tree does not need us. The log does.' The adoption is signed in the log's first page by every custodian present, with the date, and the first fixed-point photograph is taken before anything else happens, because every later photograph is measured against it.

Baseline round, the year's numbers: the trunk's circumference is measured at a marked height (a ribbon tied loosely, never nailed, never taped tight to bark, at chest height, recorded in the log so every later measurement is taken at the same honest place); the canopy's spread is paced out in two directions; the ground beneath is described in the log's plain categories, leaf litter, bare earth, grass, fallen fruit or seed, signs of visitors. Every measurement is taken twice, by two different custodians, and if the two disagree, both are written down and a third is taken: the log's rule is stated now and kept all year. 'We write what we measured, not what we expected. A surprising number is data. A copied number is fiction.'

The monthly protocol, established at the first visit so every later visit runs the same way and the months stay comparable: photograph from the fixed point first; circumference at the ribbon; canopy noted; then the month's phenology page. The year's real events, in the order the tree does them: first bud, first leaf, full leaf, flower if it flowers, fruit or seed if it sets any, first colour change, first leaf fall, bare. Each event gets the date it was FIRST seen and the name of the custodian who saw it, because 'first seen by' is the log's honour system and it makes sharp-eyed custodians of the whole group. A month where nothing has changed is written up as exactly that, 'March: no change at the ribbon; buds still shut; the log is not disappointed', because a year log that only records drama is a story, not a record.

Season pages, four across the year, written at the visit nearest each turn: each season page answers the same three questions in the custodians' own words, what is the tree doing, what is living on or under it, what has the weather done to it since the last season page, and the fixed-point photographs for the season are described in words beside their dates (the log is paper; the photographs live with the adults, and the descriptions are how the log keeps them). Disagreements are recorded as disagreements: if two custodians read the canopy differently, both readings go in, signed. The log is teaching a discipline most adults never learn. That a careful record of one ordinary tree, kept for one whole year, is a scientific document, and that its authority comes from its honesty about the boring months, not despite them.

Final visit, the handover: the year's last photograph is taken, the ribbon is checked and left as found, and the group writes the log's closing page together. The year's three biggest changes, the measurement they trust most and why, the question they are handing on unanswered ('the hollow on the north side: we never learned what lives there'), and one piece of advice to next year's custodians, earned the slow way. The log is handed over at full ceremony when the new group adopts the tree, read aloud at the trunk, the closing page first, and the outgoing custodians' names stay on the adoption page permanently: 'Kept by' is the title this record gives its workers, and it is earned monthly, in all weathers, at the pace a tree keeps.
activities.tagline: One tree, adopted for a whole year: measured monthly, watched through every season, and handed on to next year's custodians with its log.

variations.easier: A term-length version: adopt for one school term with visits every fortnight, the protocol identical, the season pages compressed, the handover made to the next term's group.
variations.harder: A two-tree version (a confident second-year group): two trees of different species kept in parallel logs, with a comparison page each season. The differences between two honest records are where the real learning compounds.

activities.inclusion: Librarianship is a desk with many chairs: the testing bench needs counters, dampness-keepers, and label-writers; the lending table needs a ledger-keeper, a packet-finder, and the adviser who gives the sowing advice, and every one of those jobs can be done seated, one-handed, by direction, or by a librarian whose strength is the ledger's memory rather than its handwriting (the audit read-back at closing is an oral honour, rotated by list). Advice and labels can be given in any register the borrowers need, spoken, written large on the packet, drawn as the sowing-depth line the library uses on every label, and the research list is read aloud in full at closing so that no librarian needs to have read handwriting to own a question. The library's founding rule helps here too: it lends to every borrower who signs, at the same ceremony, with the same honest label.

materials.item: the seed stock (saved seed from the site's own beds, donated packets within date, or a seed swap's surplus, sorted by the librarians before opening day; unknown-origin seed is welcomed but labelled as unknown, in ink, on the packet)
plain paper envelopes, one per packet (hand-folded is fine and traditional, the librarians fold the stock in the first session and the folding becomes the library's house style)
the germination-test kit (shallow trays or plates, paper towel, a spray bottle of water, and counter space out of direct sun. The test bench, set up a full week before opening day)
the ledger (a ruled notebook that is the library's memory: packet, borrower, date out, and the return column, seed returned from what the borrower grew, which is how a library of seeds is repaid)

activities.name: Seed Library Opening Day

photo.alt: Benbrook Public Library Seed Library
photo.caption: Benbrook Public Library Seed Library.
photo.credit: Photo: Aspensmonster, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Seeds are stock, not food: nothing on the table is eaten, tasted, or snacked on. Some seed is treated, some is simply not food, and the librarians' rule covers all of it without needing a list. Hands are washed after handling stock and always before eating anything else, and any tray that turns mouldy during its test week is composted whole by an adult wearing the bench's gloves. Its variety is retested from a fresh count, and the mould is recorded in the log as a result, not hidden as an embarrassment. Packet labels carry the variety's plain name and the test result; nothing is labelled with a claim the bench did not make, and any seed of unknown origin or unknown treatment is labelled unknown in ink, borrowers deserve to know what the library does not know. The ledger holds borrowers' real names because it is a working record kept by the adults between sessions, under the site's ordinary rules for such things.
activities.setup: Start a week before opening day, because the library's whole claim to honesty is made then: for every variety the library will lend, the librarians run the germination test themselves, ten seeds counted onto damp paper towel, kept damp in a labelled tray, checked daily, and counted again when the week ends. The number that sprouted is the number that goes on the packet, as a plain percentage, with the test's date: a packet labelled 'germination tested 8/10, this March' can be trusted in a way a packet of promises cannot. Sort the stock at the same bench: varieties separated, dead stock and anything mouldy composted without ceremony, and any variety whose test fails outright (two or fewer sprouts from ten) withdrawn from lending and logged as withdrawn. The library's first act of librarianship is refusing to lend seed it knows is spent. Set the opening-day table like a library, not a market stall: packets in variety order, the ledger open, the test trays on display, because the evidence is part of the exhibit.
steps: Opening framing, said at the table before the first loan: 'This is a library. It lends seeds the way the other library lends books: you borrow a packet, you grow what grows, and you repay the library the way seed libraries have always been repaid, with seed from your strongest plant, dried and brought back, so next year's borrowers grow from this year's best. Every packet on this table was tested by us, this month, and the test is on the label: eight out of ten sprouted means eight out of ten sprouted. If a packet says untested, it means exactly that too. This library does not exaggerate, because a gardener plans a bed around what a packet says, and a bed is a season you cannot have back.' The librarians introduce the ledger and its columns, and the borrowing rules are stated whole: one packet per borrower per visit, the ledger signed in real names, returns welcomed whenever the season gives them.

The testing story, told from the trays: before any lending begins, the librarians walk the first borrowers through the test bench, the trays still on display, sprouted and unsprouted side by side, and each librarian presents one variety's evidence: how many were counted, how the week ran, what the count was, and what the label therefore says. Questions are answered from the trays, not from memory. A variety whose label says 6/10 is presented at exactly its worth, with its honest use named ('six from ten is a packet you sow thickly and thin. The label tells you so, which is what labels are for'), because the library's credibility is built precisely where a lesser operation would quietly round up.

Lending round: borrowers choose, librarians lend. Each loan is a small ceremony of the ledger, packet named, borrower named, date written, and the librarian's one piece of earned advice given with it, drawn from the packet's own evidence and the season: sowing depth in plain words, indoor start or direct sow, and the honest wait ('germination in about a fortnight if the soil is warm, the test took six days on the bench, and a cold bed is slower; the packet is not late, the spring is'). Librarians who do not know an answer say so and write the question in the ledger's back page, the library's research list, the second founding habit: a library that records what it does not know yet will know it by next season.

Returns-and-savings desk, explained before it is needed: the librarians demonstrate the repayment craft on a demonstration plant's worth of seed heads. How to tell ripe seed from green, how drying is done (a paper bag, a warm shelf, a week of patience, a shake to hear the rattle), and how a return is received: variety, grower, the plant it came from described in one line ('the tallest of the row, north bed'), and the returned seed logged as next year's stock with its parentage on its future packet. A borrower whose crop failed entirely owes the library nothing but the story, and the story is entered in the ledger too, a failed bed with a recorded reason ('sown before the last frost, our error, the label now says so') is stock of another kind, and the library keeps it.

Closing the opening day: the table is counted, packets out, packets remaining, the ledger's loans read back aloud by the librarians in the session's official audit shape, and the research list is read with it, each question assigned to a librarian to answer before the next lending day, from a book, a grower, or next month's test bench. The tell-back is said over the ledger: 'The library opened with tested seed and honest labels. Nothing on this table promises more than its tray grew. What comes back will be better than what went out, seed from the strongest plants, and stories from the rest, and next spring's librarians will inherit a ledger that tells the truth. That is the whole institution. It runs on that.' The ledger and the remaining packets are stored dry, dark, and labelled with the librarians' names and the season, where next year's bench will find them.
activities.tagline: A real lending library of seeds: every packet germination-tested, honestly labelled, and lent out on a ledger the teen librarians keep.

variations.easier: A paper-only version (no seed available yet): the librarians build the whole institution as a rehearsal, packets folded, a test run on a single donated variety, the ledger opened, so the library's first lending day, when stock arrives, opens on a running system.
variations.harder: A swap-day version: opening day doubles as a seed swap. Outside growers bring surplus, every incoming variety is benched for a week's test before it joins the lending stock, and the ledger's first pages fill with donors, who are the library's founding friends.

activities.inclusion: A team navigates with every sense it owns: the navigator's job rotates by design, and it divides cleanly, one reads the needle, one counts the paces aloud, one keeps the card and calls the leg, so a navigator who cannot walk the leg can still be the team's needle-reader at each standstill, arriving by the route that suits them and taking the reading the whole team walks on. Bearings can be called in any register, spoken, signed, held up as the card's next line pointed to by its keeper, and the calibration strip teaches every body's own pace honestly, including the pace of wheels over the strip's length, which the setter's conversion treats as exactly what it is: that navigator's ruler, as valid as any pair of legs. Courses are set on ground chosen for step-free lines wherever the site allows, and a leg that cannot be made accessible is re-set by its setters as a matter of craft, not concession. A course only some teams can run is a badly set course, by this record's definition.

materials.item: sighting or baseplate compasses, one per team (real instruments, checked by the adult before the session: a compass whose needle sticks or swings lazy is retired, because a course set on a lying compass teaches lying)
three flags on poles per course (bright, tall enough to be seen from the bearing's line and no taller. A flag you can see from anywhere makes the bearing pointless)
course cards and pencils (each leg written as a bearing and a pace count, nothing else. The card is the whole instruction, and its clarity is the setter's craft)
a pace-count calibration strip (a measured 50 paces' worth of ground the adult has taped or paced out in advance, where every navigator learns their own honest pace count before any course is set)

activities.name: Compass Course, Three Flags

photo.alt: Het duimkompas met kaart
photo.caption: Het duimkompas met kaart.
photo.credit: Photo: Laurine1122, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Boundaries are the record's first law and they are geographic, not advisory: the course area is one bounded space the adult has walked, teams stay inside it and stay together, and any leg that points a team at a road, water, a car park, or out of the area stops the course on the spot. Reporting a bad leg is a result, forcing it is a breach, and the adult's framing says so before a flag is planted. Compasses are read standing still, always: nobody walks while watching a needle, nobody runs a leg, and the terrain is chosen so that a teenager looking up from a settled reading has nothing to fall off, into, or across within the course's lines. The sun and the session's length are planned like any outdoor record. Water at the start point, a hard finish time, and a whistle signal that means return to the start point now, rehearsed before the setting round so it never needs explaining in the moment. Flags and poles are carried point-down and planted by hand pressure only; a pole that needs force stays unplanted and its point is re-chosen.
activities.setup: Walk the whole ground yourself first, with the session's eyes: the course area must be one bounded, permitted space where every leg can be walked in a straight line without crossing roads, water, other groups' games, or any place a teenager following a needle might not notice arriving, deep mud, a slope that hides a drop, an out-of-bounds fence with a gap in it. Mark the single shared start point where all courses begin. Then calibrate yourself: walk the strip and count your paces over its known length, twice, because you will teach the calibration and a teacher whose own count is vague teaches vagueness. Check every compass against a bearing you know, a fence line, a building edge whose direction you have verified, and set the failures aside without a second thought. Decide the boundaries out loud to yourself in plain words ('nothing beyond the hedge, nothing across the path') so the framing can carry them exactly.
steps: The framing, at the start point, compasses still in the adult's hands: 'A bearing is a promise your feet keep. This instrument does not know where you are going. It knows one thing, perfectly: which way is which. Today each team sets a course of three flags for another team: three legs, each written as a bearing and a pace count, nothing more. The team that runs your course will find your flags if your numbers are honest and your reading of this ground is true, and they will not find them if either is sloppy, and they will know whose work it was. Then you run theirs. Setters first, runners second, everybody both.' The laws are stated whole: 'Teams stay together, always, inside the boundaries as named. Walking pace on a leg. A compass is read standing still, and running with your eyes on a needle is how ankles and friendships end. If a leg runs you at a boundary, a building, or anywhere the course should not go, stop: a course can be wrong, and reporting that, with your card, is a result. Forcing it is not.'

Calibration round, before any flag is planted: every navigator walks the measured strip and counts their own paces over its known length, twice, and writes their personal count on their course card, because a pace is not a standard unit, it is a property of a pair of legs, and a leg written as '40 paces' means the SETTER's 40 unless the card is walked by the setter's own measure. Teams therefore write legs in metres as well as paces where they can (the strip teaches the conversion on the spot: your count over the known length is your ruler), and a setter who skips calibration has built their course on sand. The round exists so nobody does. The adult watches the strip work like a hawk: counting aloud, head up between counts, eyes returning to the needle only at a standstill.

Setting round: each team walks the ground with its three flags, chooses its three points, each one a place a bearing can honestly reach and a flag can honestly stand: not hidden (this is navigation, not camouflage), not trivial (visible from the start point is not a leg, it is a view), and works backwards from each flag to write the leg that reaches it: the bearing read standing at the previous point with the needle settled, the distance paced and converted. The card is written as the runners will receive it: leg one from the start, leg two from flag one, leg three from flag two, and a finish line that brings the runners back to the start point by a stated bearing, setters walk their own finish leg before they hand the card over, because a course that strands its runners has failed its only examination. Cards are exchanged between teams by the adult, unedited: the setters' handwriting is part of the test, and legibility is a navigation skill.

Running round: teams run the courses they were given, in the order written, at walking pace, compass read at a standstill at each flag before the next leg is begun. The running team's navigator rotates at every flag, the card passes, the compass passes, and the reading is done aloud by the new navigator while the team checks the needle's settling together ('the needle settles before the feet move' is the round's working sentence, said at every leg until it becomes the team's own). A flag that cannot be found gets fifteen honest minutes of re-reading, bearing re-taken from the last certain point, paces re-counted, before it is reported missed, with the card brought back to the adult: a missed flag is a finding about the course, the running, or both, and the debrief will sort it without blame, because both teams know their own card is out there being read the same way.

Debrief at the start point, cards in hand: each course is marked by its runners in the session's official shape, flags found, legs disputed, and the single hardest reading on the card named precisely ('leg two said 140 degrees from the oak; the flag stood at 150 by our needle, one of our instruments or readings was out, and here is our evidence'). Setters answer with their setting notes. Where two compasses disagree, they are checked on the spot against the known bearing from calibration, and the instrument that lied is retired in front of everyone, kindly and permanently. The record's closing lesson, said whole: 'Navigation is a chain of honest numbers. A pace counted carelessly, a needle read while it was still swinging, a bearing written from memory, the chain breaks at its weakest link, and it breaks out there, at walking pace, with the flag in sight of nobody. Today you felt where chains hold. That feeling is the skill.' Flags are collected by their setters, the ground is left as found, and the cards are kept: a well-set course is run again next season, credited to its setters by name.
activities.tagline: Real bearings, counted paces, three flags to find: teen teams set an orienteering course, then run each other's, navigation, not wandering.

variations.easier: A one-flag version: a single out-and-back leg to one flag and home by the reverse bearing, the whole discipline of calibration, settling, and honest counting inside twenty minutes, for a first session with new instruments.
variations.harder: A night version (a dark evening session, with the adults' full permission and lit boundaries): the same courses run by torchlight, flags fitted with a reflective band. The needle read by torch held to the side, never waved across a partner's eyes, and every leg suddenly worth twice its daylight price.

activities.inclusion: Officiating is this record's great leveller: the whistle, the sheet, and the auditor's chair are full tournament jobs that ask for judgement, eyes, and a steady hand with numbers. A player whose body is sitting this fixture out can hold its authority instead, and the rotation is drawn so that officiating is never the consolation shift but the honour it is, with the panel's most trusted names taking the final. Calls and scores can be kept in any register the official works in, the sheet can be marked by a partner scribe at the referee's word, scores called aloud for the auditor to write, a raised coloured card backing the whistle for players who follow sight better than sound, and the protocol's shape protects everyone equally: one sentence of reason, play resumes, grievances in writing. The fixture card is read aloud in full at the framing, so no player's afternoon depends on having read small print on a clipboard.

materials.item: whistles, one per referee (washed before the session and issued one per official. A whistle is personal equipment for the afternoon, never passed mouth to mouth)
scoresheets and pencils on clipboards (the tournament's official record: fixtures, scores, and the initials of the referee who kept each one, kept by the referees, audited by the table)

a set of short games the group already knows, chosen by the referees' panel in advance (games of ten minutes or less with scoring a spectator can follow and no elimination. The panel's list, approved by the adult, is the tournament's whole fixture card)
bibs or sashes in two colours (so teams, referees, and spectators can read the afternoon at a glance)

activities.name: Referee-Run Round Robin
activities.safety: The adult's backstop is stated in the framing and kept narrow and real: safety calls, a dangerous tackle, a player hurt, a game heating past its rules, are the adult's instantly, whistle or no whistle, and every other call belongs to the officials, because a backstop that swallows the tournament teaches the officials nothing. The fixture list itself is a safety document: no contact games, no elimination games, no game whose whole field a referee cannot see, and playing areas walked beforehand for the ordinary hazards of the ground. Whistles are washed before issue, issued one per official, and never shared mouth to mouth within the session; a dropped whistle is washed or swapped, not licked clean and reused. Heat, water, and rest are the table's standing business between fixtures, called by the auditor on schedule rather than by the first player to flag. A tournament that runs itself still drinks on a timetable.
activities.setup: Build the fixture card before anyone arrives: the referees' panel (two or three teens who will lead the session, briefed earlier or simply first) lists the afternoon's games, every one short, every one already known to the group, every one scored in points rather than eliminations, so no player sits out and every referee's sheet fills with numbers instead of arguments. Draw the rotation on paper and check it the way the session's fairness depends on: every team plays the same number of games, every referee officiates the same number, and nobody referees a game their own team is playing. That last rule is structural, set now, because a dispute protocol is a poor substitute for a fixture list that never puts an official in it. Wash the whistles, sharpen the pencils, and walk the playing areas: boundaries marked, spectator line marked, water at the table. If a game on the list cannot be refereed by a teenager with a clear view of its whole field, it comes off the list at setup, not during a dispute.
steps: The framing, whistles still on the table: 'Today the tournament runs itself, and here is what that means. The referees keep the scores, settle the disputes, and sign their sheets. The whistle is a service, not a weapon: it stops the game so the game can be fair, and a referee who enjoys stopping the game will not be given it twice. Players: the referee's word ends the argument, not necessarily because the referee is right, but because a game where every call is appealed forever is not a game, it is a meeting. The protocol is: call, one sentence of reason, play resumes. Anything still burning at the end goes to the table, in writing, after the fixture, and the table's ruling is about the record, never a replay.' The adult's own role is named plainly too: 'I am the table's backstop. I will overrule a referee only for safety, and everyone will hear why. Everything else is yours.'

First fixture, refereed at full ceremony: the opening referee states the game, the scoring, and the boundary calls in one breath before play starts. Most disputes are born in unstated rules, and the statement is the referee's first skill. Play runs to the sheet: the referee calls what they see, gives the one-sentence reason without being asked twice ('Foot on the line. Throw retaken'), and the scoresheet fills in their hand, initialled at the final whistle. The table (an adult and a rotating teen auditor) checks the first sheet line by line at the changeover, arithmetic, initials, the score as the teams remember it, because the tournament's trust is built on its first audited sheet, and a discrepancy found early is a lesson, while one found at the final is a scandal.

Rotation round: fixtures proceed down the card, referees rotating as drawn, players rotating through refereeing with the same ceremony. A new official's first call is backed by the table visibly and without comment, because authority lent early is authority that holds later. The auditor's job grows teeth in this round: sheets are totalled fixture by fixture, the running table is kept where players can read it, and any player may inspect any sheet at any changeover. The record is public, which is most of why it stays honest. Referees learn the afternoon's hardest skill in this round and are told so while they learn it: the call you did not see is the call you do not make. 'I didn't see it', said plainly, play resumed from the last fair point, is a complete and honourable sentence in an official's mouth, and the framing honours it at full size the first time a referee uses it.

Dispute drill and the disputed fixture: the panel schedules one deliberate practice moment. A genuinely arguable call, walk-through slow: the referee states the call and the sentence, the captains hear the protocol's next step (play resumes; the grievance goes to the table in writing after the fixture), and the whole group watches a dispute end in ninety seconds without a raised voice. When a real dispute comes later, and the record does not pretend it won't, it is handled by the same shape, and the table's written ruling joins the sheets: what was claimed, what the referee saw, what the record now says. A referee whose call is overturned by the table loses nothing: the ruling corrects the record, not the official, and the debrief will say so in those words.

Finals and the audit: the last fixtures run, the sheets are gathered, and the table is totalled in public. The auditor reads every sheet aloud, captains confirm their own scores as read, and the tournament's winner is announced from the audited record and not a moment before it exists. The closing tell-back names the real result under the result: 'This afternoon ran on your calls, your sheets, and your protocol. The scores are the scores because the record says so, and the record says so because officials signed it. Any one of you can now be handed a whistle, a sheet, and a game full of your friends, the hardest officiating there is, and run it fairly. The tournament was the practice. That was the tournament.' Whistles are collected and washed, sheets are filed by the table, and any grievance still on paper gets its written answer before the group leaves. A tournament that answers its mail is one players will officiate again.
activities.tagline: Teens officiate their own tournament: whistles, scoresheets, a dispute protocol, and a rotation where everybody referees and everybody plays.

variations.easier: A two-game version: one game, two fixtures, referees swapped at half time, the whole protocol (statement, sheet, audit) inside thirty minutes for a first refereeing group.
variations.harder: A league version (across a term): the same sheets carry forward week to week, the table accumulates, and referees earn fixtures. A group's most trusted officials take the term's final, by the panel's nomination and the sheets' evidence.

activities.inclusion: The DJ position welcomes every kind of musician: a set can be played by a DJ who directs a partner's hands at the controls ('fade on my count, now'), the set list can be built and presented in any format its author works in, and the handover's call can be a raised hand, a tapped shoulder, or a signed count, the exchange zone runs on agreed signals, and agreeing them is part of the pair's planning, written on both lists before the session. The floor is equally open: dancing, moving in a chair, listening from the edge with the programme in hand are all floor behaviour the DJs are taught to read and serve, and the session's arc is programmed for the room that is actually there. A set that lifts a seated floor has done the job exactly as a set that lifts a standing one. The mid-session review is held at the position with every DJ present in whatever way they attend best, and its changes are read aloud from the paper, so no DJ's set depends on another's handwriting.

materials.item: one speaker the room can dance to, run from the adult's device or account (the session's single source. Every track comes through it, which is how the volume cap and the lyrics rule are actually enforceable)
each DJ's set list, written on paper in advance (three or four tracks, in order, with the planned joining track marked. A set that exists only in a DJ's head cannot be handed over)
a visible clock (the set is ten minutes and the handover lands on it. Time is an instrument in this record and it is played in the open)
floor markers for the DJ position and the handover point (so the change of hands happens at one known place, like a relay exchange zone)

activities.name: Ten-Minute Set, Clean Handover
activities.safety: Volume is this record's one physical risk and it is governed structurally, not by reminders: the cap is set and marked on the equipment by the adult before the first track, the speaker is positioned away from the floor's ears (never at head height beside the dancers), and a person at the room's edge must be able to hold a conversation without shouting, if they cannot, the level comes down, by the adult's hand, without debate, and the session continues at the cap. All music comes through the single screened source: no personal devices plugged in mid-session, no unscreened requests taken live, because the lyrics rule can only be kept on music that has been heard entire by the adult in advance. The floor itself follows the house's ordinary movement sense. Space to move, water available, anybody free to step off the floor at any moment without it being an event; stepping off is listening from the edge, and the DJs are taught to read it as programming information, never as failure.
activities.setup: Screen the sets before the session, every track, all the way through: each DJ submits their list in advance and the adult hears each track entire. The session's rule is absolute and is set now, not negotiated mid-set: every lyric is clean enough to be played to the whole room's families, and a track that fails is swapped by its DJ before the day, with the swap treated as programming, not censorship ('a working DJ's whole craft is playing the right record in the room they're actually in'). Set the volume cap with the speaker in the actual room, the level at which a person at the floor's edge can still speak to a partner without shouting, and mark it on the dial or the screen, physically, so the cap survives enthusiasm. Order the DJs and post the running order where the floor can see it; programme the arc of the whole session across the sets (opener's energy, the peak in the middle DJs' hands, a closer who lands the room) and tell each DJ where their set sits in that arc, because a handover is planned from the running order, not improvised at the exchange.
steps: The framing, at the DJ position, floor gathered: 'A set is a promise to a floor: ten minutes where the music never dies, never clashes, and never wanders off. Today you each play three or four tracks and then you do the hardest thing in the craft. You hand over. The next DJ's first track begins as your last one ends: matched in energy, joined on the beat or on the breath between songs, with both of you at the position, hands ready, like a relay exchange. The floor never notices the join. That is the whole standard. A gap is a dropped baton. A clash is two promises broken at once. And the set you play is the set on your paper: the floor is dancing to a plan, and the plan is what makes the plan's surprises land.' The volume cap and the lyrics rule are stated as the session's constitution, once, without apology: 'The cap is marked. The lists are screened. Inside those two lines, the floor is yours.'

First set, played at full ceremony by the first DJ with the adult alongside for this one alone: the DJ announces nothing, the music does the announcing, and plays their list as written, watching the floor the way the craft requires (heads, feet, the edges where energy leaks) and riding their planned joining track into the exchange zone as the clock runs down. The handover is walked through at full size this first time, narrated quietly by the two DJs themselves: the incoming DJ at the position a full track early, listening, naming the join point to themselves ('on the last chorus. There'), the outgoing DJ's hand leaving the controls as the incoming track takes the floor, both staying at the position until the join has landed and the floor has taken it. Whether it lands clean or rough, the debrief sentence is the same shape: what the join did, in the floor's terms, 'the floor kept moving' or 'the floor checked', because the floor is the only reviewer this record recognises.

Rotation round: sets proceed down the running order, each DJ arriving at the position during the previous set's penultimate track, set list in hand, and each handover judged by the floor's behaviour and nothing else. DJs learn the round's central discipline in their hands: your last track is not your favourite track. It is the bridge, chosen when the list was written, at the energy the NEXT set needs to start from; a DJ who peaks on their closer has spent the next DJ's opening, and the floor pays for it. The adult's only interventions are the constitution's two lines, a hand drifting above the marked cap is pointed at, silently, once, and the lyrics rule has no second warnings because it was screened, not trusted. Between sets there is no applause break and no announcement: the session is one continuous piece of music with many authors, and it is reviewed as such.

The arc reviewed, mid-session, in two minutes with the music paused exactly once: the DJs gather at the position and read the session so far as one work, where the floor's energy rose, where it sagged, which join carried it and which one cost it, and the remaining DJs may retime (never re-screen) their lists' order within their own sets in light of the evidence, marking the change on their paper in ink so the plan stays a plan. This is the record's programming lesson, and it is stated while the paper is out: 'A set list is a hypothesis. The floor is the experiment. Changing the order because the floor told you something is the craft. Changing it because you got bored is noise.'
