The closer lands the session: the final DJ plays the room down deliberately, the last track chosen when the list was written to be the session's full stop, energy spent honestly rather than switched off, and the floor is thanked by the DJs collectively, by name and set, in the tell-back's shape: 'Nobody heard a join break. The floor danced through six pairs of hands and the music never died once, that is not six sets, that is one session, and building one thing out of many people's taste, without a seam showing, is the entire job of every DJ, programmer, and host who will ever follow you at it.' Set lists are kept and filed with the running order: a session that landed is programmed again, credited to its DJs, and its joining tracks, the bridges that held. Are the first thing next session's DJs study.
activities.tagline: Teen DJs each play a short set and hand the floor to the next DJ without a gap, a clash, or a dead second. The join is the skill.

variations.easier: A two-DJ version: two sets and one handover, rehearsed twice, once walked through narrated, once live, inside twenty-five minutes; the join gets the whole session's attention, which is where a new group's attention belongs.
variations.harder: A silent-disco version (headphones for the floor, two channels): DJs hand over on one channel while the other runs long. The joins multiply, the floor's channel-switching becomes part of the evidence, and the debrief reads the switches like votes.

activities.inclusion: Architecting is a writer's desk with room for every kind of mind: clues can be drafted in words, in code, in counted things, in drawn maps, the master sheet requires one line of intended reasoning per clue, and that line can be dictated to the team's scribe as fully as it can be written. On the run, the log-keeper, the envelope-keeper, and the reader-aloud are real jobs at the chain's pace, and a runner who travels the building differently still reads the clue the whole team works from. Solutions in this record are spoken into the log by whoever reaches them, in whatever register they arrive. The watching architects' silence protects everyone equally, including architects who communicate by gesture or board: the no-hinting law names every channel, kindly, in the framing, so nobody's ordinary voice is treated as an interruption. Bounds and hiding places are set for the building as the whole group actually uses it, a clue placed where only some runners can reach it fails the fairness tests on its face, by the architects' own law.

materials.item: sealed envelopes, eight to ten per chain (numbered on the outside, the clue inside written by the architects. The seal matters: a clue that can be peeked out of order is a chain that can be cheated, and honest difficulty needs honest seals)

the architects' master sheet (the whole chain written out by its designers, solution by solution, with each clue's intended reasoning in one line. The document the debrief will mark against, kept by the adult until the run is done)

a destination worth arriving at (a small, real prize agreed in advance, the choice of tomorrow's music, a reserved window seat for the week, a trophy of magnificent worthlessness, placed where the final clue honestly leads)
pencils and the runners' log (one per running team, where every clue's working is written as it is solved, because the architects need the runners' reasoning, not just their times)

activities.name: Indoor Clue Chain Architects
activities.safety: The territory is agreed with the adult before any designing begins and the bounds are constitutional: no clue points into toilets, staff areas, food preparation, store rooms, or anywhere a runner would be out of the ordinary sight of the session, and no envelope is hidden anywhere that requires climbing, reaching inside machinery or furniture, moving another group's or person's belongings, or blocking, even briefly, even slightly, a door, an exit route, or a corridor's flow. Envelopes are placed in the adult's sight during the design round and the master sheet's locations are checked against the bounds before the run starts; a location that fails is re-hidden before the exchange, kindly and without debate, because the architects' laws bind the architects first. Running is walking: a chain is a thinking race, not a foot race, and the log is written at each clue, which builds the pauses into the form. The destination's prize is agreed in advance so no chain can promise what the session cannot deliver.
activities.setup: Survey the building as an architect, which means as a safety officer first: the chain's whole territory is agreed with the adult in advance, the rooms and corridors in bounds, and the places no clue may ever point (toilets, staff-only areas, anywhere with food preparation, anywhere a searching teenager would be alone and unwatched, and anywhere near an exit door, a stairwell's far side, or another group's session). Decide the destination and its prize with the adult and place nothing yet. Set the chain's length honestly, eight clues is a full session's design and run; a chain of twenty is two sessions wearing a trench coat, and prepare the master sheet's format so every team designs to the same standard: each clue lists its location, its text, its intended reasoning, and the one thing that would make it unfair. Read the existing shelf's hunts before designing (the indoor scavenger hunt is a list of things to find; an escape room is a room to get out of) so the architects know what a chain is by knowing what it is not: a sequence, where each solution is the only key to the next clue's whereabouts.
steps: The framing, envelopes on the table: 'A clue is fair when a stranger could solve it, not easily, not instantly, but completely, from what is written and what can be seen, with no knowledge that lives only in the designer's head. Today each team architects a chain: eight clues, sealed, numbered, each one hiding the next, the last one leading to the prize. Then the chains are exchanged, and your chain will be run by people who did not design it, while you watch. These are the architects' laws, and they are absolute: you watch in silence, no hints, no faces, no meaningful coughing, because a chain that needs its architect in the room has already failed, and your silence is how you find out. And when the run is done, the runners will mark your chain clue by clue, from their log, and every mark will cite evidence. Design accordingly.' The fairness tests are stated whole: 'Every clue must pass three questions. Could a stranger solve it from what's here? Is there exactly one reading that works? And is the hiding place in bounds, reachable, and dignified, nobody solves a clue by climbing, reaching into anything, or disturbing anyone's work.'

Design round: teams build their chains backwards, the way chains are honestly built, destination first, final clue written to lead there, then each earlier clue constructed to deliver its successor's location as its solution. Clue types are varied by design and the master sheet requires the variety: a riddle whose answer names a place; a code that yields a direction; a counting clue that only arithmetic the room can see will satisfy; a quotation with its source findable in the room; an observation clue that sends runners to look properly at something everybody walks past. Each clue is drafted, then read aloud within the team by a member who did not write it, the team's own stranger test, and any clue the reader cannot parse is redrafted on the spot, because if your own teammate needs it explained, the runners are already lost. Hiding is done last, in bounds, envelopes numbered and sealed in the adult's sight, locations logged on the master sheet and nowhere else.

The run: chains are exchanged by the adult, master sheets held back, and the running teams take the first envelope and their log and begin. The architects follow at a distance, in silence, log-keepers of their own design: where the runners hesitate, where they misread, where a clue that 'couldn't be misunderstood' is misunderstood in a way the architects must write down verbatim, because that sentence is the session's most valuable data. A chain that stalls completely gets the protocol, stated in the framing and kept exactly: fifteen minutes on one clue earns the runners the right to the architects' single pre-written hint, every chain carries one, sealed separately, written at design time for the clue its architects privately judged hardest, and beyond the hint, a stalled chain is broken open by the adult and marked as broken, without drama: a chain that cannot be run is a result, and the debrief will perform its autopsy with respect.

The marking: runners mark the chain clue by clue from their log, in the session's official shape, solved clean, solved by luck, solved after the hint, misread (with the misreading quoted), unfair (with the failed test named), and the architects answer each mark from their master sheet: the intended reasoning, stated in one line, no defence beyond it. The two documents side by side are the session's whole education, and the debrief draws the general laws out of the specific wounds: clues fail at pronouns ('it', 'the big one'), at assumed knowledge, at hiding places that reward searching over thinking, and they succeed where the reasoning was made of things the runners could see, count, or read in the room itself. The best clue of the day, by the runners' vote across both chains, is read aloud entire and its architects named: a clue strangers solved with pleasure is a piece of writing that worked on minds it never met.

Finish with the prize honoured and the archive made: the destination is reached by whoever the chains brought there, the prize is awarded as agreed (shared by the running team that earned it, however the group has ruled such things), and both master sheets and both runners' logs are filed together as the session's record. The tell-back closes the design office: 'You wrote for strangers today, and strangers read you. Where they solved you, your thinking travelled. Where they stumbled, you found the exact place your thinking stayed home. That is the whole craft of every instruction, sign, rule, and direction ever written, and you have now done it with the evidence in your hands.' A chain that marked well is preserved as the house chain for a future group to run, credited to its architects on the first envelope, in ink.
activities.tagline: Teams design a chain of sealed clues that leads somewhere real. Then watch, silent, while another team runs it and finds every weak link.

variations.easier: A four-clue version: a half-chain around one room, designed and run inside thirty minutes, the stranger test and the silent watch intact, the length the only thing reduced.
variations.harder: A cross-age version: chains architected by the teens for a younger group to run, with the fairness tests applied at the runners' reading level. Designing down honestly is the hardest brief an architect can take, and the marking is done by the young runners' own log-keeper.

activities.inclusion: The seat is taken in whatever way its sitter communicates best: answers can be spoken, signed, written on the spot and read by a chosen voice, or given as the briefest signal the laws protect. One word is a whole answer here, by constitution. Asking is an equal discipline: a questioner can read their card, hand it to the adult to read verbatim, or point to the card drawn for them, and the question loses nothing by its route. The pass token works for every sitter identically, raised, not spoken, which is precisely why the pass was designed as an object: nobody in this record has to find words in order to decline. The arc is arranged so the seat faces the group at whatever height and distance its next sitter chooses, the chair is an ordinary chair among chairs, and membership of the session, asking, listening, naming the glad-to-know sentence at each seat's end, is complete from any position in the arc, including the position of never sitting at all.

materials.item: the question cards (written by the group in a prior five minutes and screened by the adult before the session. Every card a question its writer would happily answer themselves, in front of everyone, which is the screening's whole test)
one chair, placed where the whole circle can see it kindly (the seat, ordinary, comfortable, and deliberately not special-looking; the attention is the event, not the furniture)
a soft pass token held by whoever sits in the seat (a smooth stone or a beanbag. Passing is done by raising it, so a pass never has to be spoken, explained, or performed)

activities.name: Hot Seat, Kind Questions
activities.safety: The constitution is the safety system and it is enforced by structure, not by vigilance alone: cards are screened by the adult before the session and the off-limits territories are named in the framing, bodies and appearance, money, family circumstances, romance, health, grades, third parties' business, so no answerer is ever ambushed by a question the room had already agreed not to ask. The pass is absolute, token-raised, unexplained, and unexamined, and the adult models it in the first seat so its honour is established before it is needed. Nothing is recorded, photographed, or repeated outside the room: the session's confidentiality law is stated in the framing and the adult keeps it visibly, including afterwards. An answer quoted back in a corridor, however affectionately, ends the record's future with that group until trust is rebuilt, and the framing says so plainly because teenagers keep laws they understand the reason for. The adult sits in the circle and watches the laughter's direction the whole session; a seat is ended early, without ceremony or blame, the moment its warmth changes character.
activities.setup: Screen the cards like the session depends on it, because it does: read every submitted question yourself and apply the record's constitution, which you will state in the framing. Questions ask about tastes, memories, skills, opinions, hopes, and harmless hypotheticals; no question touches bodies or appearance, money, family circumstances, romance, health, grades, or anybody else's business, and no question is a dare, a ranking of people in the room, or a story its answerer has not volunteered to tell. Cards that fail are removed quietly, without naming their writers. The screening is a filter, not a court. Shuffle the survivors, count them against the session's length (a seat runs about four questions; programme fewer seats than the group wants, so the record ends with appetite, a discipline every good host learns), and arrange the chair and circle so the seated person faces friends, not a firing line: a shallow arc, the adult seated inside the circle as a member with a job, never opposite the seat like an interviewer.
steps: The framing, the seat empty, the group in its arc: 'This is the hot seat, and in this room the name is a lie we are correcting together: the seat is warm, never hot. One person sits. The group asks. The questions are on these cards, every one of them screened, every one of them a question its writer would answer themselves. And these are the seat's laws, which outrank everybody's curiosity, including mine: the pass is a complete answer. Raise the token, the card is gone, no reason given, no reason asked, ever. An answer can be as long or as short as its owner makes it. One word is a whole answer. Nobody repeats what is said in the seat outside this room: we are practising the difference between a group that knows things about each other and a group that trades in them, and only the first kind is being built here.' The first seat is taken by the adult or a confident volunteer, at full ceremony, so the laws are seen working, including a pass, used early and used proudly, before anyone warier is asked to sit.

The asking round: cards are drawn by the questioner, read aloud exactly as written, and answered from the seat. The group's craft is listening at full size, no follow-up interrogation, no cross-examination disguised as interest; one follow-up is allowed, and its form is fixed: 'say more about that, if you'd like', an invitation whose refusal costs nothing and is taken at face value the instant it is given. Laughter is welcome where the answer invites it and is checked where it doesn't, and the adult's ear is the session's thermostat: the moment a laugh lands ON somebody rather than WITH them, the next card is drawn and the moment is over, kindly and finally. Answers that surprise the group, the quiet person's enormous opinion, the joker's serious hope, are received at the size they are given, because receiving is the skill the seat exists to teach.

Rotation: seats change by volunteer and by gentle invitation, never by assignment or acclamation. Nobody is put in the seat by the group's enthusiasm, which is pressure wearing a friendly coat. A person who declines the seat holds full membership of the session: they draw cards, they ask, they listen, and the framing protects the symmetry ('asking well is half this record; some of its best practitioners never sit'). Each seat ends the same way: the group names, briefly and specifically, one thing it now knows that it is glad to know, 'I did not know you could juggle; I am glad I know', and the seated person steps back into the arc to that sentence, which is the seat's whole social architecture: you were attended to, you were received kindly, and now you are one of us who knows it can be survived, even enjoyed.

The question-craft stretch, once the rotation has warmed: the group reviews the cards that landed best, not the funniest answers, the best QUESTIONS: the ones whose answers nobody could have predicted and everybody wanted to hear, and the session names what made them good, in the group's own words, recorded by the adult on the back of the running order: openness (a hundred honest answers fit through it), safety (its answerer could not lose by answering), and surprise (it asked about a country nobody knew the person had visited in their own life). Each member then writes one new card to that standard, screened on the spot, and the session's final seat is taken, by a volunteer the new cards have tempted, using only the new deck: the group asks its own best questions last, and feels the difference in the answers.

Closing: the cards are gathered, the pass token is retired to its place, and the tell-back is said with the seat empty at the circle's centre: 'We know more about each other than we did, and none of it cost anybody anything. Every pass was honoured, every answer was sized by its owner, and what was said here stays here. That is not a small thing. Most rooms a person will ever sit in do not run on those laws. This one did, because you kept them.' The screened deck is kept as the group's own deck, added to over the year, its constitution unchanged: a deck of questions a group wrote for itself, to its own standard, is a portrait of what that group finds interesting about being people. Worth keeping as carefully as the answers were heard.
activities.tagline: One chair, the whole group's kind attention, and questions screened in advance. The seat is warm, never hot, and the pass is absolute.

variations.easier: A three-question version: one seat, three cards, the laws at full strength inside ten minutes. A standing opener a group can run whenever a new member joins, with the new member asking first and sitting only if they offer.
variations.harder: A written version (a group that prefers paper): seats are taken in writing. A member's name drawn, the group writes kind questions anonymously to the screened standard, the seated member chooses three to answer aloud and passes the rest unread by anyone else, ever.

activities.inclusion: The benches are built for every kind of hand: a repair can be led by a repairer who directs a partner's fingers through the fine work while keeping the finding, the sequence, and the verdict in their own judgement. The chart is signed by the mind that ran the repair, and the cafe says so. The receiving desk and triage, the cafe's examining honours, where the institution's authority actually sits, are fully seated work, as are the chart-keeping and the closing audit, which is read aloud entire so its record does not depend on any one person's reading. Owners state symptoms in any register they use, spoken, written on the chart at the desk's pen, pointed out on the patient itself, and the handover report is given the same way it was received, with the chart's plain language available to be read aloud by the repairer as the standard shape. Bench heights, lighting, and magnifiers are setup decisions made before opening, because a cafe that plans its welcome mends more than objects.

materials.item: the mending bench kit (needles in a pincushion, counted out and counted in, thread in the common colours, buttons in a sorted tin, fabric patches, sharp scissors that live at the bench and travel nowhere, pins in a magnetic dish)
the paper-and-binding bench kit (tape for spines, glue sticks, a bone folder or the back of a spoon, clamps or heavy books for pressing repairs flat)
the general bench kit (a screwdriver set for battery covers and loose fittings, pliers, a soft brush and cloth for cleaning mechanisms, sticky labels for parts that must go back in order)

the patient charts (one card per item received: owner, item, what is wrong as the owner describes it, the triage verdict, the repairer's name, and the outcome, fixed, improved, or beyond this cafe, signed by the repairer and read to the owner at handover)

activities.name: Repair Cafe, First Session

photo.alt: Reading Repair Cafe DIY workshop
photo.caption: Reading Repair Cafe DIY workshop.
photo.credit: Photo: Karen Blakeman, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The constitution's exclusions are absolute and are the cafe's core safety law: nothing that plugs into a wall socket is ever opened, repaired, or plugged in at a bench, no exceptions for 'just the cord', and nothing with a heating element, a pressurised part, or a blade that must be drawn toward the body enters the benches at all; such patients are referred at triage, kindly, and the referral is recorded as good service. Sharps run on the counting law, needles, pins, and scissors counted out, counted at every change, counted in by two voices at closing, with the cafe staying open until counts agree; needles live in the pincushion or in cloth, never loose on a bench, in a lap, or in a pocket. Glue and cleaning materials are the ordinary low-odour kind, used at ventilated benches, off skin and out of eyes, with hands washed at closing; small parts from a patient's insides stay on its tray, are never mouthed or pocketed, and leave with the patient or in the bin the owner approves. Owners keep responsibility for their own items throughout, the chart records it, and anything of real financial or sentimental value is triage-referred to professionals before a learner's hands learn on it.
activities.setup: Set the cafe up as a working institution, because its credibility is its layout: a receiving desk at the door where charts are opened, a triage bench where every patient is examined before any repair is promised, the three benches behind it with their kits laid out, and a waiting area where owners stay, owners watch their repairs in this cafe, by design, because a repair explained is a repair taught. Draw the cafe's constitution on one big sheet and hang it where everyone can read it: what the cafe mends (seams, buttons, hems, bindings, paper, loose fittings, dirty mechanisms, squeaks that a brush and patience can reach); what it never touches (anything that plugs into the wall, anything with a heating element, anything whose repair needs a blade drawn toward a body, anything valuable enough that a learner's mistake would be a loss, those are referred, kindly, to professionals, and the referral is a cafe service, not a failure); and the counting law for sharps, needles and scissors are counted out at opening, counted at every bench change, and counted in at closing, aloud, by two voices. Brief the repairers on the verdict language before the doors open: fixed is a verdict the owner gives, not the repairer. The repairer reports what was done; the owner, using the thing, says whether it is fixed.
steps: Opening and triage: the cafe opens with its constitution read aloud by the receiving desk, what it mends, what it never touches, how a chart works, and the first patients are received one at a time, examined at triage in the owner's hearing: the symptom as described, the bench's own finding stated plainly ('the seam has gone along the pocket, here, that is bench work, twenty minutes'), and the verdict BEFORE repair begins: mendable here, mendable with a risk the owner must accept in words ('the fabric is worn thin around the tear; a patch will hold and will show, your call'), or beyond this cafe, with the reason and the referral said at full respect. No chart is opened on a promise triage cannot keep. An owner who accepts a risk signs the chart's line; an owner who declines takes their patient home with the triage finding written on the chart as the cafe's gift. A clear account of what is wrong is worth having, and the cafe gives it free.

Bench work, first round: repairs proceed at the benches, each repairer with one patient at a time, the chart beside the work, parts labelled as they come off and laid in order on the bench's tray, the discipline that separates a repair from a scattering is taught in the hands: photograph or sketch the arrangement before touching it, work on the tray, and stop the moment a repair reveals something triage missed, because stopping is a bench skill: the chart is amended, the owner is called over, and the verdict is re-given with the new evidence, exactly as before. Owners watch, ask, and, where the repairer invites it and the bench allows, do the final stitches, turns, or wipes themselves, guided: a repair its owner finished is a repair its owner can repeat, and the cafe counts that as its best outcome and says so on the chart.

The honest middle: every first session produces at least one patient that defeats the bench, and the record treats that patient as the session's most important teaching case rather than its embarrassment. When a repair fails or a verdict must change to beyond this cafe, the repairer completes the chart in full, what was attempted, what the attempt revealed, why the bench stops here (a part that would need ordering, a material that will not take a stitch, a mechanism whose fault is internal and sealed), and the handover conversation is rehearsed once with the receiving desk if the repairer wants it, because delivering an honest no is a professional skill and professionals practise it. The language is the cafe's own: 'Here is what we found. Here is what we tried. Here is where our bench honestly ends, and here is who can take it further.' Nothing is hidden, nothing is blamed on the patient, and the item goes home in no worse state than it arrived: a cafe that makes things worse has broken its first law, and benches check their work against the chart's arrival notes before any handover.

Handover round: patients are returned one at a time, chart in hand, the repairer reporting in the cafe's shape, what was wrong, what was done, what the owner should know ('the stitching will outlast the fabric around it; when it goes again, it will go there, and now you know the stitch'), and the owner uses the thing, here, at the desk: wears the garment, opens the book, runs the mechanism, and gives the verdict the chart was waiting for: fixed, improved, or, rarely, and honourably recorded, not yet. The repairer signs, the owner signs, and the chart is filed. A cafe's file of charts is its memory and its advertisement both, and the closing audit will read its numbers without fear because every line in it was earned in the open.

Closing audit and the tell-back: sharps are counted in, aloud, by two voices, and the cafe does not close until the counts agree with opening. A missing needle is found before anyone leaves, by the whole cafe, calmly, because the counting law exists precisely so that this sentence can be boring. Charts are tallied in the session's official shape, received, fixed, improved, beyond this cafe, referred, and read aloud by the receiving desk. The tell-back is said over the tally: 'Things came in broken and were looked at honestly. Some left fixed. Some left with the truth about themselves, which is also a service, and the hardest one to give well. You ran benches, kept charts, and signed your work. Whoever learns to repair learns the secret underneath every made thing: it was made by hands, so hands can mend it, and knowing which things your hands should not mend is not the opposite of that skill. It is the skill, finished.' Charts are filed by date, benches are packed as they were found, and the constitution sheet comes down last, to be re-hung, amended if the session taught it anything, at the next opening.
activities.tagline: Teens run a working repair cafe: triage, mending benches, honest verdicts, and owners who leave with fixed things and real explanations.

variations.easier: A one-bench version: mending only, a seams-and-buttons cafe for a first session with new repairers, the full institution (triage, charts, audit) at its smallest honest size.
variations.harder: A themed version: a book-repair morning before the library's sale, or a costume-repair session in the week before a show, one patient class, benches specialised, the constitution re-drawn for the theme and hung the same way.

activities.inclusion: Hosting divides into honours at every reach: a city's host can strike the bell, say the greeting, give the sentence, place the marker, and sign the card, or direct any of those by a partner's hands while keeping the city theirs. The route card names one host per city, and the name is what the record honours. Greetings are prepared in large print on the cards and practised in advance, so a host who communicates best by showing the card, pointing to the route, or leading the room's repeated reply by gesture is leading it fully; the room's answer-back is choral by design, which carries every voice at the size it arrives. The gap-filling business, predictions, questions, envelopes, is table work at the room's own pace, writable, drawable, or dictatable, and the evening is seated throughout: midnight walks the map so that nobody else has to. The route card is read aloud in full at the closing, so the evening's record belongs to everyone who was in the room, not only to those who read it along the way.

materials.item: a big wall map of the world's time zones (hand-drawn and hand-coloured by the hosts in preparation is best, the drawing is half the learning, with the session's route cities marked and the local time of their midnights worked out and double-checked in advance)

the route card (the evening's running order: each city's midnight in YOUR local time, in sequence, with its host named, computed beforehand, verified by a second host, and treated as the evening's script)
a clock the whole room can see, and a bell or chime for each midnight (one strike per city, struck by that city's host. The evening's recurring ceremony)

greeting cards for each route city (the correct New Year greeting in the city's own language, written large, with its pronunciation worked out and practised in advance, plus one true sentence about how that city actually celebrates, researched, not invented)

activities.name: Midnight Around the World
activities.safety: The evening is a simulation at civilised hours and says so in its framing: nobody's sleep, health, or family arrangements are spent on the theme, and the session ends when it is scheduled to end however far the route has travelled. The route card is built to the session's real hours, never the other way round. Toasts are raised in the room's ordinary drinks; nothing about the theme changes what is served, and any food the hosts add follows the house's ordinary allergy discipline, labelled and asked about in advance, with the themed dishes' ingredients known to the hosts who introduce them. Greetings and customs are researched from reliable sources beforehand and checked for accuracy: no invented traditions, no costume versions of a culture, no accents. The record's law is compliments, not imitations, and a host uncertain of a fact leaves the sentence out rather than embellishing it. The map, cards, and bell live on walls and tables; nothing about the ceremony involves darkness, candles, or moving around a dimmed room, and the clock-watching is seated, sociable work.
activities.setup: Build the route a day ahead, because the evening's magic is arithmetic and arithmetic is unforgiving: choose eight to twelve cities whose midnights fall inside your session's hours when converted to local time (a session in the early evening can catch the Pacific and Asia; a later one crosses Europe and the Atlantic), and work every conversion twice, by two different hosts, from a reliable zone reference, a route card with one wrong hour in it is discovered by the whole room at the worst possible moment, so the checking is done at a desk, not on the night. Research each city's greeting and its real celebration honestly: what the greeting actually is and how it is pronounced (audio checked if any doubt exists, and a greeting nobody can say properly is replaced by a respectful English greeting with the city's own words written on its card, displayed, not mangled), what people there genuinely eat, watch, or do at midnight, and one sentence of it, true and checkable, for the card. Draw and hang the map, mark the route, and brief the hosts: each host owns one city, its minute, its greeting, its sentence, and rehearses the strike, the greeting, and the sentence aloud before the room fills.
steps: The framing, the room gathered before the map, the first midnight still minutes away: 'Tonight this room is staying up around the world, at a civilised hour. Midnight is a place before it is a time: right now it is standing in the Pacific, and all evening it will walk west across this map, one time zone at a time, and we are going to meet it in every city on our route. When the clock reaches a city's hour, its host strikes the bell once, greets the city properly in its own words, and tells us one true thing about how the year turns there. Between midnights, the route is ours: we eat, we talk, we watch the clock, like every good New Year's room in every city on this map, most of the evening is the waiting together, done well.' The house rules are stated whole: 'Greetings are said properly or not at all, we do not do accents, and we do not laugh at a language: a pronunciation practised and offered respectfully is a compliment; an imitation is a insult wearing a party hat, and this room does not wear it. And nobody performs hunger or thirst for the theme: the drinks are ours, the toasts are real, and the evening is a simulation of midnight, not a test of anybody's endurance.'

First midnight, at full ceremony: as the clock reaches the first city's converted hour, its host steps to the map, strikes the bell once, places a marker on the city, says the greeting at full size, practised, plain, offered to the city as if the city could hear, because the room's imagination is doing honest work, gives its one true sentence, and leads the room's reply: the greeting repeated back by everyone, once, together, as well as the room can say it, which is the point of the practising. The host signs the route card beside their city, with the actual minute, and the evening's record has begun. The room toasts the city with whatever is in its glasses and the map has its first marker: midnight has a location, the room has met it there, and the route west is open.

The route round: midnights proceed down the card at their computed minutes, some arrive in a rush where zones bunch, some leave long sociable gaps, and the hosts learn the evening's real hosting craft in the gaps: the route is filled, by design, with the room's own New Year business, resolutions written for the room's time capsule or letter box if the group keeps one, the year-in-review conversation the hosts have seeded with three good questions on cards at the tables, predictions for the coming year sealed in envelopes with names on, to be opened at next year's session. A host whose city approaches keeps one eye on the clock and gives the room its one-minute warning ('Auckland has a minute to live in the old year') so every midnight lands on a gathered room, never on a scattered one: the warning, the gathering, the strike. The ceremony's rhythm becomes the evening's heartbeat, and by the fourth city the room is running it like a newsroom that loves its story.

The home midnight, rehearsed by the whole evening: when the route reaches the room's own city, the final marker, timed to the session's close or to the real hour if the session runs late enough to earn it, the ceremony is given its fullest form: every host strikes once in route order, the greetings of the whole route are repeated back down the line of the map like a roll of honour, and the room's own greeting is said last and loudest, in its own words, to its own year. The tell-back belongs to this moment and is said before the last toast: 'We have met midnight in a dozen cities and it was the same minute everywhere and a different year in every language. The year turns whether anyone watches. Tonight we watched, properly, with the arithmetic checked and the greetings practised. Which is to say, we treated the whole turning world as worth preparing for. That is the entire skill of hosting anything.'

Closing the route: the route card, signed by every host beside every city, at the actual minutes, is read back aloud in full, because the evening's record is a small true document (where midnight was met, when, by whom, in what words) and reading it aloud is how the room files it. Envelopes of predictions are sealed and stored with the card, the map comes down last and is kept flat with the session's papers, and the hosts are thanked by name, city by city, in the order of the route. The final line is the evening's own: 'Next year, midnight will walk the same road. Whoever hosts it, host it like this, prepared, accurate, and glad. Happy New Year, in every time zone there is.'
activities.tagline: One hosted evening that follows midnight across the time zones: live arithmetic, a wall map, and each city greeted properly as its year turns.

variations.easier: A four-city version: a short route across one ocean, the full ceremony at a smaller radius, ideal for a first hosting team, who will learn more from four cities landed cleanly than from twelve chased.
variations.harder: A daytime classroom version: the route runs on a school-day clock with midnights compressed to a lesson's sequence of cities whose hours suit it, the same preparation and ceremony, and the map kept up for the rest of the week as the class's working geography.

activities.inclusion: The trials run on jobs at every reach: blade design can be led by the mind that draws the pattern while a partner's hands do the cutting to their line, the sheet credits the design to its team, and the pattern is the design's signature. Counting is doubled by design, which makes the second counter, the sheet-keeper, and the clip-loader full experimental roles rather than spare parts; a run's numbers enter the record through voices as readily as through hands, and the sheet-keeper's reading-back of each run before it is inked is the protocol that lets every team member verify what the sheet says. The rig's measures are announced aloud as standard practice, revolutions and clips called, not just written, so the evidence is public to the whole room in the moment it lands. Pitch is set with a protractor jig the adult prepares for any hand that needs one, and the workload final's presentation, each team's story from its sheet, can be given by any member, in any register, from a sheet that was kept to be read aloud.

materials.item: one desk fan with a guarded grille, three speeds, positioned by the adult and moved by nobody else (the wind source, constant, caged, and the trials' whole weather system)
a test hub on a stand (a dowel axle in a heavy base, spinning freely, with paper clips hanging from a thread wound on the axle. Lifted clips are the turbine's workload and the trials' second measure)

blade stock (stiff card in several weights, scissors that live at the bench, rulers, protractors for pitch angles, tape and a glue stick, every blade cut to a recorded pattern so a winner can be re-cut exactly)

the trials sheet (one per team: blade count, length, pitch, and shape for every run, with columns for revolutions in thirty seconds and clips lifted. The sheet is the experiment, and a run that is not written down did not happen)

activities.name: Wind Turbine Blade Trials

photo.alt: Wind turbine design 001
photo.caption: Wind turbine design 001.
photo.credit: Photo: Gulraize1, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The fan is the weather and it is caged weather: the grille stays on, the fan is positioned and switched by the adult or at the adult's word, and no hand, blade, pencil, or trials sheet goes near the rig while it is running. Blades are changed only with the fan off and the hub still, and a blade that leaves the hub during a run stops the session's rig until the adult has re-checked the mounting, because a loose blade at fan speed is the one accident this record designs out in advance. Blade stock is card, cut at the bench with the bench's scissors, and finished blades are checked for the stiffness that keeps them out of the grille: a blade that flexes into the fan's face is retired at inspection, before it can be tested into trouble. The rig's stand is weighted and its fall zone kept clear; threads and clips are small parts that live on the tray and are counted at clearing-up like any bench's small stock. The generator variation, if used at all, is low-voltage hobby equipment assembled by the adult beforehand. No mains electricity is anywhere near this record's benches, ever.
activities.setup: Set the rig up like an instrument, because it is one: the fan goes at a measured distance from the hub, marked on the floor or the bench with tape, in metres, and recorded on every trials sheet, because a rig that drifts between runs makes liars of all the data downstream. Test the hub yourself: it must spin freely for several seconds from a breath of air, the thread must wind evenly on the axle, and the clip load must rise without snagging. Cut the control blade set before the teams arrive, three identical plain blades at a middling pitch, and run the rig three times with it, recording your own numbers: those three runs are the session's honesty anchor, the proof that the rig gives the same design the same answer twice, and any rig that cannot repeat its own control numbers is fixed at setup, not argued with during the trials. Decide the variable list on paper now, blade count, blade length, pitch angle, blade shape (width and curve), because the framing will restrict each team to changing them one at a time, and a restriction announced after the first run is a rule invented to spoil somebody's result.
steps: The framing, at the rig, the control numbers on display: 'This fan is the weather, and it does not play favourites: same speed, same distance, every run. Your turbine will be judged by two measures and no opinions, revolutions in thirty seconds, counted; and paper clips lifted on the thread, counted. Here is the law that makes this engineering instead of tinkering: one variable at a time. Change the blade count OR the pitch OR the length, run it, write it down, and you will learn what that variable does. Change two things and you have learned nothing twice. The sheet will not tell you which change did it, and neither will I. Every run goes on the sheet with its full design written out, because a winning blade nobody can re-cut is a rumour, and this room deals in designs.' The control set is run once more, live, and its numbers compared with setup's: the rig repeats, the room sees it repeat, and the trials begin from trust in the instrument. The foundation every honest experiment stands on.

First trials, the blade-count question: each team runs the control design, then their count variants, two blades, three, four, six, at the control's own pitch and length, three runs each, sheet filling in the open. The counting craft is taught while the numbers land: revolutions are counted by two counters independently and compared before they are written (a count the counters dispute is a run repeated, not averaged. The sheet has no column for guesses), and clips are added one at a time until the turbine stalls or the thirty seconds end, with the stalled number recorded as honestly as any success ('lifts four, stalls at five' is data; 'about five' is not). Teams present their count findings in the session's official shape, the best count, its numbers, and the margin, and disagreements between teams are settled at the rig, by re-running, never by seniority.

Second trials, pitch and length: with blade count settled by each team's own evidence, teams take up pitch, the angle of the blade to the wind, set with the protractor and recorded in degrees, working their angle up in steps across runs and watching the two measures answer differently, because pitch is where the sheet starts teaching the session's real lesson: the design that spins fastest is not always the design that lifts most, and a turbine's job decides which measure matters. Length follows the same discipline. The adult's bench talk in this round is all design-of-experiments: interactions are named when the data hints at them ('your long blades only beat the short at the steeper pitch. That is an interaction, write it exactly that way'), and every claim in the room is required to carry its run numbers like a passport.

The workload final: each team declares its champion design, chosen from its own sheet, re-cut exactly from its recorded pattern, because the final runs fresh blades, not the battered heroes of the trials, and the champions meet the session's stated workload: the standard clip load, lifted against the clock, revolutions counted, three runs each, at the fan's standard setting on the standard marks. The final's rules were the framing's rules and no new ones appear: one design, as documented; any failure, a blade tearing, a thread slipping, is recorded as the run's result and the design's sheet carries it, because a champion that fails under test conditions has told the room something the room paid a session to learn.

The debrief, sheets in hand: each team presents its design's story as the sheet tells it, the variable that mattered most, the result that surprised them, the run they would stake their name on, and the room builds the session's conclusions on the wall from the sheets alone: fastest design, strongest design, and the design each team would actually build if the turbine had a real job, with the job named, because the session's last lesson is that engineering answers are answers to a purpose. The tell-back closes the trials: 'You came in with opinions about blades and you are leaving with evidence. You changed one thing at a time, you wrote everything down, you let a load of paper clips overrule your favourites, and the designs on this wall can be re-cut by strangers and will do again what they did today. That is the whole difference between making something that works and knowing why it works. The second one is engineering, and you have done it.' The champion sheets and blade patterns are filed together as the rig's permanent record, first page of the next session's evidence.
activities.tagline: One fan, one hub, many blades: change a single variable at a time and let two honest measures, revolutions and lifted clips, judge every design.

variations.easier: A two-variable version: blade count only, three designs, three runs each, the whole discipline of the sheet inside thirty minutes, for a first trials group or a short session.
variations.harder: A generator version (a confident group, with the adult's electrical discipline absolute): the hub drives a tiny hobby motor as a generator and a meter replaces the clip count as the second measure. Read by the adult's setup, never rewired by the teams; the variables, the sheet, and the law are identical.

activities.inclusion: The hand in this record is any hand, or none: a passage can be copied by the keeper's own writing, dictated to a willing scribe at the keeper's exact words (the entry is the keeper's; the penmanship is a detail the book does not grade), typed and pasted in where that is the keeper's way of keeping, or held as a photographed page the keeper transcribes later. The copying's slowness is the mechanism, and every route that preserves the close reading preserves the record. The index, the book's real engine, is pure judgement and is open at full size to every keeper: themes are chosen, named, and searched in whatever register the keeper thinks in, and a theme given as a drawing, a colour, or a single held-up word at indexing time is filed as truly as a written one. The sharing round runs by invitation in every register, read, signed, shown from the keeper's own hands at the distance the keeper chooses, and passing is a complete contribution, protected in the framing's own words. A keeper whose whole session is one passage, well chosen and honestly indexed, has used the record at its full depth, and the closing says so in general terms so that it is heard by the person it belongs to.

materials.item: a blank book worth keeping (hardback, paper that takes ink without bleeding. The keeper's own, chosen, not issued; a commonplace book kept in a book its keeper dislikes is a diary of resentment)
a pen the keeper likes writing with (the copying is by hand and by design, so the instrument matters and the choice of it is part of the first session)

source material to hunt in (the room's books, poems, speeches, song lyrics the keeper knows by heart, family sayings, lines remembered from anywhere. The hunt is the keeper's taste at work, and no canon is issued)
index pages reserved at the back from the first day (the book's second half of genius: every entry will be findable, by theme, in the keeper's own words)

activities.name: Commonplace Book, First Pages

photo.alt: Commonplace Book of Kate Chopin, 1867 1870 DPLA 11b8c9d52810bb6e1a8b00e05178ad2e (page 122)
photo.caption: Commonplace Book of Kate Chopin, 1867 1870 DPLA 11b8c9d52810bb6e1a8b00e05178ad2e (page 122).
photo.credit: Photo: Chopin, Kate, 1850-1904, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The book's privacy is its safety system and it is absolute: a commonplace book is read by its keeper and by nobody else without the keeper's invitation, given freely for that reading, not borrowed, not passed around in the sharing round, not photographed, not quoted back at its keeper in jest, and the adult keeps their own book under the same law and is seen to keep it. Provenance honesty is the record's other law, taught as craft rather than policed as crime: a passage copied from memory is labelled from memory, a source half-remembered is written as half-remembered, and nothing in a keeper's book may be dressed in a grander source than it has, because the book's whole authority, decades from now, rests on its keeper being able to trust what its younger self wrote. Materials are ordinary and personal, pens chosen by their keepers, books kept by their owners, and the session's only physical rule is the room's ordinary one: a silent working room is arranged so that anyone who needs to move, stretch, or step out can do so without ceremony or explanation.
activities.setup: Prepare the room, not the content: this record's adult work is almost entirely restraint. Gather a spread of source material rich enough to hunt in, poetry, speeches, essays, reference books with strong sentences in them, the texts the group is already studying, and resist, completely, the urge to prepare a list of quotations worth copying: the moment the adult supplies the passages, the book becomes homework with a ribbon in it. Prepare instead the book's architecture on a demonstration page you will show and then put away: a passage copied entire, its source named honestly beneath it (author, work, and where you found it), a keeper's note of a line or two saying why this one, and, demonstrated last, because it is the point, its index entry at the back, under a theme word the keeper chose. Set the session's privacy law in the room's arrangement itself: books open on laps and tables, read by their keepers only, and the sharing round later is by invitation, from the keeper's own mouth, never by passing books around.
steps: The framing, books still closed: 'For about five hundred years, people who intended to think for a living kept a book like this. Not a diary, a diary records your days. A commonplace book records other minds: the sentences you meet that are too good to leave behind, copied out by your own hand, in your own order, under your own themes. A commonplace book is a conversation with people who are not in the room, some of them dead for centuries, all of them still talking, because you copied them down. Your hand matters: copying is slow, and the slowness is the mechanism. A passage you have written out letter by letter has been read more closely than anything you have ever photographed with your eyes. The laws: you choose everything. Nothing is assigned, nothing is graded, and spelling a great sentence slightly wrong because you copied it from memory is not an error in this book. It is evidence of what your mind kept, and you will note 'from memory' beside it like an honest scholar.'

First pages, the hunt: keepers open their books and hunt. The room's work is silent and various, reading, pausing, the particular stillness of a person deciding whether a sentence earns a page. Each keeper copies their first passage entire, names its source beneath it as honestly as they can (found in a named book, remembered from a song, 'overheard, author unknown'. Every provenance is acceptable except a false one), and writes their keeper's note: why this one, in a line or two, addressed to nobody ('because it is the truest thing anyone has said about losing'; 'because I want to be able to say it like this one day'). The adult keeps a book too, in the same silence, under the same laws, a room where the adult also hunts is a room where hunting is real work and not a task with a warden. Time is protected: nobody is asked how many they have found, and a keeper who copies one passage in the whole session and notes it well has used the session exactly right.

The index, the book's engine: with the first entries made, keepers turn to the reserved back pages and index what they have copied, not by author, but by the theme they would one day search under when they needed the sentence again: courage, home, weather, beginning again, how to lose. This is the session's quietly radical work, and the adult names it while it happens: 'Your index is your philosophy. Two keepers can copy the same passage and file it under different themes, and both filings are true. The theme is where YOU would look for it in a bad week, and nobody can assign that.' A theme with one entry is a promise; a theme that starts collecting entries across the year becomes the keeper's portrait of what they care about, drawn without their ever sitting for it. Keepers are shown the demonstration index once more if they want it. Then the demonstration book is put away for good, because the architecture is theirs now to keep or quietly change.

The sharing round, by invitation only: the adult opens it by reading one entry from their own book, passage, source, note, and its index theme, modelling the full ceremony at full size, including the honesty entries ('from memory, and I may have it wrong'). Then the invitation passes around the room and is declined as easily as it is accepted: a keeper may read a passage they copied, or describe a theme that has started in their index without reading anything filed under it, or pass, and all three are complete contributions. Nothing is passed hand to hand. A passage read aloud is received with the room's one permitted response, the keeper is thanked by name for the find ('thank you for finding that'), because the find is the keeper's work even where the words are not, and the record is careful to honour the right thing.

Closing, and the book's life after the session: keepers write the date on the inside cover with a line the adult dictates and the room adopts, 'Begun on this date, kept honestly, added to whenever a sentence earns it', and the session's practical future is settled in the open: where books live between sessions (with their keepers; the book that stays in a drawer at school is a book that stops growing), and the standing invitation that opens future sessions, the first five minutes of any later gathering can be commonplace minutes, hunts and indexing, whenever the keepers call for them. The tell-back is said with the books closed in their keepers' hands: 'You have each started the only book that will ever contain exactly your taste. It will argue with you at twenty, you will find passages your older self cannot believe you loved, and themes you cannot believe you named so early, and that argument is not the book failing. That argument is the book working, across the longest distance a school exercise ever travels: the distance between who is copying today and who will be reading then.'
activities.tagline: Other people's best sentences, copied by hand into a book that is yours: a centuries-old way to build a mind, and an index that argues back.

variations.easier: A first-pages-only version: the framing, one passage hunted and indexed, the inside-cover line, the whole founding ceremony inside twenty minutes, for a group that will keep its books in later sessions of its own.
variations.harder: A themed version: a session whose hunt is fenced to one territory, beginnings, at the start of a year; leave-takings, at its end, with keepers' indexes afterwards showing how differently one theme can be stocked by different minds.

activities.inclusion: Teaching pairs are built for every kind of teacher: the demonstrator and the room-watcher are equal halves of the craft, and a pair can divide them as their strengths run, the partner who watches attention, times the minutes, and moves to the stuck child is doing the work experienced teachers call the real job. Explanations can be given in speech, in gesture and demonstration (the session's preferred channel for young children anyway), with picture-step cards the pair draws for their own plan, or by a partner's voice at the demonstrator's direction, the youngers judge the teaching by whether their hands can do the thing, and every clear channel passes that test at full marks. The debrief's evidence, the promise kept or not, in the youngers' hands, is the same for every pair and is read aloud from the cards, so no pair's standing depends on fluent self-presentation. A pair whose session fails honestly and whose debrief reads the failure precisely has learned the record's deepest content, and the closing protects that truth by naming it in general terms, at full size, where the pair it belongs to can hear it.

materials.item: the teach-back plans (one per teaching pair, on one page: what the youngers will be able to DO at the end that they could not do at the start, one skill, named in one sentence, the steps to it, and the plan's honest timing, rehearsed against a clock)
materials for the skill, in the youngers' sizes and numbers (prepared by the teaching pair, counted, with spares. A session that runs out of materials teaches only that its teachers ran out)

the youngers themselves, a small group by arrangement with their own adult (six to ten children, whose adult stays in the room throughout. The session's safeguarding shape, stated to everyone in advance)
a feedback card for the youngers' adult (three prompts only: where the youngers' attention was fullest, where it thinned, and one thing the teachers did that worked, observed, specific, and kind)

activities.name: Teach-Back to the Youngers
activities.safety: The safeguarding shape is structural and is stated to everyone in advance: the youngers' own adult is present in the room for the entire session and retains all authority over their group. The teen teachers are never alone with the younger children, never responsible for their discipline, toileting, medication, or movement outside the session's room, and any need of that kind is handed to the youngers' adult immediately and kindly. Physical contact is limited to what a younger child initiates (a high-five, a handshake), teachers demonstrate on materials and on their own hands, guide by pointing and by showing again, and never adjust a child's body, hands, or posture. Skills are chosen from the safe shelf for the youngers' actual age: no sharps, no heat, no small parts for the youngest groups, no food, and the teaching pairs' materials are checked against that list by the adult when the plans are approved. A plan that is brilliant and unsafe is rewritten, and the rewriting is presented as the profession working, because it is. The youngers' names and the session's details stay inside the arrangement: no photographs except under the youngers' setting's own ordinary permissions, arranged through their adult, and the feedback card names situations, never children's shortcomings.
activities.setup: Arrange the session like the responsibility it is: agree the youngers' group, their adult's constant presence, the room, and the time with everyone concerned before any planning begins. The teach-back never happens by ambush, and the youngers' adult is a partner in it, briefed on the plan and holding their ordinary authority throughout. Set the planning bar in advance and in writing: ONE skill, small enough to be true ('by the end, the youngers will be able to tie a reef knot / fold a paper crane that flies / keep a four-count rhythm and stop together'), teachable in ten minutes to the age they actually are, and require each pair to state the youngers' age and plan to that age's real attention, real hands, real vocabulary, which the pairs research by asking the youngers' adult three questions beforehand (what do they love, what do they find hard, what words won't land). Prepare the room for two audiences at once: the youngers' working space at their height, the teachers' standing places, and a clock the teachers can see, because the ten minutes is a promise.
steps: The framing, to the teaching pairs before the youngers arrive: 'Teaching is the final exam nobody grades. You have planned a session for real children, who will not pretend to learn to be polite. Their attention is the honest mark scheme: when it is full, your teaching is working; when it thins, that is information about the teaching, in the moment, and good teachers read it and adjust. They do not blame the class. The laws are these, and they are the profession's own: the youngers' adult is in charge of the youngers, always. Discipline is never your job, behaviour is never your problem to solve in front of the room, and any child who needs something beyond your session goes to their adult with your help, kindly, at once. You never touch the youngers except a offered handshake or high-five they initiate. You teach in pairs so one of you can always be watching the room while the other demonstrates. And you will open by learning their names, because a teacher who does not know the class's names is performing at them.'

Rehearsal, with the clock: pairs run their sessions to each other, full size, at the youngers' imagined height and pace, demonstrations done slowly, instructions given in the short sentences the plan promised, and the watching pairs marking against the plan's one question: could a child DO the next step from what was just said and shown, without guessing? Every place a watching pair has to guess is a place the plan is rewritten, in the room, before the youngers come near it. Timing is rehearsed honestly: a session that runs fourteen minutes in rehearsal is a ten-minute session with four minutes of somebody's material still in it, and the cutting is done at rehearsal, kindly and by its owners. A tighter session that lands beats a complete one that dissolves, and the youngers' thinning attention at minute eleven will deliver the same verdict less kindly if the pairs do not deliver it first.

The session itself: the youngers arrive with their adult, are greeted by name as the pairs learn them, and the teach-back opens with the teachers' one-sentence promise, said to the children directly: 'By the end, you will be able to, ' and the skill, named plainly, so the youngers know what the ten minutes is FOR. Teaching proceeds by the rehearsed shape, show it whole once, slowly; break it into its steps; the youngers do each step with the teachers moving among them, one teaching, one watching the room exactly as rehearsed; errors are corrected as information ('the loop goes the other way, like this. Yes, that is it') and never as verdicts. The watching teacher's eyes are the session's management: a child finished early gets the plan's extension, a child stuck gets a teacher beside them, and the room's energy is read like weather and answered by pace, faster where it flags, a breath where it frazzles, because classroom craft is weather work and these ten minutes are the pairs' first honest shift at it.

The youngers' verdict and the close: the session ends when its promise is testable, and it is tested by the children doing the skill unaided, all at once, at their teachers' invitation, the reef knot tied, the crane flown, the rhythm kept and stopped together, while the teachers watch their own promise kept or not kept in other people's hands, which is the moment the record exists for. Applause is given to the youngers, by name as far as the teachers can manage it, for specific things ('you held the rhythm through the hard bar'), and the youngers leave with their work, their adult, and the teachers' thanks. The feedback card is completed by the youngers' adult before anyone disperses and handed to the pairs unread by anyone else first: it is theirs, it is specific, and its three prompts were chosen so that it tells them where their teaching actually landed, from the one professional witness in the room.

The debrief, pairs and cards together: each pair reads its card, then gives its own account in the session's official shape, the promise, whether the youngers' hands kept it, the moment attention was fullest and what the teaching was doing then, the moment it thinned and what they did, and the adult's only marks are questions that return the pairs to their own evidence. The tell-back closes the record: 'You stood in front of real learners with something to give them, and you gave it in their size, at their pace, under their adult's eye, and you watched their hands to find out if it worked. Most people talk about teaching for years before anyone lets them discover that attention cannot be commanded, only earned, minute by minute, by the clarity of what you show. You have the discovery now, at full size, with a card to prove where it landed. Whatever you teach next, a class, a team, a younger sibling at a kitchen table, starts from what your hands learned today.' Plans and cards are filed by pair, as the first documents of a teaching portfolio the pairs may be building longer than they know.
activities.tagline: Teens prepare and deliver a real ten-minute session for younger children: rehearsed, supervised, and marked only by the youngers' attention.

variations.easier: A five-minute version: one micro-skill (a knot, a clapping pattern, a fold) taught to a group of four youngers, the full shape (promise, rehearsal, verdict) at the smallest honest size, for a pairs' first teach-back.
variations.harder: A return version: the same pairs teach the same youngers a second session a month later, building on the first skill. The feedback card's second reading, against the first, is where the pairs can watch their own teaching change, which is the deepest lesson the record offers.

activities.inclusion: Heap work divides into jobs at every strength: the thermometer is read by one pair of hands and called aloud to the ledger-keeper, who may be seated at the bay's edge in the dry with the book, the readings, the weather column and the stall reasoning are the heap's intellectual core, and they are a seated job done at full authority. Turning itself scales honestly: a fork can be worked by a pair sharing the lift, the sieve can be shaken by turns or rocked by two, and the barrow runs to the beds go at the carrier's pace over the route the crew has walked for firm, step-free ground before building day. The ledger welcomes every register. A turning note can be written, dictated to the keeper verbatim, or given as the round's spoken report the keeper records with the reporter's name attached. The rota is published a season ahead, so every crew member's weeks are known, swappable by agreement, and never sprung on anyone. A heap kept by rota is a heap nobody has to be surprised by.

materials.item: a compost bay or a marked heap site in a corner the adults approve (shaded, drained, reachable with a full fork in all weathers, and far enough from eating areas that the heap's working smell is the heap's own business)
a long-stem compost thermometer (the heap's instrument, pushed to the core, left to settle, read in place; no other thermometer in the building reaches the middle of a heap and survives)

greens and browns stock, kept separately until layering (grass clippings, kitchen vegetable scraps with no meat, no dairy and no oils among them; and dry leaves, shredded card, or straw. The browns bin should never be the empty one)
a garden fork per turning pair, work gloves for every hand that touches the heap, and the ledger (a hardback book that lives with the adults. The heap's memory across the whole season)

activities.name: Compost Heap Temperature Ledger

photo.alt: A gloved hand lifting compost in a straw-covered heap, a temperature gauge resting in the pile
photo.caption: Reading the heap: a hand turns the compost while the temperature gauge sits in the pile doing its job.
photo.credit: Photo: SuSanA Secretariat, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Gloves are the heap's uniform: no bare hand goes into the heap, ever, because a working heap holds sharp surprises, glass, thorns, the fork somebody lost, alongside its citizens, and its warmth is not a cleanliness certificate. Forks travel point-down, rest point-down, and are counted out and back like the tools they are; turning pairs keep a fork's length from each other and nobody forks toward another person. The scraps rule is absolute and hygienic as much as horticultural: no meat, no dairy, no oils, no cooked food. A heap fed wrongly draws the wrong visitors and earns the wrong smells, and a violation found is removed the day it is found. Hands are washed with soap after every heap session, before food, without exception or shortcut, and the thermometer is washed after every reading round for the same reason. Anyone with a cut on a working hand covers it before gloves go on; the heap will still be there next week, and the rota has understudies by design.
activities.setup: Walk the site before the group is offered the heap, and choose it like the season-long commitment it is: the bay must drain after rain rather than drown, sit where a loaded fork can be carried without crossing play space, and stand on bare earth if the land allows, because a heap is in conversation with the ground under it. Stock the two bins before building day, a heap cannot be layered from good intentions, and test the thermometer in warm water against a second reading so the crew's first core temperature is taken on an instrument that has already told the truth once. Read the scraps rule to yourself until you can say it without notes: vegetable matter only, nothing that was ever meat, dairy, oil or cooked food, because the rule is what keeps a heap a heap instead of a nuisance. Set the ledger's first pages up in advance, build date, layers as planned, the turning rota's empty grid, and the temperature table with its date, weather, and reading columns, so the book is ready to be the record from the first forkful.
steps: Building day, the framing said at the empty bay: 'The heap is alive, and the ledger is how you know. A compost heap is not a rubbish pile with good PR. It is a city of small lives eating what we layer, and like any city it has a temperature, a diet, and weather. We build it in layers today: browns, greens, browns, greens, each layer damp as a wrung cloth, nothing packed down hard, air left in the structure because the citizens breathe. Then we keep it. A rota turns it, a thermometer reads it every week on the same day, and the ledger records what the heap actually did, rose, fell, stalled, because a heap you only visit when it smells interesting is a story, and a heap with a ledger is a season of evidence.' The layers go in as described, each one named aloud as it lands, the first temperature taken at the core before the group leaves, however unimpressive the number. Day one's reading is the baseline every later reading is honest against.

The weekly round, run by the rota pair whose names head that week's page: the thermometer goes to the core at three points, settles, and is read in place, and all three readings go in the book with the day's weather beside them, because a heap read without its weather is a number without a season. The pair inspects as they read: moisture squeezed from a gloved handful (a drop or two is right; a stream means too wet and the remedy is browns and a turn; dust means too dry and the remedy is water and a turn), and the heap's smell reported in the ledger's plain categories, earthy, sweet, sharp, wrong, with sharp or wrong triggering a turning there and then rather than a note for next week. Readings are never rounded toward the interesting: a falling temperature is written as falling, in the same ink as a rise, because the ledger's authority is exactly that it does not care which way the news points.

Turning day, when the rota calls it or the readings demand it: the heap is forked from one bay to the next (or onto its sheet and back), outside to the middle, middle to the outside, so every part of the city gets its season in the hot core and its season at the cool edge. Turners work in pairs with gloves on, forks carried point-down between lifts, and anything that should not be there, the plastic, the stray can, the scraps-rule violation somebody's lunch left behind, is lifted out and recorded in the ledger without drama: contamination found is a finding, and the book keeps findings. A turn is also the heap's census: the pair notes what has vanished (layered greens rarely survive a fortnight recognisable), what persists (woody browns keep their shape longest, which is information about carbon, not failure), and what has arrived, the worms, the beetles, the white threads of the heap's working citizens, each written as observed, never as decoration.

The stall protocol, taught before the first stall so nobody improvises: when the ledger shows two flat or falling readings in a row, the crew reads the book backwards before touching the heap, moisture notes, the last turn's date, the layers since, and names the likeliest cause in the ledger from the evidence the book itself holds: too dry, too wet, too many greens, too few, cold weather slowing the whole city honestly. One remedy is applied, one only, and written beside the prediction it carries ('added two barrows of browns and turned, expect a rise within the week'), so the next reading can grade the reasoning and not just the heap. A stall that survives two honest remedies is reported to the adults as a stall, with the book open at the evidence. The record's rule is that a heap is allowed to refuse, and a crew that reports a refusal with its workings has done the job properly.

Season's end, the harvest of the heap: the finished material is sieved by the crew, the fine, dark, earthy fraction goes to the beds in barrows, credited in the ledger with its weight or barrow count and the beds it fed, and the coarse fraction goes back as the starter layer of the next heap, carrying the city's citizens with it. The closing page is written together at the bay: the season's highest core reading and its date, the fastest rise after a turn, the stall that taught the most, and the one instruction the crew would hand the next crew, earned at fork length. The tell-back is said over the closed book: 'This heap ate a season of what the site threw away and paid it back as soil, and we know that the way you know anything, because we measured it, weekly, in the rain, and wrote down the readings we did not like in the same ink as the ones we did. The heap was alive. The ledger is how we know. Next season's crew starts from your book, not from zero.' The thermometer is washed, dried, and stored with the ledger where the next crew will find both together.
activities.tagline: A working compost heap run by teens: built in layers, turned on a rota, and read weekly by thermometer. The heat is the evidence it is alive.

variations.easier: A two-bay version (sites with a second bay): two heaps run a fortnight apart on the same rota, and the ledger keeps a comparison page, two cities, one weather, and the differences between their curves are where the season's real reading lives.
variations.harder: A winter-watch version: the heap is built in autumn and only read, never turned, through the cold months, the ledger tracks how long the core holds its heat against the season, and the spring turn is graded against the winter's curve.

activities.inclusion: Forecasting is a desk of many chairs by design: the evening round needs a thermometer reader, a sky witness, a wind witness, a keeper of the ledger and the forecaster who signs, and the signing, the desk's highest honour, belongs to whoever weighed the evidence best that week, not to whoever walked furthest to gather it. Readings can be called from the garden path while a partner reads at the beds; evidence can be given in any register, spoken, written on the round's slate, pointed to on the ledger's own comparison pages, and the morning verdict is read aloud in full at the board, so no member's season depends on small print in cold hands. The rota is published for the whole season ahead, pairs are fixed so nobody rounds alone, and a forecaster who cannot make an evening hands the witnesses' slate to their pair with the desk's blessing recorded in the book: the forecast is the desk's, whoever the dusk sends.

materials.item: a minimum thermometer at bed height in the garden or growing area (the desk's instrument. Read at dusk, reset after reading, its overnight minimum is the number the morning check will grade)
