the desk's sources (an adult-checked weather service forecast for the site, looked at together each evening. The desk uses it as one witness among several, never as the answer)
the forecast board and ledger (the board where tonight's signed forecast is posted for the gardeners; the ledger where forecasts, evidence and morning verdicts accumulate across the frost season)
fleece and covers, ready folded by the beds (the forecast has a purpose: when the desk calls frost, the gardeners who read the board can act on it. A forecast nobody can use is a diary)

activities.name: First Frost Forecast Desk

photo.alt: Frost-covered trees beside a railway bridge over a misty river at sunrise
photo.caption: A hard frost morning: the white rime the forecast desk tries to call the night before.
photo.credit: Photo: Teemu Vehkaoja (TeVe), CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Evening rounds run in the season's real dark and cold, and are planned like it: the route to the thermometer is walked in daylight first, torches are carried by the reader and a partner, nobody goes to the beds alone, and the desk's hour is early enough that the round is a task, not an expedition. Cold is dressed for, not endured as a point of pride. The round is twenty minutes of standing readings, and a forecaster who is shivering reads nothing accurately, including themselves. The thermometer is handled as glass instruments are handled, over the beds and never over paths, and if it is a spirit thermometer it is still treated as fragile kit; a breakage is reported to the adults the same evening, not discovered by the morning check. The desk advises; it never acts on other people's plants. Covers are lifted and laid by the gardeners who own the beds, because a forecast desk that starts moving other growers' fleece has mistaken its authority, and the boundary is stated in the framing before the first forecast is signed.
activities.setup: Set the thermometer before the season's first cold nights are due, at the height frost actually strikes, down among the beds, not up at eye level on a warm wall, and read it yourself for three evenings running to learn what its numbers mean against the mornings that follow, because a desk that has not calibrated its own instrument will sign forecasts it does not understand. Agree with the gardeners, in person, what the board is for: the desk forecasts the overnight minimum at the beds and calls FROST or NO FROST by a stated hour each evening; the gardeners decide what to cover; the desk never touches another grower's plants. Choose that hour so the forecast is usable, early enough to cover by, late enough that the evening's evidence is in, and fix the season's span in the ledger now: first forecast date, last forecast date, and the rule that the desk publishes every night in between, cold-looking or mild, because a forecast desk that only appears when drama threatens is a fair-weather friend with a thermometer. Prepare the board where gardeners actually pass, with the signature line at its foot: every forecast is signed by the forecaster who issued it.
steps: The framing, at the board, on the season's first evening: 'A forecast is a promise you check in the morning. This desk does not predict the weather in general. It answers one question for the people who grow here: will frost touch the beds tonight, and how cold will the coldest hour be? We answer it from evidence: the thermometer's own record, the sky at dusk, the wind or its absence, and the official forecast read as one witness, cross-examined like the others. Then we sign it. Tomorrow morning, before anything else, the desk reads the minimum the night actually left and grades its own forecast in the ledger, right, wrong, or lucky, and lucky is a grade, and it is not a compliment. Gardeners will cover real plants on our word. That is the weight this board carries, and it is why the signature is on it.' The first evening's evidence is gathered and the first forecast signed at full ceremony, however mild the night looks. The desk's habits are built on the easy nights so they hold on the hard ones.

The evening round, run the same way all season so the forecasts stay comparable: the thermometer is read from last night and reset; tonight's witnesses are taken in order. The sky (clear skies let the ground's heat escape; cloud is a blanket and the desk says which it sees), the wind (moving air mixes the cold away from the beds; a still, clear dusk is the frost's favourite weather and the round names it exactly so), the feel of the air at bed height compared with the desk's own record of similar evenings in the ledger, and the official forecast, read aloud and minuted with its number, neither worshipped nor ignored. The forecaster on duty weighs the witnesses in the open, in front of the desk, and states the call and the predicted minimum as one signed sentence on the board: a call that cannot be written as a number and a word, FROST or NO FROST, has not been made yet.

Disagreement round, used whenever the witnesses argue: when the official number says safe and the dusk says danger (or the reverse), the desk does not average its witnesses into mush, it names the disagreement on the board under the forecast ('official minimum 4 degrees; desk calls frost in the hollow beds, clear, still dusk and our thermometer's record'), because gardeners deserve the argument, not just the verdict, and because the morning grade is twice as instructive when the losing witness is on record. The desk also grades by place, not just by night: frost is a local animal that settles in hollows and spares slopes, so the ledger keeps its verdicts bed by bed where the thermometer's rounds allow a second reading. A forecast can be right for the top beds and wrong for the low ones on the same night, and a desk that learns its garden's cold corners is worth more each week of the season.

The morning check, the desk's conscience, done before the board is touched: the minimum thermometer is read first, last night's coldest truth at bed height, and the verdict is entered in the ledger against the signed forecast in the season's official shape: RIGHT (the call and the number both held), WRONG (either failed), or LUCKY (the call held for reasons the evidence did not contain, a cloud bank that arrived unscripted at midnight), with lucky recorded at exactly the same size as right, because a desk that hides its luck will start believing its own legend by November. The board is then cleared and the streak kept honestly at its head, forecasts issued, calls right, where every gardener can watch the desk's record grow at the same speed as its reputation, and never faster.

Season's end, the audit evening: when the last forecast date passes, the desk reads its whole ledger aloud to the gardeners, the record entire, the best call of the season and the evidence that carried it, the worst miss and what it taught, the hollow beds' final tally against the slope's, and hands the garden its closing page: the first frost's actual date, the coldest night's actual minimum, and the desk's one earned instruction to next year's forecasters, written by the people the mornings graded. The tell-back closes the season at the board: 'We promised the garden a checked forecast every night, and the mornings checked us back. Some nights we were right, some nights we were wrong, and every one of them is in the book in the same handwriting. A forecast you never grade is a guess with a signature on it. Ours were graded. That is the whole desk.' The thermometer is cleaned, the board stored with the ledger, and the fleece stays folded for the gardeners, whose beds the desk served and never touched.
activities.tagline: Teens run a frost forecast for real gardeners: evening readings, a signed prediction, and a morning check that grades it honestly.

variations.easier: A two-week version (a short cold snap expected): the desk runs for one fortnight around the likeliest frost dates, the full round, signed forecasts and morning grades, compressed into the nights that matter most.
variations.harder: A classroom-window version (no beds to serve): the desk forecasts for a row of tender plants on an outdoor sill the group itself grows. The gardeners are the class, the covers are real, and a miss costs the desk its own seedlings, which is the honest tuition.

activities.inclusion: The preserving line is a row of real jobs at every reach: washing and sorting can be done seated at the table's low end; the day book, the batch's memory and the day's conscience, is kept by a seated keeper whose entries the adult reads before any jar is processed; labelling is fine, unhurried work done sitting, with labels written large, dictated to a partner scribe, or lettered from the batch's stamp set where the site keeps one. The recipe is read aloud entire at the framing and the card stands at the line's centre in the largest clear print the room can make, so no hand's work depends on another's eyes or memory. Tasting is offered, never owed. A crew member who does not taste loses no standing, and the tasting notes take 'not tasted' as a complete entry. The cooling racks and the larder run are arranged on the route the crew walks together for step-free passage before the first jar is filled, so the day's proudest trip, summer, carried to its shelf, is a trip every member of the crew can make.

materials.item: the glut itself (a surplus the site or its gardeners actually have, soft fruit, tomatoes, cucumbers, whatever the season is giving away faster than it can be eaten; sound produce only, chosen by the crew, with anything mouldy or spoiled composted before it reaches the table)

jars and new lids, washed and kept hot as the recipe directs (one size, matching the recipe. Preserving is not the day to improvise with odd jars, because the processing time belongs to the jar as much as to the food)

ONE tested recipe from a recognised preserving authority, printed or copied onto the day's single recipe card (the day's whole law: its quantities, its acid, its processing time, chosen by the adult in advance for the produce in hand)
labels, a marker that survives the larder, and the day book (contents, recipe source, date, batch count, and the crew's names, every jar traceable to its day and its page)

activities.name: Summer Glut Preserving Day

photo.alt: Making Blueberry Jam 6
photo.caption: Making Blueberry Jam 6.
photo.credit: Photo: Quadell, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The recipe's authority is this record's first safety system and it is structural, not advisory: one tested recipe from a recognised preserving authority, followed exactly, quantities, acid, jar size, headspace, processing time, because preserving safety lives in ratios and minutes that cannot be tasted, smelled or guessed, and no crew member, however confident, alters any of them; a change anyone wants is a different tested recipe, chosen by the adult before the day, never an edit made at the pan. All heat processing, the processor, the boiling water, the lifting of hot jars, is the adult's work alone, at a station the crew observes from the marked line; jars are carried cool, two-handed, one at a time. Knives are counted out and back, live only at the chopping station, and washed by their own user. Allergies are checked before the day and again before the tasting, and recorded at the day book's head; produce is sound or it is compost, the sort throws away anything mouldy or spoiled entire, never trimmed-and-kept, because the glut is plentiful and the jars are few. Any jar whose seal fails, whose batch deviated unrecorded, or whose history the book cannot vouch for is fridge-first and eaten within days, and that ruling has no appeal at the table.
activities.setup: Choose the recipe before you choose the day, and choose it the way this record insists: from a recognised preserving authority's tested instructions, matched to the produce the glut actually offers, with its processing method the adult running the session is equipped and willing to run. Read it entire, twice, once for the work and once for the traps: the jar size it assumes, the acid it requires, the headspace it specifies, the processing time at the day's method, because on the day itself the card will be followed, not interpreted, and anything unclear gets settled now, with the authority's text, not at a boiling pan. Count jars against produce honestly (a glut always looks bigger before it is washed), wash and inspect every jar for chips and cracks, a flawed jar is retired to the recycling without a speech, because it will fail at the worst moment or not at all, and neither is acceptable, and lay the room out as the recipe's line: washing, chopping, packing, processing, cooling, labelling, in that order, with the knife station between washing and packing and the adult's processing station at the line's end. Check allergies for every hand and every future taster before a single jar is filled, and write them at the day book's head.
steps: The framing, at the washed and laden table: 'A jar sealed properly is summer kept. Today the glut becomes the larder, and the whole day runs on one law: the recipe is not a suggestion. Its quantities are not flavour preferences we may tune, the acid, the sugar, the time in the processor are the difference between a jar that keeps and a jar that merely looks kept, and nobody at this table can taste that difference, which is exactly why we do not improvise it. We follow the card exactly, we write down what we did, and the jars we cannot vouch for get labelled for the fridge and eaten first, proudly, at the top of the day book, not hidden at the back of a shelf. Teens prep, pack and label. The processing, the boiling, the timing, the seal check, is the adult's station and the adult's alone. Inside those lines, this is your preserving day, and what keeps from it will still be summer in the middle of winter.' The recipe card is read aloud entire by the day's reader before the first knife is lifted, so every hand knows the law it is working under.

Prep line, run at kitchen discipline: produce is washed, sorted a second time at the table (the sort is kinder before washing than after), and chopped or packed to the card's specification, sizes matter here, because the processing time was tested on pieces of the size the recipe names, and a crew that doubles the chunks has quietly rewritten the card. Knives are counted out, used at the chopping station only, washed by their user, and counted back; the line's pace is set by its slowest careful hand and nobody hurries a blade to catch up a pan. Jars are packed as the card directs, the headspace measured with the gauge or marked stick the recipe assumes, rims wiped clean before lids, because a rim with a seed on it is a seal that will fail politely in the dark months later. Every batch is announced to the day book as it is packed: time, jar count, any deviation, and the book's rule is that a deviation is written at the moment it happens, in the open, where the adult at the processing station can rule on it before the jars go in, not after.

Processing, the adult's station, watched and learned from at a respectful distance: the crew observes the full ceremony, jars in as the method directs, the timer set aloud and its start spoken, the processing time kept entire without the lid lifted for curiosity, because the card's minutes are a wall, not a window. While the processor runs, the day's teaching happens at the cooling end of the line: why the acid is in the recipe and what it guards, why the times lengthen with jar size, why a tested recipe from an authority outranks a confident video. The crew is being taught the shape of the knowledge, not encouraged to freelance with it, and the distinction is stated plainly while the jars tick and settle. Jars come out to the cooling racks untouched, undisturbed for the hours the card specifies, with the cooling zone marked and defended: a jar knocked while it is sealing is a jar for the fridge list, and the crew learns to walk around a cooling rack the way sailors walk around a sleeping watch.

Seal check and labelling, the next session or the day's late hour as the card allows: the adult checks every seal by the authority's test and the verdicts are entered batch by batch, sealed, or fridge-first, with the fridge-first jars labelled as such in the same proud hand as the rest, because the day book's honesty is the batch's real shelf life. Labels are written at the table by the crew: contents in plain words, the date, the recipe's source, the batch number from the day book, and any allergen the recipe carries, lettered to be read in a dim larder by somebody who was not here. A jar without a complete label does not leave the room. An anonymous jar is a question nobody should have to open to answer. The first jar of the day is opened and tasted at the table there and then (allergies already checked, the adult tasting first), because a preserving crew that never tastes its own work has kept summer and learned nothing about it.

Closing the day, the larder shelf and the book: sealed jars are carried to their shelf in one trip each, two hands per jar, and the shelf is photographed or listed in the day book, the batch's official existence, with the fridge-first jars at the list's head and a date by which they will be eaten, assigned to a real meal the group will actually have. The closing tell-back is said over the day book: 'This morning this was a glut. More summer than anybody could eat. Tonight it is jars with names, dates and a book that can vouch for every one of them, because we followed one tested recipe exactly and wrote down the day we did it. What keeps from today will be opened in the cold months by people who will read the label and know whose summer it was. That is preserving: not defeating the season, but keeping faith with it.' The recipe card is filed inside the day book's cover. Next glut's crew starts from this day's page, its deviations, its verdicts and its tasting notes, not from an empty table and a confident memory.
activities.tagline: A glut becomes jars: teens wash, chop, pack and label under one tested recipe followed exactly, while the adult runs the processing, summer, kept.

variations.easier: A fridge-only version (no processing equipment or no adult free to run it): the crew makes a refrigerator preserve the card vouches for, a quick pickle or fridge jam by a tested recipe, labelled fridge-first by design, dated short, and eaten within its stated days at a real shared meal.
variations.harder: A labelling-and-audit version (a larder already stocked from earlier days): the teen crew audits the shelves against the day books. Every jar's label checked against its batch page, anonymous or doubtful jars moved to the front for the adults to rule on, and the larder list rewritten true.

activities.inclusion: Crew work divides by strength and reach as honestly as the path divides into stretches: the crew book itself, findings, initials, the outstanding list, the sentence to the owners, is a full keeper's job done walking or seated at the stretch's rest point, at the authority of the person who will be believed by the owners. Drainage pairs share lifts by agreement; waymark renewal is standing, unhurried, one-mark-at-a-time work that suits a member who paces themselves; the stranger test can be walked, wheeled over the stretches the ground allows, or directed. A tester who reads marks from the path's edge and calls what a stranger would miss is doing the test's sharpest job. The route in and out is chosen at setup for the firmest, most step-free line the site offers, and the rota of stretches is published before the pass so every member knows their ground, its length and its rest points in advance. Findings may be dictated to the book-keeper verbatim; no crew member's standing on the pass depends on their handwriting, their pace, or the weight they can fork.

materials.item: the permission, in writing from whoever owns or manages the path (the crew's founding document. Which stretch, what work is welcome, what is not to be touched; carried on the day and its limits stated in the framing)
hand tools only, counted out and back (loppers and secateurs for the overgrowth the permission names, a rake and a spade for drainage work, gloves for every hand, no power tools on a teen crew, ever)
waymarking materials exactly as the permission specifies (the path's own paint, discs or tape standard. The crew renews the path's marks in the path's own language, never invents a prettier one)
the crew book (a hardback log: stretch by stretch, what was found, what was done, what was left for the next crew and why. The path's memory, kept by its keepers)

activities.name: Trail Crew, First Pass

photo.alt: First log moved, and drain created during a trail work party on Herman Creek and Nick Eaton Trails spring 2018. (26943965147)
photo.caption: First log moved, and drain created during a trail work party on Herman Creek and Nick Eaton Trails spring 2018. (26943965147).
photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Forest Service- Pacific Northwest Region, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The permission is the crew's boundary and it is geographic and specific: the named stretch only, the named work only, and any job that turns out bigger than the paper, a fallen tree, a collapsed bank, a broken bridge board, is book work, reported to the owners, never hero work attempted by teenagers with loppers. Tools are counted out and in aloud, travel closed and point-down, and are set down blades-in whenever walkers pass; loppers and secateurs are used two-handed, on wood the user can see entire, never above shoulder height, and never on anything under tension the crew has not read first. Nobody works alone on a stretch, pairs minimum, within call of the adult, and the weather call is the adult's: lightning, ice on the tread, or wind strong enough to bring branches down ends the pass, and the book records the ending as a finding, not a failure. Gloves stay on for clearing and cutting alike; hands are washed before food; and anything sharp the path surrenders, glass, wire, the walker's lost knife, goes into the sharps tin the adult carries, by the adult's gloved hand, never a crew member's pocket.
activities.setup: Get the permission before you promise the crew anything, and get it specifically: walk the stretch with the owner or manager if they will walk it, agree the two ends of the crew's ground by landmarks both parties can name, and write down what is welcome (clearing the drainage grips, cutting back the named overgrowth, renewing waymarks) and what is not (no tree work, no rerouting, no touching fences, walls or signage beyond the marks agreed). Walk the stretch again alone with the crew book and grade it the way the first pass will: drainage grips choked or running, branches at face height by their count, waymarks faded, missing or misleading, litter by the handful or the bagful, so the framing can promise the group a true picture and the work can be divided into stretches a crew can finish. Check the tool store and the gloves, count everything, and decide the carry order now: tools travel closed, point-down, in the middle of the line, and nobody carries a blade and a conversation at the same time.
steps: The framing, at the stretch's near end, permission in the adult's pocket: 'Leave the path better than the weather left it. This path is not ours. It is lent to us for one pass, by the people who own it, and the permission has edges we will respect exactly: this stretch, this work, these marks. A trail crew is not a tidy-up with boots on. We work the path the way its walkers need it: water off the tread, branches off faces, marks a stranger can follow in the rain. Everything we do goes in the crew book, stretch by stretch, including what we find and cannot fix, a collapsed grip, a rotten post, because the book goes back to the path's owners, and a crew that reports honestly is a crew that gets invited back. Walkers pass us all day. We step aside, tools down, and let the path's real users through first: it is their path. We are its guests with forks.' The stretches are assigned, the tool count is called aloud, and the first crew book entry, date, weather, crew names, permission reference, is written before a blade opens.

Drainage round, the pass's first work: the crew walks its stretch slowly and reads the water's intentions. Every grip, ditch and cross-drain is found, and choked ones are cleared by hand and spade: leaves, silt and the season's debris lifted out and scattered downhill off the path, never piled where the next rain will wash it straight back. The rule taught at the first grip and repeated at every one: 'We do not fight water; we remind it where it agreed to go.' Treads that have become channels are noted, not rebuilt, rebuilding a tread is beyond this crew's permission and the book says so plainly where it matters, and any stretch where water is winning outright gets the book's fullest entry: where, how far, what the crew believes it needs, written for the owners as a work order from the people who stood in it. A grip cleared is initialled in the book by the pair who cleared it; drainage is unglamorous and the initials are its honours list.

Overgrowth and waymark round: with drainage running, the crew turns to faces and marks, branches reaching into the walking line at head height are cut back with loppers to the permission's line, cut clean at the collar and the arisings scattered off-path; nothing taller than the crew can reach from the ground is touched, nothing with a nest, a notice or a doubt about it is touched at all, and doubt always wins. Waymarks are renewed as the permission specifies, the path's own colour, the path's own pattern, and every mark is checked from a walker's eye, at a walker's pace, in both directions: a mark you can only find by already knowing the way is a decoration, and the crew repaints or reports it accordingly. Missing marks are entered in the book with their location described the way a stranger would need it ('after the second gate, where the farm track joins'), because the book is written for the owners' next work party as much as for the record.

The stranger test, the pass's examination: when the work is done, the crew walks its whole stretch once as strangers, at walking pace, tools carried closed, following only the path and its marks, reading the tread the way the rain will read it. Whatever the test finds goes in the book without varnish: the grip that still ponds, the mark that hides behind the new growth the crew itself just cut, the stretch where the crew's own boots have churned the edge. Fixed on the spot if it is within permission and minutes, entered as outstanding if it is not. The crew also counts its litter honestly, what it carried out, bagged and weighed by the handful if no scale offers, and enters that too, because a path's first pass is measured partly in what left the path that should never have been on it.

Closing the pass, the book goes back: tools are counted in aloud against the morning's count, washed of mud, and stored; the crew book's final page for the day is written at the path's end, stretches worked, grips cleared by their initials, marks renewed, the outstanding list entire, and the crew's one sentence to the owners, earned at fork length. The tell-back is said on the tread the crew has just worked: 'This path is older than everyone standing on it and busier than we are, and today it drains where it should, spares the faces that pass, and shows its way in both directions, because a crew of teenagers treated it as a responsibility instead of a backdrop. The book says what we did and what we did not do, in the same handwriting. Leave the path better than the weather left it: done, and written down.' A copy of the day's pages goes to the owners with the crew's thanks for the permission. The invitation to a second pass is earned exactly there.
activities.tagline: Teens maintain a real path under permission: drainage cleared, waymarks renewed, and every stretch of work logged in the crew book.

variations.easier: A one-stretch version (a short path or a first crew): a single stretch worked entire, one drainage run, one waymark line, one stranger test, inside the hour; the whole discipline at a length a new crew can finish and sign.
variations.harder: A second-pass version (a returning crew): the crew works from its own book. Last pass's outstanding list is the work order, last pass's cleared grips are inspected first, and the book gains a second handwriting, which is the moment a crew becomes a tradition.

activities.inclusion: Hosting a sky is work at every body's measure: the lead host's tour is a spoken craft learned from the chart in daylight and given standing, seated on the field's stool, or from a chair at the dark zone's edge, the pointing travels by relay hosts around the field, so no guest's view depends on one host's position or reach. The tally slate, the story stops, the cocoa round and the re-finding of lost guests are full host jobs, several of them lying-down jobs on the blankets among the guests, where a host whose place is on the ground is at the party's exact centre. Stories and the tour can be given in the registers the guests need, spoken, signed by a host, told close and quiet to one family at a time, and the chart work in daylight welcomes every hand: drawing the night's sky is preparatory hosting at full standing. A guest who cannot lie back views from a reclined chair the hosts place in the field's front row at setup, by design rather than by exception, because the sky is the one ceiling every seat in this venue faces equally.

materials.item: red torches only, one per host plus spares (torch beams wrapped in red film or red-cellophane. White light is the party's one banned substance, because night vision takes twenty minutes to grow and one careless beam to spend)

the night's own chart (a planisphere set for the date or a chart drawn for that evening's actual sky. The hosts tour what is really up there tonight, checked against an almanac or the adult's sky app in daylight, never a generic poster sky)
blankets and a groundsheet constellation (the viewing field laid out in daylight: where guests lie, where hosts stand, where the drinks table sits outside the dark zone's edge)
a telescope or binoculars if the site has them, host-handled only (guests look; hosts aim, an instrument passed hand to hand in the dark ends the evening looking at the ground)

activities.name: Star Party Hosts

photo.alt: 2024 Night Sky Festival (54072609419)
photo.caption: 2024 Night Sky Festival (54072609419).
photo.credit: Photo: Joshua Tree National Park, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Darkness is managed, never merely enjoyed: the party field is one bounded space the hosts have walked in daylight, its edges known to every guest at the framing, and nobody leaves the field alone or unannounced. A guest who needs the lit path goes with a host, red torch low, because a dark field's one real danger is friendly people moving at different heights and speeds among blankets, ropes and each other. Trip hazards are marked or removed in daylight; the drinks table and its hot cocoa sit outside the dark zone with the adult, and hot drinks travel to the field's edge, never across lying guests. Red light only is a safety rule as well as a courtesy, white beams at face height steal the vision everyone present is walking by. The weather call is the adult's and it is final: cold guests end parties early without debate, the session's length is set for the season's night temperatures, and lightning anywhere in the sky closes the field on the spot. A star party under a storm is not brave, it is finished.
activities.setup: Plan the party in daylight, twice over: first the sky, then the ground. The sky: choose the date for the moon before anything else. A young or absent moon leaves the sky dark for the faint guests, and the hosts build the tour from an almanac's word on what will actually be up: which planets are out and when they set, which constellations stand where at party hour, and one deep guest worth the telescope's time, rehearsed on the chart until every host can find the tour's stops with their eyes shut at noon. Late summer is this record's favoured season, warm dark, the summer triangle overhead, and in August the Perseid meteors falling for anyone patient, but any clear, moon-thin night the almanac vouches for will do. Then the ground, walked in daylight with a host's suspicion: trip hazards marked or moved, the dark zone's edges defined, a lit path, dim, low, and pointed at the ground, from the door to the field, the drinks table placed where its lamp never sees the viewing field, and the cancellation rule agreed in advance and printed on the invitation: cloud decides, the hosts announce by a stated hour, and a cloudy party becomes a story night indoors rather than a fraud under a ceiling of grey.
steps: The framing, at the field's edge as the light goes: 'Darkness is the venue; the hosts protect it. Tonight this field is the darkest room our guests will be in all year, and everything in it works by rules that protect the dark: red light only, voices low, no screens, no beams at faces, because your eyes are instruments that take twenty minutes to tune, and the party is tuned around them. We hosts will walk you up the sky in order: the bright signposts first, then the shapes they anchor, then one guest through the telescope who repays the queue. The stories we tell are told as stories. The old names, the old plots, labelled as the treasures they are, while the things themselves hang over us being none of them and all the brighter for it. If the sky clouds, we will say so, and the party becomes stories and cocoa, honestly announced. Look up when you are ready. The first star you find on your own is yours, and pointing it out to a host is the party's first ceremony.' Guests are given the dark twenty minutes then, lying back, eyes tuning, hosts silent, because a star party that starts talking immediately has mistaken its venue.

The tour, walked in the order rehearsed: the lead host takes the signposts. The evening's planets first, named and pointed with the red torch's beam laid briefly on the grass, never waved at the sky; then the anchor constellations, traced slowly, one line at a time, with the guests' eyes given the full count of ten between lines because a shape drawn too fast is drawn on nobody's sky. Each stop carries its story told at story length, ninety seconds, no more, and told honestly: 'the hunters and bears and queens are the names the old sky-keepers gave; the stars are suns, and both of those are true at once, in different departments.' Hosts stationed around the field repeat the pointing for guests whose angle differs, and the tour doubles back for anyone who lost a shape without embarrassment or comment: losing the thread in a dark sky is the normal condition of beginners, and the party's hosts treat a request to re-find as the compliment it is.

The telescope guest and the meteor watch: the night's deep guest, a planet's rings, a cluster, the moon's edge if the moon is out, is viewed in an ordered queue the hosts run like a gallery: one guest at the eyepiece, hosts aiming and re-aiming between looks because the sky turns under a fixed instrument, every guest told what they are seeing before their eye goes down, so the looking has somewhere to land. Nobody touches the instrument; a bumped telescope is re-aimed by its host without a word of blame, because the queue's mood is part of the optics. Then the formal party dissolves into its second half, by design: blankets, low talk, and the meteor watch. Counting in the open, a tally kept on the hosts' slate, streaks claimed only by the counter who saw them whole. The tally is the party's souvenir and its honesty check: a quiet sky's count of three is entered as three, celebrated as three, and never improved in the retelling on the hosts' side of the slate.

The mid-party reading, a host's quiet round: halfway through, the hosts read the field the way they rehearsed reading it, who is cold (blankets from the store, offered before asked), who is lost (a host lies down beside them and re-finds one bright anchor, conversationally, as one sky-watcher to another), whose children are flagging (the drinks table's cocoa makes its round), and whether the sky has changed its offer, cloud creeping gets announced early and kindly, with the story-night shape ready: 'the sky has closed its second half; the parlour opens with the Perseus story and the chart.' A party that reads its guests can change its shape without breaking its spell, and the hosts practise the announcement as a piece of hospitality, not an apology.

Closing under the sky: the last look is collective, the whole field on its back for the tour's brightest stop revisited in silence, sixty full seconds of it, and then the hosts close the party standing, by name and by thanks, in the tell-back's shape: 'You gave this field your twenty quiet minutes while your eyes tuned, and the sky spent the evening repaying you. Planets by their names, the old shapes standing where the almanac promised, a tally of meteors we counted together and did not improve. We hosted the dark and the dark hosted us. Next clear night, you own the first steps yourselves: one bright signpost, patience, red light, and looking up. The sky keeps office hours every night it is clear. Tonight you learned its address.' White light returns by ceremony, the door lamp first, faces averted, guests given their moment to blink back into the lit world, and the field is cleared by red torch until the last blanket is in, so the venue is left as dark and clean as it was lent.
activities.tagline: Teens host a stargazing evening for families: red-light discipline, a rehearsed sky tour, and the old stories told as stories under the things themselves.

variations.easier: A story-night version (cloud decides, as the invitation promised): the party moves indoors exactly as announced, the chart on the wall, the tour walked in words at the same stops in the same order, the stories told entire, and the telescope guest replaced by the hosts' best account of it, honestly labelled as a description of a thing nobody saw tonight.
variations.harder: A meteor-night version (a shower's peak): the tour shortens to the signposts and the party becomes the watch entire, blankets in a circle, the tally slate at its centre, cocoa at the hour, and the count read aloud at closing as the night's whole result.

activities.inclusion: The watch divides into stations as fairly as the round divides into measures: the thermometer and the clarity cord can be read by a watcher stationed at the bank's firmest point, chosen at setup for step-free arrival, with a partner working the net stations and bringing each tray to the reading point, where the identifying, counting and sheet-keeping happen seated, at full authority, with the guide in the reader's hands. Verdicts are composed aloud by the whole watch from the sheet's readings, so the round's judgement never depends on one member's handwriting, eyesight at the tray, or footing at the edge. Calls in the tray can be pointed, described, or sketched for the guide-keeper to name; an 'unidentified' entered honestly outranks a guess, and the sheet says so, a rule that levels the tray for everyone at it. The rota of rounds is published by season so every watcher knows their dates, their station and their understudy in advance, and the record outlives any single watch's attendance, which is rather the point of keeping one.

materials.item: a stream thermometer on a cord (read in the current, in shade, at mid-depth. The watch's first instrument, lowered from the bank and never carried loose near water)
a clarity tube or a marked white disc on a cord (the round's second measure: how far down the white stays visible, read in the stream's own light and recorded in centimetres, not adjectives)

a long-handled kick net and two white trays (the bank-side sampling kit: the net works from the bank or the shallowest edge the adult approves, the trays hold stream water and whatever the net honestly brings up)

the identification guide and the round sheet (a trusted freshwater guide from the site's shelf, and the watch's record: date, weather, last rain, the three measures, the creatures found by kind and count, and the names of the watch who took them)

activities.name: Stream Watch Testing Round

photo.alt: Water Quality Testing Activity (35760148324)
photo.caption: Water Quality Testing Activity (35760148324).
photo.credit: Photo: Shenandoah National Park from Virginia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Water sets this record's laws and they are read aloud at the bank before the kit opens: the watch works from the bank or the shallowest edge the adult has approved for that day's level, nobody wades, nobody enters water above the ankle, and nobody reaches out over deep or fast water for a dropped anything; a lost thermometer is a lost thermometer, entered in the sheet with regret, and retrieved by an adult or not at all. The go/no-go rule is the adult's and it is not debated at the bank: flood water, a bank collapsing underfoot, or lightning anywhere ends the round, and the cancellation is a respectable entry. Boots with grip are the uniform; the bank is walked, never run, because wet grass over moving water is the round's whole hazard in one sentence. Hands that have held nets and tray water are washed before food, cuts are covered before the bank, and nothing from the stream, no water, no plant, nothing the net brings up, is tasted, ever, by anyone, for any reason the tray can invent. Creatures are returned within the round, in their own water, at their own station; a specimen kept 'to look at later' is a citizen removed, and the watch does not remove citizens.
activities.setup: Choose the reach before the season starts and choose it like a watchkeeper: a stretch of stream the group may legally and safely stand beside, with a bank a teenager can work from without scrambling, water the adult has seen at its ordinary level, and an upstream the adults can describe. What drains into this water is half the reading, and a watch that cannot name its upstream is measuring a rumour. Walk the reach after rain once yourself, or take local word for its temper: the adult's go/no-go rule is set now and never argued at the bank, heavy recent rain, high or discoloured flood water, or any bank made greasy and collapsing cancels the round, which is recorded in the book as cancelled-by-weather with the same respect as a completed round. Set the round sheet's fixed points in advance, the same shaded spot for temperature, the same still edge for clarity, the same net stations, because a round's value is comparability: a stream read at wandering points is a new stream every visit, and the watch is keeping one stream's record, season by season.
steps: The framing, at the bank, kit still closed: 'The stream grades itself; the watch just reads the marks. This water is being marked every day by everything that lives in it, and the fairest markers are the small creatures, because they cannot leave when the water worsens and they cannot pretend when it improves. Some kinds only live where the water is generous; some endure almost anything. So today we take the stream's three measures, its temperature, its clarity, and its citizens, at the same points we always take them, in the same way, and we write down what we find, including the kinds we hoped for and did not find, especially those. Absence is evidence. A tray with only the tough kinds in it is the stream saying something, and our job is to hear it accurately, not to cheer it up. We sample kindly: everything that comes up in the net goes back where it came from, in the water it came from, before we leave this bank. We are the stream's watch, not its collectors.' The go/no-go check is made aloud at the bank, level, colour, bank state, so the crew learns that the watch's first measurement is whether to measure at all.

The measures round, taken in the sheet's order at the fixed points: temperature first, in shade at mid-depth, the thermometer left to settle a full minute while the reader watches the current do its work. A reading snatched early is a reading of the bank's air, and the sheet says so in its margin. Clarity second, at the still edge: the white disc lowered on its cord until it honestly vanishes, the cord marked at the surface, the length read on the bank in centimetres and entered as a number. Two readers take it independently and both numbers go in, disagreements and all, because the sheet grades the readers as kindly as the stream. The weather and the last rain are entered from the watch's own record and the adults' word, never reconstructed from memory at the bank: a round that cannot state its last-rain honestly marks the line 'unknown', which the sheet treats as a complete and respectable entry.

The sampling round, the watch's heart: at each net station, the net is worked from the bank or the shallowest approved edge, a short kick of the streambed's edge stones by booted foot where the adult's rule allows, or a sweep through the marginal plants where it does not, and what the net brings up is tipped gently into a tray of the stream's own water. The tray is given a full minute of stillness before anyone reads it, because the citizens declare themselves by moving, and a tray stirred is a tray silenced. Reading is done with the guide open and the sheet beside it: kinds are named only as far as the evidence allows, the guide's families, not hopeful species, and counted by kind, with 'unidentified, small, swimming' entered as exactly that where the tray defeats the book. Every uncertain call is settled toward the duller answer, by the sheet's standing rule: a watch that inflates its finds is writing fiction in a record book, and the stream will be graded by strangers on this sheet someday.

The verdict, written at the bank before anything is packed: the watch reads its three measures together and enters the round's verdict in the sheet's own shape. What the temperature says against the season, what the clarity says against the last round, and what the citizens say overall: which expected kinds were present, which were absent, and whether the tray's balance has shifted since the last round and in which direction. The verdict names its confidence like a professional: 'three measures agree' or 'the trays argue with the tube, clarity down, citizens steady, recorded as seen.' Then the return: every tray is carried to its own station and tipped back at the water's edge, stones the net disturbed are set back as they lay, and the bank is left without a sign of the watch but the sheet. The round's ethic is stated at the water as the last tray empties: 'We took nothing but readings. The stream keeps its citizens; the watch keeps its word.'

Closing the round, at the table where the sheets live: the new sheet is read against the last two rounds aloud, the stream's short story so far, in numbers and kinds, and the watch enters one line of expectation for the next round ('if the clarity holds, expect the mayfly kinds back at station two'), signed by the round's readers, so the next watch inherits a prediction to grade as well as a protocol to follow. The tell-back closes the round over the filed sheet: 'Today this stream was measured three ways at its own points, by its own rules, and its citizens were counted and returned unharmed. The sheet says what we found and what we failed to find in the same handwriting, and the next round will be graded against it. That is what a watch is: not a visit, a vigilance, the same eyes, the same points, season after season, until the stream's story is long enough to be true.' The net is rinsed in the stream's water, dried off the ground, and stored with the guide and the sheets where the next watch will find the whole kit together.
activities.tagline: Teens test a real stream, its temperature, its clarity, and the small creatures whose presence grades water, and file the round's evidence.

variations.easier: A bank-only version (high water season, a young watch, or a fragile bank): the two instrument measures are taken entire and the sampling is done with a long-handled net from the bank's firmest point. The round's comparability survives, because the points were chosen for exactly this reach.
variations.harder: A two-stream version (a confident second-season watch): a second reach, ideally the same stream above and below a known influence, a drain, a farm, a joining brook, read on the same day by the same watch, with the comparison page written before either verdict is allowed to borrow the other's confidence.

activities.inclusion: Designing is this record's great leveller, and coaching is its second: the panel's jobs, inventory, card-writing, tally-keeping, cue-calling, the ledger's revision page, are full course authority exercised by members whose bodies may be sitting the run out entirely, and the rotation is drawn so design and coaching are honours, not consolations. Every station card carries its easier and harder doors by law, stated in the same size of writing, so an athlete's route through the course is a set of choices the course itself offers, never an exception negotiated in public. Cues can be called, shown on the card held high, or demonstrated by a partner at the station; the clock's changes are signalled by sound and by the coaches' raised hands together, so no athlete's round depends on hearing one voice in a loud room. The map is walked by the whole group before the clock starts, at walking pace, which means every athlete, including any whose movement is wheeled, aided or slow, has rehearsed their own route and their own doors before a single rep is counted.

materials.item: the station stock (the room's honest equipment: mats, cones, ropes, light balls, benches, inventoried by the designers before a single station is proposed, because a circuit designed for equipment that does not exist is fan fiction)

station cards and a marker per station (each card states the move, the count or time, the form cue in five words or fewer, and the easier and harder doors, written by the designers, readable at a glance by a tired athlete)
the course clock (one visible timer for the whole room. Work and rest are the circuit's heartbeat and everybody, athletes and coaches alike, runs on the same pulse)
the design ledger (proposals, test results, cuts and keeps with their reasons. The course's memory, so next term's designers inherit evidence instead of folklore)

activities.name: Circuit Course, Designed and Coached
activities.safety: Form is this record's safety system and it is structural: every station is tested on the designers before any athlete touches it, the adult rules the station list in advance, bodyweight and light equipment only, no maximal efforts, no loads overhead, nothing whose failure is a fall, and any station whose tenth rep cannot be done well is rebuilt or cut in the ledger, in the open, before the course opens. The rest station is a real station on the map with a card of its own, and taking it needs no permission, no explanation and no witness; an athlete who sits out a whole run on it has used the course exactly as designed. Spacing is walked at setup: stations far enough apart that a drifting athlete enters nobody's swing, floor checked dry, equipment checked whole. Water lives at the rest station, the clock's intervals are set for the room's actual fitness and the day's actual heat, and the adult's whistle stops the whole course instantly for any form that risks a body. A stoppage the coaches are taught to welcome as the system working, never as a verdict on their station.
activities.setup: Inventory before imagination: the design panel walks the room and lists what the circuit may honestly use, every mat, cone, rope and square metre of floor, and the adult rules the boundaries in the same walk: no maximal lifts, no heavy loads, nothing thrown at anybody, no station whose failure mode is a fall. The panel then drafts its long list of candidate stations against the course's shape, which is set now and never negotiated mid-session: stations in the high single digits, work intervals short enough that form survives the last one, a rest station designed in as a real station with a card of its own, and every station required to offer an easier door and a harder door on its card, so the course fits the room that arrives rather than the room the designers imagined. Each candidate station is written up provisionally, move, count, cue, and the ledger opens with the whole long list, because the testing round is about to kill a third of it and the dead deserve a record.
steps: The framing, cards in hand, athletes and designers one group: 'A station earns its place by being doable well when tired. Today this course is designed, not dealt: every station on this floor was proposed by somebody here, tested on the designers' own bodies, and kept or cut by what the test showed, and the cuts are in the ledger with their reasons, because a course that hides its rejects teaches nothing. Coaches: your station, your cue, your count. You watch form the way referees watch lines, and a tired athlete's sloppy tenth rep is your information, not their failure. Athletes: the doors are yours. Every card has an easier way in and a harder way up, and taking either is the course working as designed. The only wrong door is the one taken to impress somebody. The clock is the heartbeat. When it speaks, we move. Form is the whole game; counts are just how we keep score of it.' The course map is walked once, station by station, by the whole group before the clock starts, so no athlete meets a station for the first time at full pulse.

Testing round, designers only, run before the course ever opens: the panel works its own long list at full honesty, each station done at the card's count, at working pace, by every designer in turn, while the others watch with the ledger and the session's one merciless question: does the tenth rep look like the first? Stations fail the test in the open and for named reasons: the cue nobody could follow, the move whose form collapsed by rep six, the station that needed a spotter the course does not have, the one that was simply a punishment dressed as exercise. Failures are cut or rebuilt on the spot, a count lowered, a cue rewritten to five honest words, a move swapped for its own foundation, and every outcome is entered in the ledger in the same ink: kept, cut, rebuilt, and the evidence for each. A designer whose favourite station dies in testing is publicly thanked for the kill at the course's opening, because the panel's pride is the course's quality, not its authors' feelings.

First run, coached at full ceremony: the clock starts, the room rotates, and each coach works their station the way the framing promised. Cue called before the count starts, eyes on form, the easier door offered by name to any athlete whose tenth rep is drifting, the harder door opened for any athlete whose form is bored. Coaches keep their station's tally in the ledger's margin as the run proceeds: how many took which door, where form broke, which cue landed and which one nobody heard. The run is data collection wearing a workout's clothes, and the coaches are told so, because a course that is never re-measured after its first run is a first draft with a fan club. The adult walks the whole course continuously and only ever intervenes on form that risks a body; every other correction belongs to the coaches, whose authority the run exists to build.

Revision round, between runs, on the ledger's evidence: the panel reads the tallies aloud and rebuilds the course in the open, the station where everyone took the easier door gets its count re-set, the cue that landed gets promoted to the card in the words that actually worked, the station whose queue formed while others stood empty gets moved or split. Athletes are heard in this round by right, not by favour: one sentence each on the station they would keep exactly as it stands, entered verbatim where the panel asks for it, because the people the course is for are witnesses the design cannot afford to waste. The revised cards are rewritten clean, the ledger's revision page is signed by the panel, and the second run goes out under the new map, shorter if the evidence says shorter, so the room feels a course improve inside a single session, which is the design lesson no lecture delivers.

Closing, the course is handed over: the final run ends on the clock, the panel reads the ledger's day entire, proposals, kills, tallies, revisions, and the course is named and dated on its map, credited to its designers, and filed for the next group that books the room. The tell-back is said at the rest station, where everyone is standing by then anyway: 'This morning this course was a list of guesses. It is a course now, because its designers tested it on themselves, killed what failed, listened to the people who ran it, and changed it in writing. Any one of you can now be handed a room, an inventory and an hour, and return a workout that fits the bodies that arrive. That is coaching, and it is mostly this: propose honestly, test on yourself, watch the tenth rep, and revise in the open.' Cards and ledger are stored together; a course with a good ledger gets re-run by other groups, whose tallies join the book behind the designers' pages.
activities.tagline: Teens design a circuit of stations, test every station on themselves, then coach it for their peers. Design is the workout before the workout.

variations.easier: A four-station version (a small room or a first panel): four stations designed, tested and coached entire inside half an hour, the whole discipline at a size where every designer can coach every station once.
variations.harder: A term-league version: the course is re-run weekly by the same group, the ledger accumulates tallies across the term, stations are promoted, relegated and retired by the evidence, and the term's final course is designed from a season of the book's own numbers.

activities.inclusion: Invention is a table with many seats, and this league's honours run through all of them: the card's five fields are written work, the log is kept at the test's edge by the designers' own recorders, a seated job with the league's whole memory in its hands, and the revision round, where games are actually won, is talk and text at the table, where a designer who never ran a fixture can be the mind that finds the patch. Play itself is built for the room: the constitution's non-elimination law means every player stays in every game, the shelf and the space are the same for all inventors, and a game's easier and harder doors, most teams design them once the strangers have shown them where the game pinches, are praised in the table's marks when they appear. Stranger tests are read aloud from the card as a rule, signals for starts are agreed per game in sight as well as sound, and fixture hosting rotates through every member who wants the whistle, the slate or the boundary line. A withdrawn game, honestly logged, stands in the honours beside the winners. The league's way of saying that judgement, in any body, is the sport.

materials.item: the league's equipment shelf (one shared, inventoried set every team designs from, soft balls, cones, bibs, ropes, hoops: a game that needs kit the shelf does not hold is a poem, not an entry)
rules cards and markers, one card per game (the game's whole law on one card: players, space, start, scoring, the end. A game whose rules need a second card is not finished being invented)
the playtest log (one page per game per test: who tested, what broke, what the designers changed. The league's memory and its real league table's evidence)
the adult's safety screen, applied to every entry before its first test (the league's one non-negotiable gate, described in the framing and never waived for a clever game)

activities.name: New Game Playtest League
activities.safety: The adult's screen is the league's first law and it gates every entry before its first stranger test, without exception or appeal at the table: no contact beyond a tag's flat touch, no projectiles aimed at heads, nothing climbed or swung from, no game whose playing speed outruns the room's stopping distance, and every game non-elimination by structure, a beaten player re-enters by the game's own rule, because a test that benches its strangers teaches designers nothing about flow. The screen is re-applied after every revision, since a patch can smuggle in what the original never carried, and any moment in any test that risks a body stops that game instantly on the adult's word, with the stoppage and its reason entered on the log as design evidence, never as a team's disgrace. Space is the screen's silent partner: fixtures are set with run-off margins the constitution names, spectators stand behind the line the hosts mark, and the shelf's hard kit stays shelved for this league regardless of what a game requests. Water and rest are scheduled between fixtures by the hosts; enthusiasm is not a hydration plan.
activities.setup: Set the league's constitution before any team invents anything, and set it where everyone can read it all season: games are played on feet in the room's real space, from the shared shelf's kit; every game must be non-elimination by structure, nobody sits out, nobody is out, a player who is beaten by a moment re-enters by the game's own rule, because a league that eliminates has confused drama with design; scoring must be countable by a spectator; and a game is not entered until its rules fit on one card and a stranger has read them. The adult's screen is defined in the same pass and published with the constitution: no contact beyond a tag's touch, no projectiles at heads, no game whose speed exceeds the room's stopping distance, nothing climbed, nothing thrown that the shelf calls hard. Lay out the season's shape now, invention round, stranger tests, revision, the league fixtures, with dates, because a league is a promise of rematches, and teams design differently when they know the strangers are coming back.
steps: The framing, shelf open, cards blank: 'A rule that only works when everyone is being nice is not a rule yet. This league does not reward the game that sounds best in its inventors' mouths. It rewards the game that survives strangers: people who did not hear the explanation, who read one card, who play to win, find the loopholes, stand exactly where the designer did not imagine, and ask the question the card cannot answer. Every team invents a game today. Then the strangers arrive, each other's teams, reading only the card, and the game gets broken in the open, and that breakage is the league's gift, not its embarrassment. Designers watch their own tests in silence, log in hand, and may not explain, plead or demonstrate: the card speaks, or the card is rewritten. At the season's end the league table ranks the games by how they played for strangers. Clarity first, because a game nobody can start is a game nobody can love.' The constitution is read aloud with the framing, the screen's rules named entire, and the silence rule for designers demonstrated once, briefly, to general discomfort and complete understanding.

Invention round: teams build from the shelf and the room, testing fragments on themselves as they go, a scoring idea tried for two minutes, a boundary moved, a start re-drawn, and the card is drafted last, from what the fragments actually did, not first from what the team imagined at the table. The card's five fields are the round's discipline: players (how many, arranged how), space (marked how, out is where), start (the exact words or signal), scoring (countable, public, kept by whom), and the end (when it stops and what is true then). A field the team cannot fill is a hole the strangers will find at full speed, and the round's coaches, the adult and the league's own first questions, push on exactly those fields: 'What happens when both reach it at once?' is the league's favourite sentence, and a card that has survived it three times is nearly a game. Entries close when every card passes the screen and the one-card law; a game held back by the screen gets its reason in writing on its log page, and its team revises and re-enters, because the gate is a design tool, not a bin.

Stranger tests, the league's examination hall: each game is set up by its designers from its card, then handed over, the designers retire to the log table, silent, while a stranger team reads the card aloud, asks the card its questions, and plays. The log page fills with the test's true events in the order they happen: where the strangers stalled, what they argued about and what the card said (or failed to say) about it, every loophole walked through at full competitive honesty, every moment the game caught fire and played itself. Those go in too, in the same ink, because a revision that only fixes faults can break the magic it did not notice. The designers' silence is total and it is the hardest rule in the building; a designer who calls out a correction has marked their own card as failed at that exact line, and the log says so, kindly and permanently, because the lesson is the league's whole point: the card must carry the game when its inventors are not in the room, and someday its inventors will not be in the room.

Revision and republication: teams take their logs home to the card and rebuild, every breakage answered by a rule, a boundary, a sentence; every patch read aloud against the log to check it mends the actual hole and not a neighbouring one; the card rewritten clean at one card still, because a game that needs its patches stapled on has been revised in the wrong tense. Revised games are re-tested by different strangers, the league never lets the same strangers certify a fix they inspired, and the log gains its second page: what survived, what broke anew (revisions breed fresh loopholes the way fresh paint shows fresh cracks, and the log expects them), and the designers' verdict on their own game, entered signed: fit for the fixtures, or back for one more round, with the evidence cited either way. A team that withdraws its game at this point, on its own log's evidence, is recorded in the league's honours with the same prominence as a fixture winner. Knowing a game is not ready, and proving it, is designing.

League fixtures and the table: the surviving games are played in fixtures across the remaining sessions, every team playing every game, hosts rotating, scores kept by the hosts on the log's fixture page, and the league table is published in its true shape, which is not a ladder of players but of games: each game ranked by the strangers' marks for clarity (could we start from the card?), fairness (did the rules treat both sides alike when pressed?), and fire (did it play itself at its best moments?), with the designers' revisions between tests counted as the league's respect, not its suspicion. The closing tell-back is said with the cards and logs on the table between the teams: 'Every game here was broken by strangers and mended in writing, some of them twice. That is not a failed afternoon of games. That is the entire history of every game anybody has ever loved, compressed into a season and done honestly. A rule that only works when everyone is being nice is not a rule yet; yours work when everyone is trying to win. Take the cards. The games are yours now, and they will outlive this room, because strangers can start them without you.' The cards and logs are filed as the league's book; next season's teams inherit them as the shelf's senior games, credited to their inventors by name.
activities.tagline: Teams invent a movement game, write its rules, watch strangers break them, revise, and republish, the league rewards the clearest game, not the loudest.

variations.easier: A one-afternoon version: two teams, two games, one stranger test and one revision each, the whole league in miniature, with the silence rule and the one-card law kept entire, because they are the league.
variations.harder: A festival version (a whole programme day): visiting groups are the strangers, fixtures run all day on a published card, and the league table is announced at the day's end. The games are marked by people who will never meet their inventors, which is the purest test the league can buy.

activities.inclusion: The bank's work is table work and book work by design, and its authority sits exactly there: the rota's reader calls each jar's state aloud while the keeper enters it, and the keeper's chair, seated, at the vault or the table, with the book, the cards and the tally, is the bank's memory and conscience, a full office held at whatever pace the keeper works. Labelling welcomes every hand: labels can be written, dictated to a scribe verbatim, or lettered from the bank's stamp set where the site keeps one, and the read-back law means no jar's truth depends on one person's handwriting or eyes. The weekly round is short, scheduled, and published a season ahead with named understudies, so no member's winter depends on never being ill, and a round missed is a round the understudy runs from the book. The book, not any person's memory, is what the next round reads. The spring test's counting can be done from photographs the rota takes of each tray, checked at the table by counters who never stood at the vault, and their counts carry the same ink: the bank grades seeds, and it does not grade its bankers.

materials.item: native or perennial seed that genuinely needs cold to germinate, chosen with a trusted seed supplier's or botanic reference's word on each kind (the bank's founding list, kinds whose packets or references state a cold period, with the stated weeks copied onto the bank's cards exactly)
small jars or sealable pots, one per kind per batch, with damp sand or vermiculite as the cold bed (damp as a wrung cloth, never wet, the seed sleeps in the damp, it does not swim in it)

labels that survive the fridge, a marker that writes on them cold, and the bank book (a hardback ledger: kind, source, date in, weeks required, date due out, and the spring test's verdict. The bank's whole memory)
a fridge shelf or cold frame agreed with the adults in advance (the bank's vault. A shelf that will not be cleared in a tidy-up, at a cold that stays cold, for the whole stated term)

activities.name: Cold Stratification Seed Bank

photo.alt: Stratification in sand of Crataegus seeds
photo.caption: Stratification in sand of Crataegus seeds.
photo.credit: Photo: Gmihail at Serbian Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 rs, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Seed is treated as what it is, a material, never a food: nothing from the bank is tasted by anyone, jars and trays are labelled BANK, NOT FOOD on the vault shelf itself, and hands are washed after every round before eating, because seed may arrive dressed or dusty from its supplier and the bank does not ask which. Only kinds from trusted suppliers or known, identified garden stock are banked. No seed is gathered from plants nobody can name, and any kind whose reference mentions toxicity is banked, if at all, in a jar marked with that fact in the adult's handwriting and handled by the rota with gloves. Damp sand and vermiculite are worked dry-handed or gloved, never blown clear and never shaken into the air of a small room; a spilled jar is swept, not breathed. The fridge rule is absolute and hygienic: bank jars live only on their agreed shelf, sealed, away from food they could touch, and a jar that has been in the bank never returns to kitchen service afterwards. Broken glass in the vault is the adult's clean-up, reported the day it is found, with the jar's seed written off in the book rather than picked through by the crew.
activities.setup: Choose the seed before you promise the bank anything, and choose it from evidence: work with the adults to list kinds whose references honestly state a cold requirement, many native flowers and perennials carry one, and copy each kind's stated weeks onto its card word for word, because the bank's whole discipline is that the cold period comes from the seed's own instructions, never from a crew member's confidence. Reject any kind whose reference is vague about the cold it needs; a bank built on guesses is a fridge full of jars. Prepare the cold beds in advance, sand or vermiculite dampened, wrung, and checked by hand, and agree the vault shelf in writing with whoever owns the fridge or the cold frame: the shelf is booked for the longest term on the list plus the test weeks, and a card on the shelf edge says what the jars are and when they may be touched, which is at the rounds and at no other time. Set the bank book's first pages up now: the intake table, the weekly round page, and the spring test's empty verdict columns, so the bank is a record from the first jar, not a memory reconstructed in spring.
steps: Intake day, the framing said at the table of seed packets and empty jars: 'Cold is an ingredient, and the calendar is the recipe. Some seeds will not grow, however warm and kind the spring, until winter has passed through them. The cold is not storage, it is instruction, and these kinds are waiting for it the way a letter waits for its address to be finished. This bank gives them that winter properly: each kind in its own jar, in damp sand, labelled with its name, its source and the exact weeks its own reference demands, and entered in the book before it goes cold. Then we wait, and waiting is the work. The bank is checked weekly, briefly, by the rota, damp checked by eye, any jar that has dried re-damped by the spoonful, any jar that smells wrong reported the same day, and no jar is opened early to see how it is getting on, because a seed mid-winter cannot report, and opening the jar only warms the winter we are supposed to be keeping.' Jars are filled, labelled and entered one kind at a time, each entry read back aloud by a second crew member before the jar joins the vault. The bank's first law is that a jar and its book entry are the same fact in two places.

The weekly round, run by the rota pair whose names head that week's page: the vault is opened once, the jars are read in book order, and each jar's state is entered in the round's plain categories, damp right, dried at the surface, too wet, suspect, with remedies applied by the book's rules and no others: a dried surface gets a spoonful of water worked in gently; a jar standing wet gets its lid rested ajar for that week only, and the book says so; a suspect jar, mould spreading beyond a spot, a smell that was not there last week, is lifted out, shown to the adult the same day, and its fate (clean seed moved to a fresh bed, or the batch honestly written off) is entered with the reason. Chill weeks are tallied per jar on the round page, counted from the intake date, so the book always knows how much winter each kind has actually had, a jar that spent a week out of the cold during a fridge failure has that week struck from its tally in the open, because the bank counts the winter the seed received, not the winter the calendar claims.

Due-out day, when a kind's tally reaches its stated weeks: the jar comes out of the vault at the round, its entry is closed with the date and the true chill tally, and the seed moves to the test, a counted sample, never the whole batch: twenty seeds where the batch allows, laid on damp paper in a labelled tray, kept at the room's ordinary warmth, and watched. The rest of the batch is sown as the kind's reference directs, in trays, in pots, or in the ground at its season, by the crew, with the sowing entered in the book beside the intake entry, so every jar's story can be read entire: in on a date, cold for so many honest weeks, out, sown, tested. A kind whose reference asks for warmth-then-cold or a second winter is not argued with at the table; the book takes the reference's side, the jar's new card is written from the reference again, and the bank's patience is extended in writing, which is what banks are for.

The spring test, the bank's examination: the counted trays are read on the book's stated days, first check at the reference's earliest honest date, then weekly, and germination is counted as it is defined on the intake card: a root out, not a swelling, not a hope. The count is entered as a number out of the number laid down, in the same ink whether it delights or disappoints, and the verdict page is written per kind: the percentage the test actually grew, the chill tally it grew from, and the bank's one earned sentence about that kind ('eleven weeks was enough; nine was not tried and will not be claimed'). Batches that fail entire are not hidden or quietly composted. The failure is entered, the likeliest cause is named from the book's own evidence (a dried week, a suspect jar forgiven too long, a reference followed at second hand), and the kind is either re-banked next winter with the correction written on its new card, or struck from the bank's list with its reason, in the open.

Closing the bank's year, the shelf and the book handed on: the vault shelf is emptied, washed and released with thanks to its owner; the sown trays and pots are labelled from the book and handed to whoever will grow them on, with their kind's page copied for the grower; and the crew writes the bank's closing page together. Kinds banked, kinds proved, the test's best and worst numbers side by side, and the one instruction next winter's bankers will need most, earned at the fridge door. The tell-back is said over the closed book: 'This bank took seeds that were waiting for winter and kept that winter honestly, labelled, logged, checked weekly, and counted by the weeks the seed actually received. Spring graded us, in numbers, tray by tray, and the book holds the grades we liked and the grades we did not in the same handwriting. Cold is an ingredient. We measured it like one.' The book is stored with the empty jars and the marker where next winter's crew will find the whole bank together.
activities.tagline: Teens give native seeds the winter they require: labelled jars of cold, damp weeks, logged chill, and a spring germination test that grades the bank.

variations.easier: A single-kind version (a first bank or a short winter): one kind, banked entire by the full discipline, intake, weekly rounds, due-out, a counted test, because one kind banked honestly teaches the whole bank.
variations.harder: A cold-frame version (no fridge shelf to be had): the jars winter outdoors in a cold frame or a buried, shaded box, the rounds read a thermometer beside the jars, and the chill tally is counted in weeks the frame actually stayed cold. The book's honesty matters more outdoors, not less.

activities.inclusion: A survey divides its authority as fairly as its line divides the ground: the book-keeper, seated at the line's end or at the table the ground allows, with the sheets, the guides and the comparison pages, holds the survey's memory and reads every entry back, which makes the keeper's the casting voice on what the book holds.
