activities.setup: Choose the variety before you promise the bed anything, and choose it from evidence: work with the adults to pick a garlic suited to the site's winters from a trusted supplier's description, and copy that description's planting and harvest guidance onto the bed book's first page word for word, because the crew's whole discipline is that the timetable comes from the crop's own instructions and the site's own frost dates, never from a crew member's optimism. Walk the ground on a dry day and test it the way growers test it: dig one trowel-depth, take a handful, and squeeze. A bed that holds a wet ball will rot cloves in a wet winter, and a drained bed a short walk away is worth more than a convenient swamp. Agree the bed's tenancy in writing now, across the whole cycle, autumn planting, winter silence, spring emergence, summer harvest, with named understudies for the spring counts, because a crop planted by one term's crew and counted by nobody is a lesson in exactly the wrong thing. Set the bed book up before a clove is broken: the map page, the planting-day page, the winter log, and the spring count's empty columns, so the bed is a record from its first row, not a memory reconstructed at harvest.
steps: Planting day, the framing said at the bed's edge, bulbs still whole in the basket: 'You plant for a harvest you will hand to summer. Nothing else in this archive asks you to work for a season you will not be in charge of, and that is why this bed matters. Garlic goes in backwards to every other crop you know: planted in autumn, rooted before the hard cold, silent all winter under its blanket, and only in spring does it tell you what the winter did. Your job today is small and exact, one clove, pointed end up, at the depth and spacing the book states, in a row the line keeps straight, and your job after today is smaller and harder: log the winter, count what emerges, and never claim a shoot you did not see. A bed planted carelessly in October is a disappointment discovered in April, when nothing can be replanted. So we plant like people who intend to be believed in spring.' Bulbs are broken at the bed, never earlier, a clove separated days ahead dries at its root plate, and each clove is inspected as it is separated, firm ones to the planting tray, rejects to the book's count, in the open.

The planting, row by row, at the book's stated depth and spacing: the line is pegged, the holes are made to a marked depth, the crew uses a dibber or trowel shaft marked with tape at the book's depth, so depth is measured, not estimated, and each clove is set pointed end up, its flat root plate down, covered, and firmed once by hand. A pointed-end-down clove will still try to grow, bent and weakened, and the framing names that honestly: orientation is not fussiness, it is the plant's geometry, and a planter who finds their own mistake re-opens that one hole and sets it right before the row moves on. The map page is drawn as the rows are planted, variety by variety where the bed holds more than one, with the row labels hammered in at the row ends in letters the winter cannot wash off. A map and its labels are the same fact in two places, and the book-keeper reads each row back against the bed before the mulch goes down.

The blanket and the winter log, the crew's long quiet job: mulch is laid to the book's measured depth across the whole bed once the ground has taken its first real cold, laid too early it shelters everything the grower does not want sheltered, and the book records the date, the depth and the weather it was laid in. Then the bed is left alone on purpose, and the winter log is kept monthly and briefly by the rota: mulch still in place or lifted by wind and re-laid, standing water after storms noted and its draining watched, any heave, a clove lifted by freeze and thaw, sitting proud of the soil, pressed gently back by an adult-guided hand and entered in the log with its row. The log's honesty rule is the bed's whole ethic: a month nobody visited is entered as a month nobody visited. The winter is the crop's, not the crew's performance, and a truthful gap in the log teaches more than a fluent invention.

Spring emergence, the bed's examination: when the book's season turns, the rota counts shoots row by row on the count's stated days, first count at the first honest sign, then fortnightly, and a shoot is counted as the planting card defines it: green growth through the mulch, from a planted position, not a weed at the row's edge and not a hope under the straw. Weeds are the count's standing temptation and the book meets it head-on: anything the counters cannot honestly call garlic is counted as unknown and sketched, never rounded into the crop. The count is entered as a number out of the number planted, row by row, in the same ink whether it delights or disappoints, and the emergence percentage the bed actually grew is written beside the variety's name. The first grade the bed earns, earned by the winter and the planting together, and claimed by neither alone.

Closing the cycle's first year, the bed handed on and the harvest promised in writing: the mulch is drawn back as the book directs, the spring feeding and watering rota, if the site's guidance calls for one, is agreed with named owners for the dry weeks, and the crew writes the bed's closing page together: cloves planted, rejects at planting, emergence by row, the winter's worst weather and what it did, and the one instruction the harvest crew will need most, earned at this bed. The tell-back is said standing at the bed's edge, shoots in rows where the mulch lay: 'In autumn we planted for a harvest we would hand to summer, one clove at a time, pointed up, at a measured depth, in rows the map still matches. Winter did its work without us and the log told the truth about the months we came and the months we did not. Spring graded us in green, row by row, counted shoot by shoot and claimed only where it was seen. The bed keeps the promise through winter, and so, it turns out, did we.' The book, the spare labels and the harvest guidance are stored together where the summer crew will find the whole bed in one place.
activities.tagline: Teens plant garlic in autumn for a summer harvest: cloves set pointed-up under mulch, the winter logged honestly, spring emergence counted shoot by shoot.

variations.easier: A single-row version (a first crew or a borrowed bed): one row planted entire by the full discipline, inspection, measured depth, map, blanket, log, counted emergence, because one row planted honestly teaches the whole cycle.
variations.harder: A container version (no open ground to be had): the deepest pots the site can overwinter outdoors, planted, mulched and logged identically, with the winter log also recording every move the pots are given. A moved pot is a changed winter, and the book says so.

activities.inclusion: A dusk count is seated, silent work by design, and its authority sits exactly there: the book-keeper, seated at the watch point's heart with the sheets, the conditions columns and the calls, runs the count's voice in a whisper economy where the keeper's written signals, agreed in daylight (a raised pencil for the minute's turn, a flat hand for the end call), carry as fully as any voice. Watchers are assigned sectors by the view their seat honestly gives them, tallies can be kept by counter clicks counted by touch, and a watcher whose dusk vision is limited takes the early, bright sector where the exit silhouettes against the strongest sky. The count is designed so every seat has a sector it can hold with honour. Sheets can be transcribed and totals reckoned at the table under full light by members whose night was the book rather than the sky; their arithmetic carries the same ink. The route to the watch point is chosen for the firmest, most step-free approach the site offers, arrival is in full daylight with unhurried settling time, and the crew's size is capped by the point's honest capacity, never by enthusiasm. A quieter count from fewer, well-seated watchers is the better count, and the book says why.

materials.item: a known, established roost the adults have confirmed with its owner or a local bat group in advance (a roost whose location may be watched from outside, at a distance the guidance sets. The count never reveals a roost's location to anyone outside the crew and its hosts)

one set watch point, chosen and marked before the count night (a spot with a clear silhouette view of the exit against the evening sky, far enough away that the watchers are furniture, not a threat. The point is paced out, marked, and drawn on the count sheet)

the count sheets and the tally book (one sheet per watcher per sector: minute rows, tally columns, weather, light and the count's start and end calls. Kept in a hardback book that is the roost's whole record across the season)

counters and quiet kit (hand tally counters where the site keeps them, clipboards and pencils that work in failing light, and a red-filtered torch held by the adult alone, used only for the walk out, never shone at the roost, ever)

activities.name: Dusk Bat Exit Count

photo.alt: Hundreds of bats streaming across a dusk sky with clouds and a rising moon
photo.caption: A real exit flight at dusk: this is the stream your tally marks are counting.
photo.credit: Photo: Tomascastelazo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: The animals set this record's first law and it is absolute: no bat is ever handled, fed, approached, lit, filmed at close range or followed, by anyone, for any reason. A grounded or apparently injured bat is never touched by the crew; it is reported to the adult, who contacts the hosts or a licensed bat carer, because bats can carry disease and are protected in many places, and bare-handed rescue is both unlawful and unsafe. Nobody enters any structure, roof space or tree hollow for this count, ever: the watch is outside, at the agreed point, at the agreed distance, and a count whose watch point cannot be held is abandoned, not improvised closer. Dusk is the working light and it is governed: the route in and out is walked in daylight first, the crew moves after dark only in file behind the adult's red light, nobody leaves the watch point alone, and a watcher who feels unwell or unsafe is escorted out by the adult with the count continuing short-handed. The book records the change and the count's honour survives it. Weather ends counts without argument: rain, high wind or a cold snap that would keep the roost home anyway postpones the night, and the postponement is entered as a decision. Insect repellent, where the site uses it, goes on before arrival and well away from the watch point, and hands that have handled it never handle the book's sheets near food afterwards, the crew eats nothing at the watch point at all, which keeps the point clean and the animals unbothered.
activities.setup: Confirm the roost before you promise the count anything, and confirm it through people who know: the adults contact the roost's owner or the local bat group, establish that the roost is active this season, agree the watch point's distance and the count's dates, and learn the local rules that protect the animals, in many places bats and their roosts are protected by law, and the count operates inside those rules by design, not by exception. Visit the watch point in daylight with the adults: walk the route in and out, find the firmest ground, settle where the crew will sit, where bags go, and how a watcher who needs to leave is escorted out without crossing the exit's skyline. Set the count's shape now and write it on the book's first page as law: arrival before sunset, silence from the first-call time, sectors assigned, tallies by the minute, and the end call given by the keeper when the exit has truly finished, not when the crew is cold. Check the season and the forecast honestly: an exit count belongs to the bats' active season and to a dry, mild evening, and a count postponed for weather is a count protected, with the postponement entered in the book as a decision, not a failure.
steps: The framing, at the watch point, light still good, voices already low: 'Count what leaves; never chase what returns. Tonight this roost empties itself into the dusk, one bat at a time and then in ribbons, and our whole job is to be a number at the end of it that somebody can trust. We count from here. We do not approach the roost, we do not shine light at it, we do not handle, feed, follow or film a single animal, and a bat that comes near us is a bat we ignore with discipline, because being ignored by us is what safety feels like to a roost. Each watcher owns one sector of sky. You count only your sector, you tally by the minute, and a bat you are unsure crossed your line is a bat you do not claim, an honest undercount from a careful crew is worth more to the people who study these animals than a heroic guess. When the light goes, the tallies keep the count; nobody needs to see the book until the end call. Settle now. Silence from the first call is the count starting.' Watchers take their sectors, pencils and counters are tested in the remaining light, and the keeper opens the book to the night's sheet.

The count, run by the book's stated calls: the keeper notes sunset, weather and the first bat's minute in the book's own columns before any tally begins, because a count without its conditions cannot be compared with any other night's. From the first call, talk stops. Each watcher tallies their sector's exits minute by minute. A counter click per bat, the minute's total written at the minute's turn where the light allows, or held as clicks and transcribed in the pause the keeper declares if the exit runs hot. Double-counting at sector edges is the count's known error and the crew meets it by the law agreed in daylight: a bat crossing a boundary is counted by the sector it leaves, never by both, and a watcher who loses a ribbon against dark sky marks that minute as lost rather than inventing its number. The book has a column for lost minutes, and using it is a skill, not a confession. The adult watches the crew, not the roost: seated postures, quiet, and the route out kept clear.

The end call and the reckoning, at the watch point while the night finishes settling: the keeper gives the end call only when the exit has been empty for the full agreed stretch, then reads the sheet's conditions back before any total is spoken, sunset, first bat, weather, lost minutes, because a total announced before its conditions is a number already escaping its evidence. Sector tallies are summed aloud, minute by minute where the exit peaked, and the book's night total is agreed between keeper and watchers from the sheets, never from anyone's memory of a spectacular minute. The crew names its surprises honestly, an earlier first bat than the season led them to expect, a sector that carried the whole exit, and its non-surprises with equal respect: a quiet night counted carefully is a finding, and the book says so, because a monitoring record is built from ordinary nights counted well, not from records broken.

The walk out and the count's afterlife, governed as strictly as the count itself: the crew leaves by the daylight-walked route, in the adult's red light, at a walk, in file, with kit counted out by the keeper, counters, sheets, book, and nothing left at the watch point that would tell the ground a crowd had been there. The roost's location is the count's confidence: it is written in the book as the hosts agreed it should be recorded, it is never posted, pinned on a map, shared in a message or pointed out to visitors, and a crew member asked about it has one answer, rehearsed without embarrassment: the count does not say where its roost is. Where the hosts or the bat group keep a monitoring scheme and want the night's sheet, the keeper copies it entire, conditions, lost minutes and all, and the book records to whom it was sent and when, because data that leaves the book should leave it honestly or not at all.

Closing the night, the book finished at the table under real light: the sheets are checked for a name, a sector and a signature on each, the transcribed minutes are re-read against the counters where counters were used, and the crew writes the night's closing page together, total counted, peak minute, first bat against sunset, lost minutes owned, and the one instruction the next count night will need most, earned in the dusk. The tell-back is said over the closed book: 'Tonight a roost emptied into the dark over our heads, and we asked nothing of it but a number. We sat where we said we would sit, we counted only what our sectors honestly held, we marked the minutes we lost instead of inventing them, and we walked out leaving no sign and telling no location. Count what leaves; never chase what returns. That is a count a stranger can build on, and the bats never knew our names.' The book, counters and sheets are stored together where the next count, this crew's or another's. Will find the whole watch in one place.
activities.tagline: Teens count bats leaving a known roost at dusk from one set watch point: sectors, silence, tallies by the minute, and no bat ever approached or handled.

variations.easier: A single-sector version (a small crew or a first count): the whole discipline at one watcher's scale, one sector, one sheet, conditions, lost minutes and the walk out, with the book opened and the laws stated, ready to grow sectors next count.
variations.harder: A return-count version (a crew in its second season at the same roost): the night's sheet is read against the same dates last season before the crew leaves the table, differences are entered as questions for the hosts or the bat group, never as conclusions of the crew's own, and the book keeps both seasons in the same order.

activities.inclusion: Tchoukball staffs its honours unusually fairly, and this session says so in the open: the keeper, caller of periods, judge of landings, holder of the slate, runs the game from the court's side at full authority, and the catching line, the game's position of honour, is work done from wherever a catcher reads best: a catcher may defend a marked ground zone from a seated or standing base agreed with the keeper, because the skill being honoured is the read and the hands, not the run that preceded them. Passing chains are built so every player touches the ball inside the pass limit, the laws themselves forbid a game of stars, and the keeper counts quiet players into the next chain by the slate's rotation, not by shouting for the ball over louder voices. Shooting and catching are both taught in the open at teaching pace for as many rehearsals as a player wants before defended play, with no audience but the coach-fed frame; a player whose day is laws, link passes and the slate is not having a lesser session: the framing said the catch is the defence, and the slate's saves column is where this game's respect is written down.

materials.item: one or two tchoukball rebound frames, or a sturdy rebound net the adults have tested for a true, even bounce (the frame is the game's whole geometry, a frame that wobbles, tips or returns the ball wildly is replaced before the session, not cursed during it)

a tchoukball or a light, grippable ball of similar size that forearms can receive without stinging (the session's ball is chosen for catching confidence. A ball players flinch from teaches flinching, not defence)

the forbidden-zone markings for each frame (tape, cones or floor lines marking the D-shaped zone in front of each frame, measured and laid before players arrive. The zone is the game's signature law and its lines do not drift mid-session)
the session slate and chalk (the game's honest record: teams, the laws taught, points by period, and every disputed landing settled and entered. Kept by the session's keeper at the court's side)

activities.name: Tchoukball First Session

photo.alt: Geneva indoors nemzetközi tchoukball torna 2024. U16 lány
photo.caption: Geneva indoors nemzetközi tchoukball torna 2024. U16 lány.
photo.credit: Photo: Jeszyagi, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: No contact is this game's law, not its aspiration, and the keeper enforces it as safety before sport: a player who reaches across an opponent, body-checks a catching line or dives into another player's ground stops play for a re-teach, and a second offence rests that player to the slate's side for a period. The game's whole safety case is that collisions are designed out, and they stay designed out only while the law is kept. The forbidden zone stays empty while a shot is live: nobody stands in the rebound's first ground, heads are never the catching plan, and a ball rebounding toward a face is a ball let go, always. The slate has never once needed a point that cost an eye. Frames are fastened firm and inspected before play and never leaned on, sat on or moved mid-period; a frame that shifts is a stoppage, reset by the adults or the keeper, not wrestled back by players with the ball live. Catchers are taught receiving arms before defended play, jewellery and watches come off forearms that will take a rebound, and the court's surface is walked at setup: a floor that slides under a full-stretch catch is a floor the session shortens its game for, in the open, before anyone learns it at speed.
activities.setup: Test the frame before you test the players: stand where a shooter will stand, throw the session's ball at playing pace, and read the rebound, true, lively and catchable, in the directions the game promises. A frame that fails that test ends the setup, not the session: repair it, re-fasten it, or run the session's teaching games against a wall the adults have approved, and say plainly why, because players calibrate their trust on the first rebound they are offered. Walk the court yourself for the game's real geography, the forbidden zones at both ends, the catching ground behind them, run-off room beyond every landing area, and clear or rule out everything inside that country before a ball is thrown. Set the session's shape in advance and write it on the slate: laws and handling first, shooting against no defence second, defended play last, because a game whose signature is the catch cannot be learned by players still guessing where they may stand. Choose the first teams mixed and balanced by the evidence of the handling round, not by friendship or reputation, the keeper announces them from the slate, and the game's no-contact law makes balanced teams a courtesy this sport can actually keep.
steps: The framing, ball at rest, the whole court in view: 'The catch is the defence. In this game nobody tackles, nobody blocks, nobody guards a player. You may not touch an opponent, intercept their pass, or step into the forbidden zone while a shot is live. You score by throwing at the frame so the rebound lands on the ground beyond the zone, untouched. They score the same way, and your whole defence is to be standing where the rebound falls and to catch it clean before it lands. That makes this the strangest honest game you will learn this year: the hardest working players are the ones reading a rebound in the air, and the bravest thing on the court is a catch taken at full stretch in front of your own frame. Passes are limited, travelling with the ball is limited, and both limits exist to keep the ball moving and the reading honest. We learn the laws first, we shoot undefended second, and only then do we play, and the slate records landings as they were judged, argued once, settled, and chalked.' The laws are walked, not just said: a volunteer shooter's shot is frozen at the rebound so the room can see the zone, the landing ground and the catching ground with their own eyes.

Handling and shooting school, the session's foundation, run before any defended play: pairs move the ball the game's way, chest-high passes, caught two-handed, feet set before the throw, the three-pass rhythm counted aloud by the keeper until it is in the players' hands rather than their worries. Shooting is taught against the frame with no defence and the zone empty as the law requires: shooters learn the frame's honest angles by evidence, ten throws each, the landing spots called and chalked where they fall, because a shooter who cannot yet place a rebound has no business being defended. Catchers rehearse the game's real skill on coach-fed rebounds, reading the ball off the frame early, moving feet before hands, receiving with giving arms that absorb rather than slap, and every player rotates through shooting and catching before anyone specialises, because a catcher who has never shot does not yet know what the rebound is being asked to do.

Defended play, built in short periods the slate keeps: teams take the court with the laws entire, no contact, no interceptions, no player in the zone while a shot is live, steps and passes as taught, and the keeper referees landings from the court's side with one standard: a point is a rebound that lands on legal ground untouched, a save is a catch, and anything disputed is re-stated once from the law, settled, chalked, and played on, because this game's disputes are about geometry, and geometry does not improve with volume. Early periods are stopped kindly and often: a catcher crowding the zone is walked back to the line without blame, a shooter travelling is shown their steps in the open, and the correction is chalked as teaching, never as shame. The slate has a column for laws learned, and it fills faster than the score column in a good first session, which the keeper says aloud so the room hears what progress looks like here.

The rotation round, when the laws are holding and only then: players rotate positions by the slate's published order, shooters to catching lines, catchers to the link passes, because the game's intelligence lives in the rotation and a player fixed in one job is learning a third of the sport. Teams are rebalanced once, in the open, if the periods have shown a mismatch the mixed start did not predict; the keeper names the evidence, moves the fewest players who will repair it, and chalks the change, because a close game teaches ten times what a procession teaches and engineering one is the keeper's craft, not a favour to the losing side. Between periods the ball rests and arms rest with it. Rebound catching is forearm work, tired arms slap and drop, and the session's pace is set by the slate before goodwill and enthusiasm can spend the players' best catching in the first period and call the rest character.

Closing, the slate read entire and the frames carried off by their crews: the keeper reads the session aloud, laws taught, periods played, points by period, saves named where the room can name them, and the laws-learned column entire, and the session's one number is agreed and chalked large: the longest rally of consecutive catches the whole court held without a landing, whether it is eleven or two, because that number, honestly counted, is the court's mark to beat next session and nobody else's business. The tell-back is said with the ball resting on the frame: 'An hour ago this game sounded impossible. Score without a goal, defend without touching anyone, win ground by catching. Now the room reads rebounds, shooters place them, catchers move before the ball arrives, and every landing on the slate was judged once, settled and chalked true. The catch is the defence. Next session the mark is waiting, and the frames will be tested before we are.' Frames are inspected as they are carried, net tension, joints, feet, faults noted to the adults, and frame, ball and slate are stored together where the next session will find the whole game in one place.
activities.tagline: A no-contact team game where shots rebound off a frame and points are scored by where the ball lands: catching, not colliding, wins the ground.

variations.easier: A one-frame version (a small group or a short hall): the whole discipline at one end, handling, undefended shooting, defended play toward a single frame with teams alternating attack, with the zone, the laws and the slate entire.
variations.harder: A target-shot version (a court whose run-off room is tight): shooters score by rebounding the ball into marked landing boxes of rising value, catchers still defend entire, and the session's reading and catching are coached at full stretch inside safer geography.

activities.inclusion: An arranging studio is built out of doors other rooms do not have: the keeper's chair, predictions entered before they are heard, verdicts in the same ink, the version page written to be re-performed from, is seated work at the studio's centre, and the arranger rotation, the session's highest honour, is an office of judgement and one stated sentence, open in whatever register its holder commands: a change can be proposed in speech, in writing on the board, or by demonstrating it on one instrument or one hummed line. Singers join at the volume and in the part their voice honestly has; the voice map is built so humming floors, counted silences and pulse parts are real arranging materials with real names in the log, not consolations, and a member may hold the pulse for the whole arranged run and be, in the version page's credits, its foundation. Instruments are assigned by the census and the job, with seated positions woven into the room's shape as ordinary furniture; tempos are agreed and counted in, never sprung, and every run's count-in is given in sight as well as sound. Nobody auditions, nobody solos without asking, and the log credits the whole room as arrangers. The studio's way of keeping its authorship as wide in fact as in the framing.

materials.item: one song the studio may honestly use, chosen and cleared before the session (a public-domain song, a traditional song, or a song the adult has permission to teach and rearrange. The song's words and melody written out on the room's board, entire, because an arrangement built on a half-remembered song is a version of a rumour)

whatever instruments and sound-makers the room truly has, gathered and tested before the studio opens (voices count first. A studio that can only arrange for instruments it wishes it had will arrange nothing; every sound in the room is listed on the board as the studio's real orchestra)

the arrangement board and the version log (the board carries the song's skeleton, sections, chord pattern, who does what, in the order the version runs; the log, one page per version, records what was changed, what it did, and what the studio decided, kept by the session's keeper)

a pitch and a pulse the whole room can find (a starting note given the same way every run, and the tempo set by a count-in the arranger of the moment gives aloud. Versions are compared at agreed tempos first, so a change of speed is a decision, never a drift)

activities.name: Song Arranging Studio, First Session
activities.safety: Volume is this studio's real hazard and it is governed like one: the room's working volume is set by the adult at the framing and marked in the log, a run that has to be shouted over is stopped and reset quieter as a craft correction, and if ears are ringing, the room was too loud. That sentence is in the log's safety page and any member may say it at any time and be thanked, because hearing is the studio's instrument and nobody spends it for a chorus. Amplification, where the site uses any, is adult-set and adult-adjusted; nobody rides a volume control mid-run. Instruments are handled as the room's tools: strings, sticks and shakers stay in their players' space, a borrowed instrument is returned to its owner's hands, and the instrument census at setup includes the honest exclusions, a cracked drum, a frayed cable, taken out of the orchestra before enthusiasm can volunteer them. Song choice is a safeguarding decision as much as a musical one: words are read entire by the adult in advance, anything the room cannot sing in front of its own families does not enter the studio, and a member who will not sing a line on conscience or comfort hums, plays, or keeps the log at full standing, without explanation owed to anyone.
activities.setup: Clear the song before you clear the room: choose a song the studio is entitled to rearrange, learn it entire yourself, melody, chord pattern, section order, and write its skeleton on the board in advance, in the plain shapes the framing will use: verse, chorus, bridge if it has one, and the chord loop under each. Take the room's instrument census honestly at setup and list what actually sounds: a keyboard with a dead octave, three shakers and fourteen voices is an orchestra with a dead octave, and the arrangement will be built for the room that exists. Set the studio's shape now and keep it: the song straight first, the skeleton mapped second, one change at a time third, a full arranged run last. An arranging studio that changes everything at once learns nothing, because nobody can say which change did the work. Agree the decision law before opinions arrive and write it on the log's first page: a change is tried entire, heard entire, and kept or cut by the studio's vote after one full hearing, with the arranger of the moment holding a casting voice only on ties, taste argued once, heard once, settled.
steps: The framing, the song's skeleton on the board, before anything is changed: 'An arrangement is an argument about what the song is. The songwriter gave us a melody, a set of chords and an order of sections. Everything else, how fast it breathes, what it is played on, which section arrives like a surprise, where the room sings and where one voice stands alone, is the arrangement, and today it is ours. We will not argue in the abstract. We will sing the song straight first, until the room owns it. Then we change ONE thing, we hear the whole song with that change, and the log records what the change did, not whether it was clever, what it did: the chorus stood taller, the verse went thin, the ending stopped landing. A version is kept because the room heard it work, and cut because the room heard it fail, and both verdicts go in the same ink, because next session's studio starts from this log, not from somebody's memory of a good idea.' The song is sung straight, entire, at the agreed tempo, and the skeleton on the board is corrected in the open if the singing finds it wrong, the board serves the song, not the other way round.

Mapping the skeleton, the studio's analytical middle: the room walks the song section by section and names what each part is doing, where the melody climbs, where the chords loop and where they break, the one moment the whole song leans on, with the keeper entering the map in the log as it is agreed. Instruments are auditioned against the skeleton, not in the abstract: each sound in the room's orchestra is tried on the job the studio is considering for it, carrying the pulse, answering the melody, filling the chorus floor, and a sound that cannot hold its job at the room's honest volume is reassigned without disgrace, because arranging is casting, and a miscast shaker is the arranger's error, not the shaker's. Singers map the voice work the same way: where the room sings together, where a section drops to a hum under a single line, where silence, a full bar of it, counted, does more than any voice could. The map is read back entire by the keeper before the first change is tried, so the studio changes a song it has agreed it understands.

One change at a time, the studio's discipline and its pleasure: the arranger of the moment, a role that rotates by the log's order, open to every member, proposes exactly one change, states what they expect it to do in one sentence, and the keeper enters the prediction before a note sounds, because a studio that predicts in writing learns twice as fast as one that only reacts. The song runs entire with the change. Then the studio judges by the framing's standard: the prediction read back, the room's verdict heard, the change kept, cut, or amended once and re-heard, and amended once means once, because a version polished by nine amendments in one session is a new song nobody voted on. Changes the room has genuinely tried in studios like this, named so first-timers can reach for them: slow the chorus and let the verse run; move the strongest section to the front and pay for it at the ending; strip the instruments out under the bridge so the voices stand alone; trade the pulse from hands to feet; sing the final chorus a step higher only if the room can truly stand there, each tried entire, predicted, logged.

The arranged run and the recording of the version, the session's summit: when the studio has kept its changes, usually fewer than the room first wanted, which the keeper notes kindly, because restraint is an arranging skill, the song runs entire in its new arrangement, standing, at performance intention, with the arranger of the final version conducting the count-in and the stops. If the site records, the adult runs one take of the full run and the log notes it; if not, the log's version page is the record, and it is written to be re-performed from: section order, tempo, who carries what, the kept changes in order, and the one change the studio cut that a future session should retry, named with its prediction, because a cut change with an honest prediction is an inheritance, not a failure. Singers and players sign the version page as arrangers, all of them, because in this studio the arrangement belongs to the room that argued it into shape.

Closing the studio, the straight song sung once more, on purpose: the room sings the song as it arrived, original tempo, original order, nobody's arrangement, and hears it with arranged ears, which is the session's real graduation. The keeper reads the log back entire: the map, the predictions, the verdicts, the final version's page. The tell-back is said with the board still carrying both skeletons, the song's and the studio's: 'This morning this song had one shape, and it was somebody else's. It has two now. We took it apart without breaking it, we changed one thing at a time and wrote down what each change did, we kept what the room heard working and we cut what it heard failing, and both kinds of hearing are in the log in the same hand. An arrangement is an argument about what the song is. Ours is in the book, signed, and ready to be argued with by the next studio. Which is exactly what arrangements are for.' The board is photographed or copied into the log before it is wiped, the instruments are counted back by their players, and the log is stored with the song's card where the next studio will find the whole argument in one place.
activities.tagline: Teens take one permitted song apart, melody, chords, structure, and rebuild it in a new arrangement the whole room rehearses and logs.

variations.easier: A voices-only version (a room with no instruments to speak of): the whole studio run on the room's first orchestra, voices, hands, feet and silence, with tempo, order, humming floors and the counted bar of silence carrying every change the session tries.
variations.harder: A two-song version (a returning studio): the same skeleton method run on a second cleared song in a contrasting shape, the two version pages compared in the log, and the studio's one transferable law, the change that worked on both, written as the book's standing advice.

activities.inclusion: A film crew is a row of different crafts at full standing, and this record staffs it as such: the keeper, consents, shot log, the plan's living state, the calls at the middle, runs the shoot from the camera's side, and the interviewer's chair, the session's voice of honour, is placed where its holder works best, with questions carried on printed cards that can be read, shown, or handed to a co-interviewer to voice at the holder's direction. Camera work can be tripod-based entire, framing, holding and calling shots from a seated position at the room's agreed vantage, and sound-watching, the crew's most sensitive craft, is headphone work at the test clip's positions, open to a member whose gift is listening rather than looking. Shot-planning and the edit argument are table work where every member's evidence counts the same: the log's verdicts, not the loudest recollection, decide what the film holds. Consent is designed for real humans: cards in large clear print, read aloud on request, a decline that can be given by word, gesture or simply stepping out of the marked filming area. The room's floor plan marks a no-camera refuge corner, ordinary furniture rather than exile, so stepping out of the film never means stepping out of the room.

materials.item: one room worth filming, chosen with its owners' agreement before the rain day is spent (a workshop, a kitchen in its working hour, a library corner, the program's own store room, a room with a real life of work, people who belong to it, and something that changes across the session the crew can honestly follow)

one camera, adult-managed (a phone or camera on a tripod or a steady rest, charged, with space cleared and tested at setup. The crew's only machine, operated under the adult's eye, with the adult holding the device and its files before, during and after the session)

the consent cards and the shot plan (a card per person filmed or interviewed: what the film is, where it will be shown, and their signed yes or their no, which is final and needs no reason, and the shot plan, one page: the film's question, its planned shots in order, its interviews, agreed before the camera rolls)

the crew log (one page per session: shots taken against the plan, interviews and their consents, anything declined and how the plan absorbed it, and the edit order the crew agreed. Kept by the crew's keeper at the camera's side)

activities.name: One-Room Documentary Crew
activities.safety: Consent and safeguarding set this record's laws and they outrank every shot: nothing is posted, shared or uploaded from the session, no stills, no clips, no behind-the-scenes photographs, by anyone, and the finished film is shown only where the consent cards said it would be shown, to the audiences they named. The device is the adult's charge throughout: it enters the room with the adult, its files are inventoried in the log, material struck or withdrawn by any subject is deleted under the adult's hand with the deletion entered in the log, and no crew member copies material to a personal device for any reason, including enthusiasm. Filming never follows anyone into private spaces, no changing areas, no toilets, no offices with closed doors, and a person entering the room who has not consented is not filmed: the camera turns away or stops, in the moment, without the moment becoming a discussion. Interviews follow the site's safeguarding shape: in the open room, within the adult's sight, at the subject's workplace, and any disclosure a subject makes that raises a concern is the adult's to act on through the site's own channels. The crew's job is to stop filming and fetch the adult, and the framing says so in those words. Equipment safety is ordinary and kept: tripod legs taped or watched in walkways, cables out of paths, no filming while walking backwards, ever. The camera's operator stands still or is guided by the sound-watcher's hand on their shoulder, because a room's real hour includes real thresholds and real kettles.
activities.setup: Choose the room before the weather chooses the session, and choose it like documentary makers: the room must have a question in it, how does this kitchen feed forty people, what does a repair morning actually repair, who keeps this library alive, because a film about a room with no question is a tour, and tours are what this record refuses to make. Agree the room with its owners and its regular people in advance, in plain words: who the crew is, what a documentary is, where the finished film will be shown (in the room, to the program, and nowhere else without fresh consent), and that any person in the room may decline to be filmed or interviewed, at any point, including after the fact, and have their material deleted in front of them if they ask. Write the film's question and the first shot plan yourself with the crew's officers before the session, plan, not script: documentary shoots a real hour, and its plan is a list of honest intentions (the room waking up, the work's hardest moment, one interview per role) that the real hour is allowed to rearrange. Test the camera in the room's real light and sound at setup: a room that sounds like a tiled cave on the test clip will sound like one in the film, and positions, not hope, fix that.
steps: The framing, camera still capped, the room's owners present or their agreement read aloud: 'Consent comes before camera, every time. Today we make a short documentary, a true film about a true room and the people whose work it is. True is the job. We do not stage moments and call them found, we do not film anyone who has not said yes on a card, we do not keep footage of anyone who changes their mind, and we do not make anybody look foolish for an audience's easy laugh, because the people in this room will watch this film in this room, and a crew that would not show its cut to its subjects has made the wrong cut. Our plan is on one page: the question, the shots, the interviews. The room's real hour will rearrange it, that is documentary happening, not the plan failing, and the log will record what we actually got and what we honestly missed. Nobody performs. Nobody is ambushed. The camera is the last thing that starts and the first thing that stops when anyone says stop.' Consent cards are offered and collected before the cap comes off, declines are entered in the log with the same respect as consents, and the shot plan is amended in the open around them.

Shooting the room's hour, the crew at its stations: the crew works the plan in its published roles. Camera, sound-watcher with the test clip's lessons in their ears, interviewer, and keeper logging every shot against the plan with its time and its honest one-line verdict. Shots are taken from the positions setup proved, the camera rests steady rather than wandering, and the crew's discipline is duration: hold a shot past the interesting moment, because rooms speak in their ordinary minutes and a crew that only grabs highlights will assemble a film about grabbing. Nobody directs the room's people to repeat an action for the camera and call it documentary, if a moment matters and was missed, the log records it missed, and the interview may ask about it, which is the honest way a film recovers a moment. The keeper calls the plan's state at the session's middle, shots held, shots lost, interviews owed, and the crew re-plans its remaining time in the open, cutting planned shots by the log's evidence rather than by panic.

The interviews, conducted as the framing promised: each interviewee sits where they work, the question list is the one the plan published, the film's question from their chair, the hardest part of the work, the thing visitors never see, and follow-ups may only chase what the person has just said, never ambush them toward a line the crew wishes it had. The interviewer states at the start of every interview, on the recording, who is filming, what for, and that the person may stop, strike an answer, or withdraw entire after the fact. Consent is re-spoken at the microphone, not just signed at the door, because a card signed an hour ago should not have to do a person's remembering for them. Interruptions, hesitations and the room's own sounds stay in the material: the crew is filming a room, not a studio, and its honesty includes the kettle. An interview that runs dry is ended kindly and early by the interviewer, thanked, and logged as it was; the film owes nobody a performance, least of all its subjects.

The edit order, agreed at the table before anyone touches a timeline: the crew watches or hears its material entire, keeper's log in hand, and argues the film's shape from evidence. Which shots actually hold the question, which interview line the whole film leans on, what the opening image promises and whether the ending pays it. The cut is planned on paper first: shots in order, lengths in honest estimates, interview extracts chosen by what was said and not by who said it most fluently, and any person who struck or withdrew material is honoured in the plan before a single frame is placed, their absence shaped around with respect rather than disguised. Where the site edits on the day, the adult drives the machine and the crew directs; where it does not, the paper cut is the session's finished work and says so. A complete, argued edit plan is a real documentary outcome, and the log records which the session achieved and why. Titles and credits are agreed with the room's people: names as they wish them written, roles as they actually are.

Closing the session, the film or the plan shown first to its subjects: the crew's standing law is that the room sees it before any other audience, a rough cut screened in the filmed room, or the paper cut read aloud there shot by shot, and corrections of fact from the room's people are entered in the log and honoured in the final shape, because a documentary about people that its people call wrong is wrong, whatever it cost to shoot. The tell-back is said in the filmed room, camera capped and put away: 'This morning this room was just where the work happens. It is a film now, or a plan for one that a stranger could finish: a question asked honestly, an hour shot without staging, interviews given freely and strikable freely, and a cut argued from what we actually got. Consent came before camera, every time, and the room saw the result before anyone else did. That is what documentary means when teenagers make it properly: true, permitted, and answerable to its subjects.' The device and its files go to the adult's keeping with the log's inventory of what exists, what was deleted at whose request, and where the finished film may be shown. The crew's last entry, made before anyone leaves the room.
activities.tagline: On a rainy day, a teen crew films a short documentary about one real room: consent first, interviews on the record, and a cut planned before it is shot.

variations.easier: A silent-film version (a room whose sound defeats recording, or a first crew): the whole discipline shot as a visual documentary, planned shots, held durations, title cards written by the crew to carry the question, with interviews replaced by observed work and the consent laws entire.
variations.harder: A rain-only version (the room is the weather's own): the crew films the rain itself through and on the building, gutters, windows, the yard's new rivers, from inside the agreed positions, a documentary with no interviewees, where the consent laws rest and the shot plan and the log carry the whole discipline.

activities.inclusion: The line was designed so that standing anywhere on it, including off it, is a full position, and the inclusion is structural rather than appended: the PASS and NOT SURE edges are laid, labelled and named in the framing with the same ceremony as the ends, a middle position is introduced as an answer in its own words, and the keeper's office at the line's side, slate, pairings, the deck's memory, is a seated role with the session's whole record in its hands. Sorting can be done at any pace and by any route: a member may take the long way behind the line, place themselves by telling the keeper their position and having a marker stood there by a volunteer at their direction, or hold a position card at the line's side in a place that corresponds to their answer. The geography is the game's, the access to it is the person's. Pairings talk at standing, seated or leaning distance as the pair agrees, the one-sentence law can be met in speech, in writing shown to the partner, or by a gesture vocabulary the pair settles in its first ten seconds, and no pairing is ever reported to the room, so nobody's explanation needs to survive an audience. Statements are read twice, slowly, and shown on a card at the line's middle for anyone who takes language in better by eye; the host faces the line while reading, every time, as a matter of the session's ordinary manners.

materials.item: one long line marked on the floor or ground, end to end, that the whole group can stand along at once (tape, a rope laid straight, or a row of cones, long enough that thirty people sorting themselves along it have room to be exact, with its two ends labelled STRONGLY and NOT AT ALL, or the pair the statement needs, in letters the whole line can read)

the statement deck, screened in advance by the adult and the host together (low-stakes, answerable, kind statements about tastes, habits and harmless preferences. Every statement read aloud twice at the screening and tested against the deck's law: nobody should be able to be embarrassed by where they stand)

the edge cards (two cards or marked mats beyond each end of the line, labelled PASS and NOT SURE, full positions with full standing, part of the line's geography from the first statement, never an apology added later)

the host's slate (the session's light record: statements used, pairings made across the line, and any statement the room found flat or surprisingly divisive, entered by the session's keeper for the deck's next screening)

activities.name: Spectrum Line Introductions
activities.safety: The deck is this record's safety system and its screening law is absolute: statements are screened in advance against the categories named at setup, no statement is ever improvised by the host mid-session to chase a laugh, and a statement that lands badly, read by the room's silence, a visible flinch along the line, laughter at a position rather than with the room, is retired on the spot by the host, kindly and without analysis, and entered on the slate as retired with its reason, because a deck improves by amputation as well as addition. Nobody's position is photographed, filmed, recorded by name or reported outside the room, and the host states that law at the framing where the whole line can hear it. The line's geography is walked at setup: step-free along its whole run, no standing on furniture to be seen, the furthest pairing reached by walking behind the line and never through a sorted crowd at a run, and the session's pace is set so sorting is a walk, always. A person may stand at the edge, sit the session at the line's side as keeper, or leave and return without any accounting. The host's attention to a quiet edge-stander is one neutral check-in, offered once, and a no is a complete answer the session honours by moving on with genuine warmth.
activities.setup: Screen the deck before you mark the line, and screen it harder than feels necessary: the host and the adult read every statement aloud, stand where they honestly would, and ask the screening's one question. Could any person in this room be hurt, exposed or singled out by standing honestly on this one? Statements about family, money, bodies, belief, romance, ability and anyone's private life fail that question by category, not by wording, and they never reach the deck however gently phrased. What survives is the deck's honest territory: mornings versus nights, sweet versus salty, doing versus watching, the best season, planning versus improvising. Tastes a room can disagree about at full volume and no cost. Lay the line for the room that exists: along the longest clear run the space offers, step-free along its whole length, the edge positions beyond both ends laid with the same care as the line itself, and walking room behind the line so people can reach a far position without climbing through the sorted. Set the session's shape in advance: the line taught with two practice statements, talked rounds between statements, the deck's order mixed so no two heavy disagreements stand back to back.
steps: The framing, the whole group standing behind the unmarked side of the line, deck in the host's hand: 'Your feet answer first; then you get to explain. I will read a statement. You will walk to the place on this line that is true for you. Strongly at this end, not at all at that end, and every honest place between, including the exact middle, which is an answer and not a failure to answer. Then, before anyone explains anything to the room, you will talk for two minutes, not to your neighbour, who mostly agrees with you, but across the line: find the person standing furthest from your spot, go to them, and each explain, in one sentence each, what put you where you are standing. You are not there to win them over. You are there to be able to say, at the end, what the room looks like from the other end of one question. The edge positions are part of the line: PASS means this one is not for you today, NOT SURE means exactly that, and both are stood in with the same standing as anywhere else. Nobody will ask you to account for either. Nobody's place is recorded by name, nobody is photographed standing anywhere, and a statement you dislike can simply be watched from the edge at full membership. Feet first. Talking second. Winning never.' Two practice statements are run entire, walk, pair across, one sentence each, return, so the room learns the shape with its feet before it trusts the shape with its opinions.

The standing rounds, the session's working rhythm: the host reads each statement twice, slowly, and the room sorts itself in its own time, no countdown, no last-person spotlight, because a line that shames its slowest sorter has stopped being an introduction and started being a race. The host reads the sorted line aloud in the neutral language the framing promised: where the room bunched, where it split cleanly, where the middle carried the day, and any cluster named by position, never by person. 'The strong end is crowded on this one' is the whole commentary a bunch earns. Surprises are the deck's gold and the host marks them without exploiting them: a statement the screening expected to split the room that lands nearly unanimous, or a harmless taste that cleaves the room in two, is entered on the slate for the deck's next screening, because a deck, like a crew, improves by being re-screened against evidence. Between standing rounds the room resets fully behind the line. A sorted line that never dissolves teaches people to defend a spot instead of answering the next question fresh.

The talking rounds, where introductions actually happen: on the host's call, each person finds the furthest standing person from their own position, the host pairs any remainder, including themselves in, so nobody is left holding their sentence with nowhere to take it, and the pairs take their two minutes where they stand or a step off the line, by the pair's own agreement. The law of the two minutes is stated once and kept by courtesy rather than policing: one sentence of explanation each first, entire and uninterrupted, what put you there, in the plainest words you have, then open talk for the remainder, which is where names, programs, common ground and the session's actual introductions are exchanged, at standing distance from the disagreement that caused them. A pair that finishes early does not drift back to its own end's comfort; the host's standing invitation is to stay and keep talking until the call, because the furthest pairing is the session's whole design and its minutes are the minutes that work. Pairs dissolve on the call without verdicts: nobody reports back, nobody is quoted to the room, and a sentence heard in a pair stays in the pair unless its speaker chooses to offer it again themselves.

The deck's deepening, used only when the room is warm and the line is trusted: the host may, twice in a session and no more, follow a statement with its one allowed sequel, 'stand where you stood a year ago', and the room re-sorts itself along the same line to its remembered position, and looks, in silence for a counted ten, at how far its members have travelled in both directions. The sequel works because it is rare, because it is about change rather than difference, and because the furthest pairing that follows it talks about journeys instead of positions; a host who reaches for it a third time is spending the room's trust to fill the session, and the slate records sequels used so the next host inherits the discipline with the deck. Statements may also be proposed by the room late in the session, and they enter the deck only through the same screening law, read aloud and tested on the spot by the host and the adult together, in the room's hearing. A proposed statement that fails is declined with its reason stated kindly and briefly, which teaches the screening better than any lecture.

Closing, the line unmarked and the slate read back: the final statement is the deck's gentlest by design, the screening saves one the room will mostly share, so the session's last picture of itself is a bunch, laughing at its own unanimity, then the pairs talk, dissolve, and the group gathers off the line entirely while the host reads the slate: statements used, the surprises, the sequels spent, and the pairings' count, with no person's position on any statement named, recorded or recalled. The tell-back is said standing where the line was, its tape still down: 'An hour ago this room was thirty strangers standing behind a line. You have sorted yourselves, honestly, a dozen times since, bunched, split, stranded at ends and crowded in middles, and every time, you walked the length of your disagreement to hear one sentence from the person furthest from your spot, and gave them yours. Nobody won a single statement. Everybody can now say what the room looks like from somewhere they do not stand. That is an introduction with the geography left in. Feet first, talking second, winning never.' The line is lifted by its ends' keepers, the deck and slate are stored together, and any statement the slate marked is re-screened before the deck is used again.
activities.tagline: New teens answer screened, low-stakes statements with their feet first. Stand somewhere on the line, then talk to the person furthest from your spot.

variations.easier: A seated-line version (a small room or a settled group): the line runs along a table or a row of chairs, positions are taken by standing a card at a place along it, and the furthest pairings talk across the table, the geography, the screening and the laws entire, at table scale.
variations.harder: A short-deck version (twenty minutes, a first meeting): six statements, practice pair included, no sequels, the whole discipline in its shortest honest form, with the closing slate and the tell-back kept entire because they are where the session's manners live.

activities.inclusion: A binding table is a row of seated, measured crafts at full standing, and the studio staffs it as such: the keeper's chair, signature counts, fault causes, the tool tally, is the session's memory and conscience, and inspection pairs are formed so that every book is read by hands other than its binder's, which makes the inspector's office, flexing, opening, reporting true, a position of trust open to any maker at the table. Folding, marking and stitching can all be done from whatever seat and at whatever table height a maker works best at; holes are always punched at the adult's station, so no maker's access to the sharp work depends on their own hands' strength or steadiness, the law that reserves the awl to the adult is an inclusion as well as a safety, and the framing says both halves of that aloud. The pattern card is drawn large and read aloud entire before the first fold, stitch order is demonstrated at a pace the whole table follows and repeated on request without ceremony, and a maker may dictate their studio-book entry, have their holes marked by a partner at their direction from their own measurements, or sew with a needle threader and a thimble from the kit the table keeps as ordinary equipment. Nobody's book is compared with another's except by the inspection's own terms, does it open, does it hold, will it last, and the closing row is spines out and makers unnamed unless a maker chooses to show their binder's mark, because the first page of a person's book is theirs to show or to keep.

materials.item: paper for the pages, chosen and counted before the session (sheets that fold kindly and take a pen, enough for each maker to bind one book of the studio's stated size, plus the practice sheets the teaching uses, because a first signature folded badly should be tuition, not tragedy)

cover stock heavier than the pages, cuttable to the book's size with a margin the pattern states (card, heavy paper, or cloth-covered board the site already keeps. Every maker's cover from the same stock family, so the studio's teaching about grain, fold and glue holds for every book on the table)

the stitching kit, counted out and back by name (blunt bookbinding or tapestry needles, strong thread or linen cord waxed where the site keeps it, and the studio's one sharp station. An adult-run table with the awl and craft knives, where holes are punched and covers trimmed under the adult's hands alone)

the pattern card and the studio book (one card per book size: fold map, hole positions measured from the fold, stitch order drawn step by step, and the studio's log, where sizes tried, faults found and their causes are entered by the session's keeper, book by book)

activities.name: Pamphlet-Stitch Bookbinding Studio

photo.alt: Bookbinding tie thread 1
photo.caption: Bookbinding tie thread 1.
photo.credit: Photo: Simon Eugster – Simon / ?! 18:07, 10 May 2008 (UTC), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Sharp points set this studio's laws and they are geographic: the awl and the craft knives live only at the sharp station, are used only by the adult, travel point-down in the tray between uses, and are counted out and back by name at the session's start and end. A count that does not agree stops the tidying until it does. Makers' own tools are blunt by design: tapestry needles for stitching, scissors where the pattern needs them used at the maker's own place, point-down in their pots when hands leave them, and thread is cut, never bitten, never snapped toward a face. Paper cuts are this craft's small honest hazard and the studio treats them without drama and without neglect: a cut is washed, dried and covered before work resumes, and a maker keeps working one-handed or keeps the studio book for ten minutes, at their own election, because thread and a stinging hand are a combination that produces bad stitches and worse tempers. Paste and glue, where the size uses them, stay at the finishing bench in their pots, off the folding tables, and hands that have handled them are washed before the books' pages are touched, a glue thumbprint on a first page is forever, and the studio's order of work exists to prevent exactly that sentence.
activities.setup: Settle the book's size before you settle the room, and settle it small: a first bound book should be finishable entire in one session, pages folded, holes marked, spine stitched, covers on, name written in it, because a bookbinding studio that sends home a folder of loose intentions has taught folding, not binding. Make one complete book yourself in advance, at the table's pace, and keep your own faults in it: the sample that shows a slightly wandering stitch line teaches more than a perfect sample, and the studio will believe a teacher whose book has a history. Lay the sharp station out of the work's flow, a separate table, adult-run, where makers bring a signature for punching and a cover for trimming and wait their turn as at a craftsman's bench, and count its tools out on the studio book's first page before a sheet is folded. Set the table for the work's real order: folding space first, the pattern cards weighted where every maker can see one, thread measured and cut in lengths the pattern states, because thread cut by enthusiasm tangles at exactly the length it was not measured to.
steps: The framing, a finished book in the host's hands, opened and shut twice so the room hears it work: 'A book is a machine you can make by hand. Spine, hinge, gatherings, covers. Every part of it has a job, every job can be done at this table, and by the end of this session every maker here will have done all of them. We bind blank books today, and blank is the point: a book you have folded, punched, stitched and covered yourself is not a notebook you bought. It is a machine you built, and what gets written in it later will be written in something your hands already know entire. The laws are three. Grain runs with the spine, always, or the book will fight its reader forever. Holes are marked before they are punched, and punched only at the sharp station, by the adult. And a fault found early is tuition, while a fault hidden is a book that fails in a stranger's hands in October, so we show our faults to the table as we find them, and the studio book records them with their causes, kindly and exactly. Fold first. Stitch second. Judge last.' Each maker's paper is counted out in their hearing, the pattern card is read aloud entire once, and the first fold is made by the whole table together, slowly, crease by crease.

Folding the signatures, the studio's patient foundation: makers fold their sheets into the book's gatherings exactly as the pattern card maps them, fold, crease with the bone folder or a thumbnail's flat, nest the folded sheets inside one another in order, and check the gathering's fore-edge for the stair-step of an honest nest honestly admitted: a gathering folded carelessly climbs out of true a sheet at a time, and the check exists to catch the first sheet, not the ninth. Grain is taught by hand at this stage and never skipped: a sheet torn in the practice pile shows its grain by tearing straight one way and wandering the other, and every maker tears the practice sheet both ways before folding a real one, because grain learned by the hands stays learned. Folded gatherings are pressed under the table's weights while the covers are prepared, a book pressed as it goes is a book that will shut like a book, and the keeper enters each maker's signature count on the studio book as it is completed and checked, in the open, so the sharp station's queue runs on knowledge rather than on whoever is loudest about being ready.

Marking, punching and stitching, the spine made real: each maker marks their holes from the pattern card, measuring from the fold with a ruler and marking in pencil on the inside of the fold, measured, never eyeballed, because the stitch that follows can only be as true as the holes it travels, then carries the gathering to the sharp station, where the adult punches the marked holes with the awl and checks each one back against the card with the maker watching, so punching is witnessed teaching, not a service window. Back at the table, the stitch is sewn by the pattern card's drawn order, step by step, the whole table sewing the first pass together at the host's counted pace: in, along, out, tension even and never hauled, a stitch pulled to splitting teaches its lesson in a torn fold at the year's middle, and the knot is tied where the pattern puts it, inside the fold's shelter, trimmed to the pattern's length. A stitch that goes wrong is unpicked and resewn while the fault is still cheap; the studio book's law is that a resewn spine is a success recorded, and makers say the fault aloud as they unpick, which is how the next table learns it free.

Covers and the finishing bench, where the book becomes a book: covers are measured against the maker's own stitched gathering, not against the pattern's promise, against the book in hand, because every hand-made book is its own size by honest millimetres, marked with the pattern's margin, and trimmed at the sharp station by the adult to the maker's own marks, the maker present and calling the measurement. Covers are attached as the pattern directs for the size, stitched through with the spine where the size is slight, or hinged and pasted under the table's weights where the stock is heavy, and every finished book is pressed flat while the studio does its last work, because the press is the binding's final teacher. The finishing law is inspection, done in pairs: each book is opened, shut, opened flat, flexed gently and read for its faults by a maker who did not bind it, a hinge that cracks, a stitch that grins, a cover a fraction shy, and the findings are told to its binder plainly and entered in the studio book with their causes, because a book inspected by a friend leaves the studio with a prognosis, not a hope.

Closing the studio, the books named and the first page claimed: each maker writes their name and the date inside their own book, on the pattern's chosen page, in their best hand, the binder's mark, the oldest page in any book's life, and the books are gathered for one minute on the table together, a row of machines built in an hour, spines out, no two exactly alike and every one of them a book. The keeper reads the studio book back: sizes bound, faults found and their causes entire, sharp-station tool count in against the morning's count out. The tell-back is said with the books still in their makers' hands: 'This morning this table held flat paper, flat card and a ball of thread, and none of it would have survived being called a book. Now every maker here holds a machine they built entire, grain with the spine, holes measured before they were punched, a stitch sewn true and inspected by a friend, a cover cut to the book in hand and not to a promise. What goes into these books from here is their makers' business. That the books will hold it, open flat for it, and still be books in October. That was today's, and it is done properly.' Tools are counted back by name, offcuts go to the practice pile for the next studio's grain lessons, and the studio book is stored with the pattern cards where the next binders will find the whole craft in one place.
activities.tagline: Teens bind a real blank book by hand: folded signatures, a stitched spine, covers cut true. A book is a machine you can make at one table.

variations.easier: A single-signature version (a first studio or a short session): the whole discipline at one gathering's scale, fold, mark, punch, stitch, cover, inspect, sign, a slighter book bound entire, with the studio book opened and the laws stated in full.
variations.harder: A cloth-spine version (a returning studio): the same binding with a reinforced spine strip of book cloth or heavy tape laid under the stitching, covers in contrasting stock, and the studio book comparing the two constructions' inspection findings side by side, a second year, argued from evidence.

activities.inclusion: A temperature trial staffs its honours across every kind of attention: the log-keeper, reader of the stated minutes, caller of temperatures, keeper of the conditions margins and the void stamp, runs the session's truth from a seat in the shade at its centre, and that seat is the experiment's highest office, because a trial is only ever as good as its log. Building is table-and-ground work that divides by strength and reach as teams agree it: measuring and marking, cutting to a line, folding, glazing, sealing, each a real craft the design depends on, and the held-constant checker's role, certifying a rival team's list, is an office of pure judgement held at full standing by whoever the session trusts with a signature. Readings can be taken by probe displays read aloud, by photographs of thermometer dials checked at the table, or by a partner's called numbers entered by the keeper. The ink is the same, because the trial grades variables, not eyesight. The session's timetable is published in advance with its shade rest built into the design, the site is chosen for step-free access to the sun the experiment needs, and there is always, in any honest yard, a sunny patch the whole crew can reach, which the adults find at setup rather than apologising for at the framing.

materials.item: oven boxes the teams build from the site's agreed stock (a sturdy box per team, dark lining material, clear film or a glass sheet for the glazing, reflective card or foil for the flap, the same base kit for every team, because a trial in which the kits differ is a trial of the kits, not of the variables)

one thermometer per oven that can be read without opening it, or a probe the adult has tested in the oven's range (the trial's whole instrument, checked against a known reading at setup, because a log kept on a lying thermometer is fiction with decimal places)

the trial log (one book for the session: the control run first, then one page per variable trial, the variable changed, everything held constant listed and signed, temperatures by the stated minutes, sun and cloud noted in the same hand)

the shade-and-rest station (water, shade and the session's timetable kept by the log-keeper. A solar trial is an hour spent attending to sunlight, and the crew's management of its own exposure is part of the experiment's honest conditions)

activities.name: Solar Oven Temperature Trials

photo.alt: Cardboard Box and Duct Tape Solar Oven
photo.caption: Cardboard Box and Duct Tape Solar Oven.
photo.credit: Photo: Hunter McNenny, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.safety: Heat sets this record's laws even though its heat arrives slowly: oven interiors are tested with the thermometer, never a hand. A focused oven's floor can be far hotter than its air reading suggests and a hand learns that once, which is once too often; ovens are opened by their teams only at the keeper's call, angled away from faces, because the day's trapped heat leaves an opened oven in one warm breath and eyes are not its audience. Reflective flaps and glazing are handled by their edges, foil's cut edge is folded under at building before it can find a finger, and no maker looks at the sun through a flap, a glazing sheet or any reflected path to check an aim. Aiming is done by shadows, always, a law the framing states and the keeper enforces without exception, because the instrument this experiment cannot replace is the crew's eyesight. The session is an hour attending to sunlight and its conditions are managed as such: shade and water are at the station from the first building minute, the timetable builds in the reckoning's shade as rest and not as reward, hats and the site's sun practice are the day's ordinary dress, and any member who feels the heat as illness, headache, nausea, dizziness, sits out in the shade and tells the adult at once, with the log noting the crew change the way it notes a cloud: as a condition, without blame. Scissors and craft knives, where the build uses them, follow the site's ordinary tool laws at the building table, and a finished oven is never left working in the sun unattended at the day's end, cooled, in the shade, stored, as the closing directs.
activities.setup: Fix the base oven before you fix the trials, and fix it in writing: one base design, drawn on the log's first page with its dimensions, its lining, its glazing and its flap angle as the session's control.
