The out player leaves to the back of the waiting line. Every player below moves up one square toward the centre, and the first in line enters at square one.
Hold the centre through as many serves as you can. The throne is rented, never owned.

variations.easier: Allow one bounce inside a player's square before the hit, and lower the frame for younger or shorter players.
variations.harder: Call your square: the hitter names the target square before hitting, and a ball landing anywhere else costs the point.

activities.safety: Eyes up, feet planted inside your own square. Collisions happen when players chase balls into a neighbour's square, so a ball that leaves your square is gone; let it go. Check the frame stands stable before every session, and nobody hangs from the bars, ever.

activities.name: Cornhole
activities.tagline: Two boards, eight bags, and the sweetest three points in the yard: a bag clean through the hole.
activities.setup: Set the two boards facing each other on flat ground. Full distance is 27 feet between the fronts of the boards; for children, pace off a shorter court, 12 to 18 feet, and stretch it back as arms grow. Players pair up: partners stand at opposite boards, with their opponents beside them.
steps: Players at one board throw in turn, one bag at a time, alternating with their opponent, underhand at the far board. Four bags each.

Score the round when all eight bags have flown. A bag through the hole is worth 3. A bag resting on the board is worth 1. A bag that touched the ground first, or hangs off the board onto the grass, scores nothing and is cleared away.
Score by cancellation: a round of 9 against 5 is worth 4 to the higher side. Losing rounds sting less and comebacks stay alive.
The other end throws back. First side to 21 wins; agree before the first bag whether an exact 21 is required.

variations.easier: Move the boards closer, let young throwers stand beside their board rather than behind its front edge, and count any bag on the board as 2.
variations.harder: Race games: first side to 21 exactly, with a bag that takes you past 21 not counting, so the endgame becomes a marksman's problem.

activities.safety: One thrower throws at a time, and nobody walks the court while bags are in the air. Bags are gathered only when both ends agree the round is done.

photo.alt: A cornhole board with bean bags resting on it, a player throwing from the far end
photo.caption: Bags on the board, one more in the air.
photo.credit: Photo: Viro, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

activities.name: Tie-Dye Shirts
activities.tagline: Twist it, band it, drown it in colour: no two shirts ever come out of the bucket alike.

materials.item: plain white cotton shirts (one per child, pre-washed)
fibre-reactive dye kit, or squeeze bottles of dye

activities.setup: Work outside or over covered tables; dye is forever on everything it touches. Follow the kit on pre-soaking. Lay out gloves, bands, and bottles grouped by colour, and write each child's name on a plastic bag before the first shirt gets wet, because a finished shirt goes straight into its own bag to rest.
steps: Lay a damp shirt flat and choose a pattern. For the classic spiral, pinch the centre, twist the shirt into a flat swirl, and band it into wedges, like a pie.
Band it tight. The sections the bands divide become the colour zones, and every white line in the finished shirt is a band that held.
Gloves on, then add dye wedge by wedge: one colour per wedge, or two where wedges meet. Push the bottle's tip into the folds so the colour reaches inside the spiral.
Slide each shirt, still banded, into its named bag and let it rest as the dye directions say; overnight gives the deepest colour.

Rinse in cool water until it runs nearly clear, unband over the rinse bucket, and hold the reveal, one shirt at a time, to the group's full gasp. Wash dyed shirts separately for their first few washes.

variations.easier: One colour per shirt and a scrunch pattern: ball the shirt up, band it loosely, dye it, and get a mottled sky that never fails.
variations.harder: Fold and clamp: accordion folds with wooden shapes clamped on both sides, dyed over the clamps, open to sharp white geometry (the itajime way).

activities.safety: Gloves on every hand, aprons or smocks over anything worth keeping, and dye mixed and poured by an adult or under an adult's eye. Spent dye water goes down a household drain or onto bare dirt away from gardens and pets, never into a storm drain, and no shirt is worn home against skin while still wet with dye.

activities.name: Chess, First Session
activities.tagline: Sixteen pieces, six kinds of moves, one quiet hour: the first game, taught so it never feels like a test.
activities.setup: One set per pair, a quiet table, and no clock anywhere in sight; first sessions run on curiosity, not time. Set up the demonstration position with the group watching: a light square at every player's right hand, and each queen on her own colour. Pair players of similar experience where you can, and let true beginners play two-to-a-side at first.
steps: Teach the board and the army first. Name every piece, set the position together twice, then have every player set it once alone. Setting up correctly is the first skill of chess.

Teach the moves one piece at a time: pawn first (forward to march, sideways to capture, dreaming of the far side), then rook, bishop, queen, king, and the knight last, because the knight's hop is the move every beginner loves.
Play pawn games before whole games: eight pawns each, first to march one home or capture all of the other's. Small games finish, and finishing teaches more than any lecture.
Then play a first full game with one house rule: any player may take back one move per game, no questions asked. Say check kindly: 'your king is in trouble' before the word check.
End the session mid-interest, never mid-exhaustion, and record nothing but who wants a rematch.

variations.easier: Mini-chess with half the army (king, queen, two rooks, pawns) and take-backs allowed freely for the first month.
variations.harder: Bring in a friendly ten-minute clock, and teach one opening idea as the session's single lesson: fight for the centre.

activities.safety: The safety here is social, and it is real: chess clubs die on mockery. A lost game is never laughed at, a win is celebrated quietly, and any player may resign with dignity at any time. Pieces stay on the table or in hands, never thrown.
activities.inclusion: Large-print and tactile sets serve players with low vision, and players may choose the piece colours they read best. A player who cannot yet sit a full game plays the pawn-game circuit at full standing.

photo.alt: Two boys playing chess over a board set between them
photo.caption: A game on the street, one move at a time.

activities.name: Dominoes, First Game
activities.tagline: Match the dots and empty your hand: the draw game that teaches counting without ever saying so.
activities.setup: A double-six set is the teaching set: 28 tiles, dots running from blank to six. Turn every tile face down on the table and shuffle them with flat hands, the wash, which children will happily do for a full minute. That minute is part of the game.
steps: Each player draws seven tiles and stands them on edge, dots facing themselves. The rest form the boneyard, the draw pile at the table's edge.
The player holding the double six, or the highest double anyone holds, lays it in the centre to start the line.
Take turns adding one tile to either open end of the line, matching the touching ends dot for dot. Doubles are laid crosswise.
No match in hand? Draw from the boneyard until you can play, or the boneyard runs out. Passing is for players who truly cannot play, and the table will check.
The round ends when one player lays their last tile (call 'domino!') or nobody can move. Count the dots still in each hand; the lowest count takes the round.

variations.easier: Play one long cooperative snake with all tiles face up, building together and cheering every fit.
variations.harder: Keep score across five rounds by leftover dots and play to a match total, or graduate the table to a double-nine set.

activities.safety: Tiles are small and hard: keep them off the floor, where bare feet and chair wheels go, and away from the youngest children sharing the room.

photo.caption: A domino line grows one matched end at a time.

activities.name: Go Fish
activities.tagline: 'Do you have any sevens?' The first card game every child learns, and still the best way to teach asking.
activities.setup: One ordinary deck, jokers out. Deal five cards to each player (seven each when only two play) and scatter the rest face down in a loose pile in the middle: the ocean. Young players may fan their cards face up on the table with a partner's help; the game forgives it completely.
steps: On your turn, choose one player and ask for a rank you already hold: 'Do you have any threes?' You may only ask for what is in your own hand.
Holding that rank? They hand over every card of it, and you ask again. A good ask earns another turn.
Holding none? They say 'Go fish!', and you draw one card from the ocean. Draw the rank you asked for and you show it and take another turn; otherwise your turn ends.
Four cards of one rank make a book. Lay books face up in front of you the moment they are complete.
When the ocean is empty and the hands run out, count the books. Most books wins, and the player with the fewest deals the rematch.

variations.easier: Play in pairs with cards face up on the table, asking together, or play to pairs instead of books of four.
variations.harder: The memory rule for older players: nothing may be written down, and a player caught asking for a rank they handed away earlier loses their next turn.

activities.safety: Cards are paper; tempers are the only hazard in the game. Keep the asking cheerful and the answers honest, and make rematches instant: the second game of Go Fish is where the learning lives.

activities.name: Kids Yoga, First Session
activities.tagline: Animal poses, slow breaths, and a room that settles itself: a first yoga session built for wiggly bodies.

materials.item: yoga mats or carpet squares (one per child)

activities.setup: Mats or carpet squares in rows with a clear lane to walk, shoes off at the door, and the lights as low as the room allows. The leader sits where every child can see. One rule covers the whole session, said at the start: your mat is your island, and nobody corrects anybody else's pose.
steps: Start seated. Breathe in while hands float up, out while they float down, five slow rounds, until the room's noise drops along with the hands.
Move through animal poses, three breaths each: cat and cow on hands and knees, downward dog, a low hissing cobra, then frog squats with three jumps at the end of the set to spend the giggles.
Standing poses next: tree (foot resting at ankle or calf, never pressed into the knee), warrior two, and airplane, tipping forward with arms out, where falling over is expected and applauded.
Close the active half with a partner pose: seated back to back, breathing slowly enough that each partner can feel the other's breath move. Thirty quiet seconds is a triumph.
Finish lying down, eyes closed or gazing up, for one minute of stillness with a picture to hold in mind: floating on a raft, snow falling. Wake the room slowly: fingers, toes, then sitting.

variations.easier: Chair yoga for the whole session: every pose takes its seated form, and the breathing rounds carry the class.
variations.harder: Flow round: link four known poses into a sequence and repeat it without the leader's voice, the group counting breaths in silence.

activities.safety: Yoga is invited, never forced: any child may rest in child's pose or sit out any move, no reason needed. No pose pushes a joint past comfort, and a child who feels dizzy sits down at once. Bodies differ; the session bends to the bodies in it, never the other way around.
activities.inclusion: Every pose here has a chair form and a standing form of equal standing, and the leader shows both. A child using a mobility aid places their mat where the lane is widest.
